title: Daniel López Cano
text:
About
Hello! I am a postdoctoral researcher in computational cosmology at the Institute of Physics of the University of São Paulo (IFUSP). My work brings together cosmological simulations, machine learning for astrophysics, survey-oriented modelling, and scientific software development. More recently, I have also been working on Ly\(\alpha\) absorption processes, fast skewer generation, and pedagogical resources that use computational tools to support the learning of theoretical physics and astrophysics.
I am currently a FAPESP Postdoctoral Fellow at IFUSP, and in 2026 I am also undertaking a FAPESP-BEPE visiting research stay at the Institut de Física d’Altes Energies (IFAE) in Barcelona. Before moving to São Paulo, I completed my PhD in Astrophysics at the Donostia International Physics Center (DIPC) after completing my BSc in physics and MSc in theoretical physics at the Autonomous University of Madrid (UAM) / Institute of Theoretical Physics (IFT). Across these stages, I developed a broad interest in combining theoretical ideas, numerical methods, and data-driven techniques to study complex problems in cosmology and astrophysics.

title: About the Author
text: I am from Vallekas, a working-class neighbourhood in the south of Madrid, and through my parents my roots reach the province of Toledo and the Sierra Oeste de Madrid. 2015BSc in PhysicsUniv. Autónoma de Madrid 2019MSc in Theoretical PhysicsIFT UAM-CSIC, Madrid 2020PhD in AstrophysicsDIPC, Donostia & UAM 2024Postdoctoral FellowIFUSP, São Paulo I studied Physics at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid (UAM), where I first worked with cosmological simulations, and spent a few months at GMV writing Python software for satellite navigation (GNSS) data. I then took a Master’s in Theoretical Physics at the Instituto de Física Teórica (IFT UAM-CSIC), specialising in astrophysics and cosmology. My PhD in Astrophysics, at the Donostia International Physics Center (DIPC) and the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid (2020–2024), was devoted to structure formation in cosmological simulations, which I approached from several angles: the internal structure of dark-matter haloes, machine-learning techniques that predict haloes directly from the initial conditions, excursion-set theory, and semi-analytic models. Since 2024 I am a FAPESP postdoctoral fellow at the Institute of Physics of the University of São Paulo (USP), where I work on machine learning bridging simulations and real survey data, and on the Lyman-\(\alpha\) forest, which also took me as visiting researcher to the Institut de Física d’Altes Energies (IFAE) in Barcelona in 2026. In computational cosmology, general relativity is the theoretical backbone of everything we do, yet it rarely appears explicitly in day-to-day work. These notes are my way of going back to its foundations, and they became the basis of the graduate course From Differential Geometry to General Relativity that I taught at the University of São Paulo in 2026. I developed these notes, together with the code, figures and animations that accompany them, to bring the mathematical foundations of modern physics to a broader audience. These foundations are not nearly as complicated as their reputation suggests. Anyone with a bachelor’s background in multivariable calculus should be able to follow them, with the computational resources as a visual aid to build intuition for every new concept. daniellopezcano.github.io \(\cdot\) github.com/daniellopezcano

title: 1 Introduction
text: I believe that the best way to learn any topic in physics is to first build a solid understanding of its mathematical foundations. Intuition matters too, but the further a physical process lies from our everyday experience, the less obvious it becomes what that intuition should look like. This is especially true for quantum mechanics and general relativity, where intuition only develops after working through (and practising with) the underlying mathematics. The same holds for topics you think you already understand: revisiting them with a firmer grasp of their mathematics, you rediscover them with new depth and a richer intuition. And because different theories often share the same mathematical framework, insight into how a mechanism works in one well-known theory can often be carried over to another. Differential geometry is one such framework. It provides a general and robust foundation for many of today’s fundamental theories in physics. It is not uncommon to find colleagues in astrophysics and cosmology who regard differential geometry merely as a “necessary evil” for learning general relativity. I cannot emphasise enough how central it is to physics as a whole: even if you can get away without it for many “basic” calculations in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, or special relativity, it is still the backbone holding these theories together. Hamiltonian mechanics lives on a symplectic manifold (phase space), Maxwell’s equations reduce to two compact equations for the electromagnetic field-strength 2-form, and special relativity is nothing but the geometry of Minkowski spacetime. Still, most undergraduate physics programmes avoid the subject, at least partially, relying instead on hand-waving arguments. In practice, crowded curricula and limited preparation time often mean that students graduate with only a superficial exposure to the topic. This brief and incomplete contact can leave the impression that differential geometry is an arcane subject best left untouched, when in reality it is an essential tool that is far more approachable than its reputation suggests. Differential geometry is a beautiful subject that can be understood with a bit of effort and patience. Don’t be put off by big words like “manifold”, “tensor”, or “connection”: they are simply precise mathematical names for intuitions you already have about the physical world, perhaps without realising it. In these lecture notes, I aim to give a compact, pedagogical introduction to the subject that equips the reader with the essential tools needed to understand the mathematical foundations of general relativity. The notes assume familiarity with linear algebra and multivariable calculus; some prior exposure to special relativity is helpful but not strictly necessary. These notes began as a personal project: I wanted to learn general relativity at a more fundamental level, acquiring along the way the mathematical tools needed to appreciate its subtleties. My starting point was the lectures by Prof. Frederic P. Schuller at the WE-Heraeus International Winter School on Gravity and Light (Schuller, 2015).1 These lectures are a fantastic introduction to the subject, and I highly recommend them to anyone interested. Schuller is a great teacher: his lectures are pedagogical and, at times, genuinely funny. While taking notes on these lectures, I started developing my own Python package to illustrate some of the concepts visually.2 I also began adding explicit calculations and examples to make the key ideas more transparent. Compared with the original lectures, these notes reorganise the material into what I find a more linear sequence of topics, add worked examples and detailed proofs in the appendices, and include computational illustrations throughout. The result is a set of lecture notes I thought were worth sharing. Before diving in, let me give you the overall picture that motivates our goals. Schuller opens his lectures with a one-sentence summary of general relativity that I find a perfect starting point: “ Spacetime is a four-dimensional topological manifold with a smooth orientable atlas carrying a torsion-free connection compatible with a Lorentzian metric and a time orientation satisfying the Einstein equations. ” Of course, that sentence is packed with jargon. But, as with most things in physics, the concepts become transparent once you break them down into smaller, more digestible parts. That is exactly what the following chapters do, each one unpacking a piece of this sentence: Chapter 2 lays the algebraic groundwork. We start with sets, maps, and algebraic structures, then move on to vector spaces, dual spaces, and tensors. These concepts may look abstract, but they are exactly what physics needs: tensors are the objects that allow us to write physical laws without committing to any particular basis (and, later, to any particular coordinate system). Chapter 3 formalises the idea of a space that looks locally like \(\mathbb{R}^n\) but can have a nontrivial global structure: the topological manifold of our opening sentence, which becomes our mathematical model for spacetime. Charts provide local coordinates, and equipping the manifold with a smooth atlas (a collection of charts whose overlaps are smoothly compatible) is what allows us to do calculus on it. Chapter 4 builds, at each point of the manifold, the stage on which vectors and covectors live. A tangent vector is defined as the velocity of a curve through the point, acting on functions as a directional derivative. The tangent vectors at a point form a vector space, the tangent space, whose dual is the cotangent space: the home of covectors such as gradients. Combining both through tensor products yields the tensor spaces at that point. Every chart induces a basis in each of these spaces, and the way components change from one chart to another, which is what distinguishes covariant from contravariant objects, is derived rather than postulated. In this sense, the chapter is the algebra of Chapter 2 applied point by point. Chapter 5 lets these objects vary from point to point. Gluing all the tangent (or cotangent) spaces together produces a new manifold, the tangent (or cotangent) bundle, and a vector, covector, or tensor field is then a smooth assignment of one such object to every point, i.e., a smooth section of the corresponding bundle. The numbers that rescale fields are now replaced by functions on the manifold, so fields form a module rather than a vector space, which explains why, in general, a basis of fields exists only locally. Fields are essential in physics, and here they are introduced without reference to any coordinate system; components appear only afterwards, as functions defined on a chart domain. This clears up a common source of confusion: treating a field and its components as the same thing. The chapter closes by fixing the compact index notation used throughout the rest of the notes. Chapter 6 addresses the problem of differentiation on manifolds. Ordinary derivatives fail because vectors at different points live in different tangent spaces, and there is no built-in way to compare them. A connection provides exactly such a prescription: the resulting covariant derivative generalises the ordinary derivative to tensors and gives a precise meaning to “straight lines” (autoparallels). Every connection comes with two characteristic tensors, its torsion and its curvature; the torsion-free condition in our opening sentence concerns the former, while the latter is the mathematical heart of gravity. A physically illuminating by-product is that pseudo-forces, such as the centrifugal and Coriolis forces, appear as connection coefficients when we change coordinates, revealing them as artefacts of the coordinate choice. In flat space they can be removed everywhere by a suitable change of coordinates; in curved space, only at a single point, a fact that will return as the equivalence principle. Chapter 7 introduces the metric tensor, the object that measures distances, angles, and durations. In general relativity the metric is the gravitational field itself, so understanding its properties and the structures it induces (light cones, proper time, geodesics) is essential for linking geometry to physical predictions. This is where the Lorentzian metric and the time orientation of our opening sentence enter. Metric and connection are, a priori, independent structures. They become linked only when we require the connection to be torsion-free and compatible with the metric, which singles out a unique connection (the Levi-Civita connection) whose straightest curves are also curves of extremal length. The metric also provides our first action principle: the length (or proper-time) functional, whose stationary curves are precisely the geodesics. Chapter 8 develops the machinery to “sum” quantities over a manifold in a coordinate-independent way. Volume forms, which require the manifold to be orientable, make integration well defined, and the general Stokes theorem unifies the fundamental theorem of calculus, Gauss’s divergence theorem, and the classical Stokes theorem of vector calculus, extending them to curved spacetime. Chapter in preparation explores the role of symmetry in geometry and physics. In general relativity, symmetries of the spacetime metric, generated by Killing vector fields, correspond to conserved quantities for particles and fields moving in that spacetime. This deep connection between geometry and conservation laws, in the spirit of Noether’s theorem, is a recurring theme in modern theoretical physics. Chapter 9 revisits Newtonian gravity from a geometric viewpoint, showing that even “classical” gravity can be understood as curvature: the curvature lives in the connection of spacetime, while space itself remains flat. This chapter bridges familiar territory and the more abstract concepts of general relativity. Chapter 10 brings everything together to present general relativity as a physical theory, completing our opening sentence: spacetime geometry governed by the Einstein equations. All the mathematical tools developed in the previous chapters now find their natural role in describing and predicting physical phenomena. Throughout these notes, we will keep returning to one key idea: coordinates are just labels, a convenient bookkeeping device with no physical substance of their own. We will see it at work in the construction of fields in Chapter 3 and in the pseudo-forces of Chapter 6, and we will make it explicit at every step, peeling away the illusion that the physics depends on a particular set of numbers. The real content lives in the geometry itself, in structures and relationships that remain untouched no matter how we choose to describe them. The rest is about building up this framework piece by piece, connecting the mathematics to the physics as we go. So, enough warm-up: let’s get our hands dirty. 1 A detailed transcription of these lectures, with supplementary material, is provided by Dadhley (2015). 2 The package, Differential Geometry Tools, is publicly available at github.com/daniellopezcano/differential_geometry. Built on JAX, it provides visualisations of manifolds, vector fields, and tensor structures, and is described in Appendix A.

title: 1.1 Roadmaps of the Notes
text:
Four infographics, on the large pages that follow, map the territory covered by these notes. Figure 1.1 gives the whole construction at a glance, with no formulas: a smooth manifold, its tangent, cotangent and tensor spaces at every point, the fields assembled from them, and the three structures that can be chosen on top of these fields, up to the Einstein curvature. The three figures after it are detailed versions of this overview. Figure 1.2 collects the algebra of Chapter 2: sets and maps, the scalars \(\mathbb{R}\), the vector space with its dual and its tensor spaces, and their components in a basis. Figure 1.3 carries the construction through Chapters 3, 4 and 5: a set with a topology becomes a topological and then a smooth manifold, whose tangent, cotangent and tensor spaces at every point are finally assembled into vector, covector and tensor fields. Figure 1.4 adds the remaining layers of structure on top of these fields, following Chapters 6, 7 and 8: a connection, which allows fields to be differentiated and compared between points and gives rise to torsion and curvature; a metric, which measures lengths and angles, allowing to compute geodesics; and finally the volume form and the integral of functions and forms over the manifold. All four figures share the same layout and are read from top to bottom, each level adding one piece of structure to the previous one, while columns align corresponding objects. Every card names the chapter or section where its concepts are defined, and every symbol carries the colour of the structure that introduces it. The overview can be read at a glance; the three detailed figures are not meant to be: they are a reference to come back to, to locate a definition, recall a notation, or see where a given object fits in the overall construction. The smooth structure alone (grey region) yields the tangent, cotangent and tensor spaces at every point and, assembled smoothly, the corresponding fields. On top of these, a connection, a metric and an orientation with a volume form are separate structures, each added independently and each with its own notion of curves or integrals (nested cards). A metric relates them: identifying the autoparallel and geodesic equations makes it determine a connection, \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\), and on an oriented manifold it fixes a volume form, \(\Omega^g\); the curvatures of \(

Grey tags give the section of each concept. title: 2 Vector Spaces
text: Motivation: Objects that do not depend on a basis Physical laws should not depend on the basis used to describe them. In \(\mathbb{R}^3\), a vector \(\mathcal{X}\) has components that change with the basis, \[ \mathcal{X} = \sum_{i=1}^{3} x^i \, \hat{x}_i = \sum_{i=1}^{3} y^i \, \hat{y}_i , \qquad x^i \neq y^i \text{ in general}, \] while \(\mathcal{X}\) itself does not. A law written in components therefore holds in every basis precisely when it is the component form of a relation between basis-independent objects. These objects will not always be arrows. The tangent vectors of Chapter 4 are directional derivatives acting on functions, yet they are added and rescaled following the same rules. The theory is thus built from these rules alone. Goal. Develop the algebra that every later chapter applies point by point on a manifold. Build, from sets and maps through groups, rings and fields, the axioms of an \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space and of linear maps. Define the dual space and tensors as multilinear maps, without reference to any basis. Introduce bases and derive how components transform under a change of basis, which distinguishes covariant from contravariant objects. At every point of a manifold, these constructions become the tangent, cotangent and tensor spaces of Chapter 4. Figure 1.2 summarizes the hierarchy of structures together with their notation, operations and component transformation laws, and Appendix C.1 works out an explicit example with polynomials.

title: 2.1 Foundations: Sets, Maps, and Algebraic Structures
text: Before formally defining vector spaces, we review some necessary set-theoretic and the algebraic structures (groups, rings, fields) upon which the concept of vector spaces is built (rows 1 and 2 of Figure 1.2). A set \(\mathcal{M}\) is a well-defined collection of elements1 \(m\in \mathcal{M}\). For example, the set of real numbers \(\mathcal{M}\coloneqq \mathbb{R}\) is formed by all real numbers: \(\mathcal{M} \coloneqq \lbrace ..., -\pi, -2.34, -1, 0, 1/2, e, 10^{27}, ...\rbrace.\) We say that \(\phi\) is a map from the set \(\mathcal{M}\) (domain) to the set \(\mathcal{N}\) (target), denoted as \begin{align*} \phi : \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{N}\\ p &\mapsto \phi(p), \end{align*} if all the elements of \(\mathcal{M}\) are mapped to elements of \(\mathcal{N}\): \begin{align*} \forall p \in \mathcal{M},\, \exists n \in \mathcal{N} : \phi(p) = n. \end{align*} \(\phi\) is injective if different elements in \(\mathcal{M}\) are always mapped to different elements in \(\mathcal{N}\): \[ \forall p_1, p_2 \in \mathcal{M},\; \phi(p_1) = \phi(p_2) \iff p_1 = p_2. \] \(\phi\) is surjective if every element of the target \(\mathcal{N}\) is covered by the map: \[ \forall n \in \mathcal{N},\; \exists p \in \mathcal{M} : \phi(p) = n. \] \(\phi\) is bijective if it is both injective and surjective, hence \(\phi\) establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the elements of \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{N}\). In this case, there exists an inverse map, \begin{align*} \phi^{-1} : \mathcal{N} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\\ n &\mapsto \phi^{-1}(n), \end{align*} such that \[ \phi^{-1} \circ \phi = \text{id}_{\mathcal{M}} \quad \text{and} \quad \phi \circ \phi^{-1} = \text{id}_{\mathcal{N}}. \] Figure 2.1: Examples illustrating the fundamental properties of maps between sets: injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity. The first panel (“NOT a Function”) shows a relation where some elements in the domain are assigned to multiple elements in the target, which violates the definition of a function. The second panel (“General Function”) depicts a valid function where elements of the domain are assigned to elements of the target, but the function is neither injective nor surjective. The third panel (“Only Injective”) shows a function where distinct elements of the domain map to distinct elements of the target (injective), but not every element in the target is covered (not surjective). The fourth panel (“Only Surjective”) presents a function that covers every element of the target (surjective), but some distinct domain elements map to the same target element (not injective). The final panel (“Bijective”) shows a function that is both injective and surjective, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between domain and target, and admitting an inverse function. Given two sets \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{N}\), their Cartesian product is the set \(\mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{N}\) of ordered pairs \((m, n)\) with \(m \in \mathcal{M}\) and \(n \in \mathcal{N}\). It satisfies the following properties: Set membership: \((m, n) \in \mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{N} \iff m \in \mathcal{M}\) and \(n \in \mathcal{N}\). Projections: There exist projection maps \[ \begin{aligned} \pi_\mathcal{M} \colon \mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{N} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{M} \\ (m, n) &\longmapsto \pi_\mathcal{M}(m, n) \coloneqq m \end{aligned} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \begin{aligned} \pi_\mathcal{N} \colon \mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{N} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{N} \\ (m, n) &\longmapsto \pi_\mathcal{N}(m, n) \coloneqq n \end{aligned} \] which extract the first and second components of each pair, respectively. Associativity: For three sets \(\mathcal{M}_1\), \(\mathcal{M}_2\), and \(\mathcal{M}_3\), the products \(\mathcal{M}_1 \times (\mathcal{M}_2 \times \mathcal{M}_3)\) and \((\mathcal{M}_1 \times \mathcal{M}_2) \times \mathcal{M}_3\) are technically different sets because their elements are nested pairs: \((m_1, (m_2, m_3))\) versus \(((m_1, m_2), m_3)\). However, there is an obvious one-to-one correspondence between them that simply reorders the parentheses: \((m_1, (m_2, m_3)) \;\leftrightarrow\; (m_1, m_2, m_3) \;\leftrightarrow\; ((m_1, m_2), m_3).\) Because of this, it is common and harmless to write \((m_1, m_2, m_3)\) without worrying about how the pairs are grouped. Extension to multiple factors: \[ \mathcal{M}^n := \underbrace{\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times \mathcal{M}}_{n\text{-times}} = \{ (m_1, \dots, m_n) \mid m_k \in \mathcal{M} \;\forall k=1,\dots,n \}. \] Cardinality: If \(|\mathcal{M}| = d_1\) and \(|\mathcal{N}| = d_2\), then \(|\mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{N}| = d_1 \cdot d_2\). This extends to products of \(n\) sets. An Abelian group is the doublet \((\mathbb{R}, +)\) where \(\mathbb{R}\) is a set, and \(+\) represents an addition operation, \(+: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfying (with \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\)): Commutativity: \(\alpha + \beta = \beta + \alpha\), Associativity: \((\alpha_1 + \alpha_2) + \alpha_3 = \alpha_1 + (\alpha_2 + \alpha_3)\), Neutral element / Unitarity / Identity: \(\exists 0 \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\alpha + 0 = \alpha\), Inverse element: \(\exists (-\alpha) \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\alpha + (-\alpha) = 0\). A Ring is a triplet \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\) composed by an Abelian group \((\mathbb{R}, +)\), equipped additionally with a multiplication operator \(\cdot: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfying: Neutral element / Unitarity / Identity: \(\exists 1 \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\alpha \cdot 1 = \alpha \cdot 1 = \alpha\), Associativity: \((\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2) \cdot \alpha_3 = \alpha_1 \cdot (\alpha_2 \cdot \alpha_3)\). And the addition and multiplication operators must also have the following properties when used in combination: Distributive (left): \(\alpha_1 \cdot (\alpha_2 + \alpha_3) = (\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2) + (\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_3)\)), Distributive (right): \((\alpha_2 + \alpha_3) \cdot \alpha_1 = (\alpha_2 \cdot \alpha_1) + (\alpha_3 \cdot \alpha_1)\). A Field is a Ring \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\) with two extra properties: Commutativity (w.r.t \(\cdot\)): \(\alpha \cdot \beta = \beta \cdot \alpha\), Inverse element (w.r.t \(\cdot\)): \(\exists (\alpha^{-1}) \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\alpha \cdot (\alpha^{-1}) = 1\). The field of real numbers \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\) serves as the prototypical example in these notes. However, in more general mathematical contexts, other fields are frequently used. Unless stated otherwise, vector spaces in these notes (see below) are always defined over the field \(\mathbb{R}\). 1 Throughout these notes, I will also often use the lowercase letter \(p\) to denote a generic element of a set \(\mathcal{M}\), and similarly use \(\mathcal{N}\) to denote another different set with generic elements denoted by \(n \in \mathcal{N}\). A brief discussion of the set-theoretic framework adopted in these notes can be found in Appendix B.1.

title: 2.2 Vector Space, Dual Space, and Tensor Space
text: We now formally define the concept of an \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space, along with the related notions of linear maps, isomorphisms, and the dual vector space (rows 3 and 4 of Figure 1.2). Note that, at this stage, the definitions are purely algebraic and do not rely on any choice of basis. See appendices C.1.1 & C.1.2 for concrete examples illustrating these definitions employing polynomials. An \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space is the triplet \((V, \oplus, \odot)\) equipped with the Field \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\). The doublet \((V, \oplus)\) forms an Abelian group, and the s-multiplication operator \(\odot: \mathbb{R} \times V \to V\) satisfies (considering \(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in V\), elements of the vector space, known as vectors, and \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\)): Associativity (w.r.t \(\cdot, \odot\)): \((\alpha \cdot \beta) \odot \mathcal{X} = \alpha \odot (\beta \odot \mathcal{X})\), Distributive 1: \((\alpha + \beta) \odot \mathcal{X} = (\alpha \odot \mathcal{X}) \oplus (\beta \odot \mathcal{X})\), Distributive 2: \(\alpha \odot (\mathcal{X} \oplus \mathcal{Y}) = (\alpha \odot \mathcal{X}) \oplus (\alpha \odot \mathcal{Y})\), Unitarity / Neutral element / Identity (w.r.t \(\odot\)): \(\exists 1 \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(1 \odot \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X} \odot 1 = \mathcal{X}\). Let \((V, \oplus_V, \odot_V)\) and \((W, \oplus_W, \odot_W)\) be vector spaces. The map \(\phi : V \to W\) is linear (w.r.t. the vector spaces we have defined, also denoted as \(\phi : V \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} W\)) \(\iff \forall \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in V; \, \forall \alpha \in \mathbb{R}\): \( \phi(\mathcal{X} \oplus_V \mathcal{Y}) = \phi(\mathcal{X}) \oplus_W \phi(\mathcal{Y}) \), and \( \phi(\alpha \odot_V \mathcal{X}) = \alpha \odot_W \phi(\mathcal{X}) \). Given two \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector spaces \((V, \oplus_V, \odot_V)\) and \((W, \oplus_W, \odot_W)\), a map \(\phi : V \longrightarrow W\) is a (vector space) isomorphism if it is linear and bijective, hence invertible. If such a map exists, we say that the vector spaces \(V\) and \(W\) are isomorphic, and we write \(V \cong W\). Intuitively, this means that \(V\) and \(W\) have the same structure as vector spaces. The Vector Space of Homomorphisms between two vector spaces \((V, \oplus_V, \odot_V)\) and \((W, \oplus_W, \odot_W)\) is the triplet conformed by the set \(\text{Hom}(V, W) := \{ \phi, \varphi : V \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} W \}\), and the operations: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \textbf{Addition } \oplus_H: \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \oplus_H : \text{Hom}(V, W) \times \text{Hom}(V, W) &\longrightarrow \text{Hom}(V, W) \\ (\phi, \varphi) &\longmapsto \phi \oplus_H \varphi \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (\phi \oplus_H \varphi)(v) := \phi(v) \oplus_W \varphi(v). \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \textbf{s-multiplication } \odot_H: \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \odot_H : \mathbb{R} \times \text{Hom}(V, W) &\longrightarrow \text{Hom}(V, W) \\ (\lambda, \phi) &\longmapsto \lambda \odot_H \phi \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (\lambda \odot_H \phi)(v) := \lambda \odot_W \phi(v). \end{array} \end{aligned} \] Given a vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\), we define its Dual Vector Space as \((V^* , \oplus^*, \odot^*)\), with \(V^* := \text{Hom}(V, \mathbb{R}) := \{ \phi : V \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathbb{R} \}\), and the addition and s-multiplication operators, \(\oplus^*\) and \(\odot^*\), following the associatted homomorphic definitions above. We will denote with \(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}\) elements of the dual vector space \(V^*\) known as covectors. Given a vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\) and its dual vector space \((V^*, \oplus^*, \odot^*)\), we define the \((r,s)\)-tensor space as the triplet \(\left( {T}^{(r,s)}, \oplus_T, \odot_T \right)\), where \({T}^{(r,s)}\) is the set of all maps of the form2 3: \begin{align*} T \colon \underbrace{V^* \times \dots \times V^*}_{r \text{-times}} \times \underbrace{V \times \dots \times V}_{s \text{-times}} &\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \dots \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R} \\ \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right) &\longmapsto T \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right), \end{align*} with the property that \(T\) is multilinear, i.e., it is \(\mathbb{R}\)-linear with respect to each of its \(r + s\) slots independently. The multilinearity condition explicitly reads: For any covector slot \(i \in \{1, \dots, r\}\): \[ \begin{aligned} T \left( \dots,\; \alpha \odot^* \mathsf{X}^{(i)} \oplus^* \mathsf{Y}^{(i)},\; \dots;\; \dots \right) = \alpha \cdot T \left( \dots,\; \mathsf{X}^{(i)},\; \dots;\; \dots \right) + T \left( \dots,\; \mathsf{Y}^{(i)},\; \dots;\; \dots \right), \end{aligned} \] for any \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) and any \(\mathsf{X}^{(i)}, \mathsf{Y}^{(i)} \in V^*\). Similarly, for any vector slot \(j \in \{1, \dots, s\}\): \[ \begin{aligned} T \left( \dots;\; \dots,\; \alpha \odot \mathcal{X}^{(j)} \oplus \mathcal{Y}^{(j)},\; \dots \right) = \alpha \cdot T \left( \dots;\; \dots,\; \mathcal{X}^{(j)},\; \dots \right) + T \left( \dots;\; \dots,\; \mathcal{Y}^{(j)},\; \dots \right), \end{aligned} \] for any \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) and any \(\mathcal{X}^{(j)}, \mathcal{Y}^{(j)} \in V\). The addition \(\oplus_T\) and the s-multiplication \(\odot_T\) in the \((r,s)\)-tensor space \(\left( {T}^{(r,s)}, \oplus_T, \odot_T \right)\) are the defined as: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \oplus_T : {T}^{(r,s)} \times {T}^{(r,s)} &\longrightarrow {T}^{(r,s)} \\ (T_1, T_2) &\longmapsto T_1 \oplus_T T_2 \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (T_1 \oplus_T T_2)(\dots) := T_1(\dots) + T_2(\dots). \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \odot_T : \mathbb{R} \times {T}^{(r,s)} &\longrightarrow {T}^{(r,s)} \\ (\alpha, T) &\longmapsto \alpha \odot_T T \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (\alpha \odot_T T)(\dots) := \alpha \cdot T(\dots). \end{array} \end{aligned} \] Given two \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector spaces \(\left( V, \oplus_V, \odot_V \right)\) and \(\left( W, \oplus_W, \odot_W \right)\), we define their tensor product as the \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space \(\left( V \otimes W, \oplus_\otimes, \odot_\otimes \right)\), whose elements are finite sums \(\tau = \sum_{k} \alpha_k \, (v_k \otimes w_k)\) of simple tensors \(v_k \otimes w_k\), with \(\alpha_k \in \mathbb{R}\), and whose operations act term by term: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \textbf{Addition} \; \oplus_\otimes: \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \oplus_\otimes : (V \otimes W) \times (V \otimes W) &\longrightarrow V \otimes W \\[2pt] (\tau_1,\; \tau_2) &\longmapsto \tau_1 \oplus_\otimes \tau_2 \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } \displaystyle\sum_{k} \alpha_k (v_k \otimes w_k) \oplus_\otimes \sum_{l} \beta_l (v'_l \otimes w'_l) := \sum_{k} \alpha_k (v_k \otimes w_k) + \sum_{l} \beta_l (v'_l \otimes w'_l). \end{array} \end{aligned} \] \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \textbf{s-multiplication} \; \odot_\otimes: \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \odot_\otimes : \mathbb{R} \times (V \otimes W) &\longrightarrow V \otimes W \\[2pt] (\alpha,\; \tau) &\longmapsto \alpha \odot_\otimes \tau \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } \alpha \odot_\otimes \displaystyle\sum_{k} \alpha_k (v_k \otimes w_k) := \sum_{k} (\alpha \cdot \alpha_k) (v_k \otimes w_k). \end{array} \end{aligned} \] Two such sums are regarded as the same element whenever one can be turned into the other using the bilinearity relations: \[ \begin{aligned} (v_1 \oplus_V v_2) \otimes w &= (v_1 \otimes w) \oplus_\otimes (v_2 \otimes w), \\[4pt] v \otimes (w_1 \oplus_W w_2) &= (v \otimes w_1) \oplus_\otimes (v \otimes w_2), \\[4pt] (\alpha \odot_V v) \otimes w &= \alpha \odot_\otimes (v \otimes w) = v \otimes (\alpha \odot_W w). \end{aligned} \] The general elements of \(V \otimes W\) are finite linear combinations: \[ \sum_{k} \alpha_k \odot_\otimes (v_k \otimes w_k), \quad \alpha_k \in \mathbb{R}. \] The tensor product formalizes the concept of bilinearity itself into a linear structure. This provides the algebraic backbone that generalizes naturally to multilinearity, which underlies the formal definition of tensors as higher-order linear maps. The tensor product enjoys the following structural properties: Universal Property: For any bilinear map, \(B : V \times W \longrightarrow Z\), into a vector space \(Z\), there exists a unique linear map \(\widetilde{B} : V \otimes W \longrightarrow Z\) such that \(\widetilde{B} (v \otimes w) = B(v, w)\) for all \(v \in V\) and \(w \in W\). Dimension Formula: If \(\dim V = m\) and \(\dim W = n\), then \(\dim ( V \otimes W ) = m \cdot n\). A basis is given by the set of tensor products of basis elements: \[ \{ \hat{x}_i \otimes \hat{y}_j \mid i=1,\dots,m;\; j=1,\dots,n \}, \] where \(\{\hat{x}_i\}\) and \(\{\hat{y}_j\}\) are bases of \(V\) and \(W\), respectively. Associativity: Tensor products are associative up to canonical isomorphism: \((V_1 \otimes V_2) \otimes V_3 \cong V_1 \otimes (V_2 \otimes V_3)\). It is customary to omit parentheses and write unambiguously: \(V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes V_3\). Distributivity over Direct Sums: Tensor products distribute over direct sums: \[ (V_1 \oplus_V V_2) \otimes W \cong (V_1 \otimes W) \oplus_\otimes (V_2 \otimes W). \] Duality Relation: There is a canonical isomorphism \(\text{Hom}(V \otimes W, \mathbb{R}) \cong \text{Bilin}(V \times W, \mathbb{R})\), where \(\text{Bilin}(V \times W, \mathbb{R})\) denotes the space of bilinear maps from \(V \times W\) to \(\mathbb{R}\). An equivalent way to define an \((r,s)\)-tensor on a finite-dimensional vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\) is as an element of the tensor product space \[ T^{(r,s)} \cong \underbrace{V \otimes \dots \otimes V}_{r\text{-times}} \otimes \underbrace{V^* \otimes \dots \otimes V^*}_{s\text{-times}}. \] Note the order of the factors: the \(r\) covector slots of the multilinear map are matched by \(r\) copies of \(V\), and the \(s\) vector slots by \(s\) copies of \(V^*\). This is because a vector \(v \in V\) can eat covectors through the canonical identification \(V \cong (V^*)^*\) discussed in the next item, \(v(\mathsf{X}) \coloneqq \mathsf{X}(v)\), while a covector eats vectors directly. Accordingly, a simple tensor with \(v_1, \dots, v_r \in V\) and \(\mathsf{v}^1, \dots, \mathsf{v}^s \in V^*\) acts slot by slot, \[ \left( v_1 \otimes \dots \otimes v_r \otimes \mathsf{v}^1 \otimes \dots \otimes \mathsf{v}^s \right) \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right) \coloneqq \mathsf{X}^{(1)}(v_1) \cdots \mathsf{X}^{(r)}(v_r) \cdot \mathsf{v}^1\big(\mathcal{X}^{(1)}\big) \cdots \mathsf{v}^s\big(\mathcal{X}^{(s)}\big), \] which is manifestly multilinear, and a general element of the tensor product space acts by extending this rule linearly (which is well defined by the universal property). The resulting linear map from the tensor product space to the space of multilinear maps defined above is an isomorphism when \(V\) is finite-dimensional: both spaces have dimension \(d^{\,r+s}\) and, as shown below, the images of simple tensors of basis elements span the space of multilinear maps. This is the precise sense in which both definitions are equivalent, and the reason for the symbol \(\cong\). In this definition, tensors are no longer described as multilinear maps, but rather as elements of a vector space constructed through tensor products. Both perspectives are fully equivalent: the first is often more intuitive for understanding the action of tensors, while the second is more algebraic and convenient for computations, particularly in component form. We can also think of tensors as follows: Given a \((1,1)\)-tensor \begin{align*} T : V^* \times V &\;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}}\; \mathbb{R}\\ \left( \mathsf{X}, \mathcal{X} \right) &\longmapsto T\left( \mathsf{X}, \mathcal{X} \right). \end{align*} We can associate to any such tensor a linear map \begin{align*} \varphi_T :V &\;\xlongrightarrow{\sim}\; V\\ \mathcal{X} &\longmapsto \varphi_T(\mathcal{X}) \coloneqq T(\cdot, \mathcal{X}), \end{align*} where the dot “\(\cdot\)” indicates that the first slot is left open. More explicitly, the map \begin{align*} T(\cdot, \mathcal{X}) : V^* &\;\xlongrightarrow{\sim}\; \mathbb{R}\\ \mathsf{X} &\longmapsto T\left( \mathsf{X}, \mathcal{X} \right), \end{align*} is a linear map that can eat a covector \(\mathsf{X} \in V^*\) and return a real number. Hence, \(T(\cdot, \mathcal{X}) \in (V^*)^*\), that is, the dual of \(V^*\). In finite-dimensional vector spaces, there exists a canonical isomorphism \((V^*)^* \cong V\) which identifies \((V^*)^*\) with \(V\) itself 4. Therefore, \(T(\cdot, \mathcal{X})\) can be interpreted as an element of \(V\). In other words, the data of a \((1,1)\)-tensor, \(T : V^* \times V \xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R}\), is equivalent to the data of the linear map \(\varphi_T : V \xlongrightarrow{\sim} V\). 2 The indices enclosed in parentheses, such as \(\mathsf{X}^{(i)}\) or \(\mathcal{X}^{(j)}\), refer strictly to the position of the argument within the tensor map \(T\). This is a purely positional convention used for clarity when expressing properties like multilinearity. Don’t confuse this with coordinate or basis indices. 3 We can equivalently write \(T \in T^{(r,s)} := \text{Hom}(\underbrace{V^* \times \dots \times V^*}_{r\text{-times}} \times \underbrace{V \times \dots \times V}_{s\text{-times}}, \mathbb{R})\) 4 This identification holds because in finite-dimensional spaces, the double dual of any vector space is naturally isomorphic to the space itself. This is not generally true in infinite-dimensional settings, where the double dual can be strictly larger than the original space, unless additional conditions (like reflexivity) are satisfied.

title: 2.3 Bases, Components, and Transformation Laws
text: Introducing a basis for a vector space allows us to express vectors, covectors, and tensors in terms of components. This leads to the explicit study of how vectors, covectors, and tensors transform under changes of basis, and how their components encode the abstract multilinear structures defined previously (row 5 of Figure 1.2). Check appendices C.1.3 & C.1.4 for concrete examples showing how to extract coordinate components, and how to work with different bases. Given a vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\), a subset \( B \subseteq V \) is a (Hamel-)5 basis if \begin{align*} \forall \mathcal{X} \in V, \, \exists ! \text{ finite } \{ \hat{x}_1, ..., \hat{x}_d \} \subset B : \exists ! \{ x^1, ..., x^d\} \in \mathbb{R} : \mathcal{X} = (x^1 \cdot \hat{x}_1) \oplus ... \oplus (x^d \cdot \hat{x}_d). \end{align*} If such a basis \(B\) exists, we call \(d\) the dimension of the vector space,and we say that \(\{ x^1, ..., x^d\}\) are the components of \(v\) w.r.t \(B\). Hence, we can decompose any vector \(\mathcal{X} \in V\) as \[ \mathcal{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d x^i \cdot \hat{x}_i \] where \(x^i \in \mathbb{R}\) are the components of \(\mathcal{X}\) w.r.t \(B\). Let \(\{\hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_d\}\) and \(\{\hat{y}_1, \dots, \hat{y}_d\}\) be two bases of a vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\). Since both are bases, each vector of one basis can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of the other. Therefore, there exists a matrix of real numbers \(J^j_{i}\) such that: \begin{align*} \hat{x}_i = \sum_{j=1}^d J^j_{i} \cdot \hat{y}_j , \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, d. \end{align*} We say that covariant objects follow this transformation law, and the matrix \(J\) defines the change of basis between \(\{\hat{x}_i\}\) and \(\{\hat{y}_i\}\). The matrix \(J^j_{i} \) is invertible– meaning that there exists a matrix \((J^{-1})^j_{i}\) such that6 \(J^i_{j} \cdot (J^{-1})^j_{i} = \delta^j_i\) – which is a direct consequence of the fact that both sets \(\{\hat{x}_i\}\) and \(\{\hat{y}_i\}\) are linearly independent and span the same vector space \(V\). Therefore, the inverse transformation law reads: \begin{align*} \hat{y}_i = \sum_{j=1}^d (J^{-1})^j_{i} \cdot \hat{x}_j, \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, d. \end{align*} Let \(\mathcal{X} \in V\) be a vector with components \(\{x^i\}\) relative to the basis \(\{\hat{x}_i\}\) and components \(\{y^i\}\) relative to the basis \(\{\hat{y}_i\}\). The decomposition of \(\mathcal{X}\) w.r.t. both bases reads: \[ \mathcal{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d x^i \cdot \hat{x}_i = \sum_{i=1}^d y^i \cdot \hat{y}_i. \] Plugging the change of basis relation this expression gives: \[ \mathcal{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d x^i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^d J^j_{i} \cdot \hat{y}_j = \sum_{i=1}^d y^i \cdot \hat{y}_i. \] Since the basis vectors are linearly independent, we can equate the components on both sides to obtain the transformation law for the vector components: \[ y^i = \sum_{j=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot x^j \longrightarrow x^i = \sum_{j=1}^d (J^{-1})^i_{j} \cdot y^j. \] We say that contravariant objects follow this transformation law. Given a basis \(B\coloneq \{ \hat{x}_1, ..., \hat{x}_d \}\) of a vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\), we can define (it’s a convenient choice) the induced dual cobasis \(B^* \coloneq \{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1, ..., \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^d\}\) of its dual vector space \((V^*, \oplus^*, \odot^*)\) as : \[ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i (\hat{x}_j) = \delta^i_j = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Hence, we can decompose any covector \(\mathsf{X} \in V^*\) as \[ \mathsf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i \] where \(\mathtt{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}\) are the components of \(\mathsf{X}\) w.r.t \(B^*\). Let \(B_1^* \coloneq \{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^d\}\) and \(B_2^* \coloneq \{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^1, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^d\}\) be the dual bases associated to the bases \(B_1 \coloneq \{\hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_d\}\) and \(B_2 \coloneq \{\hat{y}_1, \dots, \hat{y}_d\}\), respectively. Since both are dual bases, each covector of one basis can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of the other. Therefore, there exists a matrix of real numbers \(J^i_{j}\) (the same as for the vectors7) such that: \begin{align*} \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i = \sum_{j=1}^d (J^{-1})^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^j \longrightarrow \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i = \sum_{j=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j, \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, d. \end{align*} As we previously defined it, we can observe that this transformation corresponds to that of a contravariant object. Let \(\mathsf{X} \in V^*\) be a covector with components \(\{\mathtt{x}^i\}\) relative to the basis \(\{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i\}\), and components \(\{\mathtt{y}^i\}\) relative to the basis \(\{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i\}\). The decomposition of \(\mathsf{X}\) w.r.t. both bases reads: \[ \mathsf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{y}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i. \] Plugging the change of basis relation into this expression gives: \[ \mathsf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{y}_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j. \] Since the basis vectors are linearly independent, we can equate the components on both sides to obtain the transformation law for the covector components: \[ \mathtt{x}_j = \sum_{i=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot \mathtt{y}_i \longrightarrow \mathtt{y}_j = \sum_{i=1}^d (J^{-1})^i_{j} \cdot \mathtt{x}_i. \] Hence, we can observe that covector components transform as covariant objects. Let \(\left\{ \hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_d \right\}\) be a basis of the vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\), and \(\left\{ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^d \right\}\) its associated dual basis in \((V^*, \oplus^*, \odot^*)\). Then the \(d^{\,r+s}\) tensors \[ \left\{ \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r} \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s} \;\Big|\; i_1,\dots,i_r, j_1,\dots,j_s \in \{1,\dots,d\} \right\} \] constitute a basis of \(T^{(r,s)}\). By the slot-by-slot action of simple tensors defined above, and \(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k}(\hat{x}_{i}) = \delta^{k}_{i}\), each of them evaluates on basis elements as \begin{equation*} \left( \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r} \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s} \right) \left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r}; \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right) = \delta^{k_1}_{i_1} \cdots \delta^{k_r}_{i_r} \cdot \delta^{j_1}_{l_1} \cdots \delta^{j_s}_{l_s}. \tag{$\star$} \end{equation*} Proof: Spanning: Given \(T \in T^{(r,s)}\), define its components by evaluation on the basis, \[ T^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s} \coloneqq T \left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{i_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{i_r}; \hat{x}_{j_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{j_s} \right) \in \mathbb{R}, \] and consider \[ S \coloneqq \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}} T^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} \cdot \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r} \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s}. \] By \((\star)\), \(S\left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r}; \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right) = T^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s} = T\left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r}; \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right)\) for every choice of indices. Two multilinear maps that agree on all tuples of basis elements agree everywhere (expand each argument in its basis and use multilinearity slot by slot), hence \(T = S\). Linear independence: Suppose a linear combination of these tensors vanishes: \[ \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}} \alpha^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} \cdot \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r} \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s} = 0. \] Evaluating both sides on \(\left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r}; \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right)\) and using \((\star)\), every term vanishes except the one with \(i_1 = k_1, \dots, j_s = l_s\), which yields \(\alpha^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s} = 0\) for all index combinations. Hence every \(T \in T^{(r,s)}\) decomposes uniquely as \[ T = \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}} T^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} \cdot \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r} \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s}, \qquad \dim T^{(r,s)} = d^{\,r+s}. \] A tensor \(T\) acts on any collection of \(r\) covectors \(\{\mathsf{X}^{(i)}\}\) and \(s\) vectors \(\{\mathcal{X}^{(j)}\}\) as: \[ \begin{aligned} T \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right) = \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}} T^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s} \cdot \mathtt{x}_{i_1} \dots \mathtt{x}_{i_r} \cdot x^{j_1} \dots x^{j_s}. \end{aligned} \] The components of a tensor \(T \in T^{(r,s)}\) transform according to: \begin{align*} {T}^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s} &= \sum_{\substack{k_1,\dots,k_r \\ l_1,\dots,l_s}} \left[ (J^{-1})^{i_1}_{k_1} \dots (J^{-1})^{i_r}_{k_r} \cdot J^{l_1}_{j_1} \dots J^{l_s}_{j_s} \cdot \widetilde{{T}}^{k_1 \dots k_r}_{l_1 \dots l_s} \right],\\ \widetilde{T}^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s} &= \sum_{\substack{k_1,\dots,k_r \\ l_1,\dots,l_s}} \left[ J^{i_1}_{k_1} \dots J^{i_r}_{k_r} \cdot (J^{-1})^{l_1}_{j_1} \dots (J^{-1})^{l_s}_{j_s} \cdot {T}^{k_1 \dots k_r}_{l_1 \dots l_s} \right], \end{align*} where \({T}\) are the components in the \(\{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i, \hat{x}_j\}\) basis and \(\widetilde{{T}}\) are the components in the \(\{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i, \hat{y}_j\}\) basis. This generalizes the transformation rules previously seen for vectors (contravariant) and covectors (covariant). 5 See Appendix B.2 for a discussion on finite versus infinite bases (Hamel vs. Schauder). 6 Where \(\delta^i_j\) is the Kronecker delta, which is \(1\) if \(i=j\) and \(0\) otherwise. 7 A formal proof that the change-of-basis matrix for the dual bases is indeed the same matrix \(J\) used for the vectors is provided in Appendix B.3.

title: 3 Topological Manifolds
text: Motivation: Doing calculus without an ambient space Spacetime should be a space on which we can do calculus without placing it inside a larger one. Calculus is defined on open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), so the minimal requirement is that every point has a neighbourhood identified, through a chart \(\mathscr{X}\), with an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Saying that a neighbourhood is open, or that a chart is continuous, already needs a topology on the space itself. A single chart rarely suffices, since a compact space such as the sphere \(S^2\) is not homeomorphic to any open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). With several charts, a function \(f\) is differentiated through its chart representatives, which on an overlap are related by \[ f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} = \big( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big) \circ \big( \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big), \] so differentiability is independent of the chart only if the chart transition maps \(\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\) are themselves differentiable. Goal. Build, from a bare set, the space on which the rest of the notes is formulated. Equip a set with a topology, which defines open sets, continuity and homeomorphisms, and with the Hausdorff and second countability conditions. Define charts and atlases, and with them a \(d\)-dimensional topological manifold, locally homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Require the chart transition maps to be \(C^\infty\), which defines a smooth manifold, together with smooth functions, curves and maps between manifolds. Spacetime will be a 4-dimensional smooth manifold, and coordinates will be nothing more than the values of its charts. Figure 1.3 summarizes the construction, and Appendix C.2 works out an explicit example of a \(d\)-dimensional smooth manifold.

title: 3.1 Topological Spaces
text: The powerset \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})\) of a set \(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of all possible subsets of \(\mathcal{M}\). The set \(\mathcal{O}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})\) defines a topology on \(\mathcal{M}\), denoted as \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\), if and only if: The topology contains the empty set and the whole space itself: \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{O}\) and \(\mathcal{M} \in \mathcal{O}\), The intersection of any two sets that belong to the topology, \(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}\in \mathcal{O}\) (referred to as open sets), is also an open set: \(\forall \mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O}\). Any union of open sets (even an infinite one) is also an open set: \(\bigcup_{\alpha}\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}\in \mathcal{O}\), where \(\alpha\) denotes an arbitrary index set. A set \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{M}\) is said to be closed under the topology \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\) if its complement is open: \(\mathcal{C} \text{ is closed} \iff \mathcal{M} \setminus \mathcal{C} \in \mathcal{O}\). Note that a set can be open, closed, both (clopen), or neither, depending on the topology. The doublet \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}\right)\) is a topological space. Given a topological space \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\), the inherited topology (or subspace topology) on a subset \(\mathcal{N} \subseteq \mathcal{M}\) is defined as \begin{align*} \left.\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}}\right|_{\mathcal{M}} \coloneqq \left\lbrace \mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{U} : \mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right\rbrace. \end{align*} That is, a subset \(\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{N}\) is declared open in \(\mathcal{N}\) if and only if it can be written as the intersection of \(\mathcal{N}\) with an open set \(\mathcal{U}\) from the ambient topology \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\). The \(\mathbb{R}^d\) standard topology, \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\), is \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d} \coloneqq \Big\{\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \;\Big|\; \forall p \in \mathcal{U}\;\exists r>0:\; B_r(p) \subseteq \mathcal{U}\Big\}, \end{align*} where the soft/open ball of radius \(r\) about \(p=(p_1,\dots,p_d)\) is \[ B_r(p) \coloneqq \Big\{ q=(q_1,\dots,q_d)\in\mathbb{R}^d \;\Big|\; \sum_{i=1}^d (q_i-p_i)^2 < r^2\Big\}. \] A topological space \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) is Hausdorff if any two distinct points can be separated by disjoint open sets: \begin{align*} \forall \, p, q \in \mathcal{M}, \; p \neq q, \;\; \exists \, \mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} : \; p \in \mathcal{U}, \; q \in \mathcal{V}, \; \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \emptyset. \end{align*} For instance, \(\left(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\right)\) is Hausdorff: take two open balls centred at \(p\) and \(q\), of radius half their distance. The map \(\phi: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathcal{N}\) is continuous w.r.t. \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) and \(\left(\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}}\right)\) if and only if the preimage of every open set in the target space \(\mathcal{N}\) is also an open set in the domain \(\mathcal{M}\), i.e. \begin{align*} \forall \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \rightarrow \mathrm{preim}_{\phi}(\mathcal{V}) \coloneqq \left\lbrace p \in \mathcal{M} \mid \phi(p) \in \mathcal{V}\right\rbrace \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}. \end{align*} This encodes the idea that \(\phi\) does not “tear” or “break” the underlying topological structure. Given two topological spaces \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\), a map \(\phi \colon \mathcal{M} \longrightarrow \mathcal{N}\), is a homeomorphism w.r.t. \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\) – if and only if: \(\phi\) is bijective, hence invertible, i.e. there exists an inverse map: \(\phi^{-1} \colon \mathcal{N} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\). \(\phi\) is continuous w.r.t. \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\). \(\phi^{-1}\) is also continuous w.r.t. \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\). A topological space \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) is second countable if its topology admits a countable basis, i.e. a countable collection \(\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\) such that every open set is a union of elements of \(\mathcal{B}\). For instance, the open balls with rational centres and rational radii form a countable basis of \(\left(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\right)\).

title: 3.2 Charts and Topological Manifolds
text: Given a topological space, \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\), and an open set \(\mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\), let’s suppose that we can define the following map: \begin{align*} \mathscr{X} \colon \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\\ p &\mapsto \mathscr{X}(p) \coloneqq \left(\mathscr{X}^{1}(p), \ldots, \mathscr{X}^{d}(p)\right) \in \mathbb{R}^d, \end{align*} where the different component functions are given by: \begin{align*} \mathscr{X}^{i} \colon \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}^{i}(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\\ p &\mapsto \mathscr{X}^{i}(p)\in \mathbb{R}. \end{align*} Now let’s endow the target space with the inherited topology from the ambient standard topology in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), i.e. \(\left. \mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})} \right|_{\mathbb{R}^d}\). From this we can define the topological space \(\left( \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}), \left. \mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})} \right|_{\mathbb{R}^d} \right)\) in the target of our map. We say that \(\mathscr{X}\) is a chart map of the chart domain \(\mathcal{U}\) if its image is open, \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\)1, and it is a homeomorphism w.r.t. \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \left. \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{U}} \right|_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}), \left. \mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})} \right|_{\mathbb{R}^d} \right)\). If so, the component functions of \(\mathscr{X}^i\) are then called coordinate maps, and the fact that \(\mathscr{X}\) is a homeomorphism guarantees the existence of a continuous inverse chart map: \begin{align*} \mathscr{X}^{-1} \colon \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d &\longrightarrow \mathcal{U}\\ \left(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_d\right) &\mapsto \mathscr{X}^{-1}\left(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_d\right) = p \in \mathcal{U}, \quad \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}. \end{align*} Charts, defined as the doublet \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right)\), provide a way to describe some local structure of \(\mathcal{M}\) in terms of standard Euclidean space. Given two intersecting charts, \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right),\) \(\left(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}\right): \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \neq \emptyset\), the chart transition maps between the two charts are defined as: \begin{align*} \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \colon \mathscr{Y}\left(\mathcal{U}\cap \mathcal{V}\right) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d &\rightarrow \mathscr{X}\left(\mathcal{U}\cap \mathcal{V}\right) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \\ \left( \beta_1, ..., \beta_d \right) &\mapsto \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\left( \beta_1, ..., \beta_d \right) \coloneqq \left(\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right) \left( \beta_1, ..., \beta_d \right), \quad \beta_i \in \mathbb{R} \end{align*} \begin{align*} \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \colon \mathscr{X}\left(\mathcal{U}\cap \mathcal{V}\right) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d &\rightarrow \mathscr{Y}\left(\mathcal{U}\cap \mathcal{V}\right) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \\ \left( \alpha_1, ..., \alpha_d \right) &\mapsto \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\left( \alpha_1, ..., \alpha_d \right) \coloneqq \left(\mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \left( \alpha_1, ..., \alpha_d \right), \quad \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R} \end{align*} Figure 3.1 illustrates the role of charts and chart transition maps. Figure 3.1: Illustration showing how charts map open sets from a topological manifold to open sets in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and how chart transition maps operate between overlapping charts. The manifold is represented by the surface at the top, with two overlapping open sets labeled \(\mathcal{U}\) (in red) and \(\mathcal{V}\) (in blue), and their intersection \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\) shaded in purple. The point \(p\) lies within the intersection \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\). The chart map \(\mathscr{X}\) maps \(\mathcal{U}\) to an open set \(\mathscr{X}\left( \mathcal{U} \right) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), and the chart map \(\mathscr{Y}\) maps \(\mathcal{V}\) to \(\mathscr{Y}\left( \mathcal{V} \right) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\). The images of the intersection, \(\mathscr{X}\left( \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \right)\) and \(\mathscr{Y}\left( \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \right)\), are shown as overlapping regions in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). The transition map \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} = \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) allows passing from the chart \(\left(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}\right)\) to the chart \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right)\) within the overlap. This diagram encapsulates the essence of local coordinate representations and the role of chart transition functions. Given some arbitrary index set \(A\), the set \(\mathcal{A} = \left\{\left(\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}, \mathscr{X}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha \in A} \right\}\) is called an atlas of the topological space \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)_d\), if the collection of chart domains \(\{\mathcal{U}_\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \}\) completely cover the manifold: \begin{align*} \bigcup_{\alpha\in A}\mathcal{U}_\alpha = \mathcal{M}. \end{align*} From this it follows that \(\forall p \in \mathcal{M},\; \exists\) a chart \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\in \mathcal{A} \mid p \in \mathcal{U}\). A \(d\)-dim. (topological) manifold is a triple \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A} \right)_d\) formed by a topological space \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) and an atlas \(\mathcal{A}\), where the topological space is required to be Hausdorff2 and second countable3. 1 Openness of the image is what later allows us to differentiate chart transition maps, since partial derivatives are only defined at interior points of their domain. Note, however, that \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\) need not be homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^d\) itself: the open annulus \(\{ q \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid 1 < q_1^2 + q_2^2 < 4 \}\) is open, but not homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (it contains loops that cannot be shrunk to a point within it). What makes a manifold locally Euclidean is that every point has some neighbourhood homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^d\), e.g. the preimage of a small open ball inside \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\), not that every chart image is. 2 Being Hausdorff does not follow from the existence of an atlas. Take two copies of \(\mathbb{R}\) and identify each \(t \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}\) of the first with \(t\) of the second. The result, the line with two origins \(0_A\) and \(0_B\), is covered by two charts, one per copy, each a homeomorphism onto \(\mathbb{R}\), with the identity on \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}\) as transition map. Every point, including each origin, has a neighbourhood homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}\), yet every neighbourhood of \(0_A\) intersects every neighbourhood of \(0_B\). Charts only control the neighbourhood of a single point, whereas being Hausdorff is a condition on pairs of points, which may lie in different charts. In these notes, the condition guarantees uniqueness of limits, hence of solutions of ordinary differential equations such as the autoparallel equation (on the line with two origins, the curve solving \(\dot{x} = 1\) with \(x(-1) = -1\) can continue through either origin), and makes compact sets closed, which allows bump functions to be extended by zero. 3 Second countability does not follow from the existence of an atlas either. The “long line”, obtained by gluing uncountably many copies of \([0,1)\) end to end, is connected, Hausdorff and locally homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}\), but it cannot be covered by countably many charts. It admits no partitions of unity, and no embedding into any \(\mathbb{R}^N\). Given the other conditions, second countability is equivalent to the existence of a countable atlas: the manifold is built from countably many charts. Unlike the Hausdorff property, nothing local fails without it. It is included in the definition so that global constructions are available on every manifold: partitions of unity, which glue local objects into global ones, such as connections, metrics, and integrals, defined as countable sums of chart integrals.

title: 3.3 Smooth Manifolds
text: An atlas is \(C^\infty\)-compatible, denoted as \(\mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\), if for any pair of charts \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right), \left(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}\right) \in \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\): Either \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \emptyset\), or \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \neq \emptyset\) and both chart transition maps, \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\), are \(C^\infty\) functions in the “ordinary multivariable calculus sense”4. A \(d\)-dim. smooth manifold (or \(C^\infty\)-manifold)5 is the triple \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, {\mathcal{A}}_{C^\infty} \right)_d\).

title: 3.3 Smooth Manifolds
text:
3.3.1 Smooth Maps and Diffeomorphisms

Smoothness of maps is defined through charts, by reducing it to ordinary multivariable calculus. A function \(f : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}\) on a smooth manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_d\) is smooth if, for every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\), its chart representative \begin{align*} f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} : \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \end{align*} is \(C^\infty\) in the ordinary multivariable calculus sense. This is where \(C^\infty\)-compatibility becomes essential: if \(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) is smooth and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) is another chart, then on \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V})\) \begin{align*} f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} = \left( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \circ \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right) = \left( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \circ \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}, \end{align*} a composition of smooth maps, hence smooth. Smoothness checked in one chart around each point therefore holds in all charts: the notion is chart-independent. On a merely topological manifold, whose transition maps are only continuous, no such chart-independent notion of differentiability would exist. More generally, given two smooth manifolds \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M} \right)_{d}\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N} \right)_{e}\), a continuous map \(\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}\) is smooth if, for every pair of charts \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M}\) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}\), its chart representative \begin{align*} \mathscr{Y} \circ \phi \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} : \mathscr{X}\big( \mathcal{U} \cap \mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{V}) \big) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^e \end{align*} is \(C^\infty\). Continuity of \(\phi\) guarantees that \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{V})\) is open, so the representative is defined on an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and the same composition argument as above shows that the notion is chart-independent. Two special cases will be used constantly: smooth functions are the smooth maps into \(\mathcal{N} = \mathbb{R}\), equipped with its standard smooth structure \(\left( \mathbb{R}, \mathcal{O}_\mathbb{R}, \{ (\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}) \} \right)_1\); smooth curves are the smooth maps \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\), with \(\mathbb{R}\) carrying the same standard structure: \(\gamma\) is smooth if and only if \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(\mathrm{preim}_\gamma(\mathcal{U})\) for every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\). A diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection \(\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}\) whose inverse \(\phi^{-1} : \mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{M}\) is also smooth. If one exists, \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{N}\) are diffeomorphic. Diffeomorphic manifolds are indistinguishable as smooth manifolds, just as homeomorphic spaces are indistinguishable as topological spaces, and isomorphic vector spaces as vector spaces. This is the notion of equivalence implicit in the footnote on exotic smooth structures above. 4 By “ordinary multivariable calculus sense” we mean that the transition maps, \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \colon \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \colon \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d\), are smooth functions between open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) in the usual calculus sense, i.e., they admit continuous partial derivatives of all orders. Useful remarks: Here we refer specifically to \(C^\infty\)-compatibility, but the notion of compatibility extends naturally to any desired degree of differentiability (\(C^k\), \(C^\omega\), etc.), depending on the structure one wishes to impose. Whitney’s Theorem states that, for \(k \geq 1\), every maximal \(C^k\)-atlas contains a \(C^\infty\)-atlas, and that the resulting smooth structure is unique up to diffeomorphism. Hence, for \(k \geq 1\), nothing is lost by working directly with \(C^\infty\)-manifolds. For \(k = 0\) the analogous statement fails: there exist topological manifolds admitting no smooth structure at all. 5 It is important to emphasize that it is possible to define two atlases, \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\), on the same topological space \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) that are both internally \(C^\infty\)-compatible, but not compatible with each other. In other words, the union \(\mathcal{A}_1 \cup \mathcal{A}_2\) does not form a valid \(C^\infty\)-atlas because the chart transition maps between charts from \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) are not smooth. In that case, each atlas defines a different smooth structure on the same topological manifold. These are then regarded as two distinct smooth manifolds with the same underlying topological space but different smooth structures. This is not just a pathological possibility: there exist topological manifolds that admit multiple inequivalent smooth structures. A famous example is \(\mathbb{R}^4\), which admits uncountably many non-diffeomorphic smooth structures, known as exotic \(\mathbb{R}^4\)’s. These are topologically homeomorphic to the standard \(\mathbb{R}^4\) but not diffeomorphic to it or to each other. Another classical example is the 7-dimensional sphere \(S^7\), for which John Milnor discovered in 1956 the existence of exotic spheres, i.e., smooth structures on \(S^7\) that are not diffeomorphic to the standard round sphere. Kervaire and Milnor later showed that \(S^7\) admits exactly 28 smooth structures up to orientation-preserving diffeomorphism (15 if orientation-reversing diffeomorphisms are also allowed). For this reason, when defining a smooth manifold, one should consider not just an arbitrary \(C^\infty\)-compatible atlas but rather the entire collection of charts that are smoothly compatible with it. This ensures that the smooth structure is fully specified. If two atlases are not compatible, they belong to different maximal atlases and define distinct smooth structures on the same topological space.

title: 4 Tangent Spaces
text: Motivation: Vectors without arrows In \(\mathbb{R}^d\), a vector \(v\) at \(p\) is an arrow from \(p\) to \(p + v\). On a manifold this picture is unavailable, since points cannot be added and there is no ambient space for the arrows to live in. What survives is the action of \(v\) on functions. In \(\mathbb{R}^d\), along the curve \(\gamma(\lambda) = p + \lambda v\), \[ (f \circ \gamma)'(0) = v^i \, \partial_i f(p) , \] and choosing for \(f\) the coordinate functions recovers every component \(v^i\). Curves and smooth functions both make sense on a manifold, so this action can serve as the definition of a vector. Goal. Build, at every point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), the vector spaces of Chapter 2. Define the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) as the set of velocities of curves through \(p\), acting on scalar fields as directional derivatives, and show that it is a \(d\)-dimensional vector space. Derive, rather than postulate, the chart-induced bases and the transformation laws of components, which distinguish covariant from contravariant objects. Construct its dual, the cotangent space \(T^*_p\mathcal{M}\), whose elements are the differentials of scalar fields, and the tensor spaces \(T^{(r,s)}_p\mathcal{M}\). The four-velocity of a particle is the velocity of its worldline at a point of spacetime, an element of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\).

title: 4.1 Tangent Space \(T_p \mathcal{M}\)
text: Figure 4.2 illustrates the construction and the role of charts and chart transition maps, and Appendix C.3 works it out on an explicit example. The \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space of scalar fields (or smooth functions) on a smooth manifold \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, {\mathcal{A}}_{C^\infty}\right)_d\) is the triplet \((C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}), \oplus, \odot)\), where \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) := \{ f: \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R} \mid f \text{ is smooth} \}\), with smoothness in the sense of Chapter 3 (\(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) is \(C^\infty\) for every chart), and the addition and s-multiplication are defined as: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \oplus : C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) \times C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) &\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) \\ (f_1, f_2) &\longmapsto f_1 \oplus f_2 \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (f_1 \oplus f_2)(p) := f_1(p) + f_2(p). \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \odot : \mathbb{R} \times C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) &\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) \\ (\lambda, f) &\longmapsto \lambda \odot f \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (\lambda \odot f)(p) := \lambda \cdot f(p). \end{array} \end{aligned} \] Figure 4.1 illustrates how two scalar fields defined upon a manifold can be multiplied and added together following the properties of a vector space. A curve on the manifold \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}\right)_d\) is a map \begin{align*} \gamma : \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\\ \lambda &\longmapsto \gamma(\lambda). \end{align*} To be able to properly define the degree of differentiability of \(\gamma\), we endow the source set \(\mathbb{R}\) with its standard smooth manifold structure \(\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{O}_\mathbb{R}, \{(\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R})\}\right)_1\), so that, by the definition of smooth maps in Chapter 3, \(\gamma\) is smooth precisely when its chart representatives \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma\) are \(C^\infty\) (and \(C^k\) when they are \(C^k\)). A curve is said to pass through a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) at parameter \(\lambda_0 \in \mathbb{R}\) if \(\gamma(\lambda_0) = p\). Given a curve \(\gamma\) at least \(C^1\) on the manifold \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}\right)_d\), its velocity at the point \(\gamma(\lambda_0) =p \in \mathcal{M}\) w.r.t. a field \(f \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\) is the linear map: \begin{align*} v_{\gamma, p} \colon C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) &\xlongrightarrow{\;\;\sim\;\;} \mathbb{R} \\ f &\longmapsto v_{\gamma, p}(f) \coloneqq \frac{d}{d\lambda} (f \circ \gamma) \Big|_{\lambda = \lambda_0} = (f \circ \gamma)' (\lambda_0), \end{align*} where the composition \((f \circ \gamma) \colon \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\) maps the curve parameter to the real line via the field \(f\). The derivative \((f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0)\) captures the rate of change of \(f\) along the curve \(\gamma\) at the point \(p\). Figure 4.1: Representation of the \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space of smooth functions \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\). Two different functions defined on the manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) are shown, \(f\) and \(g\). These two functions are added together (and the function \(g\) is multiplied by a scalar) to obtain a new function \(h = f \oplus 3.5 \odot g\), which is also a smooth function on the manifold \(\mathcal{M}\). The addition and scalar multiplication operations are defined pointwise, meaning that for each point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), the value of the function \(h\) at \(p\) is given by \(h(p) = f(p) + 3.5 \cdot g(p)\). The tangent (\(\mathbb{R}\)-vector) space to \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}\right)_d\) at \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) is a triplet \((T_p \mathcal{M}, \oplus_T, \odot_T)\), where \(T_p \mathcal{M} := \{ v_{\gamma, p} \mid \gamma \text{ is a smooth curve that passes through } p \}\) – hence \(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p \mathcal{M}\) is a vector – and the operations \(\oplus_T\) (addition) and \(\odot_T\) (s-multiplication) are defined as1: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \oplus_T : T_p \mathcal{M} \times T_p \mathcal{M} &\to T_p \mathcal{M} \\ (v_{\gamma_1, p}, v_{\gamma_2, p}) &\mapsto v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p} \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p})(f) := v_{\gamma_1, p}(f) + v_{\gamma_2, p}(f). \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \odot_T : \mathbb{R} \times T_p \mathcal{M} &\to T_p \mathcal{M} \\ (\alpha, v_{\gamma, p}) &\mapsto \alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma, p} \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (\alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma, p})(f) := \alpha \cdot v_{\gamma, p}(f). \end{array} \end{aligned} \]

title: 4.1 Tangent Space \(T_p \mathcal{M}\)
text:
4.1.1 Basis and Coordinate Components for \(T_p \mathcal{M}\)

At this point, we introduce a notational convention that, while extremely convenient and widely used, can be deceptively suggestive. It creates the illusion that the abstract objects we have defined are intrinsically tied to coordinates, when in fact, this is merely an artifact of expressing them in terms of a chart. Keeping this in mind, let us proceed.
