Given a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around the point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) such that \(p \in \mathcal{U}\), we can expand the velocity of the curve \(\gamma\) at \(p\) acting on a scalar field \(f\) as2: \begin{align*} v_{\gamma, p} (f) := (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) = \big( (\underbrace{f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}}_{\mathbb{R}\longleftarrow\mathbb{R}^d}) \circ (\underbrace{\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma}_{\mathbb{R}^d\longleftarrow\mathbb{R}}) \big)' (\lambda_0) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \underbrace{(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma)_i'(\lambda_0)}_{\dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda_0)} \underbrace{\cdot \partial_i \left[f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right] (\mathscr{X}(p))}_{\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (f)}. \end{align*} This motivates the following expression: \begin{align*} v_{\gamma, p} (f) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (f) &\longrightarrow v_{\gamma, p} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \underbrace{\dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)}_{\substack{\text{i-th component} \\ \text{of } v_{\gamma, p} \text{ w.r.t. } \mathscr{X}}} \cdot \underbrace{\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}}_{\substack{\text{i-th basis element} \\ \text{on } T_p\mathcal{U} \text{ w.r.t. } \mathscr{X}}} \end{align*} We refer to the elements \(\dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\in \mathbb{R}\) as the i-th coordinate component of \(v_{\gamma, p}\) w.r.t. the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\); and the terms \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}\in T_p\mathcal{U}\) as the i-th basis element of \(T_p\mathcal{U}\) w.r.t. the same chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\). The set \begin{align*} e \coloneqq \left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \right)_{p},\; \ldots,\; \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^d} \right)_{p} \right\rbrace \end{align*} is the chart-induced basis of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) associated with the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\). The proof that this set constitutes a basis for \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) is given in Appendix B.5. From this, it follows that the dimension of the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) coincides with the dimension \(d\) of the smooth manifold3 \(\mathcal{M}\). Given a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around the point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), we can extract the components, \(\dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\in \mathbb{R}\), of the tangent vector \(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\) as4: \begin{align*} &\sum_{j=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^j_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_{p} (\mathscr{X}^i) = v_{\gamma, p} (\mathscr{X}^i) \longrightarrow \dots\\ \sum_{j=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^j_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) &\cdot \underbrace{\partial_j \left[\mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right] (\mathscr{X}(p))}_{\delta^i_j} = (\mathscr{X}^i \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) \longrightarrow \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) = (\mathscr{X}^i \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) \in \mathbb{R} \end{align*} Given two intersecting charts \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), with \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \neq \emptyset\), the Jacobian of the chart transition map \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \coloneqq \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\) at a point \(p \in \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\) is defined as follows: \begin{align*} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{j}\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \coloneqq \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_p = \underbrace{\partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right]}_{ \left(\mathbb{R}^d\right)_\mathcal{U} \longleftarrow \left(\mathbb{R}^d\right)_\mathcal{V} } \big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big). \end{align*} Similarly, the Jacobian of the inverse transition map \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \coloneqq \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) is given by: \begin{align*} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^i_{j}\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) \coloneqq \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p = \underbrace{\partial_j \left[ \mathscr{Y}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right]}_{ \left(\mathbb{R}^d\right)_\mathcal{V} \longleftarrow \left(\mathbb{R}^d\right)_\mathcal{U} } \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big). \end{align*} By construction, Jacobians satisfy the following property: \begin{align*} \sum_{k=1}^{d} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{k} \left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^k_{j} \left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) &= \sum_{k=1}^{d} \left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \right)_{p} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_{p} \right\rbrace\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{d} \left\lbrace \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{Y}^k \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \cdot \partial_k \left[ \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big) \right\rbrace\\ &= \partial_j \left[ \left( \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right) \circ \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big)\\ &= \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^i \circ \left( \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \circ \mathscr{Y} \right) \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big)\\ &= \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) = \delta^i_j. \end{align*} This expresses the fact that the Jacobian of the transition map \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\) is the inverse of the Jacobian of the transition map \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\); in particular, both are invertible at every point of the overlap. This is a consequence of the \(C^1\)-compatibility of the two charts (the chain rule applied to two mutually inverse differentiable maps), not a criterion for it. It is, however, a useful sanity check when computing Jacobians explicitly. The chart-induced basis transforms as follows between two intersecting chart domains \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) containing a point \(p \in \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\). Given two charts \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), the basis vectors induced by \(\mathscr{X}\) and \(\mathscr{Y}\) at the point \(p\) are related by: \begin{align*} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (f) &\coloneqq \partial_i \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) = \partial_i \left[ \left( f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right) \circ \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big)\\ &= \sum_{j=1}^{d}\left\lbrace \partial_i\left[ \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right]_j (\mathscr{X}(p)) \cdot \left\lbrace \partial_j \left[ f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\right] \circ ( \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \right\rbrace (\mathscr{X}(p)) \right\rbrace\\ &= \sum_{j=1}^d \left\{ \partial_i \left[ \mathscr{Y}^j \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \cdot \partial_j \left[ f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big) \right\}\\ &= \sum_{j=1}^d \left\{ \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} (f) \right\}. \end{align*} Since this holds \(\forall f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), we conclude the transformation law for the basis vectors: \begin{align*} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} = \sum_{j=1}^d \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} = \sum_{j=1}^d \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^j_{i}\left(\mathscr{X}(p)\right) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p}. \end{align*} We say that covariant objects follow this transformation law. Correspondingly, the vector components transform as follows between two intersecting chart domains \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) containing a point \(p \in \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\). Given a vector \(v_{\gamma, p}\) expressed in the chart-induced bases of \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), we have: \begin{align*} v_{\gamma, p} &= \sum_{i=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_{p}. \end{align*} Substituting the basis change derived previously into the left-hand expression for \(v_{\gamma, p}\), we get: \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \sum_{j=1}^{d} \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_{p}. \end{align*} Since the basis vectors \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p}\) are linearly independent, we can equate the components on both sides to obtain the transformation law for the vector components: \begin{align*} \dot{\gamma}^k_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} \cdot \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^k_{i}\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) \cdot \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0). \end{align*} We say that contravariant objects follow this transformation law. Figure 4.2: Visual summary of a tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) and the components of curve velocities in different charts. A smooth manifold is shown in blue, with the overlap between two charts \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\) shaded in purple. The point \(p\) is marked by a black dot, and the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) is depicted as a purple tangent plane at \(p\). Two curves, \(\gamma\) (yellow) and \(\delta\) (green), pass through \(p\); their velocities at different points are drawn as arrows tangent to the surface. This common visual device is meant to aid intuition: in reality, tangent vectors act on smooth functions over the manifold as directional derivatives and are not fundamentally “attached arrows” on the surface. However, at the chart level these arrows do have a precise meaning: they represent the coordinate components of the curve velocities in a chart–induced basis. For example, \(\dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\) and \(\dot{\delta}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\) are the components of the velocities of \(\gamma\) and \(\delta\) in the basis \(\big\{\big(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}\big)_{p}\big\}\) induced by the chart \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right)\). The bottom panels show the curves in the coordinate domains \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}\cap\mathcal{V})\) (left) and \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U}\cap\mathcal{V})\) (right) with the curve velocities in the corresponding coordinate bases.

title: 4.1 Tangent Space \(T_p \mathcal{M}\)
text:
4.1.2 Notation

At this point in the notes, we introduce a new notation that, while standard in differential geometry, may initially obscure the true nature of the objects we have previously defined. Up until now, I have deliberately avoided this notation to emphasize the fundamental nature of these objects. However, as we progress, continuing with the previous notation will become increasingly cumbersome. Thus, it is necessary to adopt the conventional notation for vectors (and in subsequent sections for covectors, and fields). Here we are not introducing any new mathematical concepts, we will just alter our previous notation to align with the commonly used language in differential geometry. First, let us introduce the Einstein summation convention, a notational rule that eliminates the need to explicitly write summation symbols. According to this convention, whenever an index appears once as an upper index and once as a lower index within a single term, a summation over all possible values of that index is implicitly understood. For example, the expression \(A^i B_i\) is shorthand for the full summation \(\sum_{i} A^i B_i\). It is worth noting that, in some contexts, this convention is occasionally extended beyond its strict form. In particular, it is common to abuse the convention slightly by allowing summation over repeated indices even when they are not “contracted”, that is, even if the repeated index appears both in upper position or both in lower position. For instance, the expression \(A^i B^i\) is often understood as shorthand for \(\sum_i A^i B^i\) despite both indices being upper. Throughout these notes, we will adopt the standard form of the Einstein summation convention, where summation is implied only when an index appears once upstairs and once downstairs within a term. We will avoid the extended usage where repeated indices are summed without contraction, in order to maintain notational clarity. Let us now apply the Einstein summation convention to express how a vector in the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) can be expanded in terms of basis elements induced by two charts \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), both containing the point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\): \begin{align*} v_{\gamma, p} = \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p = \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p. \end{align*} This expression reflects the fact that the tangent vector \(v_{\gamma, p}\) is an intrinsic geometric object, while its representation in terms of components and basis vectors depends on the particular chart employed. Now let us suppose that we have another curve \(\delta \colon \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathcal{M}\) that passes through the same point \(p\). Then, the tangent vector \(v_{\delta, p}\) can be expressed in terms of the basis elements induced by the charts \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\), and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\) as: \begin{align*} v_{\delta, p} = \dot{\delta}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p = \dot{\delta}^i_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p. \end{align*} For simplicity, from now on we will typically denote these vectors in \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) by the symbols \(\mathcal{X}_p \coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}_p \coloneqq v_{\delta, p}\). This avoids repeatedly writing expressions like \(v_{\gamma, p}\), which carry unnecessary clutter when the geometric role of the object is already clear from context. Now we introduce yet another shorthand notation for the basis elements induced by the charts \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), respectively: \(\partial{x_i} \coloneqq \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p\) and \(\partial{y_i} \coloneqq \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p\). Taking all these notation changes into account, we can produce the following summary table: Vector notation Basis vectors In chart \(\mathscr{X}\) In chart \(\mathscr{Y}\) \(\mathcal{X}_p \coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}\) \(\left(\partial{x_i}\right)_p \coloneqq \left( \dfrac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p\) \(x^i_p \coloneqq \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\) \(y^i_p \coloneqq \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0)\) \(\mathcal{Y}_p \coloneqq v_{\delta, p}\) \(\left(\partial{y_i}\right)_p \coloneqq \left( \dfrac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p\) \(\tilde{x}^i_p \coloneqq \dot{\delta}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\) \(\tilde{y}^i_p \coloneqq \dot{\delta}^i_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0)\) With this convention, the basis expansions of the two vectors reads: \[ \mathcal{X}_p = \underbrace{ x^i_p \cdot \left(\partial{x_i}\right)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{X}} = \underbrace{ y^i_p \cdot \left(\partial{y_i}\right)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{Y}}, \qquad \mathcal{Y}_p = \underbrace{ \tilde{x}^i_p \cdot \left(\partial{x_i}\right)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{X}} = \underbrace{ \tilde{y}^i_p \cdot \left(\partial{y_i}\right)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{Y}}. \] It is important to remark once again the different roles played by the symbols \(\mathscr{X}\), \(\mathcal{X}_p\), \(x^i_p\), \(\tilde{x}^i_p\), and \(\left(\partial{x_i}\right)_p\), despite their similar appearance. The symbol \(\mathscr{X}\) refers to the chart map itself, i.e., the homeomorphism that assigns coordinates to points in the manifold. By contrast, \(\mathcal{X}_p\) and \(\mathcal{Y}_p\) are abstract tangent vectors at the point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\)—geometric objects that are independent of any chart. The symbols \(x^i_p\) and \(\tilde{x}^i_p\) denote the numerical components of the vectors \(\mathcal{X}_p\) and \(\mathcal{Y}_p\), respectively, with respect to the basis induced by the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) (and similarly \(y^i_p\) and \(\tilde{y}^i_p\) in the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\)). Meanwhile, \(\left(\partial{x_i}\right)_p \coloneqq \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p\) and \(\left(\partial{y_i}\right)_p \coloneqq \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p\) represent the basis vectors of the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) associated with each chart. Despite the visual similarity of these symbols, they refer to fundamentally different mathematical objects5. With this notation in place, the rules governing changes of coordinates between charts become: \[ \left(\partial{x_i}\right)_p = \underbrace{\left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}}_{ \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^j_{i}\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) } \cdot\; \left(\partial{y_j}\right)_p \] Similarly, the transformation law for the components of a vector: \[ y^i_p = \underbrace{ \left(\frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j}\right)_{p} }_{ \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^i_{j}\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) } \cdot\; x^j_p. \] The same rule applies to the components \(\tilde{x}^i_p\) and \(\tilde{y}^i_p\) of the vector \(\mathcal{Y}_p\), since the transformation rule depends solely on the change of basis induced by the chart transition, not on the particular vector. In this compact notation, the correspondence between the transformation of basis vectors (covariant) and the transformation of components (contravariant) becomes immediately apparent. Up to this point in the notes, I have not placed indices arbitrarily up or down, but rather deliberately in positions that reflect their transformation behavior: upper indices for contravariant objects, and lower indices for covariant objects. 1 The fact that the sum and scalar multiplication defined in this way yield well defined velocity vectors inside of \(T_p \mathcal{M}\) is not trivial. It requires proving that for any pair of smooth curves \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) passing through \(p\), there exists a third smooth curve whose velocity at \(p\) realizes the sum \(v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p}\), and similarly for the s-multiplication. A constructive proof of this fact is provided in Appendix B.4. 2 Multivariable chain rule: Given two functions \(f\) and \(g\) defined as: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} g : \mathbb{R}^D &\to \mathbb{R}^d \\ (x_1, ..., x_D) &\mapsto g(x_1, ..., x_D) := \left(g_1(x_1, ..., x_D), ..., g_d(x_1, ..., x_D)\right) \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} f : \mathbb{R}^d &\to \mathbb{R} \\ (x_1, ..., x_d) &\mapsto f(x_1, ..., x_d) \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] Let us define a function \(h : \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(h(x) := (f \circ g)(x_1, ..., x_D)\), the multidimensional chain rule states that \[ \partial_\alpha h(x_1, ..., x_D) = \partial_\alpha(f \circ g)(x_1, ..., x_D) = \sum_{i=1}^d\left\lbrace \partial_\alpha{g_i}(x_1, ..., x_D) \cdot \left[ \partial_i f \circ g \right](x_1, ..., x_D) \right\rbrace, \] where \(\partial_\alpha h\) represents the derivative w.r.t the \(\alpha\) input variable of \(h\) (the same applies to \(\partial_\alpha g_i\)). If \(D=1\), \(g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^d\), and for simplicity of notation, we can substitute the differentiation symbol “\(\partial_\alpha\)” directly by “\({}'\)”: \[ {h}'(x) = (f \circ g)'(x) = \sum_{i=1}^d\left\lbrace {g_i}'(x) \cdot \left[ \partial_i f \circ g \right](x) \right\rbrace, \] 3 It is important to emphasize that this fact does not stem solely from the existence of a single chart around the point \(p\). Rather, it is a global structural property of the manifold: the requirement that there exists an atlas \(\mathcal{A}\) whose charts cover \(\mathcal{M}\) and are each homeomorphic to open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) ensures that the local Euclidean structure — and hence the dimension \(d\) — is consistent across all points. This guarantees that the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) has the same dimension \(d\) at every point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\). In other words, the notion of dimension for a smooth manifold is globally well-defined, not merely a property observed in a single coordinate patch. 4 The step marked with an underbrace in the equation above is a direct consequence of the fact that the function \begin{align*} \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^d &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\\ \left( \alpha^1, \dots, \alpha^d \right) &\longmapsto \left(\mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right) \left( \alpha^1, \dots, \alpha^d \right) = \alpha^i. \end{align*} is simply the projection onto the \(i\)-th coordinate, hence, computing its partial derivative with respect to the \(j\)-th coordinate yields the Kronecker delta \(\delta^j_i\). 5 I might be overdoing this a little bit but I assure you that fundamental misconceptions in the future will be avoided if the reader interiorizes this. Don’t be fooled by this evil notation, it’s horrible but it’s what we have, if you think you can do better, go ahead and try, but I’ve spent no little time trying to figure out a better notation and this is the best I managed to do.

title: 4.2 Cotangent Space \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)
text: The cotangent (\(\mathbb{R}\)-vector) space \(\left(T_p^* \mathcal{M}, \oplus_{T}^*, \odot_{T}^* \right)\) of the manifold \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}\right)_d\) at a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) is the dual (\(\mathbb{R}\)-)vector space of the tangent (\(\mathbb{R}\)-vector) space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), this is, the set of all linear maps from \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\): \(T_p^*\mathcal{M} := \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{R}}(T_p\mathcal{M}, \mathbb{R})\). Each element \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) is called a covector (or cotangent vector) at the point \(p\). Covectors are canonically produced as the differentials (or gradients) of smooth scalar fields6. Given a function \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), its differential at \(p\) is the covector \begin{align*} (df)_p : T_p \mathcal{M} &\xlongrightarrow{\;\;\sim\;\;} \mathbb{R} \\ v_{\gamma, p} &\longmapsto (df)_p (v_{\gamma, p}) := v_{\gamma, p}(f), \end{align*} which evaluates the directional derivative of \(f\) along \(v_{\gamma, p}\) at the point \(p\). This construction is not a special case but an exhaustive one: every element of \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) is the differential at \(p\) of some \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)7. Locally, this is made explicit in Subsection 4.2.1, where the differentials \((d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\) of the coordinate maps are shown to form a basis of \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\).

title: 4.2 Cotangent Space \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)
text:
4.2.1 Basis and Coordinate Components for \(T^*_p \mathcal{M}\)

Given a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), the set of differentials \begin{align*} \epsilon \coloneqq \left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^1)_p, \dots, (d\mathscr{X}^d)_p \right\rbrace, \end{align*} constitutes the dual chart-induced basis8 for \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\). This means that any covector \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) at \(p\) can be written as: \begin{align*} \mathsf{X}_p = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i^p (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p, \end{align*} Therefore, at the level of a point, the cotangent space is completely and rigorously characterized as the dual of the tangent space, with gradients of scalar fields providing a natural generating set. Note that, employing the dual chart-induced basis we can recover single components of \(v_{\gamma, p}\): \begin{align*} (d\mathscr{X}^{i})_p (v_{\gamma, p}) = (\mathscr{X}^{i} \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) = (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma)_j'(\lambda_0) \cdot \underbrace{\partial_j \left[\mathscr{X}^{i} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right] (\mathscr{X}(p))}_{\delta^i_j} = (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma)_i'(\lambda_0) = \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda_0). \end{align*} Given a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) with \(p \in \mathcal{U}\), we can extract the components, \(\mathtt{x}_i^p\), of the covector \(\left(df\right)_p\) as: \begin{align*} &\sum_{j=1}^d \mathtt{x}_j^p (d\mathscr{X}^j)_p \left( \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} \right) = \left(df\right)_p \left( \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} \right) \longrightarrow \dots\\ \sum_{j=1}^{d} \mathtt{x}_j^p &\cdot \underbrace{\partial_i \left[\mathscr{X}^j \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right] (\mathscr{X}(p))}_{\delta^j_i} = \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (f) \longrightarrow \mathtt{x}_i^p = \partial_i \left[f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right] (\mathscr{X}(p)) \in \mathbb{R}. \end{align*} Given two charts \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), the basis covectors induced by \(\mathscr{X}\) and \(\mathscr{Y}\) at the point \(p\) are related as follows. Let us compute the action of the covector \((d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\) on an arbitrary tangent vector \(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\): \begin{align*} (d\mathscr{X}^{i})_p (v_{\gamma, p}) &\coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}(\mathscr{X}^{i}) = (\mathscr{X}^{i} \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0)= \big( \underbrace{ \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} }_{\mathbb{R} \longleftarrow \mathbb{R}^d} \circ \underbrace{ \mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma }_{\mathbb{R}^d \longleftarrow \mathbb{R}} \big)' (\lambda_0)\\ &= \sum_{j=1}^{d} \left\lbrace \underbrace{(\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma)_j'(\lambda_0)}_{v_{\gamma, p}(\mathscr{Y}^j)} \cdot \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^{i} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] (\mathscr{Y}(p)) \right\rbrace\\ &= \sum_{j=1}^{d} \left\lbrace (d\mathscr{Y}^{j})_p (v_{\gamma, p}) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} \right\rbrace. \end{align*} Since this holds for any tangent vector \(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\), we conclude the transformation law for the dual basis: \begin{align*} (d\mathscr{X}^{i})_p = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} \cdot (d\mathscr{Y}^{j})_p \right\rbrace = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{j} \left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot (d\mathscr{Y}^{j})_p. \end{align*} In Section 4.1.1, we defined that contravariant objects transform exactly like this, hence, the dual chart-induced basis elements are contravariant, in contrast to tangent basis vectors which transform covariantly. Correspondingly, the covector components transform as follows between two intersecting chart domains \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) containing a point \(p \in \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\). Given a covector \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) expressed in the chart-induced bases of \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), we have: \begin{align*} \mathsf{X}_p &= \sum_{i=1}^{d} \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \mathtt{y}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p. \end{align*} Substituting the basis change derived previously into the left-hand expression for \(\mathsf{X}_p\), we get: \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{d} \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot \sum_{j=1}^{d} \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} \cdot (d\mathscr{Y}^j)_p = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \mathtt{y}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p. \end{align*} Since the basis covectors \((d\mathscr{Y}^j)_p\) are linearly independent, we can equate the components on both sides to obtain the transformation law for the covector components: \begin{align*} \mathtt{y}_j^p = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} \cdot \mathtt{x}_i^p = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{j}\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot \mathtt{x}_i^p. \end{align*} In Section 4.1.1, we defined that covariant objects transform exactly like this. Hence, covector components are covariant, in contrast to vector components, which transform contravariantly. Figure 4.3: Visual summary of the cotangent space \(T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) at a point \(p\) of the smooth manifold \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}\right)_d\). Top: the manifold carries the level sets of two scalar fields, \(f\) (solid, light blue) and \(g\) (dashed, dark red), together with a curve \(\gamma\) through \(p\) and the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) at that point. The velocity \(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\) is drawn as an arrow, while the covectors \((df)_p\) and \((dg)_p \in T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) are drawn as the lines they annihilate inside \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), each one tangent at \(p\) to the level set of the corresponding scalar field. A covector is a linear map acting on \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), not an element of it, so this is the picture that matches the object: drawing it as an arrow would be misleading. Bottom: the same objects seen through the charts \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) (left) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) (right), which also show the chart images of both chart domains, \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\), \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{V})\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U})\), \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V})\). The green arrows indicate the transition maps \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\) relating the two coordinate representations, and the hatched bands mark coordinates lying outside the image of the polar chart \(\mathscr{Y}\). Components, directions and spacings change from one chart to the other; what does not change is the value of the pairing, \((df)_p\left(v_{\gamma, p}\right) = \mathtt{x}_i^p \, \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) = \mathtt{y}_i^p \, \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda_0)\).

title: 4.2 Cotangent Space \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)
text:
4.2.2 Notation

As we did for the tangent space in Subsection 4.1.2, we now introduce a simplified notation for the cotangent space \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\), which will streamline expressions involving basis elements and components. While the underlying geometric structures remain unchanged, this notation mirrors the choices adopted earlier for the tangent space. Applying the Einstein summation convention (see Subsection 4.1.2) to express how a covector in the cotangent space \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) can be expanded in terms of the dual chart-induced bases associated with two charts \(\left( \mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y} \right)\), both containing the point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\): \begin{align*} \mathsf{X}_p = \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p = \mathtt{y}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p. \end{align*} This representation reflects the fact that the covector \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) is an intrinsic geometric object, while its representation in terms of components and basis covectors depends on the particular chart employed. Now suppose we have another covector \(\mathsf{Y}_p \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\). It can be expanded similarly in the basis induced by either chart: \begin{align*} \mathsf{Y}_p = \tilde{\mathtt{x}}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p = \tilde{\mathtt{y}}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p. \end{align*} For covectors, the only new shorthand concerns the basis covectors, \[ (dx^i)_p \coloneqq (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p, \qquad (dy^i)_p \coloneqq (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p, \] while the covectors \(\mathsf{X}_p\), \(\mathsf{Y}_p\) and their components \(\mathtt{x}_i^p\), \(\mathtt{y}_i^p\), \(\tilde{\mathtt{x}}_i^p\), \(\tilde{\mathtt{y}}_i^p\) keep the names already introduced. Hence, the expansions of the two covectors become: \[ \mathsf{X}_p = \underbrace{ \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (dx^i)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{X}} = \underbrace{ \mathtt{y}_i^p \cdot (dy^i)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{Y}}, \qquad \mathsf{Y}_p = \underbrace{ \tilde{\mathtt{x}}_i^p \cdot (dx^i)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{X}} = \underbrace{ \tilde{\mathtt{y}}_i^p \cdot (dy^i)_p }_{\text{in chart } \mathscr{Y}}, \] and the transformation law for the basis covectors, derived in the previous section, reads: \[ (dx^i)_p = \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_{p} \cdot (dy^j)_p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{j}\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot (dy^j)_p. \] Similarly, the transformation law for the components of a covector is: \[ \mathtt{y}_i^p = \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^j}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_{p} \cdot \mathtt{x}_j^p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^j_{i}\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot \mathtt{x}_j^p, \] The same relation holds for the components \(\tilde{\mathtt{x}}_i^p\) and \(\tilde{\mathtt{y}}_i^p\) of the covector \(\mathsf{Y}_p\), since the transformation depends exclusively on the basis change induced by the transition between charts. Employing this notation, the correspondence between the transformation behavior of covector basis elements (contravariant) and covector components (covariant) becomes immediately apparent depending on the index position (superscript or subscript). To conclude, the notational conventions introduced for both the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) and the cotangent space \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) are summarized in the notation cards at the bottom of the roadmap in Figure 1.3 (Section 1.1). (Subsections 4.1.2, and 4.2.2 respectively). It is crucial to remember that different symbols, while visually similar, represent fundamentally different mathematical objects despite their similar appearance. This table serves as a concise reference, provided the reader remains mindful that all components and bases are chart-dependent representations of intrinsically coordinate-free geometric objects. 6 Proof that differentials are linear maps: Consider any two velocity vectors \(v_{\gamma_1, p}, v_{\gamma_2, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\) and any scalar \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\). Using the definition of vector space operations in \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) (see Section 4.1), the linearity of \((df)_p\) amounts to verifying that it is linear over the sum and scalar multiplication; we check both conditions at the same time below: \begin{align*} (df)_p \left( \alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p} \right) &= \left( \alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p} \right)(f) \\ &= \alpha \cdot v_{\gamma_1, p}(f) + v_{\gamma_2, p}(f) \\ &= \alpha \cdot (df)_p (v_{\gamma_1, p}) + (df)_p (v_{\gamma_2, p}) \quad \square \end{align*} 7 Proof: Let \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) and let \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) be a chart around \(p\). By Subsection 4.2.1, \(\mathsf{X}_p = \sum_{i} \mathtt{x}_i^p (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\) for some \(\mathtt{x}_i^p \in \mathbb{R}\). The obvious candidate, \(\sum_{i} \mathtt{x}_i^p \mathscr{X}^i\), is only defined on \(\mathcal{U}\), so we extend it to \(\mathcal{M}\) with a bump function: a \(\psi \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) with \(\psi = 1\) on an open neighbourhood \(\mathcal{W} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\) of \(p\), and \(\psi = 0\) outside a compact set \(\mathcal{K} \subset \mathcal{U}\). Such a \(\psi\) is built by pulling back a bump function on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) through \(\mathscr{X}\) and extending it by zero; the extension is smooth because \(\mathcal{K}\), being compact in a Hausdorff space, is closed, so that \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{M} \setminus \mathcal{K}\) are two open sets covering \(\mathcal{M}\), on each of which the function is smooth. Define \(f \coloneqq \psi \cdot \sum_{i} \mathtt{x}_i^p \big( \mathscr{X}^i - \mathscr{X}^i(p) \big)\) on \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(f \coloneqq 0\) on \(\mathcal{M} \setminus \mathcal{U}\); by the same argument, \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\). For any curve \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma(\lambda_0) = p\), continuity gives \(\gamma(\lambda) \in \mathcal{W}\) for \(\lambda\) close to \(\lambda_0\), where \(f = \sum_{i} \mathtt{x}_i^p \big( \mathscr{X}^i - \mathscr{X}^i(p) \big)\). Since \((f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0)\) only depends on \(f \circ \gamma\) near \(\lambda_0\), \[ (df)_p(v_{\gamma, p}) = (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) = \sum_{i} \mathtt{x}_i^p \, (\mathscr{X}^i \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) = \sum_{i} \mathtt{x}_i^p \, (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p(v_{\gamma, p}) = \mathsf{X}_p(v_{\gamma, p}), \] hence \((df)_p = \mathsf{X}_p\). \(\square\) The argument requires \(\mathcal{M}\) to be Hausdorff, an assumption made explicit in the definition of a topological manifold in Chapter 3. 8 See Appendix B.6 for the formal proof that \(\left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\rbrace\) constitutes the induced dual basis for \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\), verifying both linear independence and spanning.

title: 4.3 Tensor Space \(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\)
text: The concept of tensors generalizes that of vectors and covectors, providing a unified framework to describe multilinear geometric objects. While the definition of tensors is often introduced globally as tensor fields, it is conceptually clearer to begin with their local version at a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), constructed purely from the tangent and cotangent spaces \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) and \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\). Tensors are often introduced as mysterious objects typically accompanied by the meaningless tautology “a tensor is an object that transforms like a tensor.” This unfortunate way of presenting tensors9 makes them appear more intimidating than they truly are. In reality, tensors are paper tigers. Given a manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A} \right)_d\), the \((r,s)\)-tensor space at \(p\) is the set of all multilinear maps of the form10 (Check Section 2.2 for the definition of multilinearity): \begin{align*} T \colon \underbrace{T_p^*\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times T_p^*\mathcal{M}}_{r \text{-times}} \times \underbrace{T_p\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times T_p\mathcal{M}}_{s \text{-times}} &\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \dots \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R} \\ \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(s)} \right) &\longmapsto {T} \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(s)} \right), \end{align*} Some particularly important cases of tensors are: \((1, 0)\)-tensors: elements of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) (vectors). \((0, 1)\)-tensors: elements of \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) (covectors). \((0, 0)\)-tensors: real numbers, i.e., elements of \(\mathbb{R}\). \((1, 1)\)-tensors: linear maps (matrices) from \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) to itself. \((0, 2)\)-tensors: bilinear forms, such as the metric (more on this in Chapter 7). Alternatively, using tensor products, the space \(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\) can be defined algebraically as the vector space (see §2.2): \[ T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} := \underbrace{T_p\mathcal{M} \otimes \dots \otimes T_p\mathcal{M}}_{r \text{-times}} \otimes \underbrace{T_p^*\mathcal{M} \otimes \dots \otimes T_p^*\mathcal{M}}_{s \text{-times}}. \] Let \(\left\{ \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p \right\}\) and \(\left\{ (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\}\) denote the bases of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) and \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) associated with a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around \(p\), and let \(\left\{ \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p \right\}\) and \(\left\{ (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p \right\}\) denote the corresponding bases associated with a different chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\). The components of a tensor \(T \in T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\) w.r.t. the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) are obtained by feeding it the basis elements of that chart, \[ \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} \coloneqq T\left( (d\mathscr{X}^{i_1})_p, \dots, (d\mathscr{X}^{i_r})_p, \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_1}} \right)_p, \dots, \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_s}} \right)_p \right) \in \mathbb{R}, \] in terms of which the tensor is expanded as \[ T = \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}} \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}} \right)_p \otimes \dots \otimes \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_r}} \right)_p \otimes (d\mathscr{X}^{j_1})_p \otimes \dots \otimes (d\mathscr{X}^{j_s})_p. \] Denoting by \(\left( T_\mathcal{V} \right)^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s}\) the components w.r.t. the chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), the transformation law for the components reads: \[ \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} = \sum_{\substack{k_1,\dots,k_r \\ l_1,\dots,l_s}} \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{k_1}} \right)_p \cdots \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_r}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{k_r}} \right)_p \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{l_1}}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_1}} \right)_p \cdots \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{l_s}}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_s}} \right)_p \cdot \left( T_\mathcal{V} \right)^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s}. \] As we saw in Subsections 4.1.1 and 4.2.1, each upper index (one per covector slot) transforms contravariantly, like the components of a vector, with a factor \(\left( \partial \mathscr{X}^{i} / \partial \mathscr{Y}^{k} \right)_p\), and each lower index (one per vector slot) transforms covariantly, like the components of a covector, with a factor \(\left( \partial \mathscr{Y}^{l} / \partial \mathscr{X}^{j} \right)_p\). By construction, the dimension of \(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\) is \(\dim T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} = d^{r+s}\). 9 Common in many physics texts, perhaps stemming from the authors’ own apprehension toward differential geometry— a subject which, as the reader may have hopefully realized by this point, is in fact both harmless and remarkably beautiful. 10 The indices enclosed in parentheses, such as \(\mathsf{X}^{(i)}\) or \(\mathcal{X}_{(j)}\), refer strictly to the position of the argument within the tensor map \(T\). They are not to be confused with coordinate indices or component labels. This is a purely positional convention used for clarity when expressing properties like multilinearity.

title: 5 Fields
text: Motivation: From a vector at a point to a vector at every point The tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) lives at a single point, whereas quantities such as a velocity field or the metric vary from point to point. Assigning a vector \(\mathcal{X}_p \in T_p\mathcal{M}\) to every \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), smoothly, requires a single smooth manifold containing all tangent spaces. Their plain union is not one, since it identifies their zero vectors, all equal to the map \(f \mapsto 0\), and carries no charts. Goal. Make “a smooth assignment of a tensor to every point” precise. Glue the tangent spaces into the tangent bundle \(T\mathcal{M}\), a \(2d\)-dimensional smooth manifold that keeps track of the base point of each vector through a projection \(\pi : T\mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}\). Define a vector field as a smooth section of \(T\mathcal{M}\), covector fields likewise through the cotangent bundle, and tensor fields as \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-multilinear maps. Since the numbers that rescale fields become scalar fields, fields form \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-modules rather than vector spaces, and bases of fields exist in general only locally. The rest of the notes is formulated with fields. The connection differentiates them, the metric is a tensor field, and the Einstein equations relate tensor fields.

title: 5.1 Vector Fields
text: Given two (smooth) manifolds \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M}\right)\), and \(\left(\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}\right)\), the triple \begin{align*} \underbrace{(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M})}_{\text{Total space}} \xlongrightarrow[]{\pi} \underbrace{(\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N})}_{\text{Base space}} \end{align*} is a (smooth) bundle if the total space \(\mathcal{M}\) and the base space \(\mathcal{N}\) are (smooth) manifolds, and the projection map \(\pi: \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}\) is a (smooth) surjective map. A fibre over \(p \in \mathcal{N}\) is the set \(\text{preim}_\pi(\{p\}) \subseteq \mathcal{M}\). A section is a map \(\sigma : \mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{M}\) such that \((\pi \circ \sigma) = \mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{N}}\) (identity map). The (smooth) tangent bundle upon the (smooth) manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})\) is: \begin{align*} (T\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{T\mathcal{M}}) \xrightarrow[]{\pi} (\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}) \end{align*} Here we are considering the following definitions: \(T\mathcal{M}\) is the disjoint union of tangent spaces \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), i.e., \begin{align*} T\mathcal{M} := \dot{\bigcup_{p \in \mathcal{M}}} T_p \mathcal{M}. \end{align*} The projection map, \(\pi\), is given by \begin{align*} \pi : T\mathcal{M} &\to \mathcal{M} \\ v_{\gamma, p} &\mapsto \pi (v_{\gamma, p}) := p, \end{align*} where \( p \) is the unique point such that \( v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p \mathcal{M} \). The bundle chart maps. For every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}\), let \(T\mathcal{U} \coloneqq \operatorname{preim}_\pi(\mathcal{U})\) be the set of all tangent vectors based at points of \(\mathcal{U}\), and define \begin{align*} \xi_{\mathscr{X}} : T\mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^{d} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2d} \\ v_{\gamma, p} &\longmapsto \xi_{\mathscr{X}} (v_{\gamma, p}), \end{align*} where \begin{align*} \xi_{\mathscr{X}} (v_{\gamma, p}) := \big( \underbrace{..., (\mathscr{X}^i \circ \pi)(v_{\gamma, p}), ...}_{\substack{i\in [1, d] \text{ terms.}\\ \text{Chart coordinates w.r.t. } (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \\ \text{for the base point } p \text{ of } v_{\gamma, p}}} ; \underbrace{..., (d\mathscr{X}^j)_{p}(v_{\gamma, p}), ... }_{\substack{j\in [1, d] \text{ terms.}\\ \text{Components of } v_{\gamma, p} \\ \text{w.r.t. the chart-induced} \\ \text{basis of } T_p \mathcal{M}}} \big) = \big( ..., \mathscr{X}^i(p), ...\, ; ..., \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda_0), ... \big). \end{align*} Each \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) is a bijection onto the open set \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\): a tangent vector is uniquely determined by its base point together with its components in the chart-induced basis of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), and every such choice of data is realized by some tangent vector. The inverse map is \begin{align*} \xi_{\mathscr{X}}^{-1} : \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^{d} &\longrightarrow T\mathcal{U} \\ (\underbrace{..., \alpha^i, ...}_{i\in [1, d]} ; \underbrace{..., \beta^j, ...}_{j\in [1, d]}) &\longmapsto \sum_{k=1}^{d} \beta^k \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k} \right)_{p=\mathscr{X}^{-1}\left(\dots, \alpha^i, \dots \right)}. \end{align*} Given a second chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}\), the overlap of the two bundle charts is \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}(T\mathcal{U} \cap T\mathcal{V}) = \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\), an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{2d}\). Writing \(\alpha = (\alpha^1, \dots, \alpha^d)\) and \(p = \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha)\), and using \((d\mathscr{Y}^j)_p\big( (\partial / \partial \mathscr{X}^k)_p \big) = \partial_k \left[ \mathscr{Y}^j \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] (\alpha)\), the transition map between bundle charts reads \begin{align*} (\xi_{\mathscr{Y}} \circ \xi_{\mathscr{X}}^{-1})(\alpha \,;\, \beta) &= \Big( \dots, \mathscr{Y}^j(p), \dots \,;\, \dots, (d\mathscr{Y}^j)_p \Big( \sum_{k=1}^{d} \beta^k \Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k}\Big)_p \Big), \dots \Big) \\ &= \Big( \dots, \big(\mathscr{Y}^j \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\big)(\alpha), \dots \,;\, \dots, \sum_{k=1}^{d} \partial_k \big[\mathscr{Y}^j \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\big](\alpha) \, \beta^k, \dots \Big) \\ &= \Big( \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}(\alpha) \,;\, \dots, \sum_{k=1}^{d} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^j_{k}(\alpha) \, \beta^k, \dots \Big). \end{align*} Base coordinates change with the chart transition map, and fibre coordinates with its Jacobian, exactly as the vector components of Subsection 4.1.1. Since \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\) is \(C^\infty\), so are the entries of its Jacobian, and the second block is linear in \(\beta\): the transition map is \(C^\infty\), and so is its inverse \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}} \circ \xi_{\mathscr{Y}}^{-1}\), by the same argument with the roles of the charts exchanged. The topology \(\mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\) on \(T\mathcal{M}\) is the one that turns every bundle chart map into a homeomorphism1: a set of tangent vectors is declared open if and only if it looks open in every bundle chart, \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}} \coloneqq \Big\{ W \subseteq T\mathcal{M} \;\Big|\; \xi_{\mathscr{X}}(W \cap T\mathcal{U}) \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}} \;\; \forall \, (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A} \Big\}. \end{align*} With this topology every \(T\mathcal{U}\) is open, every \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) is a homeomorphism onto \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\pi\) is continuous, since \(\operatorname{preim}_\pi(\mathcal{U}') \in \mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\) for every \(\mathcal{U}' \in \mathcal{O}\). Note that \(\mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\) is strictly finer than the collection \(\{ \operatorname{preim}_\pi(\mathcal{U}) \mid \mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{O} \}\), the initial topology w.r.t. \(\pi\) alone. The latter only contains unions of entire fibres. It therefore cannot separate two different vectors based at the same point, and w.r.t. it the maps \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) would not even be continuous: e.g. \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}^{-1}\big( \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times (0,1)^d \big)\), the set of vectors over \(\mathcal{U}\) whose components all lie in \((0,1)\), is not a union of fibres. The information about directions within each fibre is precisely what the bundle charts add. The smooth atlas \begin{align*} \mathcal{A}_{T\mathcal{M}} \coloneqq \{ (T\mathcal{U}, \xi_{\mathscr{X}}) \mid (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A} \}. \end{align*} Its chart domains cover \(T\mathcal{M}\) because the chart domains of \(\mathcal{A}\) cover \(\mathcal{M}\). Its chart maps are homeomorphisms onto open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^{2d}\), and they are pairwise \(C^\infty\)-compatible by the transition computation above. Hence \((T\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{T\mathcal{M}})_{2d}\) is a \(2d\)-dimensional smooth manifold. A smooth vector field is a smooth section on the tangent bundle \begin{align*} \mathcal{X} : \mathcal{M} &\to T\mathcal{M} \\ p &\mapsto \mathcal{X}(p) := v_{\gamma, p}, \end{align*} with \((\pi \circ \mathcal{X}) = \mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{M}}\). In the compact notation of Subsection 4.1.2, \(\mathcal{X}(p) = \mathcal{X}_p\). We will employ the following notation to define the action of a vector field \(\mathcal{X}\) upon a function \(f \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{X} : C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) &\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) \\ f &\longmapsto \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil \colon \begin{aligned}[t] \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ p &\longmapsto \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) \coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}(f). \end{aligned} \end{align*} That is, \(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil\) is itself a scalar field, returning at each point the directional derivative of \(f\) along the vector that \(\mathcal{X}\) places there. We can therefore think of a vector field in three equivalent ways, depending on which argument we supply first: Point first: as a section, eating points \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) and returning tangent vectors \(\mathcal{X}(p) = v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\). Function first: as an operator, eating scalar fields \(f \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\) and returning, \(\mathbb{R}\)-linearly, new scalar fields \(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\). Both: once \(f\) is fixed, \(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil\) eats points \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) and returns the real numbers \(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) \in \mathbb{R}\). All three readings meet in the same number, \(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) = \mathcal{X}(p)(f) = v_{\gamma, p}(f)\). Recall that in Section 4.1 we equipped the set of scalar fields \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\) with a point-wise addition and s-multiplication, yielding the triplet \((C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}), \oplus, \odot)\), where the operations are defined as: \begin{align*} (f \oplus g)(p) \coloneqq f(p) + g(p), \qquad (\alpha \odot f)(p) \coloneqq \alpha \cdot f(p), \qquad \forall \, f, g \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}), \; \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \; p \in \mathcal{M}. \end{align*} Together with the field \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\), these operations satisfy all axioms of an \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space. However, now we are interested in defining directly the triplet \((C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}), \oplus_{C^{\infty}}, \odot_{C^{\infty}})\), with the operations defined as: \begin{align*} (f \oplus_{C^{\infty}} g)(p) \coloneqq f(p) + g(p), \qquad (f \odot_{C^{\infty}} g)(p) \coloneqq f(p) \cdot g(p), \qquad \forall \, f, g \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}), \; p \in \mathcal{M}. \end{align*} Note that, in this triplet, both operations act within \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\): the role of the scalars is now played by scalar fields themselves, rather than by elements of the field \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\). Its axioms are inherited point-wise from \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\), with the zero field \(0 \colon p \mapsto 0\) as neutral element of \(\oplus_{C^{\infty}}\) and the unit field \(1 \colon p \mapsto 1\) as neutral element of \(\odot_{C^{\infty}}\), making it a commutative, unitary ring. It is, however, not a field: the inverse \(f^{-1}\) with \(f \odot_{C^{\infty}} f^{-1} = 1\) exists only if \(f(p) \neq 0\) for every \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), so any scalar field that vanishes at some point without being the zero field has none. The real numbers have not disappeared, though: identifying each \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) with the constant field \(p \mapsto \alpha\), the old s-multiplication is recovered as a special case of the new product, \(\alpha \odot f = \alpha \odot_{C^{\infty}} f\). Both structures therefore coexist compatibly: \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\) is simultaneously an \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space and a commutative, unitary ring, a structure known as a commutative, unitary \(\mathbb{R}\)-algebra. Correspondingly, the modules below are also \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector spaces, a fact that will matter for connections (Chapter 6), which are \(\mathbb{R}\)-linear, but not \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\)-linear, in their second argument. The \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\)-module \(\Gamma T \mathcal{M}\) is the triplet \((\Gamma T \mathcal{M}, \oplus_\Gamma, \odot_\Gamma)\), built over the commutative, unitary ring \((C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}), \oplus_{C^{\infty}}, \odot_{C^{\infty}})\) of the previous item. Since its scalars now come from a ring rather than from a field, the result is a module rather than a vector space. Here \(\Gamma T \mathcal{M} \coloneqq \{\mathcal{X} : \mathcal{M} \to T\mathcal{M} \mid \text{smooth vector field}\}\), and, writing \(\mathcal{X}_1(p) = v_{\gamma, p}\), \(\mathcal{X}_2(p) = v_{\sigma, p}\) and \(\mathcal{X}(p) = v_{\gamma, p}\), the operations \(\oplus_\Gamma\) (addition) and \(\odot_\Gamma\) (s-multiplication) are: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \oplus_\Gamma : \Gamma T \mathcal{M} \times \Gamma T \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \Gamma T \mathcal{M} \\ (\mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2) &\longmapsto \mathcal{X}_1 \oplus_\Gamma \mathcal{X}_2 \end{aligned} \\[12pt] \begin{aligned} \text{with } (\mathcal{X}_1 \oplus_\Gamma \mathcal{X}_2)\left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) &\coloneqq \left(\mathcal{X}_1\left\lfloor f \right\rceil \oplus_{C^{\infty}} \mathcal{X}_2\left\lfloor f \right\rceil\right)(p) \\ &= v_{\gamma, p}(f) + v_{\sigma, p}(f), \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \odot_\Gamma : C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) \times \Gamma T \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \\ (f, \mathcal{X}) &\longmapsto f \odot_\Gamma \mathcal{X} \end{aligned} \\[12pt] \begin{aligned} \text{with } (f \odot_\Gamma \mathcal{X})\left\lfloor g \right\rceil(p) &\coloneqq \left( f \odot_{C^{\infty}} \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor g \right\rceil\right)(p) \\ &= f(p) \cdot v_{\gamma, p}(g), \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] for all \(f, g \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\) and \(p \in \mathcal{M}\). Important remark regarding modules: In Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice (ZFC) – the set theory we are using – every vector space has a basis. This result does not extend to modules in general. In particular, globally there is no guarantee that we can find vector fields \(\left\lbrace \mathcal{X}_1, ..., \mathcal{X}_d \right\rbrace \subset \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\) such that every \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T \mathcal{M}\) decomposes uniquely as \(\mathcal{X} = \sum_i f_i \odot_\Gamma \mathcal{X}_i\) with \(f_i \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), i.e. \(\Gamma T\mathcal{M}\) need not be a free module. Manifolds for which it is are called parallelizable. Nevertheless, such a decomposition always exists locally, over a chart domain \(\mathcal{U}\) (see below). A famous obstruction is the hairy ball theorem: every smooth vector field on the sphere \(S^2\) (more generally, on any even-dimensional sphere) vanishes at least at one point; colloquially, “you can’t comb a hairy ball flat without creating a cowlick”. One can show that the elements of a global basis would have to be linearly independent, and in particular nonzero, at every point, so \(S^2\) admits no global basis: \(\Gamma TS^2\) is not free. The hairy ball theorem is thus one instance of the general phenomenon, not its definition: the circle \(S^1\), the torus \(T^2\) and the sphere \(S^3\), for example, are parallelizable, while \(S^2\) is not. This leaves us with a practical rule: we only expand a vector field in components w.r.t. a basis over a domain where such a basis exists, typically a chart domain. Nothing essential is lost, since the expansion was never needed in the first place: \(\mathcal{X}\) is defined intrinsically, and its components are merely one representation of it. For a single tangent vector one could still argue that it is enough to go into a chart, since every \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) lies in some chart domain; for vector fields this is no longer true, as a chart provides a basis only over its own domain, and in general no single basis covers all of \(\mathcal{M}\). Locally, though, every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) does provide such a basis. Dropping the point \(p\) from the chart-induced basis vectors of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), we define the chart-induced basis vector fields \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} : \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow T\mathcal{U} \\ p &\longmapsto \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p, \end{align*} which are smooth, and in terms of which every vector field decomposes over \(\mathcal{U}\) as \begin{align*} \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_{\mathcal{U}} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} x^i \odot_\Gamma \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}, \qquad \text{with component functions} \quad x^i \coloneqq \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_{\mathcal{U}} \left\lfloor \mathscr{X}^i \right\rceil \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{U}). \end{align*} More generally, a frame over an open set \(\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{M}\) is a set of \(d\) smooth vector fields \(\{ e_1, \dots, e_d \} \subset \Gamma T\mathcal{U}\) whose values \(\{ e_1(p), \dots, e_d(p) \}\) form a basis of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) at every \(p \in \mathcal{U}\). Equivalently, it is a basis of the \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{U})\)-module \(\Gamma T\mathcal{U}\): every vector field decomposes uniquely as \(\left. \mathcal{X} \right|_{\mathcal{U}} = \sum_{a=1}^{d} w^a \odot_\Gamma e_a\), with component functions \(w^a \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{U})\). A frame is thus the field-level counterpart of a basis: a basis belongs to a single tangent space, whereas a frame smoothly assigns one to every point of \(\mathcal{U}\). The chart-induced basis vector fields form the chart-induced frame \(\{ \partial / \partial \mathscr{X}^i \}\) over \(\mathcal{U}\), but not every frame is chart-induced (an example is given in Appendix C.5). In this language, the remark above on modules states that a frame over the whole of \(\mathcal{M}\) exists if and only if \(\mathcal{M}\) is parallelizable. This does not contradict the previous remark: the frame \(\{ \partial / \partial \mathscr{X}^i \}\) lives only on \(\mathcal{U}\). Note also that the existence of a global frame and the existence of a global chart are different questions. The torus \(T^2\) admits a global frame, given by the two angular basis fields, which are well defined everywhere even though the angles themselves are not. Yet no single chart covers \(T^2\): being compact, it cannot be homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The sphere \(S^2\), in contrast, needs at least two charts and admits no global frame at all. Figure 5.1: Tangent bundle of a one-dimensional manifold (\(d = 1\)): a ring \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_d\) embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), which sits inside the total space as its zero section. Left: the total space \(\left( T\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{T\mathcal{M}} \right)_{2d}\), drawn as a cylinder by displaying every fibre vertically – a purely visual choice, faithful here because \(TS^1 \cong S^1 \times \mathbb{R}\). The green line is the fibre \(T_p\mathcal{M} = \operatorname{preim}_\pi(\{p\})\), which the projection \(\pi\) collapses onto \(p\). The shaded strip is \(T\mathcal{U} = \operatorname{preim}_\pi(\mathcal{U})\) over a chart domain \(\mathcal{U}\). The magenta curve is a vector field \(\mathcal{X}\), i.e. a section, which meets every fibre exactly once; over \(p\) it picks the vector \(v_{\gamma, p} = \mathcal{X}_p\) (blue arrow, tip marked with a star). Right: the image \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}(T\mathcal{U}) = \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2d}\) of the bundle chart. Its base block is the chart map \(\mathscr{X}\), which sends \(p\) to \(\mathscr{X}(p)\) on the horizontal axis \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\mathcal{U}\) to the interval marked in red. Its fibre block is \((d\mathscr{X}^1)_p\), which sends \(v_{\gamma, p}\) to its component \(\dot{\gamma}^1_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\) (vertical blue arrow). The field itself becomes the graph of its component function \(X^1 \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\). Since \(\mathscr{X}\) is not linear, both blocks distort the picture, and the right panel is not a mere copy of the strip \(T\mathcal{U}\). 1 See Appendix B.7 for the proof that this is indeed a topology, and that it has the properties listed here.

title: 5.2 Covector Fields
text: The (smooth) cotangent bundle upon the (smooth) manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})\) is: \begin{align*} (T^*\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{T^*\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{T^*\mathcal{M}}) \xrightarrow[]{\pi^*} (\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}) \end{align*} Here we are considering the following definitions: \(T^*\mathcal{M}\) is the disjoint union of cotangent spaces \(T^*_p\mathcal{M}\), i.e., \begin{align*} T^*\mathcal{M} := \dot{\bigcup_{p \in \mathcal{M}}} T^*_p \mathcal{M}. \end{align*} The projection map, \(\pi^*\), is given by \begin{align*} \pi^* : T^*\mathcal{M} &\to \mathcal{M} \\ \mathsf{X}_p &\mapsto \pi^* (\mathsf{X}_p) := p, \end{align*} where \( p \) is the unique point such that \( \mathsf{X}_p \in T^*_p \mathcal{M} \). The bundle chart maps. For every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}\), let \(T^*\mathcal{U} \coloneqq \operatorname{preim}_{\pi^*}(\mathcal{U})\) and define \begin{align*} \xi^*_{\mathscr{X}} : T^*\mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^{d} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2d} \\ \mathsf{X}_p &\longmapsto \xi^*_{\mathscr{X}} (\mathsf{X}_p), \end{align*} where \begin{align*} \xi^*_{\mathscr{X}} (\mathsf{X}_p) := \big( \underbrace{..., (\mathscr{X}^i \circ \pi^*)(\mathsf{X}_p), ...}_{\substack{i\in [1, d] \text{ terms.}\\ \text{Chart coordinates w.r.t. } (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \\ \text{for the base point } p \text{ of } \mathsf{X}_p}} ; \underbrace{..., \mathsf{X}_p\left(\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_{p}\right), ... }_{\substack{j\in [1, d] \text{ terms.}\\ \text{Components of } \mathsf{X}_p \text{ w.r.t. the}\\ \text{dual chart-induced basis}}} \big) = \big( ..., \mathscr{X}^i(p), ...\, ; ..., \mathtt{x}^p_j, ... \big), \end{align*} a bijection onto the open set \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\), with inverse \begin{align*} {\xi^*_{\mathscr{X}}}^{-1} : \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^{d} &\longrightarrow T^*\mathcal{U} \\ (\underbrace{..., \alpha^i, ...}_{i\in [1, d]} ; \underbrace{..., \beta_j, ...}_{j\in [1, d]}) &\longmapsto \sum_{k=1}^{d} \beta_k \, (d\mathscr{X}^{k})_{p=\mathscr{X}^{-1}\left(\dots, \alpha^i, \dots \right)}. \end{align*} Given a second chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}\) and \(p = \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha)\), using \((d\mathscr{X}^k)_p\big( (\partial / \partial \mathscr{Y}^j)_p \big) = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^k_{j}\big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big)\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(p) = \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}(\alpha)\), \begin{align*} (\xi^*_{\mathscr{Y}} \circ {\xi^*_{\mathscr{X}}}^{-1})(\alpha \,;\, \beta) = \Big( \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}(\alpha) \,;\, \dots, \sum_{k=1}^{d} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^k_{j}\big( \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}(\alpha) \big) \, \beta_k, \dots \Big), \end{align*} which is \(C^\infty\), being built from the smooth maps \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\) and the entries of \(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\), and linear in \(\beta\). Fibre coordinates now change with the inverse Jacobian, as the covector components of Subsection 4.2.1. The topology \(\mathcal{O}_{T^*\mathcal{M}}\) is defined exactly as for the tangent bundle, as the one turning every bundle chart map into a homeomorphism, \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}_{T^*\mathcal{M}} \coloneqq \Big\{ W \subseteq T^*\mathcal{M} \;\Big|\; \xi^*_{\mathscr{X}}(W \cap T^*\mathcal{U}) \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}} \;\; \forall \, (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A} \Big\}, \end{align*} and the proof of Appendix B.7 applies verbatim, with \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) replaced by \(\xi^*_{\mathscr{X}}\). The smooth atlas \(\mathcal{A}_{T^*\mathcal{M}} \coloneqq \{ (T^*\mathcal{U}, \xi^*_{\mathscr{X}}) \mid (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A} \}\) is \(C^\infty\)-compatible by the transition computation above, so that \((T^*\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{T^*\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{T^*\mathcal{M}})_{2d}\) is a \(2d\)-dimensional smooth manifold. A smooth covector field is a smooth section of the cotangent bundle, \begin{align*} \mathsf{X} : \mathcal{M} &\to T^*\mathcal{M} \\ p &\mapsto \mathsf{X}(p) := \mathsf{X}_p, \end{align*} with \((\pi^* \circ \mathsf{X}) = \mathbb{I}_{\mathcal{M}}\), i.e. a smooth assignment of a covector \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) to every point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\). As for covectors at a single point, sans-serif capitals \(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}, \dots\) denote generic covector fields, so that \(\mathsf{X}_p = \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (dx^i)_p = \mathtt{y}_i^p \cdot (dy^i)_p\) at every point \(p\) in the corresponding chart domains (Subsection 4.2.2). The most important examples are the differentials of scalar fields \(f \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\), \begin{align*} df : \mathcal{M} &\to T^*\mathcal{M} \\ p &\mapsto df(p) := (df)_p, \end{align*} and covector fields of this form, \(\mathsf{X} = df\), are called exact. At a single point there is no difference between the two notions: every covector is the differential of some scalar field, \(\mathsf{X}_p = (df)_p\) (Section 4.2). However, the scalar field \(f\) achieving this depends in general on the point \(p\), and a covector field need not be the differential of a single, globally defined scalar field2. We will employ the following notation to define the action of a covector field \(\mathsf{X}\) upon a vector field \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\), writing \(\mathcal{X}(p) = v_{\gamma, p}\): \begin{align*} \mathsf{X} : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) \\ \mathcal{X} &\longmapsto \mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor \colon \begin{aligned}[t] \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ p &\longmapsto \mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor(p) \coloneqq \mathsf{X}_p(v_{\gamma, p}). \end{aligned} \end{align*} That is, \(\mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor\) is itself a scalar field, returning at each point the value of the covector \(\mathsf{X}_p\) on the vector that \(\mathcal{X}\) places there. We can therefore think of a covector field in three equivalent ways, depending on which argument we supply first: Point first: as a section, eating points \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) and returning covectors \(\mathsf{X}(p) = \mathsf{X}_p \in T^*_p\mathcal{M}\). Vector field first: as an operator, eating vector fields \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\) and returning, \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\)-linearly, new scalar fields \(\mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\). Both: once \(\mathcal{X}\) is fixed, \(\mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor\) eats points \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) and returns the real numbers \(\mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor(p) \in \mathbb{R}\). All three readings meet in the same number, \(\mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor(p) = \mathsf{X}(p)\big(\mathcal{X}(p)\big) = \mathsf{X}_p(v_{\gamma, p})\). For an exact covector field this number equals, by definition of the differential, \(v_{\gamma, p}(f)\); hence \(df\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil\). The \(C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\)-module \(\Gamma T^* \mathcal{M}\) is the triplet \((\Gamma T^* \mathcal{M}, \oplus^*_\Gamma, \odot^*_\Gamma)\), built over the same commutative, unitary ring \((C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}), \oplus_{C^{\infty}}, \odot_{C^{\infty}})\), so that, as for \(\Gamma T\mathcal{M}\), the result is a module rather than a vector space. Here \(\Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} \coloneqq \{\mathsf{X} : \mathcal{M} \to T^*\mathcal{M} \mid \text{smooth covector field}\}\), and, writing \(\mathcal{X}(p) = v_{\gamma, p}\), the operations \(\oplus^*_\Gamma\) (addition) and \(\odot^*_\Gamma\) (s-multiplication) are: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \oplus^*_\Gamma : \Gamma T^* \mathcal{M} \times \Gamma T^* \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \Gamma T^* \mathcal{M} \\ (\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}) &\longmapsto \mathsf{X} \oplus^*_\Gamma \mathsf{Y} \end{aligned} \\[12pt] \begin{aligned} \text{with } (\mathsf{X} \oplus^*_\Gamma \mathsf{Y})\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor(p) &\coloneqq \left(\mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X}\right\rfloor \oplus_{C^{\infty}} \mathsf{Y}\left\lceil \mathcal{X}\right\rfloor\right)(p) \\ &= \mathsf{X}_p(v_{\gamma,p}) + \mathsf{Y}_p(v_{\gamma,p}), \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \odot^*_\Gamma : C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M}) \times \Gamma T^* \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \Gamma T^* \mathcal{M} \\ (h, \mathsf{X}) &\longmapsto h \odot^*_\Gamma \mathsf{X} \end{aligned} \\[12pt] \begin{aligned} \text{with } (h \odot^*_\Gamma \mathsf{X})\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor(p) &\coloneqq \left(h \odot_{C^{\infty}} \mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor\right)(p) \\ &= h(p) \cdot \mathsf{X}_p(v_{\gamma,p}), \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] for all \(h \in C^{\infty}(\mathcal{M})\), \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\) and \(p \in \mathcal{M}\). Figure 5.2: Tangent and cotangent bundles of the ring of Figure 5.1, drawn in the same ambient space. The tangent fibres are displayed vertically, as before (cylinder, green fibres, \(\pi\)). The cotangent fibres are displayed radially, transverse both to the ring and to the tangent fibres. Because the two directions are transverse, a pair \(\big( v_{\gamma, p}, \mathsf{X}_p \big) \in T_p\mathcal{M} \times T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) can be drawn as a single point. The orange sheets are the planes \(T_p\mathcal{M} \times T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) over six base points, attached along the corresponding tangent fibres. The blue curve is a vector field \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\), with its values \(\mathcal{X}(p) = v_{\gamma, p}\) drawn over those six points. The orange arrows are the values \(\mathsf{X}(p) = \mathsf{X}_p\) of a covector field \(\mathsf{X} \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\), each drawn from the tip of the vector \(v_{\gamma, p}\) it acts on. The orange curve is the pair of sections \(p \mapsto \big( \mathcal{X}(p), \mathsf{X}(p) \big)\). Dropping its radial displacement gives back \(\mathcal{X}\). Dropping its vertical displacement gives \(\mathsf{X}\) alone, as a section of the total space \(\left( T^*\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{T^*\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{T^*\mathcal{M}} \right)_{2d}\); in this drawing that total space is the horizontal annulus around the ring, not shown. 2 See Appendix B.8 for a detailed discussion of which covector fields are differentials.

title: 5.3 Tensor Fields and notation
text: A (smooth) \( (r,s) \)-tensor field is a \( C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \)-multilinear map \[ T : \underbrace{\Gamma T^* \mathcal{M} \times \dots \times \Gamma T^* \mathcal{M}}_{r\text{-terms}} \times \underbrace{\Gamma T\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times \Gamma T\mathcal{M}}_{s\text{-terms}} \overset{\scriptstyle \begin{array}{c} \sim \\[-10pt] ... \\[-6pt] \sim \end{array}}{\longrightarrow} C^\infty(\mathcal{M}). \] In particular, a \((0,1)\)-tensor field is a covector field, i.e. an element of \(\Gamma T^* \mathcal{M}\), and a \((1,0)\)-tensor field is a vector field, i.e. an element of \(\Gamma T \mathcal{M}\) (since the dual of \(\Gamma T^* \mathcal{M}\) is \(\Gamma T \mathcal{M}\)). So far, given a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around \(p\), we have expanded vectors and covectors at that point in the chart-induced bases of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) and \(T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) which, in the compact notation of Subsections 4.1.2 and 4.2.2, read \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} v_{\gamma, p} = x^i_p \, (\partial x_i)_p \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad ; \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} (df)_p = \mathtt{x}_i^p \, (dx^i)_p, \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] with \(x^i_p = \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)\), \((\partial x_i)_p = \left( \partial / \partial \mathscr{X}^i \right)_p\), \(\mathtt{x}_i^p = (df)_p\big((\partial x_i)_p\big)\) and \((dx^i)_p = (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\), and where the Einstein summation convention is implied. Both the components and the basis elements refer to the single point \(p\). At the level of fields, each of these expressions splits into two parts, both of which are promoted from the single point \(p\) to the whole chart domain \(\mathcal{U}\): Basis fields. Dropping the point \(p\), as done in Section 5.1, the basis elements become smooth sections over \(\mathcal{U}\), the chart-induced basis vector and covector fields: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} : \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow T\mathcal{U} \\ p &\longmapsto \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad ; \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} d\mathscr{X}^i : \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow T^*\mathcal{U} \\ p &\longmapsto (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p. \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] On the overlap \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\) with a second chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), they transform as \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \, \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad ; \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} d\mathscr{X}^i = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, d\mathscr{Y}^j, \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] where the entries of the Jacobian are now functions rather than numbers: \begin{align*} \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} : \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ p &\longmapsto \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_p = \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big), \end{align*} i.e. \(\left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{j} \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V})\), and correspondingly for \(\partial \mathscr{Y}^j / \partial \mathscr{X}^i = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^j_{i}\). Component functions. The components, real numbers at \(p\), become smooth functions on \(\mathcal{U}\), obtained by letting each field act on the basis of the other kind: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} x^i \coloneqq \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} \left\lfloor \mathscr{X}^i \right\rceil \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}) \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad ; \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \mathtt{x}_i \coloneqq \left. df \right|_\mathcal{U} \left\lceil \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right\rfloor \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}), \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] so that, at each point \(p\) with \(\mathcal{X}(p) = v_{\gamma, p}\), they return the components above, \(x^i(p) = x^i_p\) and \(\mathtt{x}_i(p) = \mathtt{x}_i^p\).
