Denoting by \(y^j\) and \(\mathtt{y}_j\) the component functions w.r.t. \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), they transform on \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\) as \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} x^i = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, y^j \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad ; \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \mathtt{x}_i = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \, \mathtt{y}_j. \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] Putting both parts together, vector and covector fields are expanded over \(\mathcal{U}\) as \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \underbrace{x^i}_{\in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})} \odot_\Gamma \underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}}_{\in \Gamma T\mathcal{U}} \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad ; \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \left. df \right|_\mathcal{U} = \underbrace{\mathtt{x}_i}_{\in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})} \odot^*_\Gamma \underbrace{d\mathscr{X}^i}_{\in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{U}}, \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] and, extending the compact notation to fields by dropping the point \(p\) from the basis elements and the s-multiplication symbols, \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad ; \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \left. df \right|_\mathcal{U} = \mathtt{x}_i \, dx^i. \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] In the same way, an \((r,s)\)-tensor field is expanded over \(\mathcal{U}\) as \begin{align*} \left. T \right|_\mathcal{U} &= T^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s} \; \partial x_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \partial x_{i_r} \otimes dx^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{j_s}, \\ T^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s} &\coloneqq T\big( dx^{i_1}, \dots, dx^{i_r}, \partial x_{j_1}, \dots, \partial x_{j_s} \big) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}), \end{align*} whose component functions transform with one Jacobian factor per index, as those of \(x^i\) (upper) and \(\mathtt{x}_i\) (lower) above. With this notation the letter “\(x\)” appears in several fonts, and its meaning depends on the context: \(\mathscr{X}^i\) are the coordinate functions of the chart, \(x^i_p\) and \(\mathtt{x}_i^p\) are real numbers at a point \(p\), \(x^i\) and \(\mathtt{x}_i\) are functions on \(\mathcal{U}\), and \((\partial x_i)_p\), \((dx^i)_p\) are basis elements at the point \(p\), while \(\partial x_i\), \(dx^i\) are the corresponding basis fields over \(\mathcal{U}\). Care must be taken to avoid misinterpretation.

title: 6 Covariant Derivative
text:
Motivation: Differentiating vector fields A vector field \(\mathcal{X}\) already differentiates scalar fields, \(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f ightceil\) being the directional derivative of \(f\) (Section 5.1). Differentiating a vector field \(\mathcal{Y}\) along \(\mathcal{X}_p\) is harder. A difference quotient along a curve through \(p\) would subtract \(\mathcal{Y}_{\gamma(\lambda)} \in T_{\gamma(\lambda)}\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}_p \in T_p\mathcal{M}\), which live in different vector spaces. Differentiating the components does not work either, because the result depends on the chart. With \(\left. \mathcal{Y} ight|_\mathcal{U} = 	ilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j\), \(\mathcal{X}_p = x^i_p \, (\partial x_i)_p\), and components \(	ilde{y}^k =  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \, 	ilde{x}^j\) in a second chart (Section 5.3), \[ \mathcal{X}_p(	ilde{y}^k) \overset{	ext{product rule}}{=} \underbrace{\left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} ight)_p \mathcal{X}_p(	ilde{x}^j)}_{	ext{transformation law of a vector}} + \underbrace{	ilde{x}^j(p) \, x^i_p \; \partial_i \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{Y}^k \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} ight]  ig( \mathscr{X}(p)  ig)}_{	ext{second derivatives of the chart transition map}} . \] The second term vanishes for all \(\mathcal{Y}\) and \(\mathcal{X}_p\) only if the chart transition map is affine, so the numbers \(\mathcal{X}_p(	ilde{x}^j)\) are not the components of a vector. Comparing tangent vectors at different points therefore requires an additional structure. Goal. Define this structure and the tensors that characterize it. A connection \(
abla\) is the rule for differentiating tensor fields along a tangent vector. In a chart it is encoded in the connection coefficient functions \(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\), whose transformation law contains the second-derivative term above. Differentiating along curves defines parallel transport and the straight curves of \(
abla\), its autoparallels. The torsion and the Riemann curvature characterize \(
abla\). The curvature measures the path dependence of parallel transport. In Newton–Cartan theory and in general relativity, free particles move along autoparallels and gravity is encoded in the connection. The part of gravity that no choice of chart removes is the curvature.

title: 6.1 Connections and Affine Manifolds
text:
A (linear) connection \(
abla\) on a smooth manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})\) assigns to every tangent vector \(\mathcal{X}_p \in T_p\mathcal{M}\), at any point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), and to every tensor field \(T \in \Gamma T^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\), of any valence \((r,s)\), a tensor at \(p\),  egin{align*} 
abla : T_p\mathcal{M} 	imes \Gamma T^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} \ (\mathcal{X}_p, T) &\longmapsto 
abla(\mathcal{X}_p, T) \coloneqq 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T, \end{align*} called the covariant derivative of \(T\) along \(\mathcal{X}_p\)1, satisfying, for all \(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{Y}_p \in T_p\mathcal{M}\), \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) and \(T_1, T_2 \in \Gamma T^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\): Action on scalar fields: \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} f = \mathcal{X}_p(f)\). Additivity in the tensor field: \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} (T_1 \oplus_\Gamma T_2) = 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T_1 \oplus_\Gamma 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T_2\). Leibniz rule: using as an example a \((1,1)\)-tensor field \(T\), for all \(\mathsf{X} \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\), \[ 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p}  ig( T(\mathsf{X}, \mathcal{Y})  ig) = (
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T)(\mathsf{X}_p, \mathcal{Y}_p) \oplus_\Gamma T_p(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X}, \mathcal{Y}_p) \oplus_\Gamma T_p(\mathsf{X}_p, 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y}), \] where the left-hand side is the covariant derivative of the scalar field \(T(\mathsf{X}, \mathcal{Y})\), and analogously for tensor fields of any valence, with one term per argument. linearity in the direction: \(
abla_{\alpha \mathcal{X}_p + \mathcal{Y}_p} T = \alpha \, 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T \oplus_\Gamma 
abla_{\mathcal{Y}_p} T\). Smoothness: for every vector field \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\), the map \(p \mapsto 
abla_{\mathcal{X}(p)} T\) is a smooth tensor field, denoted \(
abla_\mathcal{X} T \in \Gamma T^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\). The two arguments play different roles. The direction enters only through a single tangent vector at \(p\), whereas the tensor field is genuinely differentiated: \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T\) depends on the values of \(T\) around \(p\). Letting the direction vary with a vector field, property 5 yields the field-level map  egin{align*} 
abla : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} 	imes \Gamma T^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \Gamma T^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} \ (\mathcal{X}, T) &\longmapsto 
abla_\mathcal{X} T, \end{align*} which, applying property 4 at each point with \(\alpha = f(p)\), is \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linear in the vector field, \[ 
abla_{f \odot_\Gamma \mathcal{X} \oplus_\Gamma \mathcal{Y}} T = f \odot_\Gamma 
abla_{\mathcal{X}} T \oplus_\Gamma 
abla_{\mathcal{Y}} T \qquad  orall \, f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M}), \; \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}. \] Many texts take this field-level map as the definition, with \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linearity as an axiom. Both definitions are equivalent2, but the pointwise one is the natural one for differentiating along curves, where the direction is the velocity of the curve, only available at the points of the curve. From now onwards, sums of fields and their s-multiplication by scalar fields are written as \(+\) and juxtaposition (instead of \(\oplus_\Gamma\), \(\odot_\Gamma\) and their starred counterparts) An affine manifold is the quadruple \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, 
abla)\), i.e. a smooth manifold equipped with a connection. Product rule. Properties 1 and 3 imply, for all \(g \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) and \(\mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\), \[ 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} (g \, \mathcal{Y}) = \mathcal{X}_p(g) \, \mathcal{Y}_p + g(p) \, 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y}, \] and likewise \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p}(g \, T) = \mathcal{X}_p(g) \, T_p + g(p) \, 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T\) for tensor fields of any valence. Indeed, regarding \(\mathcal{Y}\) as a \((1,0)\)-tensor field, \(\mathcal{Y}(\mathsf{X}) \coloneqq \mathsf{X}\left\lceil \mathcal{Y} ightfloor\), the Leibniz rule reads \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p}  ig( \mathcal{Y}(\mathsf{X})  ig) = (
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y})(\mathsf{X}_p) + \mathcal{Y}_p(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X})\). Applying it to \(g\,\mathcal{Y}\), and evaluating the left-hand side with property 1 and the product rule of tangent vectors acting on products of scalar fields3,  egin{align*}  ig( 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p}(g\,\mathcal{Y})  ig)(\mathsf{X}_p) + g(p) \, \mathcal{Y}_p(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X}) &= 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p}  ig( g \, \mathcal{Y}(\mathsf{X})  ig) = \mathcal{X}_p(g) \, \mathcal{Y}_p(\mathsf{X}_p) + g(p) \, \mathcal{X}_p ig( \mathcal{Y}(\mathsf{X})  ig) \ &= \mathcal{X}_p(g) \, \mathcal{Y}_p(\mathsf{X}_p) + g(p) \, (
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y})(\mathsf{X}_p) + g(p) \, \mathcal{Y}_p(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X}). \end{align*} The terms \(g(p) \, \mathcal{Y}_p(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X})\) cancel and, since every covector at \(p\) is the value of some covector field (Section 4.2), the product rule follows. 1 In this text, the terms covariant derivative and connection are used interchangeably. In these notes the connection is the whole structure \(
abla\), while the covariant derivative is what it produces, \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T\). In a more general setting, however, a connection is a strictly more general notion than a covariant derivative; see Appendix B.9. 2 \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linearity implies that \((
abla_\mathcal{X} T)(p)\) depends on \(\mathcal{X}\) only through \(\mathcal{X}(p)\): in a chart, \(\left. \mathcal{X} ight|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i\) gives \((
abla_\mathcal{X} T)(p) = x^i(p) \, (
abla_{\partial x_i} T)(p)\). Hence \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T \coloneqq (
abla_\mathcal{X} T)(p)\), for any \(\mathcal{X}\) with \(\mathcal{X}(p) = \mathcal{X}_p\), is well defined. 3 \(\mathcal{X}_p(g h) = \mathcal{X}_p(g) \, h(p) + g(p) \, \mathcal{X}_p(h)\), which follows from the product rule of ordinary derivatives applied to \( ig( (g h) \circ \gamma  ig)'(\lambda_0)\).

title: 6.2 Connection Coefficient Functions
text:
Let \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) be a chart. Since a connection is local4, it also acts on tensor fields defined only over \(\mathcal{U}\), such as \(\partial x_j\) and \(dx^j\). To determine the freedom left by the axioms, consider \(\mathcal{X}_p = x^i_p \, (\partial x_i)_p\) and \(\left. \mathcal{Y} ight|_\mathcal{U} = 	ilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j\). Property 4 and the product rule give \[ 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y} = x^i_p \, 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p}  ig( 	ilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j  ig) = \mathcal{X}_p(	ilde{x}^j) \, (\partial x_j)_p + x^i_p \, 	ilde{x}^j(p) \, 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \partial x_j . \] The first term is fixed by the axioms. The only data left free are the vectors \(
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \partial x_j \in T_p\mathcal{M}\), whose components define the connection coefficient functions of \(
abla\) w.r.t. the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\):  egin{align*} \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk} : \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \ p &\longmapsto \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk}(p) \coloneqq (dx^i)_p ig( 
abla_{(\partial x_k)_p} \partial x_j  ig), \end{align*} i.e. \(
abla_{(\partial x_k)_p} \partial x_j = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk}(p) \, (\partial x_i)_p\), or, at field level, \(
abla_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk} \, \partial x_i\). Note the index convention: the last lower index labels the direction of differentiation. The components of \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y}\) therefore read \[ \left( 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y} ight)^k \coloneqq (dx^k)_p ig( 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y}  ig) = \mathcal{X}_p(	ilde{x}^k) + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^k_{ji}(p) \, 	ilde{x}^j(p) \, x^i_p , \] or, letting the direction vary with a vector field \(\left. \mathcal{X} ight|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i\), \(\left( 
abla_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} ight)^k = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor 	ilde{x}^k ightceil + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^k_{ji} \, 	ilde{x}^j \, x^i\). The \(\dim(\mathcal{M})^3\) functions \(\left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk}\) thus fully determine the action of \(
abla\) on vector fields over \(\mathcal{U}\). Analogously, for a covector field \(\left. \mathsf{X} ight|_\mathcal{U} = \mathtt{x}_j \, dx^j\), \[ 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X} = x^i_p \, 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p}  ig( \mathtt{x}_j \, dx^j  ig) = \mathcal{X}_p(\mathtt{x}_j) \, (dx^j)_p + x^i_p \, \mathtt{x}_j(p) \, 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p} dx^j , \] where the data left free are now the covectors \(
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p} dx^j \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\), with components  egin{align*}  ig(	ilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X} ig)^i_{jk} : \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \ p &\longmapsto  ig(	ilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X} ig)^i_{jk}(p) \coloneqq  ig( 
abla_{(\partial x_k)_p} dx^i  ig) ig( (\partial x_j)_p  ig), \end{align*} i.e. \(
abla_{\partial x_k} dx^i =  ig(	ilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X} ig)^i_{jk} \, dx^j\). These, however, are not independent of the \(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\)’s. Applying the Leibniz rule to the constant functions \(dx^j\left\lceil \partial x_k ightfloor = \delta^j_k\), whose covariant derivative vanishes by property 1, \[ 0 = 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p} ig( dx^j \left\lceil \partial x_k ightfloor  ig) =  ig( 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p} dx^j  ig) ig( (\partial x_k)_p  ig) + (dx^j)_p ig( 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \partial x_k  ig) =  ig(	ilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X} ig)^j_{ki}(p) + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^j_{ki}(p), \] so that \(	ilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X} = -\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\), and the components of \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X}\) read \[ \left( 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X} ight)_k \coloneqq \left( 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X} ight) ig( (\partial x_k)_p  ig) = \mathcal{X}_p(\mathtt{x}_k) - \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^j_{ki}(p) \, \mathtt{x}_j(p) \, x^i_p . \] Repeated use of the Leibniz rule gives the action of \(
abla\) on tensor fields of any valence: every upper index contributes a \(+\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\) term, and every lower index a \(-\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\) term. For instance, for a \((1,1)\)-tensor field with components \(T^i_j\), \[ \left( 
abla_\mathcal{X} T ight)^i_{j} = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor T^i_{j} ightceil + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{m\ell} \, T^m_{j} \, x^\ell - \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^m_{j\ell} \, T^i_{m} \, x^\ell. \] Let us now derive how the connection coefficient functions transform under a change of chart. On \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\), with the transformation laws of Section 5.3, \(dy^i =  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \, dx^l\) and \(\partial y_j =  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \partial x_s\), the \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linearity in the direction and the product rule give  egin{align*} \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}ight)^i_{jk} &\coloneqq dy^i\left\lceil 
abla_{\partial y_k} \partial y_j ightfloor =  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \,  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \, dx^l\left\lceil 
abla_{\partial x_p} \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \partial x_s ight) ightfloor \ &=  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \,  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \, dx^l\left\lceil \partial x_p\left\lfloor  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} ightceil \partial x_s +  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, 
abla_{\partial x_p} \partial x_s ightfloor \ &=  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^s} \, \underbrace{ rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \, \partial x_p}_{\partial y_k} \left\lfloor  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} ightceil +  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \,  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \,  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \underbrace{dx^l\left\lceil 
abla_{\partial x_p} \partial x_s ightfloor}_{\left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^l_{sp}}, \end{align*} where we used \(dx^l\left\lceil \partial x_s ightfloor = \delta^l_s\). The first term contains the basis field \(\partial y_k\) acting on the smooth function \( rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} : p \mapsto \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} ight]  ig( \mathscr{Y}(p)  ig)\). Since \( rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} = \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} ight]\), the definition of the chart-induced basis gives \[  rac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}(p) \coloneqq \partial y_k\left\lfloor  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} ightceil (p) = \partial_k \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} ight]  ig( \mathscr{Y}(p)  ig), \] an ordinary second partial derivative of the chart transition map \(	extrm{unic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\), which is smooth since the atlas is \(C^\infty\)-compatible, and symmetric in \(j\) and \(k\) by Schwarz’s theorem. We thus arrive at the transformation law \[ \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}ight)^i_{jk} =  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^s} \,  rac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} +  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \,  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \,  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^l_{sp}. \] The second term is exactly the transformation law of the components of a \((1,2)\)-tensor field. The first one, involving second derivatives of the chart transition map, shows that the connection coefficient functions are not the components of a tensor field. Normal coordinates. The inhomogeneous term can be exploited to simplify the connection coefficient functions at a chosen point. Let \(p \in \mathcal{U}\) and assume, w.l.o.g. (translating the chart), \(\mathscr{X}(p) = (0, \dots, 0)\). Define a new chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) around \(p\) through the transition map \[ \left( \mathscr{Y}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} ight)(\alpha^1, \dots, \alpha^d) \coloneqq \alpha^i +  rac{1}{2} \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{(jk)}(p) \, \alpha^j \alpha^k, \qquad \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{(jk)} \coloneqq  rac{1}{2} \Big[ \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk} + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{kj} \Big], \] which, by the inverse function theorem (the Jacobian of this transition map at \(\mathscr{X}(p) = 0\) is the identity), defines a chart on some neighbourhood \(\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\) of \(p\), \(C^\infty\)-compatible with every chart of \(\mathcal{A}\). It therefore belongs to the maximal atlas determined by \(\mathcal{A}\) (see the footnote to the definition of a smooth manifold in Chapter 3), which is the atlas we always tacitly work with5. Its first and second derivatives at \(p\) are \[ \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} ight)_p = \delta^i_j = \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} ight)_p, \qquad \left(  rac{\partial^2 \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k \, \partial \mathscr{X}^j} ight)_p = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{(jk)}(p). \] Writing the transformation law with the roles of the two charts exchanged, and evaluating it at \(p\), \[ \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk}(p) = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{(jk)}(p) + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}ight)^i_{jk}(p) \, \longrightarrow \, \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}ight)^i_{jk}(p) = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{[jk]}(p) \coloneqq  rac{1}{2} \Big[ \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{jk}(p) - \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^i_{kj}(p) \Big]. \] The symmetric part of the connection coefficient functions can thus always be made to vanish at any chosen point, whereas the antisymmetric part cannot: it is, up to a factor \(-1/2\), the torsion introduced below, a tensor field, which vanishes in one chart if and only if it vanishes in all of them. Note also that this holds at the single point \(p\) only: the derivatives of the \(\Gamma\)’s cannot, in general, be removed, which is related to the curvature introduced below. 4 If \(T\) vanishes on an open neighbourhood \(\mathcal{W}\) of \(p\), then \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T = 0\). Indeed, take \(\psi \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) with \(\psi(p) = 0\) and \(\psi = 1\) outside a compact subset of \(\mathcal{W}\) (one minus a bump function around \(p\)). Then \(T = \psi \, T\), and the product rule gives \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T = \mathcal{X}_p(\psi) \, T_p + \psi(p) \, 
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T = 0\), since \(T_p = 0\) and \(\psi(p) = 0\). Hence \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T\) only depends on \(T\) near \(p\). 5 In much of the literature, “normal coordinates” refers to the coordinates built from the autoparallels through \(p\) (the exponential map). The quadratic construction used here is the minimal one achieving \(\left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}ight)^i_{(jk)}(p) = 0\), which is all we need.

title: 6.3 Parallel Transport and Autoparallels
text:
Let \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} 	o \mathcal{M}\) be a smooth curve, with velocity \(v_\gamma : \lambda \mapsto v_{\gamma(\lambda)}\). Since the direction of \(
abla\) is a single tangent vector, \(
abla_{v_{\gamma(\lambda)}} \mathcal{Y}\) is defined for every \(\mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\). The quantities one wants to differentiate along \(\gamma\), however, starting with \(v_\gamma\) itself, are not vector fields on \(\mathcal{M}\), but vector fields along \(\gamma\), i.e. maps  egin{align*} \mathcal{X}_\gamma : \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow T\mathcal{M} \ \lambda &\longmapsto \mathcal{X}_\gamma(\lambda) \in T_{\gamma(\lambda)}\mathcal{M}, \end{align*} whose component functions \(x^i_\gamma(\lambda) \coloneqq (dx^i)_{\gamma(\lambda)} ig( \mathcal{X}_\gamma(\lambda)  ig)\) are smooth (for those \(\lambda\) with \(\gamma(\lambda) \in \mathcal{U}\)). Examples are the velocity \(v_\gamma\), with component functions \(\dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)\), and the restriction \(\mathcal{Y} \circ \gamma\) of a vector field \(\left. \mathcal{Y} ight|_\mathcal{U} = 	ilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j\), with component functions \(	ilde{x}^j \circ \gamma\). The converse fails: if \(\gamma(\lambda_1) = \gamma(\lambda_2)\) but \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma(\lambda_1) 
eq \mathcal{X}_\gamma(\lambda_2)\), as for the velocity of a figure-eight curve at its crossing point, \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\) is not the restriction of any vector field on \(\mathcal{M}\), and \(
abla\) cannot be applied to it directly. There exists a unique operator \(
abla_{v_\gamma}\), the covariant derivative along \(\gamma\), mapping smooth vector fields along \(\gamma\) to smooth vector fields along \(\gamma\), such that, for all \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma\) along \(\gamma\), \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) and smooth \(	extrm{unic ᚱ} : \mathbb{R} 	o \mathbb{R}\): \(\mathbb{R}\)-linearity: \(
abla_{v_\gamma} (\mathcal{X}_\gamma + \alpha \, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma) = 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma + \alpha \, 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{Y}_\gamma\). Leibniz rule: \(
abla_{v_\gamma} (	extrm{unic ᚱ} \, \mathcal{X}_\gamma) = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}' \, \mathcal{X}_\gamma + 	extrm{unic ᚱ} \, 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma\). Compatibility with \(
abla\): if \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma = \mathcal{Y} \circ \gamma\), then \( ig( 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma  ig)(\lambda) = 
abla_{v_{\gamma(\lambda)}} \mathcal{Y}\). In a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) it reads  egin{equation*}  ig( 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma  ig)(\lambda) = \Big(  rac{d x^k_\gamma}{d\lambda}(\lambda) + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}ight)^k_{ji} ig( \gamma(\lambda)  ig) \, x^j_\gamma(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \Big) (\partial x_k)_{\gamma(\lambda)}. 	ag{$\ast\ast$} \end{equation*} Proof. As for \(
abla\), \(
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma\) at \(\lambda\) only depends on \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\) near \(\lambda\), so it suffices to work on an interval of parameters along which \(\gamma\) stays in \(\mathcal{U}\). Uniqueness: there, \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma = x^j_\gamma \, (\partial x_j \circ \gamma)\), so properties 1 and 2, then 3, and finally property 4 of \(
abla\) force \[  ig( 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma  ig)(\lambda) =  rac{d x^j_\gamma}{d\lambda}(\lambda) \, (\partial x_j)_{\gamma(\lambda)} + x^j_\gamma(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, 
abla_{(\partial x_i)_{\gamma(\lambda)}} \partial x_j, \] which is \((\ast\ast)\). Existence: define \(
abla_{v_\gamma}\) chart by chart through \((\ast\ast)\). Properties 1 and 2 are immediate. For property 3, the expansion of \(
abla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y}\) derived above, at \(\mathcal{X}_p = v_{\gamma(\lambda)}\), coincides with \((\ast\ast)\) for \(x^j_\gamma = 	ilde{x}^j \circ \gamma\), since \(v_{\gamma(\lambda)}(	ilde{x}^k) = (	ilde{x}^k \circ \gamma)'(\lambda)\). On chart overlaps, both chart expressions satisfy properties 1–3, so by uniqueness they coincide. \(\square\) We define, for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\): \[  egin{array}{c|c}  egin{array}{c} 	ext{A vector field } \mathcal{X}_\gamma 	ext{ along } \gamma 	ext{ is}\ 	ext{	extbf{parallelly transported} along } \gamma 	ext{ if} \end{array} &  egin{array}{c} 	ext{A smooth curve } \gamma 	ext{ is}\ 	ext{	extbf{autoparallelly transported} if} \end{array} \[8pt] 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma = 0. & 
abla_{v_\gamma} v_\gamma = 0. \[12pt] \hline \[-6pt]  egin{array}{c} 	ext{A vector field } \mathcal{X}_\gamma 	ext{ along } \gamma 	ext{ is}\ 	ext{	extbf{parallel} along } \gamma 	ext{ if} \end{array} &  egin{array}{c} 	ext{A smooth curve } \gamma 	ext{ is}\ 	ext{	extbf{autoparallel} if} \end{array} \[8pt]  ig( 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma  ig)(\lambda) = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(\lambda) \, \mathcal{X}_\gamma(\lambda). &  ig( 
abla_{v_\gamma} v_\gamma  ig)(\lambda) = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(\lambda) \, v_{\gamma(\lambda)}. \end{array} \] where \(	extrm{unic ᚱ} : \mathbb{R} 	o \mathbb{R}\) is a smooth function. We define the acceleration of the curve \(\gamma\) as \(a_\gamma(\lambda) \coloneqq  ig( 
abla_{v_\gamma} v_\gamma  ig)(\lambda) \in T_{\gamma(\lambda)}\mathcal{M}\). Parallel transport cannot, in general, be phrased in terms of vector fields on \(\mathcal{M}\): transporting a vector around a closed curve typically returns a different vector, so the transported vectors are not the values of any single vector field on \(\mathcal{M}\). This failure to return, the holonomy of \(
abla\), is closely related to the curvature introduced below. Applying \((\ast\ast)\) to \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma = v_\gamma\), whose component functions are \(x^k_\gamma = \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}\), with \( rac{d}{d\lambda} \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) =  ig( \mathscr{X}^k \circ \gamma  ig)''(\lambda) \eqqcolon \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)\), and using that the \((\partial x_k)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\) form a basis of \(T_{\gamma(\lambda)}\mathcal{M}\), the autoparallel condition \( ig(

When all the \(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\)’s vanish, as for the Euclidean plane in the cartesian chart with its standard connection, its solutions are straight lines.

title: 7 Metric
text: Motivation: Distances, geodesics, and the variational principle A connection decides which curves are straight, but not how long they are, nor the angle between two vectors. On \(\mathbb{R}^d\), in Cartesian coordinates, the length of a curve is computed from the components of its velocity, \[ L_{[a,b]}[\gamma] = \int_a^b \sqrt{ \delta_{ij} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) } \; d\lambda , \] i.e. by evaluating the Euclidean inner product \(\delta_{ij}\) on the velocity \(v_{\gamma(\lambda)}\) at every \(\lambda\). On a manifold, the velocity \(v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \in T_{\gamma(\lambda)}\mathcal{M}\) is available (Chapter 4), but nothing yet turns it into a number: a tangent space is a vector space, with no lengths or angles, and the components \(\delta_{ij}\) only take this form in Cartesian charts. The missing ingredient is a symmetric, non-degenerate bilinear form on every tangent space, varying smoothly from point to point. Positive definiteness is not required, so that the Lorentzian case, the one of spacetime, is included. Goal: construct this structure and relate it to the connection. Define the metric \(g\), whose components \(g_{ij}\) replace \(\delta_{ij}\), and classify it by its signature. Define the length of curves and, as its extremal curves, the geodesics, using \(g\) alone, independently of any connection. Single out a connection whose straight curves are the geodesics: the Levi-Civita connection \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\), determined by \(g\), and characterized as the only torsion-free, metric-compatible connection. In general relativity, \(g\) is the gravitational field, and the curvatures of \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\), built from \(g\) at the end of this chapter, are the objects entering the Einstein equations.

title: 7.1 Metric
text: A metric \(g\) on a smooth manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})\) is a \((0,2)\)-tensor field \begin{align*} g : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \times \Gamma T\mathcal{M} &\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \\ (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) &\longmapsto g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}), \end{align*} satisfying the following two conditions: Symmetry: \(g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = g(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{X})\) for all \(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\). Invertibility of the musical map: the musical map \begin{align*} \flat : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} \\ \mathcal{X} &\longmapsto \flat(\mathcal{X}), \qquad \text{with } \flat(\mathcal{X})\left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor \coloneqq g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}), \end{align*} is an isomorphism of \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-modules. Explicitly, \(\flat\) must be (a) \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linear: \(\flat(f \, \mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Y}) = f \, \flat(\mathcal{X}) + \flat(\mathcal{Y})\) for all \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) and \(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\); (b) bijective: \(\forall \, \mathsf{X} \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} \;\, \exists! \, \mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M} : \flat(\mathcal{X}) = \mathsf{X}\)1. That \(\flat(\mathcal{X})\) is indeed a covector field, and condition (a) follow from the \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linearity of \(g\) in its second and first slot, respectively. The actual requirement is (b). A metric manifold is the quadruple \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, g)\), i.e. a smooth manifold equipped with a metric. In a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), the components of the metric are the functions \[ g_{ij} \coloneqq g(\partial x_i, \partial x_j) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}), \] with \(g_{ij} = g_{ji}\) by symmetry. For \(\left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i\) and \(\left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \tilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j\), \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-bilinearity gives \(\left. g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \tilde{x}^j \, g_{ij}\). When two charts are involved we write \((g_\mathscr{X})_{ij}\) and \((g_\mathscr{Y})_{kl}\); as for any \((0,2)\)-tensor field, on \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\), \[ (g_\mathscr{Y})_{kl} = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \, \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^j}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^l}\, (g_\mathscr{X})_{ij}. \] Since \(\flat\) is an isomorphism, there exists the inverse musical map \begin{align*} \flat^{-1} : \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \\ \mathsf{X} &\longmapsto \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}), \end{align*} which is \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linear as well (apply \(\flat^{-1}\) to \(\flat\big( f \, \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) + \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big) = f \, \mathsf{X} + \mathsf{Y}\)). It defines the inverse metric \(g^{-1}\), the \((2,0)\)-tensor field \begin{align*} g^{-1} : \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} \times \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} &\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \\ (\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}) &\longmapsto g^{-1}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}) \coloneqq \mathsf{Y}\left\lceil \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \right\rfloor . \end{align*} It is symmetric: writing \(\mathsf{Y} = \flat\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big)\) and using the symmetry of \(g\), \[ g^{-1}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}) = \flat\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big)\left\lceil \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \right\rfloor = g\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}), \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \big) = g\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}), \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big) = g^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}, \mathsf{X}), \] which also shows that \(g^{-1}\) is simply \(g\) evaluated on the vector fields corresponding to \(\mathsf{X}\) and \(\mathsf{Y}\) under \(\flat^{-1}\). Its components in a chart are \((g^{-1})^{ij} \coloneqq g^{-1}(dx^i, dx^j) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\). In components, the inverse metric is characterized by \(g_{ij} \, (g^{-1})^{jk} = \delta_i^k\)2. The matrix of components of \(g^{-1}\) is the inverse of the matrix of components of \(g\). Musical maps in components. For \(\left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^j \, \partial x_j\) and \(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \mathtt{x}_j \, dx^j\), the components of \(\flat(\mathcal{X}) \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\) and \(\flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\) are \begin{align*} \flat(\mathcal{X})_i &\coloneqq \flat(\mathcal{X})\left\lceil \partial x_i \right\rfloor = g(x^i \partial x_i, \partial x_j) = x^j \, g_{ji},\\ \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X})^i &\coloneqq dx^i\left\lceil \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \right\rfloor = g^{-1}(\mathtt{x}_j dx^j, dx^i) = \mathtt{x}_j \, (g^{-1})^{ji}. \end{align*} This is what is usually called “lowering” and “raising” indices with \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\). In these notes the results always keep their own names, \(\flat(\mathcal{X})_i\) and \(\flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X})^i\), and are never written as \(x_i\) or \(\mathtt{x}^i\).

title: 7.1 Metric
text:
7.1.1 Signature

Unlike a \((1,1)\)-tensor field, \(g\) has no eigenvalues. For a \((1,1)\)-tensor \(T_p\) at \(p\), the eigenvalue equation in components, \[ T^i_j(p) \, x^j_p = \lambda \, x^i_p , \] equates the components of two vectors, \(T_p(\cdot, \mathcal{X}_p)\) and \(\lambda \, \mathcal{X}_p\). It is thus the component form of a chart-independent equation, and \(\lambda\) is the same in every chart. For the metric, the analogous equation \[ g_{ij}(p) \, x^j_p = \lambda \, x^i_p \] equates the components of the covector \( lat_p(\mathcal{X}_p)\) with those of the vector \(\lambda \, \mathcal{X}_p\), which live in fundamentally different spaces. What survives is the so-called signature, as stated by Sylvester’s law of inertia (proved in Appendix B.12): at every \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) there exists a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) with \(p \in \mathcal{U}\) whose components at \(p\) are \[ g_{ij}(p) = 0 \;\; 	ext{for } i 
eq j, \qquad g_{ii}(p) \in \{+1, -1\}, \] i.e. in which the chart-induced basis \(\{ (\partial x_1)_p, \dots, (\partial x_d)_p \}\) of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) “diagonalizes” \(g_p\), and the number \(n_+\) of \(+1\)’s (and hence the number \(n_-\) of \(-1\)’s) does not depend on the chart chosen. No zeros appear because \(g_p\) is non-degenerate3, so \(n_+ + n_- = \dim(\mathcal{M})\). The doublet \((n_+, n_-)\) is the signature of \(g\) at \(p\). It is, in fact, the same at all points of a connected manifold4, so we simply speak of the signature of \(g\). Metrics are classified according to it: If \(n_+ = \dim(\mathcal{M})\), the metric is Riemannian. It is then positive-definite, \[ g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) > 0 \qquad  orall \, \mathcal{X}_p 
eq 0, \;\;  orall \, p \in \mathcal{M}, \] so each \(g_p\) is an inner product on \(T_p\mathcal{M}\). (If \(n_- = \dim(\mathcal{M})\), the metric is negative-definite and \(-g\) is Riemannian; this case is conventionally included.) If \(0 < n_+ < \dim(\mathcal{M})\), the metric is pseudo-Riemannian. Then there exist non-zero null vectors, \(g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) = 0\) with \(\mathcal{X}_p 
eq 0\): if \(g_{aa}(p) = +1\) and \(g_{bb}(p) = -1\) in such a chart, take \(\mathcal{X}_p = (\partial x_a)_p + (\partial x_b)_p\). Each \(g_p\) is thus symmetric, bilinear and non-degenerate, but not positive-definite: a pseudo-inner product. In the special case \(n_+ = 1\) or \(n_- = 1\) (with \(\dim(\mathcal{M}) \geq 2\)) the metric is Lorentzian; both sign conventions, \((1, d-1)\) and \((d-1, 1)\), are common in the literature. 1 This can be checked pointwise. At each \(p\), \( lat_p : T_p\mathcal{M} 	o T_p^*\mathcal{M}\), \( lat_p(\mathcal{X}_p)(\mathcal{Y}_p) \coloneqq g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{Y}_p)\), with \( lat(\mathcal{X})_p =  lat_p(\mathcal{X}_p)\). Since \(\dim T_p\mathcal{M} = \dim T_p^*\mathcal{M}\), (b) \(\iff\) (i) \( lat_p\) is an isomorphism \( orall \, p\) \(\iff\) (ii) \(\ker  lat_p = \{0\} \;\,  orall \, p\), i.e. \(g\) is non-degenerate: \(g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{Y}_p) = 0 \;\,  orall \, \mathcal{Y}_p \Rightarrow \mathcal{X}_p = 0\) \(\iff\) (iii) \(\det ig( g_{ij}(p)  ig) 
eq 0 \;\,  orall \, p\), in every chart. (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (b): \( lat^{-1}(\mathsf{X})_p \coloneqq  lat_p^{-1}(\mathsf{X}_p)\) is smooth, its components being \(\mathtt{x}_j\) times the entries of \( ig( g_{ij}  ig)^{-1}\). (b) \(\Rightarrow\) (i): if \( lat_{p_0}\) were singular, any \(\mathsf{Y}\) with \(\mathsf{Y}_{p_0} 
otin \operatorname{im}  lat_{p_0}\) (constant components near \(p_0\) times a bump function) would have no preimage, as \( lat(\mathcal{X})_{p_0} =  lat_{p_0}(\mathcal{X}_{p_0})\). Strictly weaker is injectivity alone, \(g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = 0 \;\,  orall \, \mathcal{Y} \Rightarrow \mathcal{X} = 0\): \(g = (\mathscr{X}^1)^2 \, dx^1 \otimes dx^1\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) satisfies it, yet \(g_0 = 0\) and \(dx^1 
otin \operatorname{im}  lat\), since \( lat(x \, \partial x_1) = (\mathscr{X}^1)^2 \, x \, dx^1 = dx^1\) requires \(x = (\mathscr{X}^1)^{-2}\), not smooth at \(0\). 2 The name “inverse” does not mean that \(g^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(g\) as a map: \(g\) is a map from pairs of vector fields to scalar fields, so it has no inverse in that sense. It refers instead to the relation between the matrices of components, which follows from \( lat^{-1}\) being the inverse of \( lat\). Since \( lat(\partial x_k)\left\lceil \partial x_l ightfloor = g_{kl}\) and \(dx^k\left\lceil  lat^{-1}(dx^j) ightfloor = (g^{-1})^{jk}\), we have \( lat(\partial x_k) = g_{kl} \, dx^l\) and \( lat^{-1}(dx^j) = (g^{-1})^{jk} \, \partial x_k\). Hence \(\partial x_i =  lat^{-1} ig(  lat(\partial x_i)  ig) = g_{ij} \, (g^{-1})^{jk} \, \partial x_k\), and similarly \(dx^j =  lat ig(  lat^{-1}(dx^j)  ig) = (g^{-1})^{jk} \, g_{kl} \, dx^l\), which, the chart-induced frames being bases, give \(g_{ij} \, (g^{-1})^{jk} = \delta_i{}^k\) and \((g^{-1})^{jk} \, g_{kl} = \delta^j{}_l\). 3 Sylvester’s law holds for any symmetric bilinear form on \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), degenerate or not: in a suitable basis it is diagonal with entries in \(\{+1, -1, 0\}\), and the numbers \((n_+, n_-, n_0)\) of each do not depend on the basis, with \(n_0 = \dim \ker  lat_p\). For a metric, \( lat_p\) is an isomorphism, so \(n_0 = 0\). Appendix B.12 proves only the non-degenerate case. 4 In a chart, the eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix \( ig( g_{ij}(p)  ig)\) must depend continuously on \(p\). Since their product, \(\det ig( g_{ij}(p)  ig)\), never vanishes, no eigenvalue can change sign, so the signature is locally constant, hence constant on a connected manifold.

title: 7.2 Length and Geodesics
text: Let \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\) be a curve, at least \(C^1\), with velocity \(v_\gamma : \lambda \mapsto v_{\gamma(\lambda)}\), on a metric manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, g)\). The sign and the speed of \(\gamma\) are the functions \begin{align*} \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma : \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \{-1, 0, +1\} & s_\gamma : \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma(\lambda) \, \coloneq \operatorname{sgn}\left( g_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)}, v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big)\right), & \lambda &\longmapsto \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma(\lambda) \, g_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)}, v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) } , \end{align*} i.e. \(s_\gamma = \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{ij} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} }\) in a chart. For a Riemannian metric, \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma = +1\) wherever \(v_\gamma \neq 0\). For an indefinite one, \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma = 0\) also for \(v_\gamma \neq 0\) (null velocities), and \(s_\gamma\) is defined piecewise on intervals where \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma\) is constant. The length of \(\gamma\) between the parameter values \(a < b\) is the functional \begin{align*} L_{[a,b]} : \{ \gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M} \mid \gamma \text{ is } C^1 \} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \gamma &\longmapsto L_{[a,b]}[\gamma] \coloneqq \int_a^b s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda , \end{align*} This satisfies that \(L_{\textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1}([a,b])}[\gamma \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}] = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma]\) for every diffeomorphism \(\textrm{\runic ᚱ} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) (Appendix B.13).

title: 7.2 Length and Geodesics
text:
7.2.1 Variations and the Euler–Lagrange Equations

Let \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\) be smooth with \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma(\lambda) \neq 0\) for all \(\lambda \in [a,b]\). Since \(\lambda \mapsto g_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)}, v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big)\) is continuous and does not vanish on \([a,b]\), \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma\) is a constant \(\pm 1\) there. Let \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) be a chart with \(\gamma([a,b]) \subseteq \mathcal{U}\)5, and denote by \(\gamma_\mathcal{U} \coloneqq \mathscr{X} \circ \gamma : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^d\) its chart representative. A variation of \(\gamma\) with fixed endpoints w.r.t. the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) is a family of curves labelled by a real deformation parameter \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} \in (-\textrm{\runic ᛊ}_0, \textrm{\runic ᛊ}_0)\), independent of the curve parameter \(\lambda\): \begin{align*} \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} : [a,b] &\longrightarrow \mathcal{U} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}(\lambda) \coloneqq \mathscr{X}^{-1}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(\lambda) \big), \end{align*} where \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ} : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^d\) is smooth with \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}(a) = \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(b) = 0\), and \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}_0 > 0\) is small enough for \(\gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) to stay in \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\). The deformation is defined through the chart: it is the chart representative that is shifted linearly in \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\), \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}\), whereas in another chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), \(\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}\) is in general not of this form. Thus \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = \gamma\), \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}(a) = \gamma(a)\), \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}(b) = \gamma(b)\) The curve \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}=0} = 0 \qquad \text{for every such } \textrm{\runic ᛉ} . \] The requirement \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \neq 0\) makes \(s_\gamma = \sqrt{\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g(v_\gamma, v_\gamma)}\) differentiable. For a Riemannian metric it only excludes \(v_\gamma = 0\). For an indefinite one it also excludes null velocities. Whether \(\gamma\) is a geodesic does not depend on the chart used to deform it: the resulting condition (see below), holds in every chart. Figure 7.1: Variation of a curve with fixed endpoints, as used in the variational definition of geodesics (Chapter 7). Top: the curve \(\gamma\) (blue) joins the points \(A = \gamma(a)\) and \(B = \gamma(b)\) of the manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) inside the chart domain \(\mathcal{U}\) (green), on which the images of the coordinate lines of \(\mathscr{X}\) are drawn. The dashed orange curves are members \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}\) of a variation, for a few values of the deformation parameter \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\); all of them share the endpoints \(A\) and \(B\). Bottom: the same objects seen through the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), where the coordinate lines become straight. Here the variation is defined: each member is the chart representative \(\gamma_\mathcal{U}\) shifted linearly in the deformation parameter, \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}\), along the vectors \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}(\lambda) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) (purple, drawn for \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 1\)), which vanish at the endpoints, \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}(a) = \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(b) = 0\). On the manifold the same family is no longer a linear shift: the deformation only has this simple form in the chart used to define it. The curve \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} \mapsto L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}]\) has vanishing derivative at \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0\) for every such \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\). On \([a,b]\), the curve \(\gamma\) and all its variations \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}\) share the same constant sign \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma\). Their speeds are therefore the values, on their velocities, of a single function on the tangent bundle, the Lagrangian6: \begin{align*} \mathcal{L} : \big\{ \mathcal{X}_p \in T\mathcal{M} \;\big|\; \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) > 0 \big\} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \mathcal{X}_p &\longmapsto \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{X}_p) \coloneqq \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) } , \end{align*} \[ s_{\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}}(\lambda) = \mathcal{L}\big( v_{\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}, \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}(\lambda)} \big), \qquad L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] = \int_a^b \mathcal{L}\big( v_{\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}, \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}(\lambda)} \big) \, d\lambda . \] In the bundle chart \((T\mathcal{U}, \xi_\mathscr{X})\) of Section 5.1, a vector \(\mathcal{X}_p = x^k_p \, (\partial x_k)_p\) is described by the \(2d\) numbers \(\xi_\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{X}_p) = \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \, ; \, x_p \big)\), i.e. the coordinates \(\mathscr{X}(p) = \big( \mathscr{X}^1(p), \dots, \mathscr{X}^d(p) \big)\) of its base point and its components \(x_p = (x^1_p, \dots, x^d_p)\). Since \(g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) = g_{ij}(p) \, x^i_p x^j_p\), the chart representative of \(\mathcal{L}\) w.r.t. \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) is \[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq \mathcal{L} \circ \xi_\mathscr{X}^{-1} : \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \, ; \, x_p \big) \longmapsto \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{ij}(p) \, x^i_p \, x^j_p } , \] a function of \(2d\) real variables: \(d\) position slots and \(d\) velocity slots. For the velocity of \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}\), \[ \xi_\mathscr{X}\big( v_{\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}, \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}(\lambda)} \big) = \big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(\lambda) \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'(\lambda) \big), \] \[ L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] = \int_a^b \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}' \big) \, d\lambda , \] and at \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0\), \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) = \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{ij}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) } = s_\gamma(\lambda)\). By Appendix B.14, \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if, on \([a,b]\), the Euler–Lagrange equations hold: \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})(\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}) \Big] - (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})(\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}) = 0 , \qquad m = 1, \dots, d , \] where \(\partial_m\) and \(\partial_{d+m}\) differentiate \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) w.r.t. its \(m\)-th position slot and its \(m\)-th velocity. For the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) of the metric, the Euler–Lagrange equations become a system of \(d\) second-order ordinary differential equations for the chart representative \(\gamma_\mathcal{U}\). Writing \(\partial_m g_{ij} \coloneqq \partial x_m \left\lfloor g_{ij} \right\rceil \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\), i.e. \((\partial_m g_{ij})(p) = \partial_m \left[ g_{ij} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right]\big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big)\), a curve with constant speed is a geodesic if and only if, on \([a,b]\), \begin{equation} \boxed{ \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \frac{1}{2} \Big( (g^{-1})^{km} \big( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} - \partial_m g_{ij} \big) \Big)\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = 0 } \tag{7.1} \end{equation} and every geodesic admits a constant-speed parametrization. This is the geodesic equation in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\). The step-by-step derivation is given in Appendix B.16. 5 For the resulting equations this is no restriction: \([a,b]\) is compact, so it splits into finitely many subintervals, each mapped by \(\gamma\) into a single chart domain, and a variation supported in one of them is a variation of the whole curve. 6 \(\mathcal{L}\) is not a covector field: on each \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) it is not linear. Functions on the tangent bundle, \(T\mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}\), depending on both the point and the velocity, are called Lagrangians, and the functionals \(\gamma \mapsto \int \mathcal{L}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) \, d\lambda\) they induce on curves are called action functionals; \(L_{[a,b]}\) is the one of this \(\mathcal{L}\).

title: 7.3 The Levi-Civita Connection
text:
The geodesic equation (7.1) has the form of the autoparallel equation (6.1), with the connection coefficient functions replaced by the Christoffel symbols of \(g\) w.r.t. \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\),  egin{equation}  oxed{  ig( \Gamma^{	ext{LC}}_\mathscr{X}  ig)^k_{ji} \coloneqq  rac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{km}  ig( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} - \partial_m g_{ij}  ig) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}). } 	ag{7.2} \end{equation} The Levi-Civita connection \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) is the connection whose connection coefficient functions are, in every chart, the Christoffel symbols. With this choice, (6.1) becomes (7.1) term by term, so the straight curves of \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) are the extremal curves of the length. Moreover, exchanging \(i \leftrightarrow j\) swaps the first two terms of the Christoffel symbols and leaves the third invariant (\(g_{ij} = g_{ji}\)), so \((\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ji} = (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ij}\), and \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) is torsion free, \(\mathtt{T}^k_{ji} = (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ij} - (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ji} = 0\). A connection \(
abla\) is metric compatible if \(
abla_\mathcal{X} g = 0\) for all \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\). In a chart,  egin{equation} (
abla_{\partial x_k} g)_{ij} = \partial_k g_{ij} - \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} - \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} . 	ag{7.3} \end{equation} As torsion freeness, metric compatibility of \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) follows from its definition: inserting the Christoffel symbols, \(\Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} =  rac{1}{2}  ig( \partial_k g_{ji} + \partial_i g_{jk} - \partial_j g_{ki}  ig)\) and \(\Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} =  rac{1}{2}  ig( \partial_k g_{ij} + \partial_j g_{ik} - \partial_i g_{kj}  ig)\), whose sum is \(\partial_k g_{ij}\). Conversely, the two properties characterize it: Theorem (Levi-Civita). \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) is the only torsion-free, metric-compatible connection on a metric manifold7. By metric compatibility, parallel transport with \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) preserves \(g\): for vector fields \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\), \(\mathcal{Y}_\gamma\) along \(\gamma\), \( rac{d}{d\lambda} \, g(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma) = g(
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma) + g(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, 
abla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{Y}_\gamma)\) (Appendix B.18.5). Along an autoparallelly transported curve, \(g(v_\gamma, v_\gamma)\), and hence \(	extrm{unic ᛇ}_\gamma\) and \(s_\gamma\), are therefore constant. Its autoparallelly transported curves with \(	extrm{unic ᛇ}_\gamma 
eq 0\) are thus exactly the constant-speed geodesics, while those with \(	extrm{unic ᛇ}_\gamma = 0\), not covered by the variational definition, are called null geodesics. For a general connection the two notions differ: autoparallels depend on \(
abla\), geodesics only on \(g\). 7 See Appendix B.17 for the proof, and for the fact that the Christoffel symbols of overlapping charts define the same connection.

title: 7.4 Curvature of the Metric
text: From now on, \(\mathrm{Riem}\) and \(\mathrm{Ric}\) denote the curvatures of \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\), both determined by \(g\) through \(g \longrightarrow \nabla^{\text{LC}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Riem} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ric}\). Using \(g\) once more, through \(\flat\), \(\flat^{-1}\) or \(g\) itself, we define: The Riemann–Christoffel curvature, the \((0,4)\)-tensor field \[ \mathrm{Riem}^\flat(\mathcal{W}, \mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) \coloneqq \mathrm{Riem}\big( \flat(\mathcal{W}), \mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \big), \qquad (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm} = g_{al} \, \mathrm{Riem}^l_{jkm} , \] the components following from \(\flat(\partial x_a) = g_{al} \, dx^l\). The Ricci scalar, the scalar field (chart independent, as \(\mathrm{Ric}\)) \[ R \coloneqq \mathrm{Ric}\big( \flat^{-1}(dx^m), \partial x_m \big) = (g^{-1})^{mk} \, \mathrm{Ric}_{km} \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M}), \] using \(\flat^{-1}(dx^m) = (g^{-1})^{mk} \, \partial x_k\). The Einstein curvature, the \((0,2)\)-tensor field \[ G \coloneqq \mathrm{Ric} - \frac{1}{2} \, R \, g , \qquad G_{ab} = \mathrm{Ric}_{ab} - \frac{1}{2} \, R \, g_{ab} . \]

title: 8 Integrals
text: Motivation: Why integrating in a chart is not enough On \(\mathbb{R}^d\), a function is integrated against the volume element \(d^d\alpha\). On a manifold, a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) turns \(f : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}\) into its chart representative \(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) on \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), which can be integrated in the ordinary sense. The question is whether the result depends on the chart. Let \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) be charts, \(\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\), and let \(\iota : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\iota(p) \coloneqq 1\) if \(p \in \mathcal{D}\) and \(0\) otherwise, be the indicator function of \(\mathcal{D}\). Its chart representative \(\iota \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\), extended by zero outside \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\), equals \(1\) on \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})\) and \(0\) elsewhere on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). It turns the integral of the chart representative of \(f\) over \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})\) into one over all of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), which can then be rewritten in the other chart: \begin{align*} \int_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})} &d^d\alpha \, \big( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \xlongrightarrow[\text{outside } \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})]{\text{extend by } 0 \text{ with } \iota \, ^{\href{#fn_Integrals_Fubini}{1}}} ... \\ ... = &\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} d^d\alpha \, \big( (\iota f) \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \xlongrightarrow[d^d\alpha \, = \, d^d\beta \, |\det ( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} )(\beta)|]{\text{change of variables} \, ^{\href{#fn_Integrals_Volume}{2}}} ... \\ ... = &\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} d^d\beta \, \Big| \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)(\beta) \Big| \, \big( (\iota f) \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) \xlongrightarrow[\text{out of } \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D})]{\iota \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \, = \, 0} ... \\ ... = &\int_{\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\beta \, \underbrace{\Big| \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)(\beta) \Big|}_{\mathclap{\text{picked up by the change of chart}}} \, \big( f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) . \end{align*} The indicator and \(f\) only become their representatives in the other chart, while the volume element picks up the factor \(\big| \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big) \big|\). The integral of a chart representative therefore depends on the chart. Goal: a notion of integration on \(\mathcal{M}\) that does not depend on the chart. Two structures achieve it: a volume form, whose chart representative picks up \(\det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)\) under a change of chart and can thus compensate the factor above; an orientation, which makes these determinants positive, so that the compensation is exact, \(|\det| / \det = 1\). Figure 8.1: Integration on a manifold, drawn for \(d = 2\). The chart domains \(\mathcal{U}\) (blue) and \(\mathcal{V}\) (green) overlap, and the region \(\mathcal{D}\) (orange outline) has its closure in \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\). The function \(f\) is defined everywhere (dotted level sets); the indicator \(\iota\) of \(\mathcal{D}\) cuts it off outside the region, and \(\iota f\) (shaded, darker for larger values) jumps to zero at the boundary of \(\mathcal{D}\). The charts \(\mathscr{X}\) and \(\mathscr{Y}\) turn \(\iota f\) into two chart representatives, related by the chart transition map, \((\iota f) \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} = \big( (\iota f) \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big) \circ \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\): they take the same value at the images of the same point \(p\), but their level sets, and the regions \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D})\), are deformed. 1 For well-behaved integrands, Fubini’s theorem allows computing it as iterated integrals, \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} d\alpha^1 \cdots \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} d\alpha^d\), each running over the whole real line. 2 \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\) is differentiable, so near \(\beta\) it acts as its Jacobian, \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}(\beta + h) = \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}(\beta) + \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}(\beta) \, h + o(|h|)\). A small box with edges \(h_k \hat{e}_k\) along the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), of volume \(d^d\beta = h_1 \cdots h_d\), is thus mapped to the parallelepiped with edges \(h_k \, \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}(\beta) \, \hat{e}_k\), of volume \(\big| \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)(\beta) \big| \, h_1 \cdots h_d\). The determinant is the signed volume spanned by the columns of the matrix, and its sign, which only records a reversal of orientation, does not enter a volume. Summing over boxes (Riemann sums) gives the result; controlling the \(o(|h|)\) terms in this limit is the content of the change of variables theorem.

title: 8.1 Volume Forms and Orientation
text:
Given a smooth manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})_d\), a volume form is a \((0,d)\)-tensor field  egin{align*} \Omega : \underbrace{\Gamma T\mathcal{M} 	imes \dots 	imes \Gamma T\mathcal{M}}_{d	ext{-times}} &\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \ \dots \ \sim}} C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \  ig( \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(d)}  ig) &\longmapsto \Omega ig( \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(d)}  ig), \end{align*} satisfying: Non-vanishing: \(\Omega_p 
eq 0\) for all \(p \in \mathcal{M}\); Total antisymmetry: exchanging any two arguments flips the sign, \[ \Omega ig( \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(a)}}_{a	ext{-th}}, \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(b)}}_{b	ext{-th}}, \dots  ig) = - \Omega ig( \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(b)}}_{a	ext{-th}}, \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(a)}}_{b	ext{-th}}, \dots  ig) \qquad  orall \, a 
eq b \in \{1, \dots, d\} . \] The \(d\)-dimensional Levi-Civita symbol is the array \(\varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} = \varepsilon^{i_1 \dots i_d}\), \(i_1, \dots, i_d \in \{1, \dots, d\}\), fixed by \(\varepsilon_{1 \dots d} = 1\) and total antisymmetry, \(\varepsilon_{\dots i_a \dots i_b \dots} = - \varepsilon_{\dots i_b \dots i_a \dots}\)3. It vanishes if two indices coincide (exchanging them gives \(\varepsilon = -\varepsilon\)), and otherwise equals the sign of the permutation \((i_1, \dots, i_d)\) of \((1, \dots, d)\). For a totally antisymmetric array \(T_{i_1 \dots i_d}\) and a matrix \(T^i_j\) (we’ll employ these properties afterwards)4: \[ \underbrace{T_{i_1 \dots i_d} = \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, T_{1 \dots d}}_{	ext{(a)}}, \qquad \underbrace{\det  ig( T^i_j  ig) = \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, T^{i_1}_1 \cdots T^{i_d}_d}_{	ext{(b)}}, \qquad \underbrace{\varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, T^{i_1}_{j_1} \cdots T^{i_d}_{j_d} = \det  ig( T^i_j  ig) \, \varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d}}_{	ext{(c)}} . \] In a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), the components of a volume form, \((\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{i_1 \dots i_d} \coloneqq \Omega ig( \partial x_{i_1}, \dots, \partial x_{i_d}  ig) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\), form a totally antisymmetric array: \[ (\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{i_1 \dots i_d} = \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, \omega_\mathscr{X} , \qquad \omega_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq (\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{1 \dots d} = \Omega ig( \partial x_1, \dots, \partial x_d  ig) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}) . \] The function \(\omega_\mathscr{X}\) is the scalar density of \(\Omega\) w.r.t. \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\). As every component is \(\pm \omega_\mathscr{X}\) or \(0\), the non-vanishing condition reads \(\omega_\mathscr{X}(p) 
eq 0\,  orall p \in \mathcal{U}\). Under a change of chart, on \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\),  egin{align} \omega_\mathscr{Y} &\coloneqq \Omega ig( \partial y_1, \dots, \partial y_d  ig) =  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^1} \cdots  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_d}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^d} \; \Omega ig( \partial x_{i_1}, \dots, \partial x_{i_d}  ig) = 	ag{8.1}\ &=  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^1} \cdots  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_d}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^d} \; (\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, =  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^1} \cdots  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_d}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^d} \, \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, \omega_\mathscr{X} \overset{(c)}{=} \det \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} ight) \omega_\mathscr{X}. 	ag{8.2} \end{align} Therefore, under a change of basis, the scalar density \(\omega_\mathscr{X}\) picks up a Jacobian determinant term.5 In particular, \(\omega_\mathscr{X}\) is not a scalar field on \(\mathcal{M}\): its values at a point depend on the chart. Let \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})_d\) be a smooth manifold, with \(\mathcal{A}\) its maximal atlas. An atlas \(\mathcal{A}^\uparrow \subseteq \mathcal{A}\), i.e. a set of charts whose domains cover \(\mathcal{M}\), is an oriented atlas if all its Jacobian determinants are positive, \[ \det \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} ight)(p) > 0 \qquad  orall \, p \in \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}, \quad  orall \, (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}), (\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}^\uparrow . \] The condition is symmetric in the two charts, since the two Jacobians are inverse matrices: \[ \det \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} ight) \, \det \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k} ight) = \det \left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k} ight) = \det  ig( \delta^i_k  ig) = 1 . \] A smooth manifold is orientable if it admits an oriented atlas6, and the triple \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}^\uparrow)\) is then an oriented manifold. 3 \(\varepsilon\) is a symbol, the same array in every chart, not the components of a tensor field. Its upper and lower versions have the same entries; the index position only allows them to enter the summation convention. 4 (a) As for \(\varepsilon\), \(T\) vanishes on repeated indices, and each exchange of two indices flips its sign. (b) \(\det  ig( T^i_j  ig) = \sum_\sigma \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) \, T^{\sigma(1)}_1 \cdots T^{\sigma(d)}_d\), the terms with repeated indices dropping out of the sum over \(i_1, \dots, i_d\). (c) Relabelling \(i_a \leftrightarrow i_b\) shows that the left-hand side is totally antisymmetric in \(j_1, \dots, j_d\); by (a) it equals \(\varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d}\) times its value at \((1, \dots, d)\), which is \(\det  ig( T^i_j  ig)\) by (b). 5 Quantities that pick up a power \(\det ig( \partial \mathscr{X}^i / \partial \mathscr{Y}^j  ig)^w\) under a change of chart are often called densities of weight \(w\). Defining what a density is, rather than how it transforms, requires intoducing the frame bundle of \(\mathcal{M}\) and the density bundles associated with it. For this chapter the transformation law is all that is needed, and \(\omega_\mathscr{X}\) can be viewed simply as function on \(\mathcal{U}\) attached to each chart. 6 Orientability is a global property: every chart domain, equipped with its single chart, is trivially oriented. The standard example of a non-orientable manifold is the Möbius strip.

title: 8.2 Integration on Manifolds
text: Let \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}^\uparrow)\) be an oriented manifold with a volume form \(\Omega\), \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}^\uparrow\), \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), and \(\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\) the open region over which \(f\) is to be integrated, with closure \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) compact and contained in \(\mathcal{U}\)7. The indicator function \(\iota\) of \(\mathcal{D}\) cuts \(f\) off outside the region: \(\iota f\) equals \(f\) on \(\mathcal{D}\) and vanishes outside it. The integral of \(f\) over \(\mathcal{D}\) is \begin{equation} \begin{split} \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega f &\coloneqq \int_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})} d^d\alpha \, \big( \omega_\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \, \big( (\iota f) \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \\ &\overset{\substack{\iota \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \, = \, 1 \text{ on } \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D}) \\ \text{and } 0 \text{ outside}}}{=} \int_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\alpha \, \big( \omega_\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \, \big( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) , \end{split} \tag{8.3} \end{equation} an ordinary integral over the open set \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), which is bounded since \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) is compact, see Figure 8.1. This definition does not depend on the chart. Let \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}^\uparrow\) be a second chart with \(\overline{\mathcal{D}} \subseteq \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\), so that \(\int_\mathcal{D} \Omega f\) can be computed in either. The chart transition map \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} = \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\), \(\alpha = \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}(\beta)\), maps \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D})\) onto \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})\), since \(\mathscr{X}\big( \mathscr{Y}^{-1}( \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D}) ) \big) = \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})\), and \begin{align*} \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega f = &\int_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\alpha \, \big( \omega_\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \, \big( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \xlongrightarrow[d^d\alpha \, = \, d^d\beta \, |\det ( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} )(\beta)|]{\text{change of variables}} ... \\ ... = &\int_{\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\beta \, \Big| \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)(\beta) \Big| \, \big( \omega_\mathscr{X} \circ \underbrace{\mathscr{X}^{-1} \circ \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}}_{\mathscr{Y}^{-1}} \big)(\beta) \, \big( f \circ \underbrace{\mathscr{X}^{-1} \circ \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}}_{\mathscr{Y}^{-1}} \big)(\beta) \xlongrightarrow[\text{at } p \, = \, \mathscr{Y}^{-1}(\beta)]{(8.1)} ... \\ ... = &\int_{\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\beta \, \underbrace{\frac{\big| \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)(\beta) \big|}{\det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)(\beta)}}_{= \, +1 \text{ in } \mathcal{A}^\uparrow} \, \big( \omega_\mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) \, \big( f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) , \end{align*} which is (8.3) in the chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\). The absolute value produced by the change of variables is cancelled by the determinant carried by \(\omega_\mathscr{X}\) only up to its sign, and the orientation makes this sign \(+1\).

title: 8.2 Integration on Manifolds
text:
8.2.1 Integral over the Whole Manifold

A function that does not vanish outside a single chart domain is first cut into pieces that do. With \(\operatorname{supp} f \coloneqq \overline{\{ p \in \mathcal{M} \mid f(p) \neq 0 \}}\) the support of \(f\), outside which \(f\) vanishes, and \(\{ \mathcal{U}_a \}_{a \in A}\) an open cover of \(\mathcal{M}\), a partition of unity subordinate to it is a family of smooth functions \(\textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n : \mathcal{M} \to [0, 1]\) such that subordinate: each \(\operatorname{supp} \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n\) is contained in some \(\mathcal{U}_a\); locally finite: every point has a neighbourhood that meets only finitely many \(\operatorname{supp} \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n\); sums to one: \(\sum_n \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n(p) = 1\) for all \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), a finite sum at every \(p\) by 2. Multiplying by \(1 = \sum_n \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n\) splits any \(f\) into the pieces \(\textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n f\), each vanishing outside a single \(\mathcal{U}_a\). Let \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}^\uparrow)\) be an oriented manifold with a volume form \(\Omega\), \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) with \(\operatorname{supp} f\) compact, and \(\{ \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n \}\) a partition of unity subordinate to the cover of \(\mathcal{M}\) by the chart domains of \(\mathcal{A}^\uparrow\), with \(\operatorname{supp} \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n \subseteq \mathcal{U}_n\) for a chart \((\mathcal{U}_n, \mathscr{X}_n) \in \mathcal{A}^\uparrow\)8. The integral of \(f\) over \(\mathcal{M}\) is \begin{equation} \int_\mathcal{M} \Omega f \coloneqq \sum_n \int_{\mathcal{U}_n} \Omega \, \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n f . \tag{8.4} \end{equation} Each term is defined by (8.3), with \(\mathcal{D}\) any open set containing \(\operatorname{supp} \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n \cap \operatorname{supp} f\) with closure compact and contained in \(\mathcal{U}_n\): this set is compact, as a closed subset of the compact \(\operatorname{supp} f\), so such \(\mathcal{D}\) exist, and \(\iota \, \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n f = \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n f\) makes the value independent of the choice. Only finitely many terms are non-zero, since the compact \(\operatorname{supp} f\) is covered by finitely many of the neighbourhoods of item 2. The result does not depend on the partition of unity chosen. 7 The closure \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) is \(\mathcal{D}\) together with its boundary points. Its compactness makes the integral finite, and its containment in \(\mathcal{U}\) makes it an ordinary integral over a bounded region of \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\). Without these conditions the integral may diverge (Appendix B.19). 8 Such a partition of unity exists because \(\mathcal{M}\) is Hausdorff and second countable (Chapter 3). The cover by all chart domains of \(\mathcal{A}^\uparrow\) is not locally finite, since infinitely many charts contain each point, but these two properties allow it to be refined to a cover in which every point has a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many of its sets, and the partition of unity is built on this refinement (Appendix B.20).

title: 8.3 The Metric Volume Form
text: Everything above holds for any volume form. On an oriented metric manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}^\uparrow, g)\), the metric singles out one, the metric volume form \(\Omega^g\), whose components in every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}^\uparrow\) are \begin{equation} \big( \Omega^g_\mathscr{X} \big)_{i_1 \dots i_d} \coloneqq \sqrt{ \big| \det g_\mathscr{X} \big| } \; \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d}, \qquad \det g_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq \det \big( (g_\mathscr{X})_{ij} \big) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}), \tag{8.5} \end{equation} i.e. whose scalar density is \(\omega^g_\mathscr{X} = \sqrt{|\det g_\mathscr{X}|}\), smooth and positive since \(g\) is non-degenerate. On \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\), with \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}), (\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}^\uparrow\), these components transform as those of a \((0,d)\)-tensor field9: \begin{align*} \big( \Omega^g_\mathscr{Y} \big)_{j_1 \dots j_d}& \coloneqq \sqrt{\big| \det g_\mathscr{Y} \big|} \; \varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d} \, \overset{\text{Ch.~7}}{=} \, \sqrt{\Big| \det \Big( \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^{i}_{k} \, \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^{j}_{l} \, (g_\mathscr{X})_{ij} \Big) \Big|} \; \varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d} \xlongrightarrow[\text{transpose: same } \det]{\det \text{ multiplicative}} ... \\ ... = &\sqrt{\det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^2} \, \sqrt{\big| \det g_\mathscr{X} \big|} \; \varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d} = \operatorname{sgn}\big( \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big) \big) \, \sqrt{\big| \det g_\mathscr{X} \big|} \; \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big) \; \varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d} \xlongrightarrow{\text{(c)}} ... \\ ... = &\underbrace{\operatorname{sgn}\big( \det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big) \big)}_{= \, +1 \text{ in } \mathcal{A}^\uparrow} \; \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^{i_1}_{j_1} \cdots \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^{i_d}_{j_d} \, \underbrace{\sqrt{\big| \det g_\mathscr{X} \big|} \; \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d}}_{( \Omega^g_\mathscr{X} )_{i_1 \dots i_d}} = \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^{i_1}_{j_1} \cdots \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^{i_d}_{j_d} \, \big( \Omega^g_\mathscr{X} \big)_{i_1 \dots i_d} . \end{align*} The chart-wise definitions thus agree on overlaps and define a single \((0,d)\)-tensor field \(\Omega^g\), totally antisymmetric, as \(\varepsilon\) is, and nowhere vanishing: a volume form. Without the orientation, the two definitions would differ by a sign wherever \(\det \big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big) < 0\). If the chart-induced basis at \(p\) is orthonormal in the sense of Sylvester’s law of inertia, \(g_{ij}(p) = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) and \(g_{ii}(p) \in \{+1, -1\}\) (Chapter 7), then \(\omega^g_\mathscr{X}(p) = 1\): \(\Omega^g\) assigns unit volume to the parallelepiped spanned by an orthonormal basis. With \(\omega^g_\mathscr{X} = \sqrt{|\det g_\mathscr{X}|}\), the integrals (8.3) and (8.4) become, writing \(\int_\mathcal{M} f \coloneqq \int_\mathcal{M} \Omega^g f\), \[ \int_\mathcal{M} f = \sum_n \int_{\mathscr{X}_n(\mathcal{U}_n)} d^d\alpha \, \sqrt{ \big| \det g_{\mathscr{X}_n} \big| \big( \mathscr{X}_n^{-1}(\alpha) \big) } \; \big( (\textrm{\runic ᚹ}_n f) \circ \mathscr{X}_n^{-1} \big)(\alpha) , \] valid for any signature. 9 The determinants are those of the matrices of components: \(\det g_\mathscr{X}\) is a function on \(\mathcal{U}\), not a scalar field, and picks up \(\det\big( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \big)^2\) under a change of chart.

title: 9 Newton-Cartan Theory
text: Motivation: Gravity as geometry: Newton’s theory on spacetime In Newtonian mechanics, a particle of mass \(m\), described in Cartesian coordinates of an inertial frame, obeys \[ m \, \ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U}(t) = f^\alpha_\gamma(t) - m \, \partial_\alpha \Phi\big( t, \gamma_\mathcal{U}(t) \big), \qquad \sum_\alpha \partial_\alpha \partial_\alpha \Phi = 4 \pi G_N \, \rho , \] where \(f^\alpha_\gamma\) are the components of the forces acting on it and \(\Phi\) is the gravitational potential, determined by the mass density \(\rho\). The gravitational term is unlike any other force: it is proportional to the very mass that measures inertia, so \(m\) drops out of free fall, \(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} = - \partial_\alpha \Phi\), and all bodies fall alike. The pseudo-forces of rotating or accelerated frames, such as the Coriolis and centrifugal forces, share this property, and they are not caused by any body: they are produced by the choice of frame. This suggests treating gravity not as a force, but as part of the geometry, as what “straight” means. On space this fails (Appendix B.21.4), but on spacetime, the speed is part of the direction of the worldline, and the idea works. Goal: reformulate Newtonian gravity on a 4-dimensional manifold, with gravity encoded in a connection. Define a Newtonian spacetime: an absolute time \(t\) and a torsion-free connection \(\nabla\) along which time flows uniformly, with no notion of spatial distance. Rephrase Newton’s axioms: free particles follow the autoparallels of \(\nabla\), forces are measured as deviations from them, and absolute time is singled out as the parameter of every worldline. In charts adapted to absolute time, identify the pseudo-forces (Coriolis, centrifugal, Euler, translational) with connection coefficient functions created by the chart alone. Place gravity in the connection: uniform gravity is a pseudo-force, removed in a freely falling chart, whereas non-uniform gravity is curvature, which no chart removes. Poisson’s equation becomes a condition on the Ricci curvature, and the Riemann curvature measures the tidal acceleration. Already in Newton’s theory, gravity is the curvature of spacetime. General relativity (Chapter 10) keeps this insight and replaces absolute time by a Lorentzian metric and time orientation.

title: 9.1 Newtonian Spacetime
text:
Given a 4-dimensional smooth manifold \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})\), an absolute time is a scalar field  egin{align*} t \colon \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \ p &\longmapsto t(p), \end{align*} \(t \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), such that \((dt)_p 
eq 0\) \( orall p \in \mathcal{M}\). It assigns to every event the universal time at which it happens, as Newtonian physics assumes, and the condition \((dt)_p 
eq 0\) ensures that time never stands still; at every event there are directions along which \(t\) increases.
