For the action below it leads to the same field equations (not shown here). 6 There, compactness of \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) makes the integral finite, and its containment in the chart domain makes it an ordinary integral over a bounded region (Appendix B.19). 7 By Sylvester’s law of inertia, \((g_{ij}(p)) = \mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \, \mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1) \, \mathbf{A}\) for an invertible \(\mathbf{A}\), so \(\det g = - (\det \mathbf{A})^2 < 0\). 8 The prefactor plays no role in vacuum; it fixes the coupling to matter (Section 10.3). With \((+, -, -, -)\) and \(\mathrm{Ric}_{ab} = \mathrm{Riem}^m{}_{amb}\), \(\kappa = - 1/(16 \pi G_N)\) (Landau and Lifshitz, 1975); with \((-, +, +, +)\), \(R\) changes sign and \(\kappa = + 1/(16 \pi G_N)\) (Poisson, 2004). The speed of light is \(1\). 9 This keeps every \(g_{	extrm{unic ᛊ}}\) a metric on all of \(\mathcal{M}\) and lets \(	extrm{unic ᛉ}\) be described in one chart. It is no restriction: \(S_\mathcal{D}[g_{	extrm{unic ᛊ}}]\) only depends on \(	extrm{unic ᛉ}\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) (Figure 10.2; Appendix B.20).

title: 10.3 Coupling to Matter
text: Matter enters through its own action, added to \(S_\mathcal{D}\). Varying the matter fields gives their equations on the curved spacetime; varying the metric gives the Einstein equations with a source, the energy-momentum tensor. The Setting is that of Subsection 10.2.2. Total action. For matter fields \(\Phi\) (tensor fields on \(\mathcal{M}\)) and a scalar field \(\mathcal{L}_M\) built from \(\Phi\), its derivatives and \(g\), \(S_M[g, \Phi] \coloneqq \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega^g \mathcal{L}_M\). The total action \(S_\mathcal{D} + S_M\) is required to be critical under two independent kinds of variations: of \(\Phi\) with \(g\) fixed, which give the matter field equations, and of \(g\) with \(\Phi\) fixed. Energy-momentum tensor. The response of \(S_M\) to a change of the metric defines the symmetric \((0,2)\)-tensor field \(T\) (Landau and Lifshitz, 1975): \[ \boxed{ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} S_M[g_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}, \Phi] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = - \frac{1}{2} \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega^g \, (T^{\flat^{-1}})^{ij} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_{ij} , \qquad (T^{\flat^{-1}})^{ij} = (g^{-1})^{ia} \, (g^{-1})^{jb} \, T_{ab} , } \] for every admissible \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\), uniquely by step 5. If \(\mathcal{L}_M\) contains no derivatives of \(g\), then \(\delta \mathcal{L}_M = \Theta^{ij} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_{ij}\) with \(\Theta\) symmetric, and panel (A) of Figure 10.3 gives \[ (T^{\flat^{-1}})^{ij} = - 2 \, \Theta^{ij} - \mathcal{L}_M \, (g^{-1})^{ij} , \] the second term coming from the volume element. Derivatives of \(g\) in \(\mathcal{L}_M\) are first moved off \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) as in step 4. Einstein equations. With \(- \kappa = 1/(16 \pi G_N)\), the variation of \(S_\mathcal{D} + S_M\) in \(g\) is \(\int_\mathcal{D} \Omega^g \big( \frac{1}{16 \pi G_N} (\hat{G})^{ij} - \frac{1}{2} (T^{\flat^{-1}})^{ij} \big) \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_{ij}\), and step 5 gives \[ \boxed{ G = 8 \pi G_N \, T . } \] \(T\) is to the metric what a current is to the electromagnetic potential: the response of the action to a change of it. The contracted Bianchi identity (Subsection B.18.10) forces \((g^{-1})^{kl} (\nabla_{\partial x_k} T)_{ln} = 0\), local conservation of energy and momentum, which a chart-independent \(\mathcal{L}_M\) guarantees through the matter field equations. The normalization of \(T\) gives the familiar energy densities and fluxes, and \(\mathrm{Ric}_{00} = 4 \pi G_N \rho\) of Chapter 9 in the Newtonian limit. Example: electromagnetism. For the potential \(\mathsf{A}\), with \(F_{ij} = \partial_i \mathtt{a}_j - \partial_j \mathtt{a}_i\) and \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{EM}} = - \frac{1}{4} F_{ab} (F^{\flat^{-1}})^{ab}\), the two kinds of variations give the Einstein–Maxwell equations (Appendix in preparation) \[ G_{mn} = 8 \pi G_N \Big( - (g^{-1})^{bd} \, F_{mb} \, F_{nd} + \frac{1}{4} \, g_{mn} \, F_{ab} \, (F^{\flat^{-1}})^{ab} \Big), \qquad (\nabla_{\partial x_a} F^{\flat^{-1}})^{ab} = 0 . \]

title: A Computational ressources
text: Almost all the figures, examples, and visualizations in these notes have been produced with Differential Geometry Tools, a Python package developed by the author alongside the text. The package is openly available at github.com/daniellopezcano/differential_geometry so that every figure can be regenerated, every example rerun, and every construction modified and explored by the reader. Open science. The repository is released under the MIT license, which allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute the code, for teaching, research, or any other purpose, with the only requirement of preserving the original copyright and license notice. This choice reflects a conviction that runs through the whole project: educational material, like scientific results, gains value when it is transparent and reproducible. Making the code public means that the figures in these notes are not illustrations to be taken on trust, but the output of computations that anyone can inspect, check, and improve. Suggestions, corrections, and contributions are warmly welcome. Design goals. The package aims at providing a collection of simple, easy-to-use classes that mirror the objects introduced throughout the lectures, from manifolds, charts, and curves to fields and the structures built on top of them. Each class is kept as close as possible to its mathematical definition, so that the code can be read side by side with the text rather than as a black box. The package is built on JAX, whose automatic differentiation computes the derivatives that pervade differential geometry (Jacobians, tangent vectors, directional derivatives, or the change of components between charts) exactly and without any manual derivation. Beyond producing the figures of these notes, the same tools can be used to build more elaborate or interactive visualizations, and to test the abstract constructions on examples of one’s own choosing. Why code matters. Differential geometry is a subject where the formalism can easily run ahead of intuition. Writing code is a remarkably effective way of closing that gap, for at least three reasons. First, a computer accepts no vague definitions: to implement a tangent vector, a covector, or a field, one must state precisely where it lives, what it acts on, and what it returns – exactly the discipline these notes try to cultivate when specifying every map through its domain and target. Second, the distinctions that are most often blurred on paper, such as the one between a geometric object and its components in a given chart, become unavoidable in code, where every component must be computed with respect to an explicitly chosen chart. Third, abstract statements become checkable: a transformation law, the chart independence of a pairing, or the smoothness of a transition map can be verified numerically in a few lines, and one can vary a chart, a curve, or a field and immediately see what changes and what does not. In this sense, the package is meant as a computational counterpart to the text: not a replacement for the formal definitions, but a laboratory in which to experiment with them. An evolving resource. The repository is actively developed, and its contents may grow beyond what is described or used in these notes. The notes present the ideas; the repository reflects the current state of the tools built around them. Readers are encouraged to explore it, adapt it to their own needs, and use it as a starting point for visualizations and experiments of their own.

title: B.1 Set Theory Foundations (§2.1)
text: This appendix expands on the brief remark made in Section 2.1 regarding the set-theoretic foundations underlying the definitions of sets, maps, and algebraic structures. It summarizes the role of axiomatic set theory—particularly the Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC)—as the formal foundation upon which modern mathematics, including the material in these notes, is built. Formally, the notions of set, element, subset, intersection, union, and related concepts are rigorously grounded in axiomatic set theory. The most commonly used framework is Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice (abbreviated ZFC). This system provides a widely accepted foundation for modern mathematics, resolving classical paradoxes such as Russell’s paradox and enabling the construction of virtually all mathematical objects encountered in fields like analysis, topology, and geometry. The Axiom of Choice (AC) plays a subtle but significant role within this framework. It is indispensable for certain results—such as Tychonoff’s theorem in topology, or the fact that every vector space admits a basis—but it also leads to counterintuitive consequences, including the existence of non-measurable sets and the Banach-Tarski paradox. Despite this, the use of AC is standard in most of pure mathematics, including the framework employed throughout these notes. It is worth noting that ZFC is not the only possible foundation for mathematics. Some branches explore alternatives such as ZF without Choice, category-theoretic frameworks like Elementary Topos Theory, or type-theoretic foundations like Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT). These frameworks differ in how they treat objects, collections, and logical inference, sometimes avoiding certain pathologies at the cost of restricting other constructions. Nevertheless, for the purposes of these notes, we adopt a pragmatic approach based on the standard ZFC framework: sets are well-defined collections of elements, and all operations we employ are assumed to be well-behaved within this context. A deep exploration of the logical and philosophical foundations of mathematics—including formal logic, model theory, and metamathematics—is essential in its own right but lies beyond the scope of this text. We must start somewhere.

title: B.2 Hamel and Schauder Bases (§2.3)
text: This appendix expands on the brief comment made in Section 2.3 regarding the nature of bases in vector spaces. Specifically, it clarifies the distinction between Hamel bases, which rely on finite linear combinations, and Schauder bases, which involve infinite sums defined only when a compatible topology is present. The concept of a basis in linear algebra—formally called a Hamel basis—requires that every vector in the space can be expressed as a finite linear combination of elements from the basis. This finite expansion is fundamental to the definition of a basis in the context of pure vector spaces. Specifically, the decomposition \[ \mathcal{X} = (x^1 \cdot \hat{x}_1) \oplus \dots \oplus (x^d \cdot \hat{x}_d) \] must always involve only finitely many terms for any vector \(\mathcal{X} \in V\). If we were to drop the requirement that only finite sums are allowed in the decomposition, the expression for a vector would become an infinite sum, i.e., an infinite series. However, the concept of summing infinitely many vectors is not meaningful in the context of pure vector spaces alone, since the axioms of vector spaces do not include any notion of limit, convergence, or closeness. To give meaning to such infinite sums, the vector space must be equipped with additional structure, specifically, a topology compatible with the vector space operations. This leads to the concept of a topological vector space, and in particular, to the notion of a Schauder basis (also called a topological basis). A Schauder basis allows vectors to be expressed as (potentially) infinite sums that converge in the topology of the space. The distinction between Hamel and Schauder bases has profound consequences: In finite-dimensional vector spaces, the two notions coincide trivially, since infinite sums do not arise. In infinite-dimensional vector spaces, a Hamel basis always exists (assuming the Axiom of Choice), but it is almost never useful in practice. Hamel bases for function spaces like \(L^2([0,1])\)—the set of all square-integrable functions on the interval \([0,1]\)—are uncountably infinite, highly pathological, and bear no relation to the orthonormal bases commonly used in analysis (such as Fourier bases), which are Schauder bases. Conversely, Schauder bases are countable (when they exist) and tied to the topology of the space. These bases enable the powerful machinery of infinite series and convergence, which is essential for functional analysis, partial differential equations, and quantum mechanics. In summary, the restriction to finite sums in the definition of a Hamel basis is not an arbitrary technicality but a fundamental reflection of the fact that pure vector spaces, as defined in algebra, do not possess any notion of convergence or topology.

title: B.3 Change of basis for the dual basis (§2.3)
text: In this appendix, we provide a formal proof that the change-of-basis matrix that relates two dual bases is the same matrix that governs the transformation of vector components (see Section 2.3). Let \(\{\hat{x}_i\}\) and \(\{\hat{y}_i\}\) be two bases of the vector space \((V, \oplus, \odot)\), related by: \begin{align*} \hat{x}_i = \sum_{j=1}^d J^j_{i} \cdot \hat{y}_j, \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, d. \end{align*} Let \(\{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i\}\) and \(\{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i\}\) be the dual bases associated to \(\{\hat{x}_i\}\) and \(\{\hat{y}_i\}\), respectively, defined by the canonical pairing condition: \begin{align*} \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i(\hat{x}_j) = \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i(\hat{y}_j) = \delta^i_j. \end{align*} We express \(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i\) in terms of \(\{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^j\}\): \begin{align*} \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i = \sum_{j=1}^d A^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^j. \end{align*} Applying both sides to \(\hat{y}_k\): \begin{align*} \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i(\hat{y}_k) &= \sum_{j=1}^d A^i_{j} \cdot \underbrace{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^j (\hat{y}_k)}_{= \delta^j_k} \longrightarrow \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i\left( \sum_{m=1}^d (J^{-1})^m_{k} \cdot \hat{x}_m \right) = A^i_{k} \\ \longrightarrow & \sum_{m=1}^d (J^{-1})^m_{k} \cdot \underbrace{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i\left(\hat{x}_m\right)}_{= \delta^i_m} = A^i_{k} \longrightarrow A^i_{k} = (J^{-1})^i_{k}. \end{align*} We conclude that the change-of-basis relation for the dual bases reads: \begin{align*} \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i = \sum_{j=1}^d (J^{-1})^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^j, \end{align*}

title: B.4 Curves realizing the vector space operations of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) (§4.1)
text: In Section 4.1 we defined the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) at a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) as the collection of velocity linear maps associated with smooth curves passing through \(p\). The algebraic structure of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) as a real vector space was introduced by endowing it with the operations of addition and s-multiplication, defined operationally via their action on smooth functions \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\): \begin{align*} (v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p})(f) &\coloneqq v_{\gamma_1, p}(f) + v_{\gamma_2, p}(f), \\ (\alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma, p})(f) &\coloneqq \alpha \cdot v_{\gamma, p}(f). \end{align*} While these definitions correctly encode the vector space axioms, an important subtlety arises from the fact that each tangent vector is itself defined via the velocity of some smooth curve passing through \(p\). Therefore, to guarantee that \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) is closed under \(\oplus_T\) and \(\odot_T\)—that is, that the result of these operations still corresponds to the velocity of a smooth curve passing through \(p\)—it is necessary to demonstrate that such curves indeed exist. In other words, we must prove the following: For any two smooth curves \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) passing through \(p\), there exists a third smooth curve \(\sigma\) whose velocity satisfies \(v_{\sigma, p} = v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p}.\) For any smooth curve \(\gamma\) passing through \(p\) and any real scalar \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), there exists a smooth curve \({\sigma}\) whose velocity satisfies \(v_{{\sigma}, p} = \alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma, p}.\) This appendix provides a constructive proof of these facts: To prove the existence of a smooth curve realizing the addition operation \(v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p}\) for two tangent vectors \(v_{\gamma_1, p}, v_{\gamma_2, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\), we proceed as follows. Let \(\gamma_1, \gamma_2 : \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\) be two smooth curves passing through \(p\), i.e., there exist parameters \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\gamma_1(\lambda_1) = \gamma_2(\lambda_2) = p\). We construct a new curve \(\sigma_{\mathscr{X}} : \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\), defined in terms of a local chart \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right)\) with \(p \in \mathcal{U}\), as follows: \begin{align} \sigma_{\mathscr{X}}(\lambda) := \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big[ (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1)(\lambda_1 + \lambda) + (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2)(\lambda_2 + \lambda) - (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1)(\lambda_1) \big] =... \tag{B.1}\\ ... = \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big[ (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_1)(\lambda) + (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_2)(\lambda) - (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\varnothing)(\lambda) \big]=... \tag{B.2}\\ ... = \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big[ \big( (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_1) + (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_2) - (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\varnothing)\big) \big] (\lambda). \tag{B.3} \end{align} Where we have defined the reparametrization functions \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_1 \colon \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_1(\lambda) \coloneqq \lambda + \lambda_1 \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_2 \colon \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_2(\lambda) \coloneqq \lambda + \lambda_2 \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\varnothing \colon \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\varnothing(\lambda) \coloneqq \lambda_1 \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] This construction corresponds, in local coordinates, to performing a vector addition of the coordinate representations of the curves’ increments around the point \(p\). It is immediate to verify that \(\sigma(0) = p\). Now applying the multidimensional chain rule (check the footnote in subsection 4.1.1) forwards and then backwards: \begin{align*} v_{\sigma_{\mathscr{X}}, p}(f) &:= (f \circ \sigma_{\mathscr{X}})'(0) = \left( f \circ (\mathscr{X}^{-1} \circ \mathscr{X}) \circ \sigma_{\mathscr{X}} \right)'(0) = \left( (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \circ (\mathscr{X} \circ \sigma_{\mathscr{X}}) \right)'(0) \\ &= \sum_{i} \left\lbrace \left[ (\mathscr{X} \circ \sigma_{\mathscr{X}})_i \right]'(0) \cdot \partial_i (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \right\rbrace \\ &= \sum_{i} \left\lbrace \left[ (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_1)_i'(0) + (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_2)_i'(0) - (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1 \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\varnothing)_i'(0) \right] \cdot \partial_i (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \right\rbrace \\ &= \sum_{i} \left\lbrace \left[ (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1)_i'(\lambda_1) + (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2)_i'(\lambda_2) \right] \cdot \partial_i (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \right\rbrace \\ &= \sum_{i} \left\lbrace (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1)_i'(\lambda_1) \cdot \partial_i (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) + (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2)_i'(\lambda_2) \cdot \partial_i (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \right\rbrace \\ &= \left( (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \circ (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1) \right)'(\lambda_1) + \left( (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \circ (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2) \right)'(\lambda_2) \\ &= \left( f \circ (\mathscr{X}^{-1} \circ \mathscr{X}) \circ \gamma_1 \right)'(\lambda_1) + \left( f \circ (\mathscr{X}^{-1} \circ \mathscr{X}) \circ \gamma_2 \right)'(\lambda_2) \\ &= (f \circ \gamma_1)'(\lambda_1) + (f \circ \gamma_2)'(\lambda_2) \\ &= v_{\gamma_1, p}(f) + v_{\gamma_2, p}(f). \end{align*} which confirms that the curve \(\sigma\) realizes the tangent vector \(v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p}\) according to the operational definition of addition in the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\). As anticipated, while the construction was carried out using a local chart, the resulting tangent vector is independent of the chosen chart, since the final expression for the velocity depends only on derivatives evaluated at \(p\), which transform covariantly under chart transitions. To prove the existence of a smooth curve realizing the scalar multiplication operation \(\alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma, p}\) for a given tangent vector \(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\) and scalar \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\), we proceed as follows. Let \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\) be any smooth curve passing through \(p\), i.e., such that \(\exists \lambda_1 \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(\gamma(\lambda_1) = p\). We construct the reparametrized curve \({\sigma} : \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\) as: \begin{align*} {\sigma}(\lambda) \coloneqq \gamma\big(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha(\lambda)\big) = (\gamma \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha)(\lambda), \end{align*} where the reparametrization function \(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha\) is defined by: \begin{align*} \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha : \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha(\lambda) \coloneqq \alpha\lambda + \lambda_1. \end{align*} It is immediate to verify that \({\sigma}(0) = \gamma(\lambda_1) = p\), so \({\sigma}\) is indeed a curve passing through \(p\). Now, applying the chain rule for the composition of smooth functions, we compute the velocity of \({\sigma}\) at \(p\) with respect to any smooth function \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\): \begin{align*} v_{\sigma, p}(f) &\coloneqq (f \circ {\sigma})'(0) = \frac{d}{d\lambda}\Big|_{\lambda=0} (f \circ \gamma \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha)(\lambda) = ...\\ ...& = \textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha'(0) \cdot (f \circ \gamma)'(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}_\alpha(0)) = \alpha \cdot (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_1) = \alpha \cdot v_{\gamma, p}(f). \end{align*} This shows that the curve \({\sigma}\) realizes the scalar multiple \(\alpha \odot_T v_{\gamma, p}\) according to the operational definition of scalar multiplication in the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\).

title: B.5 Chart-induced basis of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) (§4.1.1)
text: In this appendix, we provide a formal proof that the set of chart-induced vectors \[ \left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \right)_p,\; \ldots,\; \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^d} \right)_p \right\rbrace \] constitutes a basis for the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) at a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), associated with a given chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) containing \(p\). While this fact is often presented as an immediate consequence of definitions, it is instructive—and mathematically rigorous—to explicitly verify that these elements indeed satisfy the conditions of a basis: Spanning: Any \(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\) can be written as a linear combination of the basis elements in \(e\). This condition holds immediately from the expression given in Section 4.1.1: \begin{align*} v_{\gamma, p} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} \end{align*} Here we show that any tangent vector \(v_{\gamma, p}\) can be represented in a chart \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right)\) as the linear combination of the basis elements \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}\). Linear independence: The only linear combination of basis elements that yields the zero vector in \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) is the trivial one where all coefficients vanish. To see this, suppose that some linear combination of the basis elements gives the zero vector: \begin{align*} 0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}. \end{align*} Our goal here is to check if this condition holds only when all the coefficients \(\alpha^i\) are zero independently (if so, we will have proven linear independence), or if there exists other possible combinations of the coefficients \(\alpha^i\) that also yield the zero vector as a result. If we now let this expression (both sides) act upon any arbitrary basis element \(\mathscr{X}^j\): \begin{align*} 0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (\mathscr{X}^j). \end{align*} At this point we need to realize that, by definition (see Section 4.1.1): \begin{align*} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (\mathscr{X}^j) = \partial_i \underbrace{\left[ \mathscr{X}^j \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right]}_{\mathbb{R} \longleftarrow \mathbb{R}^d} (\mathscr{X}(p)) = \delta^j_i. \end{align*} This is a direct consequence of the fact that the operator \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p\) measures the rate of change of any function along the \(i\)-th coordinate direction at the point \(p\). When applied to the coordinate function \(\mathscr{X}^j\), which simply “extracts” the \(j\)-th coordinate, it yields \(1\) if it differentiates with respect to its own direction (\(i = j\)), and \(0\) otherwise. Substituting everything on our original expression we have: \begin{align*} 0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (\mathscr{X}^j). \;\iff\; 0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \delta^j_i = \alpha^j \quad \forall j=1,\dots,d. \end{align*} The conclusion \(\alpha^j = 0\) for all \(j\) follows immediately because we have let the original expression act upon any arbitrary basis element \(\mathscr{X}^j\). Therefore, the assumption that the linear combination vanishes implies that each individual coefficient must be zero independently. This guarantees that no non-trivial linear dependence exists among the basis elements, completing the proof of linear independence.

title: B.6 Chart-induced basis of \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) (§4.2.1)
text: In this appendix, we provide a formal proof that the set of chart-induced covectors \[ \left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^1)_p,\; \ldots,\; (d\mathscr{X}^d)_p \right\rbrace \] constitutes a basis for the cotangent space \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) at a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), associated with a given chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) containing \(p\). This amounts to verifying that these elements satisfy the conditions of a basis, additionally, we also show here that this set is the dual basis induced by the tangent basis \(\left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \right)_p, \dots, \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^d} \right)_p \right\rbrace\): Duality pairing with the tangent basis: First, we recall that the covector \((d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\) acts on the chart-induced vector \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p\) as: \begin{align*} (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p &= \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p (\mathscr{X}^i) = \delta^i_j. \end{align*} This holds because the action of \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p\) on the coordinate function \(\mathscr{X}^i\) yields \(1\) if \(i = j\) and \(0\) otherwise (see Section B.5). This result immediately guarantees that the set \(\left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\rbrace\) forms the dual basis to \(\left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p \right\rbrace\). Linear independence: Suppose that some linear combination of the covectors yields the zero covector: \begin{align*} 0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p, \qquad \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}. \end{align*} Our goal here is to check if this condition holds only when all the coefficients \(\alpha^i\) are zero independently (if so, we will have proven linear independence), or if there exists other possible combinations of the coefficients \(\alpha^i\) that also yield the zero vector as a result. Let this expression act on any arbitrary basis vector \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p\): \begin{align*} 0 &= \left( \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right) \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot \delta^i_j = \alpha_j. \end{align*} Since this holds for arbitrary \(j = 1, \dots, d\), it immediately follows that \(\alpha_j = 0\) for all \(j\). Therefore, the set \(\left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\rbrace\) is linearly independent. Spanning: Let \(\mathsf{X} \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) be an arbitrary covector. Since \(\mathsf{X}\) is a linear map on \(T_p\mathcal{M}\), its action is fully determined by its values on the basis vectors \(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p\). These values are real numbers: \begin{align*} \mathtt{x}^i \coloneqq \mathsf{X} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad \forall i = 1, \dots, d. \end{align*} We call these the covector components of \(\mathsf{X}\) in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\). We now claim that the covector \begin{align*} \tilde{\mathsf{X}} \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \end{align*} coincides with \(\mathsf{X}\). Let us verify that \(\tilde{\mathsf{X}}\) and \(\mathsf{X}\) agree upon acting on any vector \(v_{\gamma,p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\). Applying \(\tilde{\mathsf{X}}\) to \(v_{\gamma,p}\): \begin{align*} \tilde{\mathsf{X}}(v_{\gamma,p}) &= \left( \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right) (v_{\gamma,p}) = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p (v_{\gamma,p}) = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \left( \sum_{j=1}^d \dot{\gamma}^j(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p \right) \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}^i \cdot \left[ \sum_{j=1}^d \dot{\gamma}^j(\lambda_0) \cdot \underbrace{(d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p}_{\delta^i_j} \right] = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}^i \cdot \dot{\gamma}^i(\lambda_0) = \mathsf{X} \left( \sum_{i=1}^d \dot{\gamma}^i(\lambda_0) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p \right) \\ &= \mathsf{X}(v_{\gamma,p}). \quad \square \end{align*}

title: B.7 The topology of the tangent bundle (§5.1)
text: We prove that \(\mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\), as defined in Section 5.1, is a topology on \(T\mathcal{M}\), and that w.r.t. it every \(T\mathcal{U}\) is open, every bundle chart map \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) is a homeomorphism onto \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\pi\) is continuous. The only inputs are that every \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) is a bijection onto the open set \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\), and that every transition map \(\xi_{\mathscr{Y}} \circ \xi_{\mathscr{X}}^{-1}\) is a homeomorphism (in fact a smooth bijection with smooth inverse) between the open sets \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\). \(\mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\) is a topology. \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}(\emptyset \cap T\mathcal{U}) = \emptyset\) and \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}(T\mathcal{M} \cap T\mathcal{U}) = \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\) are open for every chart, so \(\emptyset, T\mathcal{M} \in \mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\). Since \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) is injective, images commute with intersections: \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\big( (W_1 \cap W_2) \cap T\mathcal{U} \big) = \xi_{\mathscr{X}}(W_1 \cap T\mathcal{U}) \cap \xi_{\mathscr{X}}(W_2 \cap T\mathcal{U})\), an intersection of two open sets. Images always commute with unions: \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\big( (\bigcup_\alpha W_\alpha) \cap T\mathcal{U} \big) = \bigcup_\alpha \xi_{\mathscr{X}}(W_\alpha \cap T\mathcal{U})\), a union of open sets. Every \(T\mathcal{V}\) is open: for every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}(T\mathcal{V} \cap T\mathcal{U}) = \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\), which is open. Every \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\) is a homeomorphism onto \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\). It is a bijection by construction. Open map: if \(W \subseteq T\mathcal{U}\) is open, then \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}(W) = \xi_{\mathscr{X}}(W \cap T\mathcal{U})\) is open by definition of \(\mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\). Continuity: let \(O \subseteq \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d\) be open and \(W \coloneqq \xi_{\mathscr{X}}^{-1}(O)\). For any chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), \[ \xi_{\mathscr{Y}}(W \cap T\mathcal{V}) = \big( \xi_{\mathscr{Y}} \circ \xi_{\mathscr{X}}^{-1} \big)\Big( O \cap \big( \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \times \mathbb{R}^d \big) \Big), \] the image of an open set under a homeomorphism between open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^{2d}\), hence open. Thus \(W \in \mathcal{O}_{T\mathcal{M}}\). \(\pi\) is continuous: for \(\mathcal{U}' \in \mathcal{O}\) and every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), \(\xi_{\mathscr{X}}\big( \operatorname{preim}_\pi(\mathcal{U}') \cap T\mathcal{U} \big) = \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{U}') \times \mathbb{R}^d\), which is open. \(\square\)

title: B.8 Which covector fields are differentials? (§5.2)
text: In Section 4.2 we saw that, at a single point, every covector is a differential: for every \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) there is some \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) with \(\mathsf{X}_p = (df)_p\). It is natural to ask whether this statement survives the promotion from a point to the whole manifold: Given a smooth covector field \(\mathsf{X} \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\), is there a single scalar field \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) such that \(\mathsf{X} = df\) everywhere? The answer is “not always”, and it depends on the scale at which the question is asked: at a single point, on a small region around each point, or on the whole manifold. We go through the three scales in turn, and see that each one brings in a new obstruction. Technical names are introduced only at the end, once the ideas behind them are clear.

title: B.8 Which covector fields are differentials? (§5.2)
text:
Two rules for computing differentials

Since \((df)_p(v_{\gamma, p}) \coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}(f) = (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0)\), differentials inherit the rules of ordinary derivatives. For all scalar fields \(f, g\) and all \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\): \begin{align*} \underbrace{d\big( f \oplus_{C^\infty} \alpha \odot g \big) = df \oplus^*_\Gamma \alpha \odot^*_\Gamma dg}_{\text{linearity}}, \qquad\qquad \underbrace{d\big( f \odot_{C^\infty} g \big) = f \odot^*_\Gamma dg \oplus^*_\Gamma g \odot^*_\Gamma df}_{\text{Leibniz rule}}. \end{align*} The first follows from the linearity of the ordinary derivative, and the second, at each point \(p = \gamma(\lambda_0)\), from the product rule, \(\big( (f g) \circ \gamma \big)'(\lambda_0) = f(p) \cdot (g \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) + g(p) \cdot (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0)\). In particular, the differential of a constant function vanishes, so constants can be moved freely in and out of \(d\). Both rules hold equally for functions defined only on an open set \(\mathcal{U}\), such as the coordinate maps \(\mathscr{X}^i\) of a chart. These two rules are all we need to understand what goes on below.

title: B.8 Which covector fields are differentials? (§5.2)
section: Scale 1: at a point, every covector is a differential
text:
Scale 1: at a point, every covector is a differential

Fix a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around \(p\). The dual chart-induced basis consists of differentials already, those of the coordinate maps, and any covector at \(p\) is a combination of them, \(\mathsf{X}_p = \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\). The coefficients \(\mathtt{x}_i^p\) are real numbers, i.e. constants, so by linearity they can be moved inside the differential: \begin{align*} \mathsf{X}_p = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p = \big( d f_p \big)_p, \qquad \text{with} \qquad f_p \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i^p \odot \mathscr{X}^i. \end{align*} In the chart, \(f_p\) is simply the linear function whose slopes are the components of \(\mathsf{X}_p\), \((f_p \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1})(\alpha) = \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i^p \alpha^i\). It is defined only on \(\mathcal{U}\), but a bump function extends it to all of \(\mathcal{M}\) without changing its differential at \(p\) (see the footnote in Section 4.2). This is why it is legitimate to think of any covector at a point as a differential.

title: B.8 Which covector fields are differentials? (§5.2)
section: Scale 2: on a region, the coefficients stop being constants
text:
Scale 2: on a region, the coefficients stop being constants

Now consider a covector field \(\mathsf{X}\). Over a chart domain it decomposes as (Section 5.3) \begin{align*} \left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^i, \qquad \mathtt{x}_i \coloneqq \left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} \left\lceil \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right\rfloor \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}). \end{align*} At every point \(p \in \mathcal{U}\), the recipe of Scale 1 produces a function \(f_p\) with \((df_p)_p = \mathsf{X}_p\), but a different one for each point, since the slopes \(\mathtt{x}_i(p)\) change from point to point. The natural attempt to glue all of them into a single function is to replace the constant slopes by the component functions, \(f \coloneqq \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i \odot_{C^\infty} \mathscr{X}^i\). But now the coefficients are no longer constants, and the Leibniz rule produces an extra term: \begin{align*} d\Big( \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \odot_{C^\infty} \mathscr{X}^i \Big) = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^i}_{\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U}} \;\oplus^*_\Gamma\; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^d \mathscr{X}^i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathtt{x}_i}_{\text{extra term}}. \end{align*} The extra term comes entirely from the variation of the components across the region. This particular attempt fails, but some cleverer function might still work. To decide whether one does, we need a criterion. A necessary condition. If \(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = df\) for some \(f\), then its components are not arbitrary: using \(df\lceil \mathcal{X} \rfloor = \mathcal{X}\lfloor f \rceil\), \begin{align*} \mathtt{x}_i = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad \mathtt{x}_i(p) = \partial_i \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big), \end{align*} so all of them are partial derivatives of one and the same function \(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\). Differentiating once more, and using that mixed partial derivatives commute (Schwarz’s theorem), we obtain \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_i \right\rceil = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_j \right\rceil \qquad \forall \, i, j = 1, \dots, d. \tag{S} \end{align*} This symmetry condition does not depend on the chart used to write it, so it is a property of \(\mathsf{X}\) itself: under a change of chart, the Leibniz rule produces extra terms containing second derivatives of the chart transition map, which are symmetric in \(i\) and \(j\) and therefore cancel in the difference of both sides of (S). Example. On \(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}^2\) with the cartesian chart \(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a, b)\), consider the covector field with component functions \((\mathtt{x}_1, \mathtt{x}_2) = (-b, a)\), i.e. \(\mathsf{X} = (-\mathscr{X}^2) \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^1 \oplus^*_\Gamma \mathscr{X}^1 \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^2\). Then \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_2 \right\rceil = 1 \;\neq\; -1 = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_1 \right\rceil, \end{align*} so there is no scalar field \(f\) with \(\mathsf{X} = df\), neither on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) nor on any open set, however small. Pointwise, of course, nothing is wrong: at a point \(p\) with \(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a_p, b_p)\), Scale 1 gives \(\mathsf{X}_p = (df_p)_p\) with \(f_p = (-b_p) \odot \mathscr{X}^1 \oplus a_p \odot \mathscr{X}^2\). What fails is that these linear functions differ from point to point, and no single function reproduces all of them at once. Exact fields do not form a module. The Leibniz rule also explains why the module \(\Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\) of Section 5.2 had to be built from all smooth sections, and not only from differentials. Differentials are closed under addition, \(df \oplus^*_\Gamma dg = d(f \oplus_{C^\infty} g)\), but not under s-multiplication by scalar fields: rearranging the Leibniz rule, \begin{align*} h \odot^*_\Gamma df = d\big( h \odot_{C^\infty} f \big) \oplus^*_\Gamma (-f) \odot^*_\Gamma dh, \end{align*} which, because of the last term, is in general not a differential. For instance, \(\mathscr{X}^1 \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has components \((\mathtt{x}_1, \mathtt{x}_2) = (0, a)\) and violates (S). The condition is also sufficient on a ball. Conversely, suppose that \(\mathsf{X}\) satisfies (S) on a chart domain whose image \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\) is a ball centred at the origin of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Writing \(\bar{\mathtt{x}}_i \coloneqq \mathtt{x}_i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) for the chart representatives of the components, we can build the missing function explicitly, by adding up the values of \(\mathsf{X}\) along the straight segment from the origin to each point \(\alpha \in \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\): \begin{align*} F(\alpha) \coloneqq \int_0^1 \sum_{i=1}^d \bar{\mathtt{x}}_i(t \alpha) \, \alpha^i \, dt, \qquad f \coloneqq F \circ \mathscr{X}. \end{align*} Differentiating under the integral sign, using (S) to exchange the indices, and recognizing a total derivative in \(t\), \begin{align*} \partial_j F(\alpha) &= \int_0^1 \Big[ \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) + \sum_{i=1}^d t \, \alpha^i \, \partial_j \bar{\mathtt{x}}_i(t\alpha) \Big] dt \overset{\text{(S)}}{=} \int_0^1 \Big[ \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) + \sum_{i=1}^d t \, \alpha^i \, \partial_i \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) \Big] dt \\ &= \int_0^1 \frac{d}{dt} \Big[ t \, \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) \Big] dt = \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(\alpha), \end{align*} i.e. \(\mathtt{x}_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \lfloor f \rceil\), and hence \(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = df\). Since every point has a chart neighbourhood whose image is a ball, we conclude that at this scale (S) is both necessary and sufficient: a covector field is a differential near every point if and only if it satisfies (S).

title: B.8 Which covector fields are differentials? (§5.2)
section: Integrating a covector field along a curve
text:
Integrating a covector field along a curve

To understand the last scale we need one more tool, which in fact we have just used: the integral \(F(\alpha)\) above adds up the values of \(\mathsf{X}\) along a segment. In general, given a smooth curve \(\gamma\) and a parameter interval \([\lambda_a, \lambda_b]\), at each \(\lambda\) the covector \(\mathsf{X}_{\gamma(\lambda)}\) can eat the velocity of the curve, producing a real number. Adding up these numbers along the curve defines the integral of \(\mathsf{X}\) along \(\gamma\), \begin{align*} \int_\gamma \mathsf{X} \coloneqq \int_{\lambda_a}^{\lambda_b} \mathsf{X}_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) \, d\lambda = \int_{\lambda_a}^{\lambda_b} \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i\big(\gamma(\lambda)\big) \cdot \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, d\lambda, \end{align*} where the second expression holds whenever the curve stays inside the chart domain \(\mathcal{U}\). If \(\mathsf{X} = df\), the integrand is, by definition of the differential and of the velocity, \((df)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) = v_{\gamma(\lambda)}(f) = (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda)\), and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \begin{align*} \int_\gamma df = f\big(\gamma(\lambda_b)\big) - f\big(\gamma(\lambda_a)\big). \end{align*} The integral of a differential only depends on the endpoints of the curve, not on the path in between. In particular, for a closed curve, one that returns to its starting point, the integral of a differential always vanishes. This also works in the opposite direction, and tells us how to build \(f\) from \(\mathsf{X}\) on a connected manifold. Fix a reference point \(p_0\), and define \(f(p)\) as the integral of \(\mathsf{X}\) along any curve from \(p_0\) to \(p\)1. This is a sensible definition precisely when the result does not depend on the curve chosen; and since two curves from \(p_0\) to \(p\) form a closed curve when the second is run backwards, this happens precisely when the integral of \(\mathsf{X}\) along every closed curve vanishes. In that case, extending a curve from \(p_0\) to \(p\) by a short segment along the \(j\)-th coordinate direction of a chart shows that \(\partial_j \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] = \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j\), i.e. \(df = \mathsf{X}\). Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathsf{X} = df \text{ for some } f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \quad \iff \quad \int_\gamma \mathsf{X} = 0 \text{ for every closed curve } \gamma. \end{align*}

title: B.8 Which covector fields are differentials? (§5.2)
section: Scale 3: on the whole manifold, local primitives must glue
text:
Scale 3: on the whole manifold, local primitives must glue

The construction on a ball worked because every point could be reached from the centre along a straight segment lying inside the region, so every closed curve in it could be shrunk continuously to a point, and (S) guarantees that the integral does not change during the shrinking, so it must vanish. On a region with a “hole”, a closed curve winding around the hole cannot be shrunk, and its integral may be non-zero even when (S) holds everywhere. In that case \(\mathsf{X}\) is a differential near every point (Scale 2), but the local functions cannot be glued into a single one. Example. On the punctured plane \(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}\), with the same two charts as in Appendix C.4 (the cartesian chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), \(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a, b)\), and the polar chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), defined off the ray \(\{a \leq 0, \, b = 0\}\)), consider the covector field with component functions \begin{align*} \left( \mathtt{x}_1, \mathtt{x}_2 \right) = \left( \frac{-b}{a^2 + b^2}, \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} \right). \end{align*} It satisfies (S) everywhere: \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_2 \right\rceil = \frac{b^2 - a^2}{(a^2 + b^2)^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_1 \right\rceil. \end{align*} By Scale 2, it is therefore a differential near every point. It is a differential on \(\mathcal{V}\): its components coincide with those of \(d\mathscr{Y}^2\), the second row of the Jacobian \(\left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^2_{j} = \partial \mathscr{Y}^2 / \partial \mathscr{X}^j\) computed in Appendix C.4. Hence \(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{V} = d\mathscr{Y}^2\): on \(\mathcal{V}\), \(\mathsf{X}\) is the differential of the polar angle \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(b, a)\). It is not a differential on \(\mathcal{M}\): along the unit circle \(\delta(\lambda) = (\cos \lambda, \sin \lambda)\), \(\lambda \in [0, 2\pi]\), whose velocity has components \(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = (-\sin \lambda, \cos \lambda)\), \begin{align*} \int_\delta \mathsf{X} = \int_0^{2\pi} \Big( (-\sin \lambda) \cdot (-\sin \lambda) + \cos \lambda \cdot \cos \lambda \Big) \, d\lambda = 2\pi \neq 0, \end{align*} although \(\delta\) is a closed curve. The would-be function \(f\) is the angle \(\theta\) itself, and it fails for a simple reason. Near every point there is a local function whose differential is \(\mathsf{X}\), namely a local determination of the angle. Following the circle, each local determination must continue the previous one, and after a full turn we come back to the starting point with \(\theta + 2\pi\) instead of \(\theta\): the local functions exist, but they cannot be glued into a single-valued, smooth function on the whole punctured plane. The polar chart avoided the problem by cutting the plane along a ray, but that cut is precisely what makes it a local description.

title: B.8 Which covector fields are differentials? (§5.2)
text:
The names of things

With the ideas in place, here is the standard vocabulary, which the reader will meet in the literature. In the language of differential forms, covector fields are called 1-forms. A covector field of the form \(\mathsf{X} = df\) is called exact. A covector field satisfying (S) is called closed. The condition is usually written as \(d\mathsf{X} = 0\), where \(d\) is the exterior derivative, an operation extending the differential \(f \mapsto df\) from scalar fields to 1-forms. We have seen that every exact field is closed. The Poincaré lemma states that on a contractible region – one that can be continuously shrunk to a point, such as a ball – every closed covector field is exact. The construction of \(F\) in Scale 2 is its proof for a ball. The first de Rham cohomology group \(H^1_{\text{dR}}(\mathcal{M})\) collects the closed covector fields, regarding two of them as equivalent when they differ by an exact one. It is trivial precisely when every closed covector field is exact, and it measures, in this sense, the “one-dimensional holes” of \(\mathcal{M}\): it is trivial for \(\mathbb{R}^d\) or any contractible manifold, and non-trivial for the punctured plane or the circle \(S^1\). In summary, the answer to our question depends on the scale at which it is asked, and each scale adds one requirement to the previous ones: At a point: every covector is a differential, \(\mathsf{X}_p = (df_p)_p\), because its components are constants and can be moved inside \(d\). Locally: once the components become functions, the Leibniz rule gets in the way, and a covector field is a differential near every point if and only if it is closed. Closed or not, every covector field is still locally a combination of differentials with function coefficients, \(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^i\): what may fail is being a single differential. Globally: a closed covector field is a differential on all of \(\mathcal{M}\) if and only if its integrals along all closed curves vanish, i.e. if and only if its local primitives can be glued together. This is guaranteed when \(H^1_{\text{dR}}(\mathcal{M})\) is trivial, e.g. on any contractible manifold, but even there only for closed fields: the field of the first example, on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), is not a differential anywhere. This is why, in the main text, generic covector fields are denoted by \(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}, \dots\), and the symbol \(df\) is reserved for exact ones. 1 Here curves are allowed to be piecewise smooth, since joining two curves end to end generally produces a corner; the integral is then computed piece by piece.

title: B.9 Connections and covariant derivatives (§6.1)
text:
In Chapter 6 the words connection and covariant derivative are used almost interchangeably: the connection is the structure \(
abla\), and the covariant derivative is what it produces, \(
abla_\mathcal{X} T\). In differential geometry at large, however, the two notions are genuinely different, the connection being the more general one. This appendix sketches the difference. Connections live on any bundle. Consider a smooth bundle \(E \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathcal{M}\), with arbitrary fibres. At each point \(e\) of the total space, the tangent space \(T_eE\) contains a canonical vertical subspace, \(V_eE \coloneqq \ker (d\pi)_e\), made of the directions along the fibre, which the projection collapses to zero. There is, however, no canonical notion of horizontal direction, i.e. of moving along \(\mathcal{M}\) without moving within the fibre. A (Ehresmann) connection is precisely such a choice: a smooth assignment of horizontal subspaces \(H_eE\) complementary to the vertical ones, \[ T_eE = V_eE \oplus H_eE . \] From it one obtains parallel transport: a curve in \(\mathcal{M}\) can be lifted uniquely to a horizontal curve in \(E\) through any chosen point of the initial fibre. Nothing in this construction requires the fibres to be vector spaces. On a principal \(G\)-bundle one additionally demands compatibility with the action of \(G\), and the connection can be equivalently encoded as a Lie-algebra-valued 1-form. Covariant derivatives live on vector bundles. A covariant derivative is a linear differential operator acting on sections of a vector bundle \(E \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathcal{M}\), \[ 
abla : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} 	imes \Gamma E \longrightarrow \Gamma E, \] \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linear in its first argument and satisfying the product rule \(
abla_\mathcal{X}(g\,s) = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor g ightceil s + g \, 
abla_\mathcal{X} s\) in its second one. Both properties require adding sections and multiplying them by scalar fields, which only makes sense when the fibres are vector spaces. Where they meet. On a vector bundle, the connections whose horizontal subspaces are compatible with the linear structure of the fibres (linear connections) are in one-to-one correspondence with covariant derivatives: \(
abla_\mathcal{X} s\) is the vertical part of the derivative of the section \(s\) along \(\mathcal{X}\), the vertical subspaces of a vector bundle being canonically identified with the fibres themselves. A connection is therefore more general in two ways: it exists on bundles where covariant derivatives cannot even be defined, most notably principal bundles, and even on vector bundles there are non-linear connections that yield no covariant derivative. A physics example. In gauge theories the gauge potential \(A\) is a connection on a principal \(G\)-bundle, not a derivative of anything. The familiar covariant derivative \(D_j = \partial_j - i A_j\) only appears when \(A\) acts on matter fields, which are sections of associated vector bundles. In general relativity all the relevant objects are sections of the tangent bundle and of the tensor bundles built from it, which are vector bundles. There the two notions coincide, and the connection can be defined directly through the axioms of a covariant derivative, as done in Chapter 6.
