abla_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{Z} - [\mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Y}]  ig) = g \, \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) + \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Y}), \end{align*} where the two non-tensorial terms \(\mp \, \mathcal{Y}\left\lfloor g ightceil \mathcal{X}\), one coming from the product rule and the other from the commutator, cancel exactly. Finally, by (a), \[ \mathtt{T}(df, g \, \mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Y}) = df\left\lceil g \, \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) + \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Y}) ightfloor = g \, \mathtt{T}(df, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) + \mathtt{T}(df, \mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Y}). \] Linearity in the third entry needs no separate proof: since \([\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{X}] = -[\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}]\), the torsion is antisymmetric in its last two entries, \(\mathtt{T}(df, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = -\mathtt{T}(df, \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{X})\), and linearity in the third entry follows from linearity in the second. Hence \(\mathtt{T}\) is a \((1,2)\)-tensor field. \(\square\)

title: B.11 Flat Torsion-Free Connections (§6.4)
text:
Proposition. A torsion-free connection satisfies \(\mathrm{Riem} = 0\) on an open set \(\mathcal{W}\) if and only if around every \(p \in \mathcal{W}\) there is a chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) with \(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y} = 0\). (\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y} = 0\), the component functions of \(\mathrm{Riem}\) vanish in \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) (Chapter 6), so the tensor field \(\mathrm{Riem}\) vanishes on \(\mathcal{V}\). (\(\Rightarrow\)) Parallel covector fields. Take a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) with \(\mathscr{X}(p) = 0\), a cube \(C = (-r, r)^d \subseteq \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{W})\), and write component functions as functions of the coordinates \(\alpha \in C\), with \(\partial_k \coloneqq \partial / \partial \alpha^k\). A covector field \(\mathsf{X} = \mathtt{x}_i \, dx^i\) is parallel, \(
abla \mathsf{X} = 0\), if  egin{align*} \partial_k \mathtt{x}_i = \Gamma^j_{ik} \, \mathtt{x}_j, \qquad  orall \, i, k. 	ag{P} \end{align*} Differentiating (P) and using it again, \(0 = \partial_m \partial_k \mathtt{x}_i - \partial_k \partial_m \mathtt{x}_i = \mathrm{Riem}^j_{imk} \, \mathtt{x}_j\), so flatness is exactly the condition for (P) to be solvable with arbitrary values at \(p\). Explicitly, solve the \(k = 1\) equation along the \(\alpha^1\)-axis, then the \(k = 2\) equation along \(\alpha^2\) from every point reached, and so on up to \(k = d\), each step being a linear system of ordinary differential equations with a unique smooth solution on \((-r, r)\). After step \(s\), the defect \(w_i \coloneqq \partial_k \mathtt{x}_i - \Gamma^j_{ik} \mathtt{x}_j\) of any earlier equation, \(k < s\), satisfies  egin{align*} \partial_s w_i = \Gamma^j_{is} \, w_j - \mathrm{Riem}^j_{isk} \, \mathtt{x}_j = \Gamma^j_{is} \, w_j, \end{align*} with \(w_i = 0\) at \(\alpha^s = 0\), hence \(w_i = 0\): all equations of (P) hold on \(C\). Parallel coframe. Starting from \((d\mathscr{X}^a)_p\), this yields parallel covector fields \(\mathsf{X}^a = \mathtt{x}^a_{i} \, dx^i\), \(a = 1, \dots, d\), with \(\det(\mathtt{x}^a_{i}) = 1\) at \(\alpha = 0\), hence non-zero on \(C\) after shrinking \(r\). Coordinates. Since \(
abla\) is torsion-free, \(\Gamma^j_{ik} = \Gamma^j_{ki}\), so (P) gives \(\partial_k \mathtt{x}^a_{i} = \partial_i \mathtt{x}^a_{k}\). On \(C\), the functions  egin{align*} F^a(\alpha) \coloneqq \int_0^1 \mathtt{x}^a_{i}(\lambda \alpha) \, \alpha^i \, d\lambda \qquad 	ext{satisfy} \qquad \partial_k F^a(\alpha) = \int_0^1  rac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ \lambda \, \mathtt{x}^a_{k}(\lambda \alpha) \Big] d\lambda = \mathtt{x}^a_{k}(\alpha), \end{align*} where the symmetry was used to recognize the total derivative. The Jacobian of \(F\) is \((\mathtt{x}^a_{k})\), invertible, so by the inverse function theorem \(\mathscr{Y}^a \coloneqq F^a \circ \mathscr{X}\) defines a chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) around \(p\) in the maximal atlas, with \(d\mathscr{Y}^a = \mathtt{x}^a_{k} \, dx^k = \mathsf{X}^a\). Vanishing coefficients. In \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), the parallel covector fields \(dy^a\) have constant component functions \(\delta^a_i\), so \(0 =  ig( 
abla_{\partial y_k} dy^a  ig)_i = - \left( \Gamma_\mathscr{Y} ight)^a_{ik}\) for all \(a, i, k\). \(\square\) Remarks. Torsion-freeness is necessary: \(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y} = 0\) implies \(\mathtt{T} = 0\), so charts with \(\Gamma = 0\) exist if and only if \(\mathrm{Riem} = 0\) and \(\mathtt{T} = 0\). The result is local: a flat torus, for instance, admits such charts around every point but no global one. Two such charts differ by an affine change of coordinates, since their transition map has vanishing second derivatives by the transformation law.

title: B.12 Sylvester’s law of inertia (§7.1.1)
text:
Let \((V, \oplus, \odot)\) be an \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space of dimension \(d \geq 1\) (we write \(+\) and juxtaposition for its operations) and let  egin{align*} b : V 	imes V &\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \ \sim}} \mathbb{R} \ (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) &\longmapsto b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) \end{align*} be a symmetric bilinear form which is non-degenerate: \(b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = 0\) for all \(\mathcal{Y} \in V\) implies \(\mathcal{X} = 0\). The case of interest in Chapter 7 is \(V = T_p\mathcal{M}\) and \(b = g_p\). Statement. (i) Existence: there exists a basis \(\{ \hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_d \}\) of \(V\) such that \(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_b) = 0\) for \(a 
eq b\) and \(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) \in \{+1, -1\}\). (ii) Uniqueness of the signs: the number \(n_+\) of basis vectors with \(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) = +1\), and hence the number \(n_- = d - n_+\) of those with \(b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) = -1\), is the same for every basis as in (i). Proof of (i), by induction on \(d\). There is a vector \(\mathcal{X}_0\) with \(b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0) 
eq 0\). Otherwise, by bilinearity and symmetry (polarization), \[ b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = 	frac{1}{2} \Big[ b(\mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Y}) - b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{X}) - b(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{Y}) \Big] = 0 \qquad  orall \, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in V, \] contradicting non-degeneracy, since \(V 
eq \{0\}\). Normalization. Set \(\hat{e}_1 \coloneqq \mathcal{X}_0 / \sqrt{|b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0)|}\). Then \(b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_1) = b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0) / |b(\mathcal{X}_0, \mathcal{X}_0)| = \pm 1\). If \(d = 1\), we are done. Splitting off \(\hat{e}_1\). Let \(W \coloneqq \{ \mathcal{W} \in V \mid b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{W}) = 0 \}\), the kernel of the linear map \(b(\hat{e}_1, \cdot) : V 	o \mathbb{R}\). This map is non-zero (it takes the value \(\pm 1\) on \(\hat{e}_1\)), hence surjective, and \(\dim W = d - 1\) by rank–nullity. Every \(\mathcal{X} \in V\) decomposes uniquely as \[ \mathcal{X} = \alpha \, \hat{e}_1 + \mathcal{W}, \qquad \alpha \coloneqq  rac{b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{X})}{b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_1)}, \qquad \mathcal{W} \coloneqq \mathcal{X} - \alpha \, \hat{e}_1 \in W, \] where \(b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{W}) = b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{X}) - \alpha \, b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_1) = 0\), and uniqueness follows by applying \(b(\hat{e}_1, \cdot)\) to two such decompositions. \(b\) restricted to \(W\) is non-degenerate. If \(\mathcal{W}_0 \in W\) satisfies \(b(\mathcal{W}_0, \mathcal{W}) = 0\) for all \(\mathcal{W} \in W\), then for every \(\mathcal{X} = \alpha \, \hat{e}_1 + \mathcal{W}\), \[ b(\mathcal{W}_0, \mathcal{X}) = \alpha \, \underbrace{b(\mathcal{W}_0, \hat{e}_1)}_{= \, b(\hat{e}_1, \mathcal{W}_0) \, = \, 0} + \, b(\mathcal{W}_0, \mathcal{W}) = 0, \] so \(\mathcal{W}_0 = 0\) by non-degeneracy of \(b\) on \(V\). Induction. Applying the induction hypothesis to \((W, b|_{W 	imes W})\) yields a basis \(\{ \hat{e}_2, \dots, \hat{e}_d \}\) of \(W\) with the required properties. Its elements satisfy \(b(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_a) = 0\) because they lie in \(W\), and by the unique decomposition above, \(\{ \hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_d \}\) is a basis of \(V\). \(\square\) Proof of (ii). Let \(\{ \hat{e}_a \}\) and \(\{ \hat{e}'_a \}\) be two bases as in (i), with \(n_+\) and \(n'_+\) positive entries, respectively. Consider the subspaces \[ V_+ \coloneqq \operatorname{span}\{ \hat{e}_a \mid b(\hat{e}_a, \hat{e}_a) = +1 \}, \qquad V'_- \coloneqq \operatorname{span}\{ \hat{e}'_a \mid b(\hat{e}'_a, \hat{e}'_a) = -1 \}, \] of dimensions \(n_+\) and \(d - n'_+\). For a non-zero \(\mathcal{X} = \sum_a \alpha^a \, \hat{e}_a \in V_+\) (sum over the positive basis vectors only), \(b(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{X}) = \sum_a (\alpha^a)^2 > 0\), while for a non-zero \(\mathcal{Y} = \sum_a  eta^a \, \hat{e}'_a \in V'_-\), \(b(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{Y}) = -\sum_a ( eta^a)^2 < 0\). Hence \(V_+ \cap V'_- = \{0\}\), and the dimension of the subspace \(V_+ + V'_- \subseteq V\) is \[ \dim(V_+ + V'_-) = \dim V_+ + \dim V'_- - \dim(V_+ \cap V'_-) = n_+ + (d - n'_+) \leq d \quad \longrightarrow \quad n_+ \leq n'_+ . \] Exchanging the roles of the two bases gives \(n'_+ \leq n_+\), so \(n_+ = n'_+\). \(\square\) Remark (eigenvalues). Given any basis of \(V\), the matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) of entries \(b(\hat{x}_i, \hat{x}_j)\) is real and symmetric, so it can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix \(\mathbf{O}\), \(\mathbf{O}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{B} \, \mathbf{O} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d)\). Since \(\mathbf{O}^{\mathsf{T}} = \mathbf{O}^{-1}\), this is at the same time a change of basis for \(b\) (a congruence), and rescaling the new basis vectors by \(1/\sqrt{|\lambda_a|}\) produces a basis as in (i). By (ii), \(n_+\) is therefore the number of positive eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{B}\), whichever basis was used to write it down. The eigenvalues themselves, however, do depend on the basis. Remark (realization by a chart). In the case \(V = T_p\mathcal{M}\), \(b = g_p\), the basis of (i) can always be realized as the chart-induced basis at \(p\) of a suitable chart. Given any chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around \(p\), write \(\hat{e}_a = A^i{}_a \, (\partial x_i)_p\), with \((A^i{}_a)\) an invertible matrix. The chart \[ \mathscr{Y}^a \coloneqq (A^{-1})^a{}_i \,  ig( \mathscr{X}^i - \mathscr{X}^i(p)  ig), \] obtained from \(\mathscr{X}\) by a linear (hence \(C^\infty\)-compatible) change of chart, satisfies \[ (\partial y_a)_p = A^i{}_a \, (\partial x_i)_p = \hat{e}_a , \] since \((\partial x_i)_p =  ig( \partial \mathscr{Y}^a / \partial \mathscr{X}^i  ig)_p \, (\partial y_a)_p = (A^{-1})^a{}_i \, (\partial y_a)_p\). In this chart, the components of the metric at \(p\) are diagonal, \(g_{ab}(p) = 0\) for \(a 
eq b\), with \(g_{aa}(p) = \pm 1\).

title: B.13 Reparametrization invariance of the length (§7.2)
text:
Let \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, g)\) be a Riemannian metric manifold, \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} 	o \mathcal{M}\) a smooth curve with speed \(s_\gamma\), and \(a < b\). Recall that \(L_{[a,b]}[\gamma] \coloneqq \int_a^b s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda\), where the integral exists because \(s_\gamma\), the square root of a continuous non-negative function, is continuous on \([a,b]\). Reparametrizations. A reparametrization is a diffeomorphism \(	extrm{unic ᚱ} : \mathbb{R} 	o \mathbb{R}\), i.e. a smooth bijection with smooth inverse. Equivalently, \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}\) is a smooth bijection with \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) 
eq 0\) for all \(	ilde{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}\): If \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1}\) is differentiable, applying the chain rule to \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1} \circ 	extrm{unic ᚱ} = \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}\) gives \((	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1})' ig( 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda})  ig) \cdot 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) = 1\), so \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) 
eq 0\). Conversely, if \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) 
eq 0\) everywhere, the inverse function theorem makes \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1}\) smooth, with derivative \((	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1})'(\lambda) = 1 / 	extrm{unic ᚱ}' ig( 	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1}(\lambda)  ig)\). A smooth bijection alone does not suffice: \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda}) = 	ilde{\lambda}^3\) is one, but \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(0) = 0\) and its inverse, \(\lambda \mapsto \lambda^{1/3}\), is not differentiable at \(0\). Since \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}'\) is continuous and never vanishes, it has a constant sign: \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}\) is either orientation preserving (\(	extrm{unic ᚱ}' > 0\)) or orientation reversing (\(	extrm{unic ᚱ}' < 0\)). In both cases \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1}([a,b])\) is a closed interval \([	ilde{a}, 	ilde{b}]\), with \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{a}) = a\), \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{b}) = b\) in the first case and \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{a}) = b\), \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{b}) = a\) in the second. Statement. For every reparametrization \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}\), the reparametrized curve \(\delta \coloneqq \gamma \circ 	extrm{unic ᚱ}\), which traces the same path as \(\gamma\), satisfies \[ L_{[	ilde{a}, 	ilde{b}]}[\delta] = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma], \qquad [	ilde{a}, 	ilde{b}] \coloneqq 	extrm{unic ᚱ}^{-1} ig( [a,b]  ig). \] Proof. Velocities. At every \(	ilde{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}\), both curves pass through the same point, \(\delta(	ilde{\lambda}) = \gamma ig( 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda})  ig)\), so their velocities live in the same tangent space. For every \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), the ordinary chain rule for the composition of the real functions \(f \circ \gamma\) and \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}\) gives \[ v_{\delta(	ilde{\lambda})}(f) =  ig( (f \circ \gamma) \circ 	extrm{unic ᚱ}  ig)'(	ilde{\lambda}) = (f \circ \gamma)' ig( 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda})  ig) \cdot 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) \cdot v_{\gamma, \gamma(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda}))}(f). \] Since this holds for every \(f\), the two velocities are proportional, \[ v_{\delta(	ilde{\lambda})} = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) \, v_{\gamma, \gamma(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda}))} \in T_{\delta(	ilde{\lambda})}\mathcal{M}. \] Speeds. By the bilinearity of \(g_{\delta(	ilde{\lambda})}\), \[ s_\delta(	ilde{\lambda}) = \sqrt{ g_{\delta(	ilde{\lambda})} ig( v_{\delta(	ilde{\lambda})}, v_{\delta(	ilde{\lambda})}  ig) } = \sqrt{ 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda})^2 \; g_{\gamma(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda}))} ig( v_{\gamma, \gamma(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda}))}, v_{\gamma, \gamma(	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda}))}  ig) } = |	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda})| \; s_\gamma ig( 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda})  ig). \] Lengths. Substituting \(\lambda = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda})\), \(d\lambda = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) \, d	ilde{\lambda}\), in the orientation preserving case, \(|	extrm{unic ᚱ}'| = 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'\), \[ L_{[	ilde{a}, 	ilde{b}]}[\delta] = \int_{	ilde{a}}^{	ilde{b}} s_\gamma ig( 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda})  ig) \, 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) \, d	ilde{\lambda} = \int_{	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{a})}^{	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{b})} s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda = \int_a^b s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma]. \] In the orientation reversing case, \(|	extrm{unic ᚱ}'| = -	extrm{unic ᚱ}'\), and the extra sign compensates the exchange of the integration limits, \[ L_{[	ilde{a}, 	ilde{b}]}[\delta] = -\int_{	ilde{a}}^{	ilde{b}} s_\gamma ig( 	extrm{unic ᚱ}(	ilde{\lambda})  ig) \, 	extrm{unic ᚱ}'(	ilde{\lambda}) \, d	ilde{\lambda} = -\int_{b}^{a} s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda = \int_a^b s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma]. \qquad \square \] Remarks. The speed itself is not invariant: \(s_\delta = |	extrm{unic ᚱ}'| \, (s_\gamma \circ 	extrm{unic ᚱ}) 
eq s_\gamma \circ 	extrm{unic ᚱ}\) in general. Only its integral is, because the factor \(|	extrm{unic ᚱ}'|\) is exactly the Jacobian of the change of integration variable. This is why the speed is a property of the parametrized curve, while the length is a property of the path it traces. The square root in the definition of \(s_\gamma\) is what produces \(|	extrm{unic ᚱ}'|\) rather than \(	extrm{unic ᚱ}'\), making the length also independent of the direction in which the path is traversed.

title: B.14 Euler–Lagrange equations (§7.2.1)
text: Setting. As in Chapter 7: \(\gamma\) is smooth, \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma = \pm 1\) on \([a,b]\), \(\gamma([a,b]) \subseteq \mathcal{U}\), and \(\gamma_\mathcal{U} = \mathscr{X} \circ \gamma\). The Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}\) is defined on the vectors over \(\mathcal{U}\) with sign \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma\), \[ D \coloneqq \big\{ \mathcal{X}_p \in T\mathcal{U} \;\big|\; \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) > 0 \big\} \subseteq T\mathcal{U} \subseteq T\mathcal{M} . \] Writing \((\alpha \, ; \beta) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d\) for the \(d\) position slots and the \(d\) velocity slots of the bundle chart \((T\mathcal{U}, \xi_\mathscr{X})\), and using \(g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) = g_{ij}(p) \, x^i_p \, x^j_p\) with \(p = \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha)\) and \(x_p = \beta\), the chart image of \(D\) is \[ D_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq \xi_\mathscr{X}(D) = \Big\{ (\alpha \, ; \beta) \in \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \times \mathbb{R}^d \;\Big|\; \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{ij}\big( \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha) \big) \, \beta^i \beta^j > 0 \Big\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d , \] and the chart representative of the Lagrangian is \begin{align*} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq \mathcal{L} \circ \xi_\mathscr{X}^{-1} : D_\mathscr{X} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ (\alpha \, ; \beta) &\longmapsto \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}(\alpha \, ; \beta) = \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{ij}\big( \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha) \big) \, \beta^i \beta^j } . \end{align*} \(D_\mathscr{X}\) is open in \(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) is smooth on it, as the square root of a smooth positive function. A point of \(D_\mathscr{X}\) is the chart description, through \(\xi_\mathscr{X}\), of a tangent vector with sign \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma\). For a smooth \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ} : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^d\) with \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}(a) = \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(b) = 0\), the length of \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}\) is \[ L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] = \int_a^b \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \underbrace{\gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(\lambda)}_{\text{position slots}} \, ; \, \underbrace{\dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'(\lambda)}_{\text{velocity slots}} \big) \, d\lambda , \] which makes sense as long as the argument of \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) lies in \(D_\mathscr{X}\) for all \(\lambda \in [a,b]\). Statement. \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if, for \(m = 1, \dots, d\) and all \(\lambda \in [a,b]\), \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) \Big] - (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) = 0 . \] Strategy. The definition of a geodesic is a condition on an integral, for every \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\). The proof turns it into a condition at every point \(\lambda\), in two moves: (I) compute the derivative at \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0\) (steps 1–4): \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = \int_a^b \sum_{m=1}^d \left\{ \left[(\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) - \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \right] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \right\} \, d\lambda ; \] (II) since \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) is arbitrary, this vanishes for every \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) if and only if (step 5): \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) \Big] - (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) = 0 . \] Proof. The deformed curves are admissible for small \(|\textrm{\runic ᛊ}|\). We need \(\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(\lambda) \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'(\lambda) \big) \in D_\mathscr{X}\) for all \(\lambda \in [a,b]\). The undeformed points form the compact set \(K \coloneqq \big\{ \big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) \;\big|\; \lambda \in [a,b] \big\} \subseteq D_\mathscr{X}\). Since \(D_\mathscr{X}\) is open, there exist a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(B_\delta(k) \subseteq D_\mathscr{X}\) for every \(k \in K\), with \(B_\delta\) the open balls of the standard topology of \(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d = \mathbb{R}^{2d}\). The deformation keeps each point of \(K\) inside its ball as long as \[ \sum_{m=1}^d \Big[ \big( \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \big)^2 + \big( \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'^m(\lambda) \big)^2 \Big] \leq \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 M_\textrm{\runic ᛉ}^2 < \delta^2, \qquad M_\textrm{\runic ᛉ}^2 \coloneqq \max_{\lambda \in [a,b]} \sum_{m=1}^d \Big[ \big( \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \big)^2 + \big( \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'^m(\lambda) \big)^2 \Big], \] which holds for \(|\textrm{\runic ᛊ}| < \textrm{\runic ᛊ}_0 \coloneqq \delta / (1 + M_\textrm{\runic ᛉ})\). For such \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\) the length above is defined, and the function of two variables \[ (\textrm{\runic ᛊ}, \lambda) \longmapsto \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(\lambda) \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'(\lambda) \big) \] is smooth on \((-\textrm{\runic ᛊ}_0, \textrm{\runic ᛊ}_0) \times [a,b]\), as a composition of smooth maps. Differentiate under the integral sign. For any \(0 < \textrm{\runic ᛊ}_1 < \textrm{\runic ᛊ}_0\), the partial derivative w.r.t. \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\) of the function of step 1 is continuous on the compact set \([-\textrm{\runic ᛊ}_1, \textrm{\runic ᛊ}_1] \times [a,b]\), so the derivative and the integral can be exchanged: \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = \int_a^b \frac{\partial}{\partial \textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \Big[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(\lambda) \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'(\lambda) \big) \Big]_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} \, d\lambda . \] Chain rule. At fixed \(\lambda\) (dropped from the notation in this step), \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\) enters all \(2d\) slots of \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\): \begin{align*} &\frac{\partial}{\partial \textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \Big[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}' \big) \Big] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{chain rule}} \; &\sum_{m=1}^d \Big[ \frac{\partial \big( \gamma^m_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m \big)}{\partial \textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \, (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}' \big) + \frac{\partial \big( \dot{\gamma}^m_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'^m \big)}{\partial \textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \, (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}' \big) \Big] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{affine in } \textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \; &\sum_{m=1}^d \Big[ \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m \, (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}' \big) + \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'^m \, (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \, \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}' \big) \Big] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} \\ \xlongrightarrow{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, = \, 0} \; &\sum_{m=1}^d \Big[ \underbrace{(\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m}_{\text{position shifted by } \textrm{\runic ᛉ}} + \underbrace{(\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'^m}_{\text{velocity shifted by } \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'} \Big] . \end{align*} Integrate by parts. The functions \(\lambda \mapsto (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big)\) are \(C^1\) (\(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) and \(\gamma\) are smooth). Inserting step 3 into step 2, \begin{align*} &\frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{steps 2, 3}} \; &\int_a^b \sum_{m=1}^d \Big\{ (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m + (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}'^m \Big\} d\lambda \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{product rule}} \; &\int_a^b \sum_{m=1}^d \Big\{ (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m + \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m \Big] \\ & \qquad - \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m \Big\} d\lambda \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{fund.\ theorem of calculus}} \; &\sum_{m=1}^d \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m \Big]_a^b \\ &+ \int_a^b \sum_{m=1}^d \left\{ \left[(\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) - \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \right] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \right\} \, d\lambda \\ \xlongrightarrow{\textrm{\runic ᛉ}(a) \, = \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}(b) \, = \, 0} \; &\int_a^b \sum_{m=1}^d \left\{ \left[(\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) - \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \right] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \right\} \, d\lambda . \end{align*} The boundary term is where the fixed endpoints are used. From the integral to every point. The bracket in the integrand of step 4 is minus the left-hand side of the Statement, and is continuous in \(\lambda\) (\(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) and \(\gamma\) are smooth). (\(\Leftarrow\)) If the Statement holds, the bracket vanishes for every \(m\) and \(\lambda\), so the derivative is \(0\) for every \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\): \(\gamma\) is a geodesic. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose, on the contrary, that \(\gamma\) is a geodesic but the bracket is non-zero for some \(m\) at some \(\lambda_0 \in (a,b)\). Since the derivative of step 4 must vanish for every admissible \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\), it must vanish in particular for the bracket itself, multiplied by \((\lambda - a)(b - \lambda)\) so as to vanish at the endpoints: \[ \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \coloneqq (\lambda - a)(b - \lambda) \Big[ (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) - \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \Big] . \] For this choice, each term of the integrand of step 4 is \((\lambda - a)(b - \lambda) \geq 0\) times the square of the bracket. The integrand is therefore non-negative on \([a,b]\), and, by continuity, positive on an interval around \(\lambda_0\), so \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = \int_a^b \underbrace{(\lambda - a)(b - \lambda)}_{\geq \, 0} \sum_{m=1}^d \underbrace{\Big[ (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) - \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \Big]^2}_{\geq \, 0, \text{ and } > \, 0 \text{ near } \lambda_0} d\lambda > 0 , \] which contradicts \(\gamma\) being a geodesic. Hence the bracket vanishes on \((a,b)\) for every \(m\), and on \([a,b]\) by continuity: this is the Statement. \(\square\) The proof only uses that \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) is \(C^2\) on an open set containing \(K\). It therefore holds for the action functional \(\int_a^b \mathcal{L}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) \, d\lambda\) of any such Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}\).

title: B.15 Higher-order Lagrangians (§7.2.1)
text: The Lagrangian of Chapter 7 is a function on the tangent bundle: it eats a tangent vector \(\mathcal{X}_p\), i.e. a base point and a velocity, and nothing else. Its chart representative therefore has only position slots and velocity slots, and the action of a curve only involves \(\gamma_\mathcal{U}\) and \(\dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}\). Higher derivatives appear as soon as the integrand also depends on the acceleration of the curve, or on even higher derivatives. This happens, for instance, for Lagrangians built from the acceleration \(a_\gamma = \nabla_{v_\gamma} v_\gamma\) of Chapter 6, whose components \(\ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U} + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}\) contain second derivatives of \(\gamma_\mathcal{U}\); when a total derivative is added to a first-order Lagrangian (item 3 of the remarks below); in field theory, where the Lagrangian of General Relativity contains second derivatives of the metric components. This appendix extends Appendix B.14 to Lagrangians depending on derivatives of \(\gamma_\mathcal{U}\) up to an arbitrary order \(k \geq 1\), following Section 2.1 of Ortín (2004), there written for fields. The case \(k = 1\) is the one of that appendix, and the proof follows the same five steps; only step 4 changes, since each order of derivative needs its own integrations by parts. Setting. Let \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) be a chart, \(\gamma\) a smooth curve with \(\gamma([a,b]) \subseteq \mathcal{U}\), and \(\gamma_\mathcal{U} = \mathscr{X} \circ \gamma\). For \(j = 0, 1, \dots, k\) write \[ \gamma^{(j)}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \coloneqq \frac{d^j}{d\lambda^j} \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \in \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad \gamma^{(0)}_\mathcal{U} = \gamma_\mathcal{U}, \quad \gamma^{(1)}_\mathcal{U} = \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}, \] where the index in parentheses counts derivatives (it is not a slot label as in Chapter 2). A Lagrangian of order \(k\) is, in the chart, a smooth function \[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} : D_\mathscr{X} \subseteq \underbrace{\mathbb{R}^d \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^d}_{(k+1) \text{-times}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \qquad \big( \alpha_{(0)} \, ; \alpha_{(1)} \, ; \dots ; \alpha_{(k)} \big) \longmapsto \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \alpha_{(0)} \, ; \alpha_{(1)} \, ; \dots ; \alpha_{(k)} \big), \] on an open set \(D_\mathscr{X}\) containing the points \(\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big)\), \(\lambda \in [a,b]\). Its \((k+1) d\) slots come in \(k+1\) blocks of \(d\) slots: block \(j\) receives the \(j\)-th derivative of the curve. Generalizing \(\partial_m\) (block \(0\)) and \(\partial_{d+m}\) (block \(1\)), \[ \partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq \text{derivative of } \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \text{ w.r.t.\ the } m\text{-th slot of block } j . \] The action of \(\gamma\) is \[ S_{[a,b]}[\gamma] \coloneqq \int_a^b \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) \, d\lambda , \] and the length of Chapter 7 is the case \(k = 1\), \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{ij}\big( \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha_{(0)}) \big) \, \alpha^i_{(1)} \alpha^j_{(1)} }\). Variations are defined as before, \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}\), so that the \(j\)-th derivative of the varied curve is \(\gamma^{(j)}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)}\); but now we require \[ \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(i)}(a) = \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(i)}(b) = 0, \qquad i = 0, 1, \dots, k-1 : \] the varied curves share with \(\gamma\) not only the endpoints, but also the first \(k - 1\) derivatives of the chart representative there. The curve \(\gamma\) is a critical curve of the action if \(\frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} S_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = 0\) for every such \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\). Remark (charts). For \(k \geq 2\) the slots beyond the velocity are not the components of tangent vectors: under a change of chart, \(\ddot{\gamma}_\mathcal{V}\) is not obtained from \(\ddot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}\) with one Jacobian, but picks up second derivatives of the chart transition map, exactly as the connection coefficient functions do (Chapter 6). Hence a Lagrangian of order \(k \geq 2\) is not a function on \(T\mathcal{M}\); its natural home is a higher-order generalization of the tangent bundle, which these notes do not need. Everything below is done in a single chart. Statement. \(\gamma\) is a critical curve if and only if, for \(m = 1, \dots, d\) and all \(\lambda \in [a,b]\), \[ \boxed{ \sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^j \frac{d^j}{d\lambda^j} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] = 0 . } \] For \(k = 1\) the left-hand side is \((\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})(\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}) - \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})(\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}) \big]\), the bracket of step 4 of Appendix B.14: minus the left-hand side of its Statement. Proof. 1–2. Admissibility, and differentiation under the integral sign. As in Appendix B.14, with the compact set \(K \subseteq D_\mathscr{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{(k+1)d}\) and the bound \(M_\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) now including all blocks: \[ K \coloneqq \Big\{ \big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) \;\Big|\; \lambda \in [a,b] \Big\}, \qquad M_\textrm{\runic ᛉ}^2 \coloneqq \max_{\lambda \in [a,b]} \sum_{j=0}^{k} \sum_{m=1}^d \big( \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)m}(\lambda) \big)^2 . \] Chain rule. At fixed \(\lambda\) (dropped from the notation), \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\) enters all \((k+1)d\) slots of \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\), block \(j\) through \(\gamma^{(j)}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)}\): \begin{align*} &\frac{\partial}{\partial \textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \Big[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(k)} \big) \Big] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{chain rule}} \; &\sum_{j=0}^{k} \sum_{m=1}^d \frac{\partial \big( \gamma^{(j)m}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)m} \big)}{\partial \textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \, (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(k)} \big) \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{affine in } \textrm{\runic ᛊ}, \; \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, = \, 0} \; &\sum_{j=0}^{k} \sum_{m=1}^d (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)m} . \end{align*} Block \(j\) contributes the \(j\)-th derivative of \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\); for \(k = 1\) this is step 3 of Appendix B.14. Integrate by parts, \(j\) times for block \(j\). The functions \(\lambda \mapsto (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big)\) are smooth (\(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) and \(\gamma\) are smooth). Inserting step 3 into step 2, the derivative of the action is a sum over the blocks, \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} S_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = \int_a^b \sum_{j=0}^{k} \sum_{m=1}^d (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)m} \, d\lambda , \] and in the term of block \(j\) the deformation enters through its \(j\)-th derivative. One integration by parts moves one derivative from \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) onto the derivative of the Lagrangian: \begin{align*} &\int_a^b (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)m} \, d\lambda \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{product rule}} \; &\int_a^b \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)m} \Big] d\lambda \\ &\qquad - \int_a^b \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)m} \, d\lambda \\ \xlongrightarrow{\text{fund.\ theorem of calculus}} \; &\Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)m} \Big]_a^b \\ &\qquad - \int_a^b \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)m} \, d\lambda \\ \xlongrightarrow{\textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)}(a) \, = \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)}(b) \, = \, 0} \; &- \int_a^b \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)m} \, d\lambda . \end{align*} The result has the same form, with one more derivative on the first factor, one less on \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\), and a factor \(-1\). Repeating the same three moves, each time using one more of the conditions \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-2)} = \dots = \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(0)} = 0\) at \(a\) and \(b\), after \(j\) integrations by parts \[ \int_a^b (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j)m} \, d\lambda = (-1)^j \int_a^b \frac{d^j}{d\lambda^j} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m \, d\lambda . \] Block \(j\) uses the conditions on \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}', \dots, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(j-1)}\), and the highest block, \(j = k\), uses all of them: this is why \(k - 1\) derivatives of \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) must vanish at the endpoints. Doing this for every block, and collecting the factor \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m\), \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} S_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0} = \int_a^b \sum_{m=1}^d \left\{ \sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^j \frac{d^j}{d\lambda^j} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] \right\} \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \, d\lambda . \] For \(k = 1\) this is step 4 of Appendix B.14: block \(0\) needs no integration by parts, block \(1\) needs one. From the integral to every point. As in Appendix B.14, with the sum over \(j\) in the integrand of step 4 in place of the bracket there. Suppose, on the contrary, that \(\gamma\) is a critical curve but this sum is non-zero for some \(m\) at some \(\lambda_0 \in (a,b)\), and choose the sum itself as the variation: \[ \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^m(\lambda) \coloneqq \big( (\lambda - a)(b - \lambda) \big)^k \sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^j \frac{d^j}{d\lambda^j} \Big[ (\partial_{jd+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} \, ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] . \] The only new point is admissibility, which now also requires \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}', \dots, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(k-1)}\) to vanish at the endpoints. This is why the prefactor is raised to the power \(k\): it vanishes to order \(k\) at \(a\) and \(b\), so its first \(k-1\) derivatives vanish there too. By the Leibniz rule, every derivative \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}^{(i)m}\) with \(i \leq k-1\) is a sum of terms, each containing a derivative of order at most \(k - 1\) of the prefactor, and therefore vanishes at \(a\) and \(b\). The rest is as there: the integrand of step 4 is the non-negative prefactor times the sum over \(m\) of the squares of these sums, positive near \(\lambda_0\), so the derivative of the action is positive, a contradiction. \(\square\) Remarks. Order of the equations and boundary data. If \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) genuinely depends on the last block, the term \(j = k\) of the Statement differentiates \(k\) more times a function of \(\gamma^{(k)}_\mathcal{U}\), so the equations contain \(\gamma^{(2k)}_\mathcal{U}\): a system of \(d\) ordinary differential equations of order \(2k\). Such a system needs \(2k\) pieces of data per component, which is exactly what the variations keep fixed: \(\gamma_\mathcal{U}, \dots, \gamma^{(k-1)}_\mathcal{U}\) at \(a\), and the same at \(b\). For \(k = 1\): second-order equations, and fixed endpoints. Total derivatives. Let \(K\) be a smooth function of the first \(k\) blocks only, \(K\big( \alpha_{(0)} ; \dots ; \alpha_{(k-1)} \big)\). Along a curve, by the chain rule, \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ K\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k-1)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \Big] = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \sum_{m=1}^d (\partial_{jd+m} K)\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k-1)}_\mathcal{U} \big) \, \gamma^{(j+1)m}_\mathcal{U} , \] the evaluation on the curve of a Lagrangian of order \(k\), linear in the last block. Its action is \(K\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(b) ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k-1)}_\mathcal{U}(b) \big) - K\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(a) ; \dots ; \gamma^{(k-1)}_\mathcal{U}(a) \big)\), by the fundamental theorem of calculus, and it is the same for all varied curves, since they share these data with \(\gamma\). Its derivative w.r.t. \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\) thus vanishes for every \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) and every curve, so, by the Statement, its Euler–Lagrange expression vanishes identically. Adding it to any Lagrangian leaves the equations unchanged. For \(k = 2\) this can be checked directly: with \(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_\mathscr{X}(\alpha_{(0)} ; \alpha_{(1)} ; \alpha_{(2)}) = (\partial_i K) \, \alpha^i_{(1)} + (\partial_{d+i} K) \, \alpha^i_{(2)}\), on the curve \[ \partial_m \tilde{\mathcal{L}}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ \partial_m K \big], \qquad \partial_{d+m} \tilde{\mathcal{L}}_\mathscr{X} = \partial_m K + \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ \partial_{d+m} K \big], \qquad \partial_{2d+m} \tilde{\mathcal{L}}_\mathscr{X} = \partial_{d+m} K , \] and the alternating sum of the Statement gives \(\frac{d}{d\lambda} [\partial_m K] - \frac{d}{d\lambda} [\partial_m K] - \frac{d^2}{d\lambda^2} [\partial_{d+m} K] + \frac{d^2}{d\lambda^2} [\partial_{d+m} K] = 0\). This is how second derivatives can sit in a Lagrangian without raising the order of its equations: a first-order Lagrangian plus \(\frac{d}{d\lambda} K(\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U})\) contains \(\ddot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}\), linearly, and still has second-order equations. The Lagrangian of General Relativity is of this kind: its second derivatives of the metric components can be collected into a total derivative, which is why the Einstein equations are of second order (the remainder, quadratic in first derivatives, is then no longer chart independent).

title: B.16 Derivation of the geodesic equation (§7.2)
text: Setting. As in Chapter 7: \(\gamma\) is smooth with constant sign \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma = \pm 1\) on \([a,b]\), \(\gamma([a,b]) \subseteq \mathcal{U}\), \(\gamma_\mathcal{U} = \mathscr{X} \circ \gamma\), and \(s_\gamma\) is smooth and positive on \([a,b]\). The chart representative of the Lagrangian is \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \mathscr{X}(p) ; x_p \big) = \sqrt{\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{kl}(p) \, x^k_p \, x^l_p}\), and \((\partial_m g_{ij})(p) = \partial_m \left[ g_{ij} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right]\big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big)\). By Appendix B.14, \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if, for \(m = 1, \dots, d\), \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) \Big] - (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) = 0 . \] Statement. \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if, on \([a,b]\), \[ \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \frac{1}{2} \Big( (g^{-1})^{km} \big( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} - \partial_m g_{ij} \big) \Big)\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = \frac{s_\gamma'(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} \, \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) . \] Every geodesic admits a constant-speed parametrization, for which the right-hand side vanishes and the geodesic equation (7.1) follows. Proof. Partial derivatives of \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\). Using \(\partial \sqrt{f} = \partial f / (2 \sqrt{f})\), in the velocity slots (\(\partial x^i_p / \partial x^m_p = \delta^i_m\), \(g_{ij} = g_{ji}\)) and in the position slots (only \(g_{ij}\) depends on them): \begin{align*} \partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} &= \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, \frac{g_{ij}(p) \big( \delta^i_m \, x^j_p + x^i_p \, \delta^j_m \big)}{2 \sqrt{\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{kl}(p) \, x^k_p \, x^l_p}} = \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, \frac{g_{mj}(p) \, x^j_p}{\sqrt{\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{kl}(p) \, x^k_p \, x^l_p}} , \\ \partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} &= \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, \frac{(\partial_m g_{ij})(p) \, x^i_p \, x^j_p}{2 \sqrt{\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, g_{kl}(p) \, x^k_p \, x^l_p}} . \end{align*} On the curve, \(p = \gamma(\lambda)\), \(x^i_p = \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)\) and \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = s_\gamma(\lambda)\): \begin{align*} (\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) &= \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, \frac{g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} , \\ (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\big( \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \big) &= \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, \frac{(\partial_m g_{ij})\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)}{2 \, s_\gamma(\lambda)} . \end{align*} Euler–Lagrange equations, after inserting step 1 and multiplying by \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, s_\gamma(\lambda) \neq 0\) (\(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma^2 = 1\)): \[ s_\gamma(\lambda) \, \frac{d}{d\lambda} \left( \frac{g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} \right) - \frac{1}{2} (\partial_m g_{ij})\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = 0 . \] Expansion of the \(\lambda\)-derivative. By the quotient rule, and since \((g_{mj} \circ \gamma)'(\lambda) = v_{\gamma(\lambda)}(g_{mj}) = \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, (\partial_i g_{mj})\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big)\), \begin{align*} s_\gamma(\lambda) \, \frac{d}{d\lambda} \left( \frac{g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} \right) &= \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big( g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \Big) - \frac{s_\gamma'(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} \, g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \\ &= (\partial_i g_{mj})\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \ddot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \\ &\quad - \frac{s_\gamma'(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} \, g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) , \end{align*} so step 2 reads \[ g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \ddot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \Big( \partial_i g_{mj} - \frac{1}{2} \partial_m g_{ij} \Big)\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = \frac{s_\gamma'(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} \, g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) . \] Symmetrization. Renaming the summed indices \(i \leftrightarrow j\), \[ (\partial_i g_{mj})\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = (\partial_j g_{mi})\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda), \] so that, taking half of each, \[ (\partial_i g_{mj})\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2} \big( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} \big)\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) , \] and step 3 becomes \[ g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \ddot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) + \frac{1}{2} \big( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} - \partial_m g_{ij} \big)\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = \frac{s_\gamma'(\lambda)}{s_\gamma(\lambda)} \, g_{mj}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) . \] Isolation of \(\ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}\). Multiplying by \((g^{-1})^{km}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big)\), summing over \(m\), and using \((g^{-1})^{km} \, g_{mj} = \delta^k_j\), we obtain the equation of the statement. All steps are reversible (\(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, s_\gamma \neq 0\), \(g^{-1}\) invertible), so \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if it holds on \([a,b]\). Constant speed. Being a geodesic does not depend on the parametrization: for \(\delta \coloneqq \gamma \circ \sigma\), the variations of \(\delta\) are the \(\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \circ \sigma\), as \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \circ \sigma = \gamma_\mathcal{U} \circ \sigma + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ} \circ \sigma\), and \(L_{\sigma^{-1}([a,b])}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} \circ \sigma] = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}]\) (Appendix B.13), so both derivatives at \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0\) coincide. Choosing \(\sigma^{-1}(\lambda) \coloneqq \int_a^\lambda s_\gamma = L_{[a,\lambda]}[\gamma]\), a diffeomorphism since \(s_\gamma > 0\), gives \(s_\delta = \sigma' \, (s_\gamma \circ \sigma) \equiv 1\). For constant speed, \(s_\gamma' = 0\), the right-hand side of the statement vanishes and (7.1) follows. \(\square\)

title: B.17 The Levi-Civita theorem (§7.3)
text:
Let \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, g)\) be a metric manifold. We show that \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) is well defined on \(\mathcal{M}\), and that any torsion-free, metric-compatible connection \(
abla\) is \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\). That \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) is torsion free and metric compatible was shown in Chapter 7. In a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), let \(\Gamma^k_{ji}\) be the connection coefficient functions of \(
abla\). Torsion freeness. \(\mathtt{T}^m_{ij} = \Gamma^m_{ji} - \Gamma^m_{ij} = 0\), i.e. \(\Gamma^m_{ij} = \Gamma^m_{ji}\). Metric compatibility. By (7.3), \((
abla_{\partial x_k} g)_{ij} = 0\) reads \[ \partial_k g_{ij} = \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} + \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} . \] Cyclic permutations. Writing the last relation for the cyclic permutations \((k, i, j)\), \((i, j, k)\) and \((j, k, i)\),  egin{align*} \partial_k g_{ij} &= \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} + \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im}, \ \partial_i g_{jk} &= \Gamma^m_{ji} \, g_{mk} + \Gamma^m_{ki} \, g_{jm}, \ \partial_j g_{ki} &= \Gamma^m_{kj} \, g_{mi} + \Gamma^m_{ij} \, g_{km}, \end{align*} adding the last two and subtracting the first, \[ \partial_i g_{jk} + \partial_j g_{ki} - \partial_k g_{ij} = \Gamma^m_{ji} \, g_{mk} + \Gamma^m_{ij} \, g_{km} + \underbrace{\Gamma^m_{ki} \, g_{jm} - \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj}}_{= \, 0} + \underbrace{\Gamma^m_{kj} \, g_{mi} - \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im}}_{= \, 0} = 2 \, g_{km} \, \Gamma^m_{ij}, \] where the underbraced terms cancel, and the remaining two coincide, by the symmetry of \(\Gamma\) in its lower indices and of \(g\). Solving for \(\Gamma\). Multiplying by \( rac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{lk}\), with \((g^{-1})^{lk} \, g_{km} = \delta^l_m\), \[ \Gamma^l_{ij} =  rac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{lk}  ig( \partial_i g_{jk} + \partial_j g_{ki} - \partial_k g_{ij}  ig) =  ig( \Gamma^{	ext{LC}}_\mathscr{X}  ig)^l_{ij} . \] The connection coefficient functions are the Christoffel symbols in every chart, so \(
abla = 
abla^{	ext{LC}}\). Well-definedness. In each chart domain \(\mathcal{U}\), the Christoffel symbols define, through the component formulas of Chapter 6, a connection on \(\mathcal{U}\), torsion free and metric compatible. On \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\), the connections of both charts are torsion free and metric compatible, so by the previous items they coincide: the Christoffel symbols of the two charts obey the transformation law of connection coefficient functions, and assemble into a single connection \(
abla^{	ext{LC}}\) on \(\mathcal{M}\). \(\square\)

Apply \(\partial x_c\) to the constant function \((g^{-1})^{ar} \, g_{rs} = \delta^a_s\) and use the Leibniz rule: \(0 = \partial_c (g^{-1})^{ar} \; g_{rs} + (g^{-1})^{ar} \; \partial_c g_{rs}\). title: B.18 Properties of \(g\) and of the L.C. connection (§§7.3–7.4)
section: B.18.2 Derivative of the determinant and contracted Christoffel symbols
text:
B.18.2 Derivative of the determinant and contracted Christoffel symbols

Let \(\det g \coloneqq \det\big( g_{ij} \big) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\), which never vanishes. Then \[ \boxed{ \partial_k \det g = \det g \; (g^{-1})^{ij} \, \partial_k g_{ij}, \qquad \big( \Gamma^{\text{LC}}_\mathscr{X} \big)^m_{mk} = \partial_k \ln \sqrt{|\det g|} . } \] Proof. For \(\mathbf{A}\) invertible, \(\det(\mathbf{A} + t \, \mathbf{B}) = \det \mathbf{A} \, \det\big( \mathbf{I} + t \, \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{B} \big) = \det \mathbf{A} \, \big( 1 + t \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{B}) + O(t^2) \big)\): in the sum over permutations, every permutation other than the identity picks at least two off-diagonal entries, each of order \(t\). Along the \(k\)-th coordinate line through \(q\), the matrix of components is \(\mathbf{A} + t \, \mathbf{B} + O(t^2)\), with \(\mathbf{A} = \big( g_{ij}(q) \big)\) and \(\mathbf{B} = \big( \partial_k g_{ij}(q) \big)\), and the derivative at \(t = 0\) gives the first formula (Jacobi’s formula). For the second, contracting the Christoffel symbols, \[ \big( \Gamma^{\text{LC}}_\mathscr{X} \big)^m_{mk} = \frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{ml} \big( \partial_k g_{lm} + \partial_m g_{lk} - \partial_l g_{mk} \big) = \frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{ml} \, \partial_k g_{lm} = \frac{\partial_k \det g}{2 \det g}, \] where the last two terms in the bracket cancel after exchanging the dummy indices \(m \leftrightarrow l\) in one of them. \(\square\) The density \(\sqrt{|\det g|}\) reappears in the chapter on integration.

title: B.18 Properties of \(g\) and of the L.C. connection (§§7.3–7.4)
section: B.18.3 Covariant derivatives commute with contractions
text:
B.18.3 Covariant derivatives commute with contractions

For any connection, contracting an upper with a lower index commutes with covariant differentiation. For \(\mathrm{Ric}_{jm} = \mathrm{Riem}^k_{jkm}\), \[  oxed{ (
abla_{\partial x_n} \mathrm{Riem})^k_{jkm} = (
abla_{\partial x_n} \mathrm{Ric})_{jm} , } \] and likewise for any other contraction. Proof. By the component rule, \[ (
abla_{\partial x_n} \mathrm{Riem})^k_{jkm} = \partial_n \mathrm{Riem}^k_{jkm} + \underbrace{\Gamma^k_{ln} \, \mathrm{Riem}^l_{jkm}}_{(\ast)} - \Gamma^l_{jn} \, \mathrm{Riem}^k_{lkm} - \underbrace{\Gamma^l_{kn} \, \mathrm{Riem}^k_{jlm}}_{(\ast\ast)} - \Gamma^l_{mn} \, \mathrm{Riem}^k_{jkl} , \] and exchanging the dummy indices \(k \leftrightarrow l\) in \((\ast\ast)\) turns it into \((\ast)\). The remaining terms are the component rule for the \((0,2)\)-tensor field \(\mathrm{Ric}\). \(\square\)

title: B.18 Properties of \(g\) and of the L.C. connection (§§7.3–7.4)
section: B.18.6 The Riemann–Christoffel curvature in normal coordinates
text:
B.18.6 The Riemann–Christoffel curvature in normal coordinates

Let \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) be a normal chart at \(p\) (Chapter 6). Since \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\) is torsion free, all its connection coefficient functions vanish at \(p\), and then, by (B.4), so do all first derivatives of the metric, \(\partial_k g_{ij}(p) = 0\). In such a chart, \[ \boxed{ (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm}(p) = \frac{1}{2} \Big( \partial_k \partial_j g_{am} - \partial_k \partial_a g_{jm} - \partial_m \partial_j g_{ak} + \partial_m \partial_a g_{jk} \Big)(p) . } \] Proof. At \(p\) the quadratic terms of \(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{jkm} = \partial_k \Gamma^i_{jm} - \partial_m \Gamma^i_{jk} + \Gamma^i_{rk} \, \Gamma^r_{jm} - \Gamma^i_{rm} \, \Gamma^r_{jk}\) vanish, and in \(\partial_k \Gamma^i_{jm}\) the term containing \(\partial_k (g^{-1})^{il}\) multiplies first derivatives of \(g\), so \[ \partial_k \Gamma^i_{jm}(p) = \frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{il} \big( \partial_k \partial_m g_{lj} + \partial_k \partial_j g_{lm} - \partial_k \partial_l g_{jm} \big)(p). \] Subtracting the same expression with \(k \leftrightarrow m\), the terms \(\partial_k \partial_m g_{lj}\) cancel by Schwarz’s theorem, and \((\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm} = g_{ai} \, \mathrm{Riem}^i_{jkm}\), with \(g_{ai} (g^{-1})^{il} = \delta^l_a\), gives the claim. \(\square\)

title: B.18 Properties of \(g\) and of the L.C. connection (§§7.3–7.4)
section: B.18.7 Symmetries of the Riemann–Christoffel curvature
text:
B.18.7 Symmetries of the Riemann–Christoffel curvature

\[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\text{(a)} \quad (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm} = - (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajmk}, &&\text{(b)} \quad (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm} = - (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{jakm}, \\ &\text{(c)} \quad (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm} + (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{akmj} + (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{amjk} = 0, &&\text{(d)} \quad (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm} = (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{kmaj}. \end{aligned} } \] (a) holds for any connection, (c) is the algebraic Bianchi identity, (b) and (d) are specific to \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\). Proof. Each identity states that a \((0,4)\)-tensor field vanishes, so it suffices to check it at an arbitrary \(p\) in a normal chart at \(p\). With \(\partial_{km} g_{aj} \coloneqq \partial_k \partial_m g_{aj}(p)\), symmetric in \(k, m\) and in \(a, j\), \[ 2 \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm}(p) = \partial_{kj} g_{am} - \partial_{ka} g_{jm} - \partial_{mj} g_{ak} + \partial_{ma} g_{jk} . \] (a): \(k \leftrightarrow m\) maps the four terms onto minus themselves. (b): \(a \leftrightarrow j\) swaps the first two and the last two terms, flipping the sign. (d): \((a,j) \leftrightarrow (k,m)\) gives \(\partial_{am} g_{kj} - \partial_{ak} g_{mj} - \partial_{jm} g_{ka} + \partial_{jk} g_{ma}\), the same four terms. (c): the three cyclic permutations of \((j,k,m)\), \[ \begin{aligned} &\partial_{kj} g_{am} - \partial_{ka} g_{jm} - \partial_{mj} g_{ak} + \partial_{ma} g_{jk} \\ + \, &\partial_{mk} g_{aj} - \partial_{ma} g_{kj} - \partial_{jk} g_{am} + \partial_{ja} g_{km} \\ + \, &\partial_{jm} g_{ak} - \partial_{ja} g_{mk} - \partial_{km} g_{aj} + \partial_{ka} g_{mj} = 0 , \end{aligned} \] cancel term by term. \(\square\) Multiplying (c) by \((g^{-1})^{ia}\), \(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{jkm} + \mathrm{Riem}^i_{kmj} + \mathrm{Riem}^i_{mjk} = 0\). Together, (a)–(d) leave \(d^2 (d^2 - 1)/12\) independent component functions (not proved here): one for \(d = 2\), six for \(d = 3\), twenty for \(d = 4\).

title: B.18 Properties of \(g\) and of the L.C. connection (§§7.3–7.4)
section: B.18.8 Symmetry of the Ricci and Einstein curvatures
text:
B.18.8 Symmetry of the Ricci and Einstein curvatures

\[ \boxed{ \mathrm{Ric}_{ab} = \mathrm{Ric}_{ba}, \qquad G_{ab} = G_{ba} . } \] Proof. With \(\mathrm{Riem}^m_{amb} = (g^{-1})^{mc} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{camb}\), (d), the relabelling \(m \leftrightarrow c\) and the symmetry of \(g^{-1}\), \[ \mathrm{Ric}_{ab} = (g^{-1})^{mc} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{camb} = (g^{-1})^{mc} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{mbca} = (g^{-1})^{cm} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{cbma} = \mathrm{Ric}_{ba} . \] \(G = \mathrm{Ric} - \frac{1}{2} R \, g\) is then a sum of symmetric tensor fields. \(\square\)

title: B.18 Properties of \(g\) and of the L.C. connection (§§7.3–7.4)
text:
B.18.9 Two dimensions

If \(d = 2\), the curvature is determined by the Ricci scalar: \[ \boxed{ (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{ajkm} = \frac{R}{2} \big( g_{ak} \, g_{jm} - g_{am} \, g_{jk} \big), \qquad \mathrm{Ric} = \frac{R}{2} \, g, \qquad G = 0 . } \] Proof. By (a) and (b), the only non-zero components are \[ \rho \coloneqq (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{1212} = (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{2121} = -(\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{1221} = -(\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{2112} . \] With \(\mathrm{Ric}_{ab} = (g^{-1})^{mc} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{camb}\) and \((g^{-1})^{11} = g_{22} / \det g\), \((g^{-1})^{12} = -g_{12} / \det g\), \((g^{-1})^{22} = g_{11} / \det g\), \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Ric}_{11} &= (g^{-1})^{22} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{2121} = \frac{\rho}{\det g} \, g_{11}, \\ \mathrm{Ric}_{12} &= (g^{-1})^{12} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{2112} = \frac{\rho}{\det g} \, g_{12}, \\ \mathrm{Ric}_{22} &= (g^{-1})^{11} \, (\mathrm{Riem}^\flat)_{1212} = \frac{\rho}{\det g} \, g_{22}. \end{aligned} \] Contracting, \(R = (g^{-1})^{mk} \mathrm{Ric}_{km} = 2 \rho / \det g\), so \(\mathrm{Ric} = \frac{R}{2} g\) and \(G = 0\). The right-hand side of the first formula has the symmetries (a), (b) and \(1212\) component \(\frac{R}{2} \det g = \rho\). \(\square\)

title: B.18 Properties of \(g\) and of the L.C. connection (§§7.3–7.4)
text:
B.18.11 The energy Lagrangian

The square root in \(\mathcal{L}\) (Chapter 7) can be dropped. The energy Lagrangian is \begin{align*} \mathcal{T} : T\mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ \mathcal{X}_p &\longmapsto \mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}_p) \coloneqq g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p), \qquad \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq \mathcal{T} \circ \xi_\mathscr{X}^{-1} : (\alpha \, ; \beta) \longmapsto \big( g_{ij} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \, \beta^i \beta^j , \end{align*} so that \(\mathcal{L} = \sqrt{\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, \mathcal{T}}\) where \(\mathcal{L}\) is defined. Its Euler–Lagrange equations are (7.1). With \(\partial_{d+m} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} = 2 \, (g_{mj} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \, \beta^j\) and \(\partial_m \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} = \partial_m (g_{ij} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \, \beta^i \beta^j\) on \((\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U})\), \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big( 2 \, g_{mj} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} \big) - \partial_m g_{ij} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} = 2 \, g_{mj} \, \ddot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} + \big( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} - \partial_m g_{ij} \big) \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} , \] splitting \(2 \, \partial_i g_{mj} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}\) symmetrically in \(i, j\). Setting it to zero and multiplying by \(\frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{km}\) gives (7.1). In practice this is the fastest way of computing the Christoffel symbols: read them off as the coefficients of \(\dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}\). Its solutions have constant \(\mathcal{T}\). Along a solution, \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} = \partial_m \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} \, \dot{\gamma}^m_\mathcal{U} + \partial_{d+m} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} \, \ddot{\gamma}^m_\mathcal{U} = \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big( \partial_{d+m} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} \, \dot{\gamma}^m_\mathcal{U} \big) = \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big( 2 \, \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} \big), \] since \(\beta^m \partial_{d+m} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} = 2 \, \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X}\). Hence \(\frac{d}{d\lambda} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} = 0\). Relation with \(\mathcal{L}\). Where \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \neq 0\), \(\partial \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \, \partial \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} / (2 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})\) for every slot, and \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = s_\gamma\) along the curve, so \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ \partial_{d+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \big] - \partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma}{2 s_\gamma} \Big( \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ \partial_{d+m} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} \big] - \partial_m \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} \, \partial_{d+m} \mathcal{T}_\mathscr{X} \Big). \] For constant speed both sets of equations coincide, and by item 2 every solution for \(\mathcal{T}\) has constant speed. The solutions for \(\mathcal{T}\) are thus the constant-speed geodesics and the null geodesics (\(\mathcal{T} = 0\), where \(\mathcal{L}\) is not differentiable). The price is that \(\int \mathcal{T}\), unlike \(L_{[a,b]}\), depends on the parametrization.

title: B.19 Compactness and the integral over a region (§8.2)
text: The integral (8.3) over a region \(\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\) assumes that \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) is compact and contained in \(\mathcal{U}\). This appendix defines the two notions involved and shows what the assumption does: it turns the definition into an ordinary integral of a bounded function over a bounded subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), which is therefore finite. Closure. The closure of \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{M}\) is the smallest closed set containing it, \[ \overline{\mathcal{S}} \coloneqq \bigcap \big\{ \mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{M} \;\big|\; \mathcal{M} \setminus \mathcal{C} \in \mathcal{O}, \; \mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{C} \big\} , \] i.e. \(\mathcal{S}\) together with its boundary points; e.g. \(\overline{(-1, 1)} = [-1, 1]\) in \(\mathbb{R}\). Compactness. A family \(\{ \mathcal{W}_a \}_{a \in A}\) of open sets, with \(A\) possibly infinite, is an open cover of \(\mathcal{K} \subseteq \mathcal{M}\) if \(\mathcal{K} \subseteq \bigcup_{a \in A} \mathcal{W}_a\). The set \(\mathcal{K}\) is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover: \[ \mathcal{K} \subseteq \bigcup_{a \in A} \mathcal{W}_a , \quad \mathcal{W}_a \in \mathcal{O} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \mathcal{K} \subseteq \mathcal{W}_{a_1} \cup \dots \cup \mathcal{W}_{a_N} \quad \text{for some } a_1, \dots, a_N \in A . \] Figure B.1 illustrates the definition and the two ways it fails in \(\mathbb{R}\): a missing endpoint, and escape to infinity. In \(\mathbb{R}^d\), the compact sets are exactly the closed and bounded ones (Heine–Borel; not proved here). Two consequences. (i) Continuous images of compact sets are compact. Let \(\phi : \mathcal{U} \to \mathbb{R}^d\) be continuous and \(\mathcal{K} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\) compact. If \(\{ \mathcal{W}_a \}\) is an open cover of \(\phi(\mathcal{K})\), the preimages \(\mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{W}_a)\) are open (continuity) and cover \(\mathcal{K}\), so finitely many of them, \(\mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{W}_{a_1}), \dots, \mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{W}_{a_N})\), cover \(\mathcal{K}\); then \(\mathcal{W}_{a_1}, \dots, \mathcal{W}_{a_N}\) cover \(\phi(\mathcal{K})\). \(\square\) (ii) Continuous functions on compact sets are bounded. If \(\mathcal{K} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) is compact and \(h : \mathcal{K} \to \mathbb{R}\) continuous, then \(h(\mathcal{K})\) is compact by (i), hence bounded by Heine–Borel: \(|h| \leq C\) on \(\mathcal{K}\) for some \(C \geq 0\). \(\square\) Statement. In the setting of Section 8.2, if \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) is compact and contained in \(\mathcal{U}\)2, then \[ \bigg| \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega f \bigg| < \infty . \] Proof. Let \(h(\alpha) \coloneqq \big( \omega_\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) \, \big( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha)\), a continuous function on \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\), since \(\omega_\mathscr{X} \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\), \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) and \(\mathscr{X}^{-1}\) is continuous. The region is bounded in the chart. \(\mathscr{X}\) is continuous on \(\mathcal{U} \supseteq \overline{\mathcal{D}}\), so \(\mathscr{X}(\overline{\mathcal{D}})\) is compact by (i), hence bounded by Heine–Borel: \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D}) \subseteq \mathscr{X}(\overline{\mathcal{D}}) \subseteq [-L, L]^d\) for some \(L > 0\). The integrand is bounded on it. \(h\) is continuous on the compact set \(\mathscr{X}(\overline{\mathcal{D}})\), so, by (ii), \(|h(\alpha)| \leq C\) for all \(\alpha \in \mathscr{X}(\overline{\mathcal{D}})\). Estimate. \begin{align*} \bigg| \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega f \bigg| &\overset{(8.3)}{=} \bigg| \int_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\alpha \, h(\alpha) \bigg| \leq \int_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\alpha \, |h(\alpha)| \\ &\overset{\text{step 2}}{\leq} C \int_{\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})} d^d\alpha \overset{\text{step 1}}{\leq} C \int_{[-L, L]^d} d^d\alpha = C \, (2L)^d < \infty . \end{align*} The integral exists in the first place, as the integral of a bounded continuous function over a bounded open set3. \(\square\) Without the assumption. Let \(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}\), with an oriented atlas containing the identity chart \((\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{X})\), \(\mathscr{X}(p) = p\), the volume form \(\Omega\) with \(\omega_\mathscr{X} = 1\), and \(f = 1\), so that, in the identity chart, \(\int_\mathcal{D} \Omega f\) is the length of \(\mathcal{D}\). Each part of the assumption can fail on its own: \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) not compact: escape to infinity (Figure B.1(c)). For \(\mathcal{U} = \mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathcal{D} = (0, \infty)\), \(\overline{\mathcal{D}} = [0, \infty)\) is closed but unbounded, step 1 fails, and \[ \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega f = \int_0^\infty d\alpha = \infty . \] \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) compact, but not contained in \(\mathcal{U}\): reaching the edge of the chart (Figure B.1(b)). Take the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{Y})\) with \(\mathcal{U} = (0, 1)\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(p) \coloneqq \tan\big( \pi (p - \tfrac{1}{2}) \big)\), compatible with the identity chart and in the oriented atlas, since \(d\mathscr{Y}/dp > 0\); and \(\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{U}\). Then \(\overline{\mathcal{D}} = [0, 1]\) is compact, but its endpoints are not in \(\mathcal{U}\). By (8.1), \(\big( \omega_\mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) = \frac{d}{d\beta} \mathscr{Y}^{-1}(\beta) = \frac{1}{\pi (1 + \beta^2)}\), and \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{R}\) is unbounded, so step 1 fails: \[ \int_{\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{D})} d\beta \, \big( \omega_\mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) \, \big( f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{d\beta}{\pi (1 + \beta^2)} = 1 . \] The value is still finite, the length of \((0, 1)\), but the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\) only yields it as an improper integral over all of \(\mathbb{R}\), whose convergence rests on the decay of the integrand, and to which the Statement does not apply. Compactness of \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) is thus what makes the integral finite, and its containment in \(\mathcal{U}\) is what makes a single chart show this through an ordinary integral over a bounded region. Figure B.1: Open covers of subsets \(\mathcal{K}\) (orange) of \(\mathbb{R}\). Open sets are drawn as bars with hollow, i.e. excluded, endpoints; filled endpoints are included. (a) The closed and bounded interval \([0, 1]\): whatever the open cover (grey), finitely many of its sets (blue) already cover it, endpoints included. (b) The interval \((0, 1)\), which lacks its endpoint \(0\): the sets \(\mathcal{W}_n = (1/n, 1)\) cover it, but any finitely many of them leave a gap \((0, 1/N]\) near the missing endpoint. (c) The unbounded set \(\mathbb{R}\): the sets \(\mathcal{W}_n = (-n, n)\) cover it, but any finitely many of them leave out the points with \(|\lambda| \geq N\), which escape to infinity. Closedness rules out (b) and boundedness rules out (c); together they characterize compactness in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (Heine–Borel). For a region \(\mathcal{D}\) of integration, (c) is a region escaping to infinity, and (b) a region reaching the edge of its chart domain, whose missing endpoints are the points of \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) outside \(\mathcal{U}\). 2 Equivalently, the closure of \(\mathcal{D}\) taken within \(\mathcal{U}\), \(\mathcal{K} \coloneqq \overline{\mathcal{D}} \cap \mathcal{U}\), is compact: the condition only involves the chart domain. Indeed, if \(\overline{\mathcal{D}} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\), then \(\mathcal{K} = \overline{\mathcal{D}}\). Conversely, a compact \(\mathcal{K}\) is closed in \(\mathcal{M}\), since \(\mathcal{M}\) is Hausdorff (Chapter 3), and contains \(\mathcal{D}\), so \(\overline{\mathcal{D}} \subseteq \mathcal{K} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{D}}\). 3 As a Lebesgue integral always; as a Riemann integral when the boundary of \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{D})\) has zero volume, e.g. when it is a smooth hypersurface.

title: B.20 Partitions of unity, paracompactness and second countability (§8.2.1)
text:
The integral (8.4) needs a partition of unity subordinate to the cover of \(\mathcal{M}\) by the chart domains of \(\mathcal{A}^\uparrow\) (Subsection 8.2.1). This appendix shows that partitions of unity subordinate to every open cover exist because \(\mathcal{M}\) is Hausdorff and second countable (Chapter 3), that the property they actually rest on is paracompactness, and that neither condition can be dropped. Compactness and closures are as in Appendix B.19. Paracompactness. A refinement of an open cover \(\{ \mathcal{U}_a \}\) is an open cover \(\{ \mathcal{W}_b \}\) with every \(\mathcal{W}_b\) contained in some \(\mathcal{U}_a\). A space is paracompact if every open cover has a locally finite refinement: finitely many sets near each point, instead of finitely many sets altogether as for compactness. This is the property partitions of unity rest on. On the one hand, a partition of unity \(\{ 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n \}\) subordinate to \(\{ \mathcal{U}_a \}\) contains one: the open sets \(\{ 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n > 0 \}\) cover \(\mathcal{M}\), since \(\sum_n 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n = 1\), each lies in \(\operatorname{supp} 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n \subseteq \mathcal{U}_a\), and they are locally finite, as the supports are. Partitions of unity subordinate to every open cover thus exist only on paracompact spaces. On the other hand, they are built on a locally finite refinement, as below, where Hausdorff and second countability are what produce it. Existence. Let \(\{ \mathcal{U}_a \}\) be an open cover of \(\mathcal{M}\). Exhaustion by compact sets (second countability). Every point has an open neighbourhood with compact closure: the preimage, in a chart, of a small open ball, whose closure lies in the preimage of the closed ball, compact, and closed since \(\mathcal{M}\) is Hausdorff. The elements of a countable basis of \(\mathcal{O}\) contained in such neighbourhoods still cover \(\mathcal{M}\) and have compact closures: call them \(\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2, \dots\). Set \(\mathcal{K}_1 \coloneqq \overline{\mathcal{B}_1}\) and \(\mathcal{K}_{j+1} \coloneqq \overline{\mathcal{B}_1} \cup \dots \cup \overline{\mathcal{B}_{m_j}}\), with \(m_j > j\) so large that \(\mathcal{B}_1, \dots, \mathcal{B}_{m_j}\) cover the compact \(\mathcal{K}_j\). Then every \(\mathcal{K}_j\) is compact, \(\mathcal{K}_j \subseteq \operatorname{int} \mathcal{K}_{j+1}\), and \( igcup_j \mathcal{K}_j = \mathcal{M}\). Compact rings. With \(\mathcal{K}_0 = \mathcal{K}_{-1} \coloneqq \emptyset\), the compact sets \(\mathcal{R}_j \coloneqq \mathcal{K}_{j+1} \setminus \operatorname{int} \mathcal{K}_j\) cover \(\mathcal{M}\), and each lies in the open set \(\mathcal{O}_j \coloneqq \operatorname{int} \mathcal{K}_{j+2} \setminus \mathcal{K}_{j-1}\). Finitely many bump functions per ring (compactness). For each \(p \in \mathcal{R}_j\), take a bump function \(\varphi_p \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), \(\varphi_p \geq 0\), \(\varphi_p(p) > 0\), with \(\operatorname{supp} \varphi_p\) compact and contained in \(\mathcal{O}_j \cap \mathcal{U}_a\) for some \(a\) (Section 4.2; its extension by zero outside a chart domain uses again that compact sets are closed). The open sets \(\{ \varphi_p > 0 \}\) cover the compact \(\mathcal{R}_j\), so finitely many suffice. Over all \(j\), this gives countably many \(\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \dots\). Local finiteness (paracompactness). Every point lies in some \(\operatorname{int} \mathcal{K}_m\), which is disjoint from \(\mathcal{O}_j\) for \(j > m\), so it meets only the supports chosen for \(j \leq m\): finitely many. The sets \(\{ \varphi_n > 0 \}\) thus form a countable locally finite refinement of \(\{ \mathcal{U}_a \}\). Normalize. Near each point, \(\sum_k \varphi_k\) is a finite sum of smooth functions, hence smooth, and it is positive everywhere, since the sets \(\{ \varphi_k > 0 \}\) cover \(\mathcal{M}\). Hence \[ 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n \coloneqq  rac{\varphi_n}{\sum_k \varphi_k} \] is a partition of unity subordinate to \(\{ \mathcal{U}_a \}\): \(0 \leq 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n \leq 1\), \(\operatorname{supp} 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n = \operatorname{supp} \varphi_n \subseteq \mathcal{U}_a\), locally finite by step 4, and \(\sum_n 	extrm{unic ᚹ}_n = 1\). \(\square\) Second countability enters in step 1, and only there: it supplies countably many sets, hence an exhaustion by countably many compact sets. Hausdorff enters in steps 1 and 3, by making compact sets closed. Compactness then reduces each ring to finitely many bump functions, and the rings, each meeting only its neighbours, make the whole family locally finite. Hausdorff cannot be dropped. title: B.21 Geometric Formulations of Newtonian Gravity (§9.1)
text:
B.21.3 Remarks

Inertial systems. Defining an inertial system as one in which free particles move uniformly along straight lines, and stating Newton I “in an inertial system”, is nearly circular. In Section 9.2, Newton I is chart independent: a single connection has all free worldlines as autoparallels. Inertial charts, \(\Gamma = 0\), become a derived notion: they are adapted to an inertial frame \(\mathcal{W} = \partial x_0\), \(
abla \mathcal{W} = 0\), and exist on an open set if and only if \(\mathrm{Riem} = 0\) there. With non-uniform gravity only charts with \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00} = 0\) along a single freely falling worldline remain (Subsection 9.5.2). Is Newtonian spacetime curved? It depends on which connection describes free motion: \(
abla^0\) (Galilean, flat) or \(
abla\) (Newton–Cartan, curved wherever there are tidal accelerations). Both predict the same motion, but Newton–Cartan theory is preferable: \(
abla\) is fixed by free fall whereas \(
abla^0\) is not; the universality of free fall is built in, since \(m\) never enters \(
abla\); and the field equation is local, whereas Poisson’s equation needs boundary conditions which cannot be imposed for a homogeneous mass distribution filling space (Neumann–Seeliger paradox).
