The curvature is of a restricted kind: the absolute spaces are flat, \(\mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{ eta\delta\kappa} = 0\).

title: B.21 Geometric Formulations of Newtonian Gravity (§9.1)
section: B.21.4 Laplace’s Question: Space versus Spacetime
text:
B.21.4 Laplace’s Question: Space versus Spacetime

Is there a connection on space whose autoparallels, \(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} + \Gamma^\alpha_{ eta\delta} \, \dot{\gamma}^ eta_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^\delta_\mathcal{U} = 0\), are the free-fall trajectories \(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} = - \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi ightceil\)? No: Velocity dependence: the \(\Gamma\)-term is quadratic in the velocity, \(\partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi ightceil\) does not depend on it. An autoparallel with vanishing velocity has vanishing acceleration, but a stone released at rest falls. Reparametrization: with \(\gamma\), also \(\lambda \mapsto \gamma(c \, \lambda)\), \(c 
eq 0\), is an autoparallel, so the path depends only on the initial point and direction. Stones thrown in the same direction with different speeds, however, follow different parabolas. On spacetime the answer is yes, because the speed becomes part of the direction: with \(\dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U} = 1\), the free-fall equation reads \(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} + \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi ightceil \dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U} = 0\), the autoparallel equation with \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00} = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi ightceil\). A stone at rest has spacetime velocity \((1, 0, 0, 0)\), on which \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\) acts, and different speeds are different spacetime directions. The same mechanism absorbs any acceleration of degree \(0\), \(1\) or \(2\) in the spatial velocity, through \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\), \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0 eta}\) and \(\Gamma^\alpha_{ eta\delta}\), provided it is the same for all particles. The Lorentz force is not, since it depends on \(q/m\); Kaluza–Klein theory absorbs it by turning \(q/m\) into a velocity component in a fifth dimension. 5 \(\Gamma^0_{jk} = 0\) by \(
abla dt = 0\). Inserting \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma = \partial x_\alpha \circ \gamma\), \(\mathcal{Y}_\gamma = \partial x_ eta \circ \gamma\) for arbitrary \(\gamma\) gives \(\Gamma^ eta_{\alpha k} = - \Gamma^\alpha_{ eta k}\). For \(k = 0\), with torsion-freeness, this is the antisymmetry of \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0 eta} = \Gamma^\alpha_{ eta0}\). For \(k = \delta\) spatial, alternating it with the symmetry in the lower indices, \(\Gamma^\alpha_{ eta\delta} = - \Gamma^ eta_{\alpha\delta} = - \Gamma^ eta_{\delta\alpha} = \Gamma^\delta_{ eta\alpha} = \Gamma^\delta_{\alpha eta} = - \Gamma^\alpha_{\delta eta} = - \Gamma^\alpha_{ eta\delta}\), so \(\Gamma^\alpha_{ eta\delta} = 0\). \(\square\) 6 A classical result, whose proof we omit: flatness gives charts with \(\Gamma = 0\), in which compatibility makes the \(h_{\alpha eta}\) constant, and a constant linear change of the spatial coordinates makes them \(\delta_{\alpha eta}\). 7 Often called Newtonian spacetime in the literature, not to be confused with Section 9.1. 8 This is Corollary VI of the Principia. See J. Earman, World Enough and Space-Time, MIT Press (1989); S. Saunders, Rethinking Newton’s Principia, Philosophy of Science 80 (2013) 22–48. 9 Sketch. By (TK1), \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0 eta}\) depends on \(t\) only, and a time-dependent rotation of the axes removes it (Subsection 9.4). In the new chart, (TK2) reads \(\partial x_ eta\left\lfloor \Gamma^\alpha_{00} ightceil = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \Gamma^ eta_{00} ightceil\), so on any ball \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00} = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi ightceil\) for some \(\phi\), and \(
abla^0\) is the connection whose coefficients vanish in this chart. See D. Malament, Topics in the Foundations of General Relativity and Newtonian Gravitation Theory, University of Chicago Press (2012), Chapter 4.

title: B.22 Torsion in Newton-Cartan Theory (§9.1)
text: Two statements about torsion are frequently encountered, and seem to contradict each other: “torsion does not affect the autoparallels, since the autoparallel equation only involves the symmetric part of the connection coefficient functions”, and “torsion does affect the autoparallels”. Both are correct. They differ in what is held fixed when torsion is introduced: either the symmetric part of the connection coefficient functions, or some other structure from which the connection is constructed, such as a metric. Torsion is written as in Chapter 6, \(\mathtt{T}^i_{jk} = \Gamma^i_{kj} - \Gamma^i_{jk}\), with \(\Gamma^i_{jk} = dx^i\left\lceil \nabla_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j \right\rfloor\). Even when torsion leaves the autoparallels unchanged, it does affect parallel transport and curvature, which is why the torsion-free condition in the definition of Newtonian spacetime matters (Subsections B.22.4 and B.22.5).

title: B.22 Torsion in Newton-Cartan Theory (§9.1)
section: B.22.1 Statement A: the Symmetric Part is Held Fixed
text:
B.22.1 Statement A: the Symmetric Part is Held Fixed

Every connection coefficient function splits into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts in the two lower indices, \begin{align*} \Gamma^i_{jk} = \Gamma^i_{(jk)} + \Gamma^i_{[jk]}, \qquad \Gamma^i_{[jk]} \coloneqq \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \Gamma^i_{jk} - \Gamma^i_{kj} \Big] = - \frac{1}{2} \, \mathtt{T}^i_{jk}, \end{align*} so the antisymmetric part is the torsion, up to a factor \(-1/2\), while the symmetric part is independent of it. Since in the autoparallel equation \begin{align*} \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U} + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} = \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U} + \Gamma^k_{(ji)} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} = 0 \end{align*} the coefficient functions are contracted with the symmetric product \(\dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}\), the antisymmetric part drops out. Statement A. Two connections with the same symmetric part, \(\tilde{\Gamma}^k_{(ij)} = \Gamma^k_{(ij)}\), have the same autoparallels, whatever their torsions. Without charts: the difference of two connections is a \((1,2)\)-tensor field \(S\) (Chapter 6), and both connections have the same autoparallels if and only if \(S\) is antisymmetric in its two vector slots, i.e. if they differ only by torsion. This is the right statement whenever the connection itself is the primary structure, freely specified by its coefficient functions, as in the Newtonian spacetime of Chapter 9.

title: B.22 Torsion in Newton-Cartan Theory (§9.1)
section: B.22.2 Statement B: a Metric is Held Fixed
text:
B.22.2 Statement B: a Metric is Held Fixed

In most physical theories the connection is not specified freely but constructed from other structures, subject to compatibility conditions. The standard case is a metric: a symmetric \((0,2)\)-tensor field \(g\) whose matrix of component functions \(g_{ij} \coloneqq g(\partial x_i, \partial x_j)\) is invertible at every point, with inverse \(g^{ij}\), \(g^{ik} g_{kj} = \delta^i_j\). A connection is metric compatible if \(\nabla g = 0\), i.e. if parallel transport preserves the lengths of and angles between vectors. Writing \(\Gamma_{kij} \coloneqq g_{km} \Gamma^m_{ij}\) and \(\mathtt{T}_{kij} \coloneqq g_{km} \mathtt{T}^m_{ij}\), the condition reads \begin{align*} 0 = \big( \nabla_{\partial x_k} g \big)(\partial x_i, \partial x_j) = \partial x_k\left\lfloor g_{ij} \right\rceil - \Gamma_{jik} - \Gamma_{ijk}. \end{align*} Given \(g\) and a prescribed torsion \(\mathtt{T}\), there is exactly one metric compatible connection with that torsion10: \begin{align*} \Gamma_{kij} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \Big[ \partial x_i\left\lfloor g_{jk} \right\rceil + \partial x_j\left\lfloor g_{ki} \right\rceil - \partial x_k\left\lfloor g_{ij} \right\rceil \Big]}_{\eqqcolon \, \mathring{\Gamma}_{kij}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \Big[ \mathtt{T}_{kji} + \mathtt{T}_{jki} + \mathtt{T}_{ikj} \Big]}_{\eqqcolon \, K_{kij}}. \end{align*} The first term is the Levi-Civita connection, the unique torsion-free metric compatible one, symmetric in \(i, j\); the second is the contorsion, linear in the torsion. Its antisymmetric part reproduces the torsion, \(K_{kij} - K_{kji} = - \mathtt{T}_{kij}\), but its symmetric part does not vanish in general: \begin{align*} \Gamma^k_{(ij)} = \mathring{\Gamma}^k_{ij} + \frac{1}{2} \, g^{km} \Big[ \mathtt{T}_{imj} + \mathtt{T}_{jmi} \Big]. \end{align*} Statement B. For a fixed metric, the autoparallels of the metric compatible connection with torsion \(\mathtt{T}\) satisfy \begin{align*} \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U} + \mathring{\Gamma}^k_{ji} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} + g^{km} \, \mathtt{T}_{imj} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} = 0, \end{align*} so torsion does affect them. The additional term vanishes for all velocities if and only if \(\mathtt{T}_{imj} = - \mathtt{T}_{jmi}\), which, combined with the antisymmetry of torsion in its last two indices, means that \(\mathtt{T}_{kij}\) is totally antisymmetric. Only then are the autoparallels those of the Levi-Civita connection.

title: B.22 Torsion in Newton-Cartan Theory (§9.1)
text:
B.22.3 Conclusion

The two statements describe different families of connections: (A) fixing \(\Gamma^k_{(ij)}\) and varying \(\mathtt{T}\) leaves the autoparallels unchanged, but in general destroys metric compatibility; (B) fixing \(g\) and \(\nabla g = 0\) and varying \(\mathtt{T}\) preserves metric compatibility, but in general changes \(\Gamma^k_{(ij)}\), hence the autoparallels. They agree precisely for totally antisymmetric torsion. Asking whether torsion affects autoparallels is therefore not meaningful until the structure from which the connection is built is specified.

title: B.22 Torsion in Newton-Cartan Theory (§9.1)
text:
B.22.4 Torsion Beyond Autoparallels

Even in case (A), torsion is not invisible to the connection: it affects the parallel transport of vectors other than the velocity. Along a curve \(\gamma\), a vector field \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\) with components \(x^k_\gamma\) is parallel transported if  egin{align*}  rac{d x^k_\gamma}{d\lambda} + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, x^j_\gamma \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} = 0, \end{align*} where \(\Gamma\) is contracted with two different vectors, so its antisymmetric part contributes. Only for \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma = v_\gamma\), which yields the autoparallel equation, does it drop out. Since the curvature measures the failure of parallel transport around closed curves, \(\mathrm{Riem}\) and \(\mathrm{Ric}\) depend on the torsion as well: if \(	ilde{
abla}\) and \(
abla\) differ only by torsion, they have the same autoparallels but, in general, different curvatures. Example. In a stratified chart of a Newtonian spacetime with all \(\Gamma^i_{jk} = 0\), i.e. without gravity, add \(	ilde{\Gamma}^\alpha_{ eta\delta} \coloneqq \varepsilon_{\alpha eta\delta}\), the totally antisymmetric symbol with \(\varepsilon_{123} = 1\). The new connection still satisfies \(
abla dt = 0\), its torsion is \(\mathtt{T}^\alpha_{ eta\delta} = - 2 \, \varepsilon_{\alpha eta\delta}\), and its autoparallels are unchanged: free particles move along straight lines at constant velocity \(u^\alpha\). A spatial vector transported along such a worldline, however, obeys \( rac{d x^\alpha_\gamma}{dt} = - \varepsilon_{\alpha eta\delta} \, x^ eta_\gamma \, u^\delta\): it rotates about the direction of motion. Correspondingly, by the component expression of \(\mathrm{Riem}\) (Chapter 6),  egin{align*} \widetilde{\mathrm{Riem}}^\alpha_{ eta\delta\kappa} = \delta_{\alpha\kappa} \, \delta_{ eta\delta} - \delta_{\alpha\delta} \, \delta_{ eta\kappa}, \qquad \widetilde{\mathrm{Ric}}_{ eta\kappa} = - 2 \, \delta_{ eta\kappa}: \end{align*} a spacetime with no gravity, in which every free particle moves exactly as in the torsion-free case, has non-vanishing curvature, and even violates the vacuum field equation \(\mathrm{Ric} = 0\). Torsion also enters two further results of Chapter 6. A chart with all \(\Gamma^i_{jk} = 0\) exists only if both \(\mathrm{Riem}\) and \(\mathtt{T}\) vanish, since torsion, being a tensor field, cannot be removed by any choice of chart. And the identification of the relative acceleration of neighbouring autoparallels with the curvature, as in the tidal acceleration of Section 9.4, acquires torsion terms, so that with torsion it no longer equals \(\mathrm{Riem}\).

title: B.22 Torsion in Newton-Cartan Theory (§9.1)
text:
B.22.5 The Newtonian Case

Uniform flow restricts torsion even before choosing the connection. The derivation \( ig( 
abla_{\partial x_i} dt  ig)_k = - \Gamma^0_{ki}\) of Section 9.3 does not use torsion-freeness, so \(
abla dt = 0\) gives \(\Gamma^0_{ki} = 0\) for all \(k, i\), and hence \(\mathtt{T}^0_{jk} = 0\): the torsion of any connection compatible with absolute time is spatial. Within Newton’s axioms, torsion is a gauge freedom. The axioms of Section 9.2 only involve worldlines, i.e. velocities transported along themselves. Free particles therefore determine \(\Gamma^k_{(ij)}\), since knowing \(\Gamma^k_{(ij)} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}\) for all velocities fixes the symmetric part, but leave the torsion completely free, and no prediction depends on it. Requiring \(\mathtt{T} = 0\) selects the unique connection determined by free particles. It is a convention, but a necessary one: only for this connection do \(\mathrm{Riem}\) and \(\mathrm{Ric}\) depend on observable quantities alone, so that \(\mathrm{Riem} 
eq 0\) signals gravity, \(\mathrm{Ric} = 4 \pi G ho \; dt\left\lceil \cdot ightfloor dt\left\lceil \cdot ightfloor\) ties curvature to matter, and \(\mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0 eta0}\) is the tidal acceleration. With torsion, the curvature would also record the unobservable rotation of the example above. Beyond Newton’s axioms, torsion is physical. If parallel transport of vectors other than the velocity is given physical meaning, torsion becomes observable, and its value is decided by experiment rather than by convention. Two instances: Gyroscopes. Postulating that the axis of a torque-free gyroscope is parallel transported, the torsion of the example would make it precess about the direction of motion. Experience shows that a torque-free gyroscope keeps its orientation w.r.t. non-rotating axes, i.e. is parallel transported by the torsion-free connection. Spatial metric. If \(
abla\) is required to be compatible with a spatial metric \(h\) (Appendix B.21), Statement B applies to the spatial indices: in a Cartesian stratified chart, spatial torsion that is not totally antisymmetric in its three spatial indices changes \(\Gamma^\alpha_{( eta\delta)}\), and hence the worldlines themselves. In both cases the torsion-free condition becomes a physical assumption, consistent with Newtonian experience. The definition of Newtonian spacetime thus fixes the gauge freedom left by the axioms in the one way compatible with these further observations. 10 Write the compatibility condition three times, cyclically permuting \((i, j, k)\), and add the first two minus the third. Replacing every \(\Gamma_{mab}\) by \(\Gamma_{mba} - \mathtt{T}_{mab}\) where needed, all terms except \(2 \, \Gamma_{kij}\) cancel or combine into torsion terms, which yields the expression given. Conversely, this expression satisfies the compatibility condition and has torsion \(\mathtt{T}\). \(\square\)

title: C.1 Example of Vector Spaces (§§2.2–2.3)
text: Consider the \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space \(\left( P_N, \oplus, \odot \right)\) equipped with the field of real numbers \((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\), where: \[ P_N := \left\{ \begin{aligned} p : \mathbb{R} &\to \mathbb{R}\\ x &\mapsto p(x) := p^0 + p^1 x + \cdots + p^N x^N,\; p^i \in \mathbb{R}, \, N \in \mathbb{N} \end{aligned} \right\}, \] \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \textbf{Pointwise addition } \oplus: \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \oplus : P_N \times P_N &\to P_N \\ (p, q) &\mapsto p \oplus q \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (p \oplus q)(x) := p(x) + q(x). \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \textbf{Pointwise s-multiplication } \odot: \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \odot_H : \mathbb{R} \times P_N &\to P_N \\ (\alpha, p) &\mapsto \alpha \odot p \end{aligned} \\[6pt] \text{with } (\alpha \odot p)(x) := \alpha \cdot p(x). \end{array} \end{aligned} \]

title: C.1 Example of Vector Spaces (§§2.2–2.3)
section: C.1.1 Check for Vector Space Properties (§2.2)
text:
C.1.1 Check for Vector Space Properties (§2.2)

We can verify that \( \left( P_N, \oplus, \odot \right) \) is a vector space over \( \mathbb{R}, +, \cdot \) by checking the required axioms: Commutativity (for \(\oplus\)): \[ \forall p, q \in P_N \longrightarrow (p \oplus q)(x) = p(x) + q(x) = q(x) + p(x) = (q \oplus p)(x), \] Associativity (for \(\oplus\)): \[ \forall p, q, r \in P_N \longrightarrow ((p \oplus q) \oplus r)(x) = (p(x) + q(x)) + r(x) = p(x) + (q(x) + r(x)) = (p \oplus (q \oplus r))(x). \] Neutral element (for \(\oplus\)): The zero polynomial \( \mathbf{0} \in P_N \), defined by \( \mathbf{0}(x) := 0 \), satisfies \[ (p \oplus \mathbf{0})(x) = p(x) + 0 = p(x), \quad \forall p \in P_N. \] Inverse element (for \(\oplus\)): For each \( p \in P_N \), define \( -p \in P_N \) by \( (-p)(x) := -p(x) \). Then, \[ (p \oplus (-p))(x) = p(x) - p(x) = 0 = \mathbf{0}(x). \] Associativity (for \(\odot\)): \[ \begin{aligned} \forall \alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}, \, p \in P_N \longrightarrow \left((\alpha \cdot \beta) \odot p\right)(x) = (\alpha \cdot \beta) \cdot p(x) = \alpha \cdot (\beta \cdot p(x)) = \left(\alpha \odot (\beta \odot p)\right)(x), \end{aligned} \] Distributivity (of \(+\) over \(\odot\)): For \( \alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R} \), and \( p \in P_N \), \[ \begin{aligned} \left((\alpha + \beta) \odot p\right)(x) = (\alpha + \beta) \cdot p(x) = \alpha \cdot p(x) + \beta \cdot p(x) = ...\\ ... = (\alpha \odot p)(x) + (\beta \odot p)(x) = \left((\alpha \odot p) \oplus (\beta \odot p)\right)(x), \end{aligned} \] Distributivity (of \(\odot\) over \(\oplus\)): For \( \alpha \in \mathbb{R} \), and \( p, q \in P_N \), \[ \begin{aligned} \left(\alpha \odot (p \oplus q)\right)(x) = \alpha \cdot (p(x) + q(x)) = \alpha \cdot p(x) + \alpha \cdot q(x) = ...\\ ...= (\alpha \odot p)(x) + (\alpha \odot q)(x) = \left((\alpha \odot p) \oplus (\alpha \odot q)\right)(x), \end{aligned} \] Unitary element (for \(\odot\)): The one polynomial \( \mathbf{1} \in P_N \), defined by \( \mathbf{1}(x) := 1 \), satisfies \[ (\mathbf{1} \odot p)(x) = 1 \cdot p(x) = p(x). \] Figure C.1: This figure provides a visual illustration of the polynomial vector space operations introduced in Appendix C.1. It depicts pointwise addition and scalar multiplication, together with their compatibility under the derivative linear map \(\delta\). Colored curves represent different elements of the vector space and their transformations.

title: C.1 Example of Vector Spaces (§§2.2–2.3)
section: C.1.2 Examples of Objects associated with a Vector Space (§2.2)
text:
C.1.2 Examples of Objects associated with a Vector Space (§2.2)

We can now provide an example of a linear map. Let’s consider the differential operator: \begin{align*} \delta : P_N &\overset{\sim}{\to} P_N\\ p &\mapsto \delta(p) := p' \end{align*} Where \(\left( P_N, \oplus, \odot \right)\), serves both as the domain and the target vector space for \(\delta\). We can explicitly check that it satisfies the properties for linear maps: \[ \delta \left[ \left(p \oplus q\right)(x) \right] = (p(x) + q(x))' = p'(x) + q'(x) = \delta(p)(x) \oplus \delta(q)(x), \] \[ \delta \left[ \left(\alpha \odot p\right) (x) \right]= (\alpha \cdot p(x) )' = \alpha \cdot p'(x) = \alpha \odot \delta(p)(x). \] We can also define the vector space of homomorphisms between the vector space \(\left( P_N, \oplus, \odot \right)\), and itself using the definitions from Chapter 2: \( \left( \text{Hom}(P_N, P_N), \oplus_H, \odot_H \right) \). For example: \(5 \odot \delta \oplus (\delta \circ \delta) \in \text{Hom}(P_N, P_N)\). The dual vector space of \(\left( P_N, \oplus, \odot \right)\) is the homomorphism between our original vector space and the real numbers, i.e, \(\left( P_N^* := \text{Hom}(P_N, \mathbb{R}), \oplus^*, \odot^* \right)\). The following operator for integration is therefore an element of the dual space, that is, a covector: \begin{align*} I : P_N &\overset{\sim}{\to} \mathbb{R}\\ p &\mapsto I(p) := \int_0^1 p(x) dx\, . \end{align*} And we need to verify if it is indeed linear: \[ I \left[ \left(p \oplus q\right)(x) \right] = I\left[p(x) + q(x)\right] = I\left[p(x)\right] + I\left[q(x)\right], \] \[ I \left[ \left(\alpha \odot p\right) (x) \right]= I\left[\alpha \cdot p(x)\right] = \alpha \cdot I\left[p(x)\right]. \] Finally, we provide an example of a higher-order tensor: The inner product on the real numbers is a \((0,2)\)-tensor over \( P_N \) defined by the (multi-)linear map: \begin{align*} g : P_N \times P_N &\overset{\sim}{\to} \mathbb{R}\\ (p, q)&\mapsto g(p, q) := \int_{-1}^{1} p(x) q(x) dx \,. \end{align*} Again, let’s verify if it is indeed (multi-)linear: \begin{align*} g\left[\left(p_1 \oplus p_2\right)(x),\; q(x)\right] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \left(p_1(x) + p_2(x)\right) q(x) dx = ...\\ &...= \int_{-1}^{1} p_1(x) q(x) dx + \int_{-1}^{1} p_2(x) q(x) dx = g(p_1, q) + g(p_2, q), \end{align*} \[ g\left[\left(\alpha \odot p\right)(x),\; q(x)\right] = \int_{-1}^{1} \left(\alpha \cdot p(x)\right) q(x) dx = \alpha \cdot \int_{-1}^{1} p(x) q(x) dx = \alpha \cdot g(p, q), \] The same is true for the second entry, confirming it’s (multi-)linear, and therefore a \((0,2)\)-tensor.

title: C.1 Example of Vector Spaces (§§2.2–2.3)
section: C.1.3 Basis, Dual Basis and Coordinate Components (§2.3)
text:
C.1.3 Basis, Dual Basis and Coordinate Components (§2.3)

If we now fix the order of our polinomials to a finite number, let’s say \( N = 3 \), we can define the following (Hamel) basis for our vector space: \[ B \coloneq \left\lbrace \hat{x}_i \right\rbrace = \left\lbrace \hat{x}_0(x) = 1, \quad \hat{x}_1(x) = x, \quad \hat{x}_2(x) = x^2, \quad \hat{x}_3(x) = x^3 \right\rbrace. \] We can express any polynomial (of degree \(N \leq 3\)) as a linear combination of these elements . The corresponding dual induced cobasis \(B^* \coloneq \left\lbrace \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i \right\rbrace = \{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^0,\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1,\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^2,\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^3\}\subset P^*\) is defined as follows: \[ \begin{aligned} \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^0 : P &{\to} \mathbb{R}, & p &\mapsto \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^0(p) := p(0),\\ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1 : P &{\to} \mathbb{R}, & p &\mapsto \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1(p) := \left.\frac{d}{dx}p(x)\right|_{x=0},\\ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^2 : P &{\to} \mathbb{R}, & p &\mapsto \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^2(p) := \left.\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}p(x)\right|_{x=0},\\ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^3 : P &{\to} \mathbb{R}, & p &\mapsto \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^3(p) := \left.\frac{1}{6}\frac{d^3}{dx^3}p(x)\right|_{x=0}. \end{aligned} \] In operator shorthand, \[ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^k \;\equiv\; \left.\frac{1}{k!}\frac{d^k}{dx^k}\right|_{x=0}, \qquad k=0,1,2,3, \] Each \(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^k\) acts on vectors (polynomials) \(p\in P_N\) and returns a real number by first differentiating and then evaluating it at a point, for example \(x=0\). We can verify that \(B^*\) is indeed the corresponding induced dual cobasis to \(B\) by explicitly checking if \(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i(\hat{x}_j) = \delta^i_j \quad \forall \, i, j \in \left[0, N\right]\): \[ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i(\hat{x}_j)= \left.\frac{1}{i!}\frac{d^i}{dx^i}x^j\right|_{x=0} =\delta^i_j. \] Now we are going to show explicitly how to extract the components of vectors in the provided basis employing the dual induced cobasis. Given any \(p\in P_N\), we write it in coordinates w.r.t. \(B\) as \[ p \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^3 p^{i}\, \hat{x}_i. \] Applying \(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j\) to both sides isolates the \(j\)-th coordinate because \(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j(\hat{x}_i)=\delta^j_i\): \[ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j(p) \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^3 p^{i}\, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j(\hat{x}_i)= \sum_{i=0}^3 p^{i}\,\delta^j_i = \; p^{\,i}. \] For a concrete instance, take the polynomial \(p(x)=1.5 - 1.5\,x - x^2 + 0.7\,x^3\). Then \[ p(0)=1.5,\qquad \left.\frac{d}{dx}p(x)\right|_{x=0}=-1.5,\qquad \left.\frac{d^2}{dx^2}p(x)\right|_{x=0}=-2,\qquad \left.\frac{d^3}{dx^3}p(x)\right|_{x=0}=4.2, \] and therefore \[ [p]_{B} =\bigl(p^{\,0},p^{\,1},p^{\,2},p^{\,3}\bigr)^\top =\left(1.5,\,-1.5,\,\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot(-2),\,\tfrac{1}{6}\cdot 4.2\right)^\top =\left(1.5,\,-1.5,\,-1,\,0.7\right)^\top \] Figure C.2: This figure illustrates the decomposition of two polynomial vectors \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\) into the canonical monomial basis \(\{1, x, x^2, x^3\}\), as discussed in Appendix C.1. The colored lines correspond to the scaled coordinate components, while the gray curves represent the normalized basis functions. Together, they show how elements of the polynomial vector space can be written as linear combinations of basis elements. For an example of how this process works in the case of a covector, let’s take the integral functional \(I\in P_N^*\) previously defined. We can obtain it’s components in the dual induced cobasis by directly evaluating how it acts upon the basis elements \(B = \left\lbrace \hat{x}_j \right\rbrace\): \[ I_j \;=\; I(\hat{x}_j)\;=\;\int_0^1 x^j\,dx\;=\;\frac{1}{j+1}, \qquad j\in [0,N]. \] hence \[ [I]_{B^*} =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & \tfrac12, & \tfrac13, & \tfrac14 \end{bmatrix} \quad \longrightarrow \qquad I \;=\; \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^0 \;+\; \tfrac12\,\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1 \;+\; \tfrac13\,\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^2 \;+\; \tfrac14\,\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^3. \] Having shown how to decompose vectors and covectors in a given basis/cobasis, we explore how these components can be employed in matrix form to perform operations—specifically, the direct integration of polynomials—via a simple matrix multiplication. Let \([I]_{B^*}\) denote the coordinate row of the integral covector and \([p]_{B}\) the coordinate column of a polynomial \(p\in P_N\) in our fixed bases. Since \(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i(\hat{x}_j)=\delta^i_j\), the pairing matrix is the identity and the action of \(I\) on \(p\) reduces to: \[ I(p) \;=\; [I]_{B^*}\,[p]_{B} \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \tfrac12 & \tfrac13 & \tfrac14 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} p^{\,0}\\[2pt] p^{\,1}\\[2pt] p^{\,2}\\[2pt] p^{\,3} \end{bmatrix} \;=\; p^{\,0}\;+\;\tfrac12\,p^{\,1}\;+\;\tfrac13\,p^{\,2}\;+\;\tfrac14\,p^{\,3}. \] Equivalently, the same computation done explicitly reads \[ I(p)\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^3 p^{\,j}\,I(\hat{x}_j) \;=\;\sum_{j=0}^3 p^{\,j}\!\int_0^1 x^j\,dx \;=\;\sum_{j=0}^3 \frac{p^{\,j}}{j+1}, \] which is exactly the scalar obtained by the vector multiplication above. We now extend the component extraction procedure to higher-order tensors. Let’s employ as an example the the inner product \(g\), a \((0,2)\)-tensor defined above. Its components in the monomial basis \(B\) are: \[ g_{ij} \;=\; g(\hat{x}_i,\hat{x}_j)\;=\;\int_{-1}^{1} x^{\,i}\,x^{\,j}\,dx \;=\;\int_{-1}^{1} x^{\,i+j}\,dx \;=\; \begin{cases} \;\;0, & i+j\ \text{odd},\\[2pt] \displaystyle \frac{2}{\,i+j+1\,}, & i+j\ \text{even}. \end{cases} \] In particular, for \(i,j\in [0, N]\) we obtain the Gram matrix \[ [g]_{B} =\begin{pmatrix} \frac{2}{1} & 0 & \frac{2}{3} & 0\\[4pt] 0 & \frac{2}{3} & 0 & \frac{2}{5}\\[4pt] \frac{2}{3} & 0 & \frac{2}{5} & 0\\[4pt] 0 & \frac{2}{5} & 0 & \frac{2}{7} \end{pmatrix}. \] Hence, for \(p=\sum_i p^{i} \hat{x}_i\) and \(q=\sum_j q^{j} \hat{x}_j\), \[ g(p, q) \;=\; \sum_{i,j=0}^3 p^{i} q^{j}\, g_{ij}. \]

title: C.1 Example of Vector Spaces (§§2.2–2.3)
text:
C.1.4 Change of Basis (§2.3)

We now consider an alternative basis of \(P_{N=3}\): the (unnormalized) Legendre polynomials on \([-1,1]\): \[ B_L \coloneq \left\lbrace \hat{y}_i \right\rbrace = \Bigl\{ \hat{y}_0(x)=1,\quad \hat{y}_1(x)=x,\quad \hat{y}_2(x)=\tfrac12(3x^2-1),\quad \hat{y}_3(x)=\tfrac12(5x^3-3x) \Bigr\}. \] First, let’s show that \(B_L\) is a basis of \(P_3\), i.e., that \(\left\lbrace \hat{y}_i \right\rbrace\) are linearly independent and span \(P_3\). To do so we are going to obtain the change-of-basis matrix by expressing each \(\hat{y}_j \in B_L\) in the monomial basis \(B \coloneq \{\hat{x}_i\}\): \[ \hat{y}_0=\hat{x}_0,\qquad \hat{y}_1=\hat{x}_1,\qquad \hat{y}_2=-\tfrac12\,\hat{x}_0+\tfrac32\,\hat{x}_2,\qquad \hat{y}_3=-\tfrac32\,\hat{x}_1+\tfrac52\,\hat{x}_3. \] Hence the change-of-basis matrix (columns are the coordinates of \(B_L\) expressed in \(B\)) is: \[ \left(J^{-1}\right)^i_j = \left(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{B \leftarrow B_L}\right)^i_j =\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -\tfrac12 & 0\\[4pt] 0 & 1 & 0 & -\tfrac32\\[4pt] 0 & 0 & \tfrac32 & 0\\[4pt] 0 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac52 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \longrightarrow \qquad \det \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{B \leftarrow B_L}\neq 0. \] Therefore the columns are linearly independent and so is \(B_L\). Since \(\dim P_3=4\) and we have \(4\) independent vectors, they span \(P_3\) and hence constitutes a basis. Figure C.3: This figure illustrates the decomposition of two polynomial vectors \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\) into the Legendre basis \(\{\hat{y}_0(x)=1,\;\hat{y}_1(x)=x,\;\hat{y}_2(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}(3x^2-1),\;\hat{y}_3(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}(5x^3-3x)\}\), as discussed in Appendix C.1.4. The colored lines correspond to the scaled coordinate components (each coefficient times its Legendre basis function), while the gray curves represent the normalized basis functions themselves. Together, they show how elements of the polynomial vector space can be written as linear combinations of Legendre polynomials. The corresponding induced dual cobasis \(B_L^* \coloneq \left\lbrace \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i \right\rbrace \subset P_N^*\) is naturally defined using orthogonality of Legendre polynomials w.r.t. the inner product \(g(p,q)=\int_{-1}^{1}p(x)q(x)\,dx\): \[ \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i : P_N \to \mathbb{R},\qquad p \longmapsto \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i(p) \;\coloneq\; \frac{2i+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x)\,\hat{y}_i(x)\,dx, \quad i \in [0, N]. \] Using \(\int_{-1}^{1}\hat{y}_i\hat{y}_j\,dx=\tfrac{2}{2i+1}\delta^i_j\), we get \(\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i(\hat{y}_j)=\delta^i_j\), so indeed \(B_L^*\coloneq\{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i\}\) is the induced dual cobasis of \(\{\hat{y}_i\}\). As previously demonstrated, we can obtain the components of a vector \(p\in P_3\) in a given basis, e.g. \(B_L\), by letting the elements of the induced dual cobasis, \(B_L^*\), act on \(p\). Writting down explicitly the components for the example polynomial we have been working with, \(p(x)=1.5 - 1.5\,x - x^2 + 0.7\,x^3\), we get: \begin{align*} \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^0\left(p\right) &= \frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \hat{y}_0(x)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \cdot 1\,dx = \frac{7}{6}\\ \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^1\left(p\right) &= \frac{3}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \hat{y}_1(x)\,dx = \frac{3}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \cdot x\,dx = -\frac{27}{25}\\ \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^2\left(p\right) &= \frac{5}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \hat{y}_2(x)\,dx = \frac{5}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \cdot \frac{1}{2}\left(3x^2-1\right)\,dx = -\frac{2}{3}\\ \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^3\left(p\right) &= \frac{7}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \hat{y}_3(x)\,dx = \frac{7}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} p(x) \cdot \frac{1}{2}\left(5x^3-3x\right)\,dx = \frac{7}{25} \end{align*} Therefore \([p]_{B_L} = \left(\frac{7}{6}, -\frac{27}{25}, -\frac{2}{3}, \frac{7}{25}\right)^T\). We can verify that this is equivalent to employing the inverse of the change of basis matrix transformation previously defined: \begin{align*} J = \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{B_L \leftarrow B} = \left(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{B \leftarrow B_L}\right)^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & \tfrac{1}{3} & 0\\[4pt] 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac{3}{5}\\[4pt] 0 & 0 & \tfrac{2}{3} & 0\\[4pt] 0 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac{2}{5} \end{pmatrix}, \quad [p]_{B_L} = J\,[p]_B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & \tfrac{1}{3} & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac{3}{5}\\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{2}{3} & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac{2}{5} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{3}{2}\\[2pt] -\tfrac{3}{2}\\[2pt] -1\\[2pt] \tfrac{7}{10} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{7}{6}\\[2pt] -\tfrac{27}{25}\\[2pt] -\tfrac{2}{3}\\[2pt] \tfrac{7}{25} \end{pmatrix}. \end{align*} Where it is immediate to verify that the inverse change of basis is indeed the one given above, since explicitly \(J \cdot J^{-1} \;=\; I_4\). The same logic applies to covectors and higher-order tensors. We leave to the reader repeating the same exercise for the components of the integral covector \(I\) in the basis \(B_L^*\).

title: C.2 Example of a \(d\)-dimensional Smooth Manifold (§§3.2–3.3)
text: Consider the 1-dim. (topological) manifold \(\left( \mathcal{S}^1, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{S}^1}, \mathcal{A} \right)_1\) constituted by: The set \(\mathcal{S}^1 \coloneqq \left\lbrace q = (q_1, q_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : q_1^2 + q_2^2 = 1 \right\rbrace\). The topology inherited from the standard topology of \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{S}^1} \coloneqq \left.\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^2}\right\rvert_{\mathcal{S}^1} = \left\lbrace \mathcal{S}^1 \cap \mathcal{W} : \mathcal{W} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^2} \right\rbrace. \end{align*} The atlas \(\mathcal{A}\) formed by four charts, whose domains are open in \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{S}^1}\) and together cover \(\mathcal{S}^1\): \[ \mathcal{A} \coloneqq \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c@{\quad} | @{\quad} c} \textbf{Upper chart $(\mathcal{U}_\uparrow, \mathscr{X}_\uparrow)$} & \textbf{Lower chart $(\mathcal{U}_\downarrow, \mathscr{X}_\downarrow)$} \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U}_\uparrow &\coloneqq \lbrace q \in \mathcal{S}^1 : q_2 > 0 \rbrace \\ \mathscr{X}_\uparrow : \mathcal{U}_\uparrow &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}_\uparrow(\mathcal{U}_\uparrow) = (-1, 1) \\ q &\longmapsto \mathscr{X}_\uparrow(q) \coloneqq q_1 \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U}_\downarrow &\coloneqq \lbrace q \in \mathcal{S}^1 : q_2 < 0 \rbrace \\ \mathscr{X}_\downarrow : \mathcal{U}_\downarrow &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}_\downarrow(\mathcal{U}_\downarrow) = (-1, 1) \\ q &\longmapsto \mathscr{X}_\downarrow(q) \coloneqq q_1 \end{aligned} \\[22pt] \hline \\[-2pt] \textbf{Right chart $(\mathcal{U}_\rightarrow, \mathscr{X}_\rightarrow)$} & \textbf{Left chart $(\mathcal{U}_\leftarrow, \mathscr{X}_\leftarrow)$} \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U}_\rightarrow &\coloneqq \lbrace q \in \mathcal{S}^1 : q_1 > 0 \rbrace \\ \mathscr{X}_\rightarrow : \mathcal{U}_\rightarrow &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}_\rightarrow(\mathcal{U}_\rightarrow) = (-1, 1) \\ q &\longmapsto \mathscr{X}_\rightarrow(q) \coloneqq q_2 \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U}_\leftarrow &\coloneqq \lbrace q \in \mathcal{S}^1 : q_1 < 0 \rbrace \\ \mathscr{X}_\leftarrow : \mathcal{U}_\leftarrow &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}_\leftarrow(\mathcal{U}_\leftarrow) = (-1, 1) \\ q &\longmapsto \mathscr{X}_\leftarrow(q) \coloneqq q_2 \end{aligned} \end{array} \right\rbrace \] Each chart map is a homeomorphism onto the open interval \((-1, 1)\), with continuous inverse \begin{align*} \mathscr{X}_\uparrow^{-1}(\alpha) &= \left( \alpha, \sqrt{1 - \alpha^2} \right), & \mathscr{X}_\downarrow^{-1}(\alpha) &= \left( \alpha, -\sqrt{1 - \alpha^2} \right), \\ \mathscr{X}_\rightarrow^{-1}(\alpha) &= \left( \sqrt{1 - \alpha^2}, \alpha \right), & \mathscr{X}_\leftarrow^{-1}(\alpha) &= \left( -\sqrt{1 - \alpha^2}, \alpha \right). \end{align*} We now check that the atlas is \(C^\infty\)-compatible, i.e. that the chart transition maps are smooth wherever two chart domains overlap. The intersection of \(\mathcal{U}_\uparrow\) and \(\mathcal{U}_\rightarrow\) is the open quarter of circle \[ \mathcal{U}_\uparrow \cap \mathcal{U}_\rightarrow = \left\lbrace q \in \mathcal{S}^1 : q_1 > 0, \; q_2 > 0 \right\rbrace, \]

title: C.3 Example of Tangent, Cotangent and Tensor Spaces (§§4.1–4.3)
text: Figure C.4: Visualization of the curves \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) (from the example in Appendix C.3) on the smooth manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_2\), with \(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}^2\), both passing through the point \(p = (1,1)\). At that point, the velocities of the curves define elements of the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\). Arrowheads indicate the local direction of each curve. This figure illustrates that although the curves can be added within a chart, the resulting curve is chart-dependent and not intrinsic to the manifold. Consider the 2-dim. (topological) manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A} \right)_2\), with \(\mathcal{M} \coloneqq \mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \coloneqq \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^2}\) the standard topology. We denote generic points of the manifold by \(q = (q_1, q_2) \in \mathcal{M}\), reserving the letter \(p\) for the specific point introduced below. The atlas \(\mathcal{A}\) is formed by the two charts: \[ \mathcal{A} \coloneqq \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c@{\quad} | @{\quad} c} \textbf{Chart $(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})$} & \textbf{Chart $(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})$} \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \\ \mathscr{X} \colon \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) = \mathbb{R}^2 \\ q &\longmapsto \mathscr{X}(q) \coloneqq (2 q_1, -q_2) \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \mathcal{V} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \\ \mathscr{Y} \colon \mathcal{V} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) = \mathbb{R}^2 \\ q &\longmapsto \mathscr{Y}(q) \coloneqq (q_1, q_2 e^{q_1}) \end{aligned} \end{array} \right\rbrace \] Both chart domains cover the whole manifold, hence \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \mathcal{M}\). Both chart maps are homeomorphisms w.r.t. the standard topologies, with continuous inverse chart maps: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \mathscr{X}^{-1} \colon \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) &\longrightarrow \mathcal{U} \\ (\alpha_1, \alpha_2) &\longmapsto \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = (\alpha_1/2, -\alpha_2) \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \colon \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) &\longrightarrow \mathcal{V} \\ (\beta_1, \beta_2) &\longmapsto \mathscr{Y}^{-1}(\beta_1, \beta_2) = (\beta_1, \beta_2 e^{-\beta_1}) \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] The atlas \(\mathcal{A}\) is \(C^\infty\)-compatible, since both chart transition maps are built from polynomials and exponentials, hence \(C^\infty\) in the ordinary multivariable calculus sense: \begin{align*} \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \colon \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \\ (\beta_1, \beta_2) &\longmapsto \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}(\beta_1, \beta_2) \coloneqq \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right)(\beta_1, \beta_2) = (2\beta_1, -\beta_2 e^{-\beta_1}), \\[6pt] \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \colon \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) &\longrightarrow \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \\ (\alpha_1, \alpha_2) &\longmapsto \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) \coloneqq \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right)(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = (\alpha_1/2, -\alpha_2 e^{\alpha_1/2}). \end{align*} Therefore \(\mathcal{A} \equiv \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\), and \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_2\) is a 2-dim. smooth manifold. Now consider the following two curves on the manifold: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \gamma_1 \colon \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{M} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \gamma_1(\lambda) \coloneqq (\lambda, 1) \end{aligned} \end{array} \quad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \gamma_2 \colon \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{M} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \gamma_2(\lambda) \coloneqq (1, 2\lambda). \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] Both curves pass through the point \(p \coloneqq (1,1) \in \mathcal{M}\): \(\gamma_1(\lambda_1) = p\) at \(\lambda_1 \coloneqq 1\), and \(\gamma_2(\lambda_2) = p\) at \(\lambda_2 \coloneqq 1/2\) (see Figure C.4). Their chart representatives, together with the coordinates of \(p\) in each chart, are: \[ \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1)(\lambda) &= (2\lambda, -1) \\ (\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_1)(\lambda) &= (\lambda, e^{\lambda}) \end{aligned} \end{array} \qquad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2)(\lambda) &= (2, -2\lambda) \\ (\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_2)(\lambda) &= (1, 2e\lambda) \end{aligned} \end{array} \qquad &\begin{array}{c} \begin{aligned} \mathscr{X}(p) &= (2, -1) \\ \mathscr{Y}(p) &= (1, e) \end{aligned} \end{array} \end{aligned} \] We can explicitly add these curves in each chart, i.e., by adding their chart representatives component-wise in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Recall that a manifold carries no notion of addition of its points: even though \(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}^2\) here, the vector-space structure of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is not part of \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_2\), and we deliberately ignore it. We define the curves \(\sigma_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathcal{V}}\) through their chart representatives in \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), respectively: \begin{align*} (\mathscr{X} \circ \sigma_{\mathcal{U}})(\lambda) &\coloneqq (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_1)(\lambda_1 + \lambda) + (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_2)(\lambda_2 + \lambda) - \mathscr{X}(p) \\ &= (2 + 2\lambda, -1) + (2, -1 - 2\lambda) - (2, -1) = (2\lambda + 2, -2\lambda - 1), \\[6pt] (\mathscr{Y} \circ \sigma_{\mathcal{V}})(\lambda) &\coloneqq (\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_1)(\lambda_1 + \lambda) + (\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_2)(\lambda_2 + \lambda) - \mathscr{Y}(p) \\ &= (1 + \lambda, e^{1 + \lambda}) + (1, e + 2e\lambda) - (1, e) = (\lambda + 1, e^{\lambda + 1} + 2e\lambda). \end{align*} Subtracting \(\mathscr{X}(p)\) (resp. \(\mathscr{Y}(p)\)) ensures that both curves pass through \(p\) at \(\lambda_0 = 0\). Mapping these chart-level curves back to the manifold with the inverse chart maps, we explicitly observe that they differ: \begin{align*} \sigma_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda) &= \mathscr{X}^{-1}\big( (\mathscr{X} \circ \sigma_{\mathcal{U}})(\lambda) \big) = (\lambda + 1, 2\lambda + 1) \longrightarrow \sigma_{\mathcal{U}}'(\lambda) = (1, 2), \\ \sigma_{\mathcal{V}}(\lambda) &= \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\big( (\mathscr{Y} \circ \sigma_{\mathcal{V}})(\lambda) \big) = (\lambda + 1, 1 + 2\lambda e^{-\lambda}) \longrightarrow \sigma_{\mathcal{V}}'(\lambda) = \big( 1, 2e^{-\lambda}(1 - \lambda) \big). \end{align*} However, what does not depend on the chart is the velocity of these curves at \(p\), i.e., the vector they define in \(T_p\mathcal{M}\). Let us explicitly check this. For any scalar field \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) we have1: \begin{align*} v_{\sigma_{\mathcal{U}}, p}(f) &\coloneqq (f \circ \sigma_{\mathcal{U}})'(0) = \sum_{i=1}^{2} (\sigma_{\mathcal{U}})_i'(0) \cdot \partial_i f\big( \sigma_{\mathcal{U}}(0) \big) = \partial_1 f(1,1) + 2 \cdot \partial_2 f(1,1), \\[6pt] v_{\sigma_{\mathcal{V}}, p}(f) &\coloneqq (f \circ \sigma_{\mathcal{V}})'(0) = \sum_{i=1}^{2} (\sigma_{\mathcal{V}})_i'(0) \cdot \partial_i f\big( \sigma_{\mathcal{V}}(0) \big) = \partial_1 f(1,1) + 2 \cdot \partial_2 f(1,1), \\[6pt] \big( v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p} \big)(f) &\coloneqq v_{\gamma_1, p}(f) + v_{\gamma_2, p}(f) = (f \circ \gamma_1)'(\lambda_1) + (f \circ \gamma_2)'(\lambda_2) \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{2} (\gamma_1)_i'(\lambda_1) \cdot \partial_i f\big( \gamma_1(\lambda_1) \big) + \sum_{i=1}^{2} (\gamma_2)_i'(\lambda_2) \cdot \partial_i f\big( \gamma_2(\lambda_2) \big) \\ &= \big( 1 \cdot \partial_1 f(1,1) + 0 \cdot \partial_2 f(1,1) \big) + \big( 0 \cdot \partial_1 f(1,1) + 2 \cdot \partial_2 f(1,1) \big) \\ &= \partial_1 f(1,1) + 2 \cdot \partial_2 f(1,1). \end{align*} Since this holds \(\forall f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), we conclude: \[ v_{\sigma_{\mathcal{U}}, p} = v_{\sigma_{\mathcal{V}}, p} = v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p}. \] That is, the curve realizing the sum \(v_{\gamma_1, p} \oplus_T v_{\gamma_2, p}\) depends on the chart used to construct it, but the element of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) it defines does not (cf. Appendix B.4). 1 Since \(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}^2\), any \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) is also a function \(f \colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) that is smooth in the ordinary multivariable calculus sense: \(f = (f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}) \circ \mathscr{X}\) is a composition of ordinarily smooth maps (equivalently, \(\mathcal{A} \cup \{ (\mathcal{M}, \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^2}) \}\) is still a \(C^\infty\)-compatible atlas). The same holds for the curves, viewed as maps \(\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2\). We can therefore apply the multivariable chain rule directly to \(f \circ \sigma \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), where \(\partial_i f\) denotes the ordinary partial derivative of \(f\) w.r.t. its \(i\)-th entry, and \((\sigma)_i'\) the derivative of the \(i\)-th component of \(\sigma\).

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
text: This appendix follows a single manifold from its definition as a set all the way up to vector fields, covector fields, their actions and a tensor field, so that every object introduced in the three sections above can be seen written out explicitly in two different charts. Point-level objects are written in the compact notation of Subsections 4.1.2 and 4.2.2, field-level objects in that of Section 5.3, and the Einstein summation convention is implied throughout.

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
text:
C.4.1 The manifold

Let us define a 2-dim. smooth manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_2\) as follows. The set \(\mathcal{M}\) is the graph of the height function \(h\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{M} \coloneqq \left\{ p = (a, b, c) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \;\middle|\; c = h(a,b) \right\}, \end{align*} where the height function \(h\) is \begin{align*} h(a,b) \coloneqq \frac{1}{2}\cos(a+b) + \frac{1}{2}\sin\left(a - b + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) + 1 = \cos a \, \cos b + 1, \end{align*} and the last equality lets us write every subsequent expression in a compact form. The topology \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}\) is the one induced from the ambient space \(\left( \mathbb{R}^3, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^3} \right)\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M} \coloneqq \left.\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^3}\right|_\mathcal{M} = \left\{ \mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{W} \;\middle|\; \mathcal{W} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^3} \right\}. \end{align*} The atlas \(\mathcal{A} \coloneqq \left\{ (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}), (\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \right\}\) is defined by the two charts2: \[ \begin{array}{c@{\;\;} | @{\;\;} c} \textbf{Chart $(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})$} & \textbf{Chart $(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})$} \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \\[2pt] \mathscr{X} \colon \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) = \mathbb{R}^2 \\ p = (a,b,c) &\longmapsto \mathscr{X}(p) \coloneqq \left( a \,,\, b \right) \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \mathcal{V} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \setminus \left\{ a \leq 0, \, b = 0 \right\} \\[2pt] \mathscr{Y} \colon \mathcal{V} &\longrightarrow \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) = (0, \infty) \times (-\pi, \pi) \\ p = (a,b,c) &\longmapsto \mathscr{Y}(p) \coloneqq \left( \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \,,\, \operatorname{atan2}(b, a) \right) \end{aligned} \end{array} \] so that the coordinate functions are \(\mathscr{X}^1(p) = a\), \(\mathscr{X}^2(p) = b\) and \(\mathscr{Y}^1(p) = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), \(\mathscr{Y}^2(p) = \operatorname{atan2}(b,a)\). Both chart maps are homeomorphisms onto their (open) images: \(\mathcal{M}\) is a graph over \(\mathbb{R}^2\), so \(\mathscr{X}\) is the restriction of the projection \((a,b,c) \mapsto (a,b)\), and \(\mathscr{Y}\) is that projection followed by polar coordinates. Their inverses are \begin{align*} \mathscr{X}^{-1} \colon \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) &\longrightarrow \mathcal{U} \\ (\alpha_1, \alpha_2)_\mathcal{U} &\longmapsto \big( \alpha_1, \, \alpha_2, \, h(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) \big)_\mathcal{M} \end{align*} \begin{align*} \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \colon \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) &\longrightarrow \mathcal{V} \\ (\beta_1, \beta_2)_\mathcal{V} &\longmapsto \big( \beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \, \beta_1 \sin \beta_2, \, h(\beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \beta_1 \sin \beta_2) \big)_\mathcal{M}. \end{align*} Since \(\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{M}\), the overlap of the two chart domains is \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \mathcal{V}\), and the two chart transition maps are \begin{align*} \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \colon \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) &\longrightarrow \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \\ \left( \beta_1 \,,\, \beta_2 \right)_\mathcal{V} &\longmapsto \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right) \left( \beta_1 \,,\, \beta_2 \right)_\mathcal{V} = \left( \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \,,\, \beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \right)_\mathcal{U} \end{align*} \begin{align*} \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \colon \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) &\longrightarrow \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}) \\ \left( \alpha_1 \,,\, \alpha_2 \right)_\mathcal{U} &\longmapsto \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \left( \alpha_1 \,,\, \alpha_2 \right)_\mathcal{U} = \left( \sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \,,\, \operatorname{atan2}(\alpha_2, \alpha_1) \right)_\mathcal{V}. \end{align*} Both are \(C^\infty\) on \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V})\) and \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{V})\) respectively (on the latter the branch cut has been removed, and \(\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2 > 0\) there), so the atlas is \(C^\infty\)-compatible, \(\mathcal{A} \equiv \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\), and \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_2\) is a 2-dim. smooth manifold.

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
text:
C.4.2 Jacobians and transformation laws

To relate the two charts we need the Jacobians of the transition maps at a point \(p \in \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\). Writing \(\mathscr{X}(p) = (\alpha_1, \alpha_2)_\mathcal{U}\), \(\mathscr{Y}(p) = (\beta_1, \beta_2)_\mathcal{V}\): \begin{align*} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) = \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p = \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{Y}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} & \dfrac{\alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \\[10pt] -\dfrac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} & \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \end{bmatrix}_\mathcal{V}, \end{align*} since \begin{align*} \partial_1 \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \left( \begin{array}{c} \alpha_1 \\ \alpha_2 \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{U} = \left( \begin{array}{c} \alpha_1 / \sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \\ -\alpha_2 / (\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2) \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{V} \quad ; \quad \partial_2 \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \left( \begin{array}{c} \alpha_1 \\ \alpha_2 \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{U} = \left( \begin{array}{c} \alpha_2 / \sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \\ \alpha_1 / (\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2) \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{V}. \end{align*} Correspondingly, for the inverse transition map: \begin{align*} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) = \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_p = \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^i \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] \left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \beta_2 & -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \\[4pt] \sin \beta_2 & \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}_\mathcal{U}, \end{align*} since \begin{align*} \partial_1 \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \left( \begin{array}{c} \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{V} = \left( \begin{array}{c} \cos \beta_2 \\ \sin \beta_2 \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{U} \quad ; \quad \partial_2 \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \left( \begin{array}{c} \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{V} = \left( \begin{array}{c} -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \\ \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{U}. \end{align*} As a consistency check, using \(\alpha_1 = \beta_1 \cos \beta_2\) and \(\alpha_2 = \beta_1 \sin \beta_2\), \begin{align*} \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{k}\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^k_{j}\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) = \delta^i_j. \end{align*} With these two matrices, the transformation laws derived in Subsections 4.1.1 and 4.2.1 become completely explicit. For the basis vectors of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) — covariant, \((\partial x_i)_p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^j_{i}\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) \cdot (\partial y_j)_p\) and \((\partial y_j)_p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_{j}\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot (\partial x_i)_p\): \begin{gather*} \begin{cases} (\partial x_1)_p = \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot (\partial y_1)_p - \dfrac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot (\partial y_2)_p \\[10pt] (\partial x_2)_p = \dfrac{\alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot (\partial y_1)_p + \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot (\partial y_2)_p \end{cases} \\[8pt] \begin{cases} (\partial y_1)_p = \cos \beta_2 \cdot (\partial x_1)_p + \sin \beta_2 \cdot (\partial x_2)_p \\[10pt] (\partial y_2)_p = -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \cdot (\partial x_1)_p + \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \cdot (\partial x_2)_p \end{cases} \end{gather*} For the basis covectors of \(T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) — contravariant, \((dx^i)_p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot (dy^j)_p\) and \((dy^i)_p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) \cdot (dx^j)_p\): \begin{gather*} \begin{cases} (dx^1)_p = \cos \beta_2 \cdot (dy^1)_p - \beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \cdot (dy^2)_p \\[10pt] (dx^2)_p = \sin \beta_2 \cdot (dy^1)_p + \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \cdot (dy^2)_p \end{cases} \\[8pt] \begin{cases} (dy^1)_p = \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot (dx^1)_p + \dfrac{\alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot (dx^2)_p \\[10pt] (dy^2)_p = -\dfrac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot (dx^1)_p + \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot (dx^2)_p \end{cases} \end{gather*} For the components of a vector \(\mathcal{X}_p \in T_p\mathcal{M}\) — contravariant, \(x^i_p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot y^j_p\) and \(y^i_p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) \cdot x^j_p\): \begin{gather*} \begin{cases} x^1_p = \cos \beta_2 \cdot y^1_p - \beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \cdot y^2_p \\[10pt] x^2_p = \sin \beta_2 \cdot y^1_p + \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \cdot y^2_p \end{cases} \\[8pt] \begin{cases} y^1_p = \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot x^1_p + \dfrac{\alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot x^2_p \\[10pt] y^2_p = -\dfrac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot x^1_p + \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot x^2_p \end{cases} \end{gather*} For the components of a covector \(\mathsf{X}_p \in T^*_p\mathcal{M}\) — covariant, \(\mathtt{y}_j^p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right) \cdot \mathtt{x}_i^p\) and \(\mathtt{x}_j^p = \left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^i_j\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) \cdot \mathtt{y}_i^p\): \begin{gather*} \begin{cases} \mathtt{y}_1^p = \cos \beta_2 \cdot \mathtt{x}_1^p + \sin \beta_2 \cdot \mathtt{x}_2^p \\[10pt] \mathtt{y}_2^p = -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \cdot \mathtt{x}_1^p + \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \cdot \mathtt{x}_2^p \end{cases} \\[8pt] \begin{cases} \mathtt{x}_1^p = \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot \mathtt{y}_1^p - \dfrac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot \mathtt{y}_2^p \\[10pt] \mathtt{x}_2^p = \dfrac{\alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot \mathtt{y}_1^p + \dfrac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot \mathtt{y}_2^p \end{cases} \end{gather*} Note that the four laws come in two pairs: basis vectors transform exactly like covector components (both with \(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\) in one direction and \(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\) in the other, contracted on the upper index), and basis covectors exactly like vector components (contracted on the lower index).

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
text:
C.4.3 Curves and velocities

With all the machinery in place we can now have some fun. Consider the two families of curves (\(x_0 \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(r_0 > 0\) fixed): \begin{align*} \gamma_{x_0} \colon \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{M} & \delta_{r_0} \colon \mathbb{R} &\longrightarrow \mathcal{M} \\ \lambda &\longmapsto \gamma_{x_0}(\lambda) \coloneqq \big( x_0, \, \lambda, \, h(x_0, \lambda) \big)_\mathcal{M} & \lambda &\longmapsto \delta_{r_0}(\lambda) \coloneqq \big( r_0 \cos \lambda, \, r_0 \sin \lambda, \, h(r_0 \cos \lambda, r_0 \sin \lambda) \big)_\mathcal{M}. \end{align*} The first family sweeps the manifold with “vertical” curves, the second one with “circles”. For \(x_0 > 0\), \(\gamma_{x_0}\) stays inside \(\mathcal{V}\), while for \(x_0 \leq 0\) it crosses the branch cut at \(\lambda = 0\); \(\delta_{r_0}\) stays inside \(\mathcal{V}\) for \(\lambda \in (-\pi, \pi)\) and leaves it when it crosses the branch cut. Following Subsection 4.1.2, we write \(\mathcal{X}_p \coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}_p \coloneqq v_{\delta, p}\) for their velocities at a point \(p\). The curve \(\gamma_{x_0}\). Its chart representative in \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) and the corresponding velocity at \(p = \gamma_{x_0}(\lambda_0)\) are \begin{align*} \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{x_0} \right)(\lambda) = \left( \begin{array}{c} x_0 \\ \lambda \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{U} \;\Longrightarrow\; \left( \begin{array}{c} x^1_p \\ x^2_p \end{array} \right) \coloneqq \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{x_0} \right)'(\lambda_0) = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{X}_p = (\partial x_2)_p. \end{align*} The same velocity can be computed through \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), for \(p \in \mathcal{V}\): \begin{align*} \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_{x_0} \right)(\lambda) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2} \\ \operatorname{atan2}(\lambda, x_0) \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{V} \;\Longrightarrow\; \left( \begin{array}{c} y^1_p \\ y^2_p \end{array} \right) \coloneqq \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_{x_0} \right)'(\lambda_0) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \dfrac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda_0^2}} \\[10pt] \dfrac{x_0}{x_0^2 + \lambda_0^2} \end{array} \right) \;\longrightarrow\; \dots \end{align*} \begin{align*} \dots \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{X}_p = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda_0^2}} \cdot (\partial y_1)_p + \frac{x_0}{x_0^2 + \lambda_0^2} \cdot (\partial y_2)_p, \end{align*} and this is exactly what the transformation law of the previous subsection produces, since at \(p = \gamma_{x_0}(\lambda_0)\) we have \(\alpha_1 = x_0\) and \(\alpha_2 = \lambda_0\): \begin{align*} \left( \begin{array}{c} y^1_p \\ y^2_p \end{array} \right) = \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right) \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \alpha_2 / \sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \\ \alpha_1 / (\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2) \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \lambda_0 / \sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda_0^2} \\ x_0 / (x_0^2 + \lambda_0^2) \end{array} \right). \quad \checkmark \end{align*} The curve \(\delta_{r_0}\). Now it is the polar chart that trivializes the computation. For \(\lambda \in (-\pi, \pi)\)3, at \(p = \delta_{r_0}(\lambda_0)\): \begin{align*} \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \delta_{r_0} \right)(\lambda) = \left( \begin{array}{c} r_0 \\ \lambda \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{V} \;\Longrightarrow\; \left( \begin{array}{c} \tilde{y}^1_p \\ \tilde{y}^2_p \end{array} \right) \coloneqq \left( \mathscr{Y} \circ \delta_{r_0} \right)'(\lambda_0) = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{Y}_p = (\partial y_2)_p, \end{align*} while in the cartesian chart \begin{align*} \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \delta_{r_0} \right)(\lambda) = \left( \begin{array}{c} r_0 \cos \lambda \\ r_0 \sin \lambda \end{array} \right)_\mathcal{U} \;\Longrightarrow\; \left( \begin{array}{c} \tilde{x}^1_p \\ \tilde{x}^2_p \end{array} \right) \coloneqq \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \delta_{r_0} \right)'(\lambda_0) = \left( \begin{array}{c} -r_0 \sin \lambda_0 \\ r_0 \cos \lambda_0 \end{array} \right) \;\longrightarrow\; \dots \end{align*} \begin{align*} \dots \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{Y}_p = -r_0 \sin \lambda_0 \cdot (\partial x_1)_p + r_0 \cos \lambda_0 \cdot (\partial x_2)_p, \end{align*} which is again the second column of \(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\left( \mathscr{Y}(p) \right)\), i.e. the transformation law applied to \((0,1)\), with \(\beta_1 = r_0\) and \(\beta_2 = \lambda_0\). In terms of the chart coordinates of the base point, \(\alpha_1 = r_0 \cos \lambda_0\) and \(\alpha_2 = r_0 \sin \lambda_0\), the same velocity reads \(\mathcal{Y}_p = -\alpha_2 \cdot (\partial x_1)_p + \alpha_1 \cdot (\partial x_2)_p\), an expression we will reuse below. Figure C.5: Curves on the manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_2\) of Appendix C.4 (top), and their chart representatives under \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) (bottom left) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) (bottom right), as indicated by the arrows labelled \(\mathscr{X}\) and \(\mathscr{Y}\). Shown are two members of each family, \(\gamma_{x_0}\) with \(x_0 = -3\pi/2\) (green) and \(x_0 = 2\pi\) (yellow), and \(\delta_{r_0}\) with \(r_0 = \pi\) (purple) and \(r_0 = \pi/3\) (grey), together with the straight line \(\gamma_{m=1}\) of slope one (light blue) used in Fig. C.6. Arrowheads indicate the direction of the velocities \(v_{\gamma, p}\) and \(v_{\delta, p}\) at sampled points; only their direction is meaningful, their length has been normalized. Each family is trivial in one chart and non-trivial in the other: the \(\gamma_{x_0}\) are vertical lines \(\mathscr{X}^1 = x_0\) in \(\mathscr{X}\), whereas the \(\delta_{r_0}\) are vertical lines \(\mathscr{Y}^1 = r_0\) in \(\mathscr{Y}\). Curves crossing the branch cut \(\{a \leq 0,\, b = 0\}\) of the polar chart, such as \(\gamma_{-3\pi/2}\) and \(\gamma_{m=1}\), appear in \(\mathscr{Y}\) as two disconnected pieces, since \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) cannot see the points where they leave \(\mathcal{V}\). Note that the arrows drawn on the manifold are not ‘real’ objects: what we can write down are the components of the velocities w.r.t. a chart, while the velocities themselves are only ‘waiting’ to act on a function in order to produce its directional derivative at each point \(p\).

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
section: C.4.4 A scalar field, its differential and the action of velocities on it
text:
C.4.4 A scalar field, its differential and the action of velocities on it

Let us now define a smooth scalar field \(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) on our manifold: \begin{align*} f \colon \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ p = (a, b, c) &\longmapsto f(p) \coloneqq c = \cos a \, \cos b + 1, \end{align*} that is, the simplest possible choice: the “height” of each point. We could identify it with a scalar field — a \((0,0)\)-tensor field — such as the temperature at each point of \(\mathcal{M}\). Its chart representatives, which are the objects we can actually differentiate, are \begin{align*} \left( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \colon \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} & \left( f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right) \colon \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ (\alpha_1, \alpha_2) &\longmapsto \cos \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_2 + 1 & (\beta_1, \beta_2) &\longmapsto \cos \left( \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \right) \cos \left( \beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \right) + 1, \end{align*} and their partial derivatives at \(\mathscr{X}(p)\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(p)\) are, by Subsection 4.2.1, precisely the components of the covector \((df)_p = \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (dx^i)_p = \mathtt{y}_i^p \cdot (dy^i)_p\): \begin{align*} \mathtt{x}_1^p = \partial_1 \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] (\alpha_1, \alpha_2) &= -\sin \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_2, & \mathtt{x}_2^p = \partial_2 \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] (\alpha_1, \alpha_2) &= -\cos \alpha_1 \sin \alpha_2, \end{align*} \begin{align*} \mathtt{y}_1^p = \partial_1 \left[ f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] (\beta_1, \beta_2) &= -\frac{\alpha_1 \sin \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_2 + \alpha_2 \cos \alpha_1 \sin \alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}}, \\[6pt] \mathtt{y}_2^p = \partial_2 \left[ f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] (\beta_1, \beta_2) &= \alpha_2 \sin \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_2 - \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_1 \sin \alpha_2, \end{align*} where in the last two lines we abbreviated \(\alpha_1 = \beta_1 \cos \beta_2\), \(\alpha_2 = \beta_1 \sin \beta_2\) and \(\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} = \beta_1\) to keep the expressions readable. The reader may check that they are related by the covariant transformation law of Subsection C.4.2. Evaluating \(f\) along the curves gives two ordinary functions of one real variable: \begin{align*} \left( f \circ \gamma_{x_0} \right)(\lambda) &= \cos x_0 \, \cos \lambda + 1, \\ \left( f \circ \delta_{r_0} \right)(\lambda) &= \cos \left( r_0 \cos \lambda \right) \cos \left( r_0 \sin \lambda \right) + 1, \end{align*} and we can now compute the action of the velocities on \(f\) without any chart at all, directly from the definition \(v_{\gamma, p}(f) \coloneqq \left( f \circ \gamma \right)'(\lambda_0)\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{X}_p(f) &= \left( f \circ \gamma_{x_0} \right)'(\lambda_0) = -\cos x_0 \, \sin \lambda_0, \\[6pt] \mathcal{Y}_p(f) &= \left( f \circ \delta_{r_0} \right)'(\lambda_0) = r_0 \sin \lambda_0 \, \sin\left(r_0 \cos \lambda_0\right) \, \cos \left(r_0 \sin \lambda_0\right) - r_0 \cos \lambda_0 \, \cos \left(r_0 \cos \lambda_0\right) \, \sin \left(r_0 \sin \lambda_0\right) \\ &= \alpha_2 \sin \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_2 - \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_1 \sin \alpha_2, \end{align*} with \(\alpha_1 = r_0 \cos \lambda_0\) and \(\alpha_2 = r_0 \sin \lambda_0\) in the last line. Of course the same numbers must come out of the chart expressions \(\mathcal{X}_p(f) = (df)_p(\mathcal{X}_p) = x^i_p \, \mathtt{x}_i^p = y^i_p \, \mathtt{y}_i^p\). For \(\gamma_{x_0}\) in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), with \((\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = (x_0, \lambda_0)\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{X}_p(f) = x^i_p \, \mathtt{x}_i^p = 0 \cdot \left( -\sin x_0 \cos \lambda_0 \right) + 1 \cdot \left( -\cos x_0 \sin \lambda_0 \right) = -\cos x_0 \sin \lambda_0, \quad \checkmark \end{align*} and in the chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) the two contributions conspire to give the same result: \begin{align*} \mathcal{X}_p(f) = y^i_p \, \mathtt{y}_i^p &= \frac{\alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \cdot \left( -\frac{\alpha_1 \sin \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_2 + \alpha_2 \cos \alpha_1 \sin \alpha_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2}} \right) \\ &\quad + \frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cdot \left( \alpha_2 \sin \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_2 - \alpha_1 \cos \alpha_1 \sin \alpha_2 \right) \\ &= -\frac{\alpha_2^2 + \alpha_1^2}{\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2} \cos \alpha_1 \sin \alpha_2 = -\cos x_0 \sin \lambda_0. \quad \checkmark \end{align*} For \(\delta_{r_0}\) it is now the polar chart that makes the check immediate: \(\mathcal{Y}_p(f) = \tilde{y}^i_p \, \mathtt{y}_i^p = \mathtt{y}_2^p\), which is the chart-free result above. ✓This is the whole point of the construction: the velocity is an intrinsic object, the components and the partial derivatives are not, and the chart dependence cancels in the contraction. Figure C.6: The scalar field \(f(p) = \cos a \cos b + 1\) of Subsection C.4.4, drawn as colour and level sets on the manifold (top) and through its chart representatives \(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) (bottom left) and \(f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\) (bottom right). The curves \(\delta_\pi\) (purple) and \(\gamma_{m=1}\) (light blue) intersect at the point \(p = \big( 2, \sqrt{\pi^2 - 4} \big)\) (black dot), where their velocities \(v_{\delta, p}\) and \(v_{\gamma, p}\) are drawn at true scale. Also at \(p\), the covector \((df)_p\) is represented by its stack of level lines (black): the thick line through \(p\) is its kernel, tangent to the level set of \(f\) through \(p\), and consecutive lines differ by one unit of \((df)_p\). On the manifold this stack lies inside the tangent plane \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) (grey), the chart-free picture of the covector. In each chart the stack and the arrows look different, since both the components \(\mathtt{x}_i^p\), \(\mathtt{y}_i^p\) of \((df)_p\) and those of the velocities change. Their contraction does not: the arrows cross the stack in the same way in both charts, giving \(v_{\gamma, p}(f) \approx 0.68\) and \(v_{\delta, p}(f) \approx -1.11\), i.e. \(\gamma_{m=1}\) climbs \(f\) at \(p\) while \(\delta_\pi\) descends it.

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
text:
C.4.5 Vector fields

Each point of \(\mathcal{M}\) lies on exactly one curve of each family (taking \(\delta_0\) to be the constant curve at the origin), so each family defines a smooth vector field, i.e. a smooth section of \(T\mathcal{M}\) assigning to every point the velocity of the curve of the family passing through it: \[ \begin{array}{c@{\quad} | @{\quad} c} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{X} \colon \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow T\mathcal{M} \\ p = (a,b,c) &\longmapsto \mathcal{X}(p) \coloneqq v_{\gamma_{a}, p} \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \mathcal{Y} \colon \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow T\mathcal{M} \\ p = (a,b,c) &\longmapsto \mathcal{Y}(p) \coloneqq v_{\delta_{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}, p} \end{aligned} \end{array} \] so that \(\mathcal{X}(p) = \mathcal{X}_p\) and \(\mathcal{Y}(p) = \mathcal{Y}_p\) are the velocities of the previous subsections. In each case the velocity is evaluated at the parameter value at which the corresponding curve passes through \(p\), namely \(\lambda_0 = b\) for \(\gamma_a\) and \(\lambda_0 = \operatorname{atan2}(b,a)\) for \(\delta_{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\) (at the origin \(\delta_0\) is constant and \(\mathcal{Y}\) vanishes). In both cases \(\left( \pi \circ \mathcal{X} \right)(p) = p\) and \(\left( \pi \circ \mathcal{Y} \right)(p) = p\) by construction, as a section must satisfy. Their component functions, \(X^i \coloneqq \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} \left\lfloor \mathscr{X}^i \right\rceil\) and \(Y^i \coloneqq \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{V} \left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^i \right\rceil\) for \(\mathcal{X}\), and \(\tilde{X}^i\), \(\tilde{Y}^i\) for \(\mathcal{Y}\), follow from Subsection C.4.3 by reading the components of the velocities at a generic point \(p = (a, b, c)\). For \(\mathcal{X}\), \begin{align*} \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = X^i \, \partial x_i = \partial x_2 \quad ; \quad \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{V} = Y^i \, \partial y_i = \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \, \partial y_1 + \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial y_2, \end{align*} and for \(\mathcal{Y}\), \begin{align*} \left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \tilde{X}^i \, \partial x_i = -b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2 \quad ; \quad \left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{V} = \tilde{Y}^i \, \partial y_i = \partial y_2, \end{align*} where the component functions are read as functions of \(p = (a, b, c)\), and the basis fields are the chart-induced ones, \(\partial x_i = \partial / \partial \mathscr{X}^i\) and \(\partial y_i = \partial / \partial \mathscr{Y}^i\). Each of the two fields is therefore an element of the chart-induced frame of one of the two charts, and an honest field with non-constant component functions in the other one. Two remarks are worth making here: \(\left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{V} = \partial y_2\) is only a frame element over \(\mathcal{V}\), but the field itself extends smoothly to all of \(\mathcal{M}\): its component functions in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), \((\tilde{X}^1, \tilde{X}^2) = (-b, a)\), are perfectly smooth across the branch cut. What does not extend is the frame: at the origin \(a = b = 0\) the field vanishes, so it cannot be part of any frame there. This is the local-versus-global statement of Section 5.1 in miniature: chart-induced frames always exist over a chart domain, and nothing guarantees that any of them extends to the whole manifold. Finally, in the tangent-bundle charts \(\xi_\mathscr{X}\) and \(\xi_\mathscr{Y}\) of Section 5.1 each of these fields is described, at the point \(p = (a, b, c)\), by \(2 \dim \mathcal{M} = 4\) numbers, the first two of which locate the base point and the last two of which are the components of the vector sitting over it: \begin{align*} \xi_\mathscr{X} \left( \mathcal{X}_p \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \left( a \,,\, b \right) \\ \left( 0 \,,\, 1 \right) \end{array} \right) \quad ; \quad \xi_\mathscr{Y} \left( \mathcal{X}_p \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \left( \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \,,\, \operatorname{atan2}(b,a) \right) \\[4pt] \left( \dfrac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}} \,,\, \dfrac{a}{a^2+b^2} \right) \end{array} \right), \end{align*} \begin{align*} \xi_\mathscr{X} \left( \mathcal{Y}_p \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \left( a \,,\, b \right) \\ \left( -b \,,\, a \right) \end{array} \right) \quad ; \quad \xi_\mathscr{Y} \left( \mathcal{Y}_p \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \left( \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \,,\, \operatorname{atan2}(b,a) \right) \\ \left( 0 \,,\, 1 \right) \end{array} \right). \end{align*} Figure C.7: The vector fields \(\mathcal{X}\) (yellow) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) (light blue) of Subsection C.4.5, obtained by assigning to every point the velocity of the curve of each family passing through it. Top: the two fields drawn over a grid of base points on the manifold; since a vector field is a section of \(T\mathcal{M}\), each arrow lives in the tangent space of its own base point. Bottom: their component functions in \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) (left) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) (right). Each field is a chart-induced basis field of one chart, with constant components \((0,1)\): \(\left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \partial x_2\) and \(\left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{V} = \partial y_2\). In the other chart it is an honest field with non-constant component functions, a rotation \((\tilde{X}^1, \tilde{X}^2) = (-b, a)\) for \(\mathcal{Y}\) in \(\mathscr{X}\), and \((Y^1, Y^2) = \big( b/\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\, a/(a^2+b^2) \big)\) for \(\mathcal{X}\) in \(\mathscr{Y}\). Arrows are normalized, so only directions are meaningful; recall that without a metric there is no intrinsic notion of the length of a tangent vector. Note that \(\mathcal{Y}\) vanishes at the origin, so it cannot be part of a frame there, even though its component functions \((-b, a)\) are perfectly smooth.

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
section: C.4.6 Action of the vector fields on the scalar field
text:
C.4.6 Action of the vector fields on the scalar field

We can now evaluate the action \(\mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil\) of these fields upon the scalar field \(f\) defined above. By definition this is the function that assigns to each point the directional derivative of \(f\) there, \(\mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) \coloneqq \mathcal{X}_p(f)\), and in a chart it is the contraction of the component functions with the components \(\mathtt{x}_i^p = \partial_i \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \left( \mathscr{X}(p) \right)\) of Subsection C.4.4, now evaluated at \((\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = (a, b)\). For \(\mathcal{X}\), whose component functions in \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) are \((0, 1)\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil \colon \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ p = (a,b,c) &\longmapsto \mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) = X^i(p) \cdot \mathtt{x}_i^p = 0 \cdot \left( -\sin a \cos b \right) + 1 \cdot \left( -\cos a \sin b \right) = -\cos a \, \sin b, \end{align*} and for \(\mathcal{Y}\), whose component functions in the same chart are \((-b, a)\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{Y} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil \colon \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\ p = (a,b,c) &\longmapsto \mathcal{Y} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) = \tilde{X}^i(p) \cdot \mathtt{x}_i^p = (-b) \left( -\sin a \cos b \right) + a \left( -\cos a \sin b \right) \\ &\qquad = b \, \sin a \, \cos b - a \, \cos a \, \sin b. \end{align*} Both results are again smooth functions on \(\mathcal{M}\), i.e. elements of \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), as they must be: a vector field eats an element of the ring and returns, \(\mathbb{R}\)-linearly, another element of the ring. Computing the same action through the other chart is a useful exercise. For \(\mathcal{Y}\), whose component functions in \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) are \((0,1)\), \begin{align*} \mathcal{Y} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p) = \tilde{Y}^i(p) \cdot \mathtt{y}_i^p = 0 \cdot \mathtt{y}_1^p + 1 \cdot \mathtt{y}_2^p = b \, \sin a \, \cos b - a \, \cos a \, \sin b, \quad \checkmark \end{align*} which is the same function, as it has to be. Note also where these functions vanish: \(\mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil = 0\) wherever the field is tangent to a level set of \(f\), which here happens along \(b = 0, \pm\pi, \dots\) and \(a = \pm \pi/2, \pm 3\pi/2, \dots\); there the flow of the field neither climbs nor descends the “eggs”. Figure C.8: Action of the vector fields \(\mathcal{X}\) (yellow) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) (light blue) on the scalar field \(f\), as computed in Subsection C.4.6. Top: both fields on the manifold, coloured by \(f\). Bottom: the new scalar fields \(\mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil = -\cos a \sin b\) (left) and \(\mathcal{Y} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil = b \sin a \cos b - a \cos a \sin b\) (right), drawn as colour maps in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), together with the level sets of \(f\) and the corresponding field. Red (blue) regions are those where the field climbs (descends) \(f\), and the white bands, where the action vanishes, are those where the field runs along the level sets of \(f\). For \(\mathcal{X}\) these are \(b = 0, \pm\pi, \dots\) and \(a = \pm \pi/2, \pm 3\pi/2, \dots\). The magnitude of \(\mathcal{Y} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil\) grows with the distance to the origin (note the different colour scales), since the component functions \((-b, a)\) of \(\mathcal{Y}\) do. Both panels illustrate that a vector field eats an element of the ring \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\) and returns another one, and by Subsection C.4.8 they equally show the actions \(df \left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor\) and \(df \left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor\) of the covector field \(df\).

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
text:
C.4.7 A covector field

The simplest way of producing a covector field is to take the differential of a scalar field, so let us consider \begin{align*} df \colon \mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow T^*\mathcal{M} \\ p &\longmapsto df(p) \coloneqq (df)_p, \end{align*} which trivially satisfies \(\left( \pi^* \circ df \right) = \mathbb{I}_\mathcal{M}\).
