Its component functions, \(\mathtt{X}_i \coloneqq \left. df \right|_\mathcal{U} \left\lceil \partial x_i \right\rfloor\) and \(\mathtt{Y}_i \coloneqq \left. df \right|_\mathcal{V} \left\lceil \partial y_i \right\rfloor\) (Section 5.3), return at each point the components of Subsection C.4.4, \(\mathtt{X}_i(p) = \mathtt{x}_i^p\) and \(\mathtt{Y}_i(p) = \mathtt{y}_i^p\), so that in each chart \begin{align*} \left. df \right|_\mathcal{U} &= \mathtt{X}_i \, dx^i = -\sin a \cos b \; dx^1 - \cos a \sin b \; dx^2, \\[6pt] \left. df \right|_\mathcal{V} &= \mathtt{Y}_i \, dy^i = -\frac{a \sin a \cos b + b \cos a \sin b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \; dy^1 + \left( b \sin a \cos b - a \cos a \sin b \right) dy^2, \end{align*} with the component functions read as functions of \(p = (a, b, c)\), and \(dx^i = d\mathscr{X}^i\), \(dy^i = d\mathscr{Y}^i\) the chart-induced basis covector fields. These two expressions are of course related by the transformation law for covector component functions of Section 5.3, \(\mathtt{Y}_j = \left( \partial \mathscr{X}^i / \partial \mathscr{Y}^j \right) \mathtt{X}_i\), where the entries of \(\textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\) are now the functions \(\partial \mathscr{X}^1 / \partial \mathscr{Y}^1 = a / \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), \(\partial \mathscr{X}^2 / \partial \mathscr{Y}^1 = b / \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), \(\partial \mathscr{X}^1 / \partial \mathscr{Y}^2 = -b\) and \(\partial \mathscr{X}^2 / \partial \mathscr{Y}^2 = a\): \begin{align*} \mathtt{Y}_1 &= \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \, \mathtt{X}_1 + \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \, \mathtt{X}_2 = \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \left( -\sin a \cos b \right) + \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \left( -\cos a \sin b \right), \quad \checkmark \\[6pt] \mathtt{Y}_2 &= -b \, \mathtt{X}_1 + a \, \mathtt{X}_2 = b \sin a \cos b - a \cos a \sin b. \quad \checkmark \end{align*} In the cotangent-bundle charts of Section 5.2 the field reads, at the point \(p = (a,b,c)\), \begin{align*} \xi^*_\mathscr{X} \left( (df)_p \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \left( a \,,\, b \right) \\ \left( -\sin a \cos b \,,\, -\cos a \sin b \right) \end{array} \right) \end{align*} \begin{align*} \xi^*_\mathscr{Y} \left( (df)_p \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} \left( \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \,,\, \operatorname{atan2}(b,a) \right) \\[4pt] \left( \dfrac{-a \sin a \cos b - b \cos a \sin b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} \,,\, b \sin a \cos b - a \cos a \sin b \right) \end{array} \right). \end{align*} Since \(\mathcal{M}\) is contractible, every covector field on it is the differential of some scalar field, so nothing is lost by this choice of example; on a manifold with non-trivial \(H^1_{\text{dR}}\) this would no longer be true (see the discussion opening Section 5.2).

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
section: C.4.8 Action of the covector field on the vector fields
text:
C.4.8 Action of the covector field on the vector fields

We can finally contract the two kinds of fields. By definition, \(df \left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor(p) \coloneqq (df)_p \left( \mathcal{X}(p) \right)\), which in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) reads \(df \left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor = \mathtt{X}_i \, X^i\) and gives \begin{align*} df \left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor(p) &= \mathtt{X}_i(p) \, X^i(p) = \left( -\sin a \cos b \right) \cdot 0 + \left( -\cos a \sin b \right) \cdot 1 = -\cos a \, \sin b, \\[6pt] df \left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor(p) &= \mathtt{X}_i(p) \, \tilde{X}^i(p) = \left( -\sin a \cos b \right) \cdot (-b) + \left( -\cos a \sin b \right) \cdot a = b \, \sin a \, \cos b - a \, \cos a \, \sin b, \end{align*} and the same two functions come out of the chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), for instance for \(\mathcal{Y}\), whose component functions there are \((0,1)\): \begin{align*} df \left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor(p) = \mathtt{Y}_i(p) \, \tilde{Y}^i(p) = \mathtt{Y}_1(p) \cdot 0 + \mathtt{Y}_2(p) \cdot 1 = b \, \sin a \, \cos b - a \, \cos a \, \sin b. \quad \checkmark \end{align*} Comparing with Subsection C.4.6 we see that \begin{align*} df \left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor = \mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil \qquad \forall \, \mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}, \end{align*} which is nothing but the definition of the differential, \((df)_p (v_{\gamma, p}) \coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}(f)\), promoted from a point to the whole manifold. The two brackets \(\left\lfloor \cdot \right\rceil\) and \(\left\lceil \cdot \right\rfloor\) are thus two readings of one and the same number at each point: either “the field differentiates the function” or “the differential of the function eats the field”. One asymmetry between the two readings is worth stressing, since it is what makes \(df \left\lceil \cdot \right\rfloor\) a tensor field, a \((0,1)\) one, whereas \(\mathcal{X} \left\lfloor \cdot \right\rceil\) is not: the vector field \(\mathcal{X}\) is a \((1,0)\)-tensor field through its action on covector fields, not through its action on scalar fields. The map \(df \left\lceil \cdot \right\rfloor\) is \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linear, \begin{align*} df \left\lceil g \odot_\Gamma \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor = g \odot_{C^\infty} df \left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor \qquad \forall \, g \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M}), \end{align*} whereas \(\mathcal{X} \left\lfloor \cdot \right\rceil\) is only \(\mathbb{R}\)-linear and satisfies instead the Leibniz rule \(\mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \odot_{C^\infty} g \right\rceil = f \odot_{C^\infty} \mathcal{X} \left\lfloor g \right\rceil \oplus_{C^\infty} g \odot_{C^\infty} \mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil\). With our example, taking \(g = f\): \begin{align*} \mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \odot_{C^\infty} f \right\rceil(p) = \frac{d}{d\lambda} \left[ \left( \cos a \cos \lambda + 1 \right)^2 \right]_{\lambda = b} = -2 \left( \cos a \cos b + 1 \right) \cos a \sin b = 2 f(p) \cdot \mathcal{X} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil(p). \quad \checkmark \end{align*}

title: C.4 Example of Fields (§§5.1–5.3)
section: C.4.9 Module operations and a tensor field
text:
C.4.9 Module operations and a tensor field

To close the example, the two \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-module operations on \(\Gamma T\mathcal{M}\) are completely explicit in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\): \begin{align*} \left. \left( \mathcal{X} \oplus_\Gamma \mathcal{Y} \right) \right|_\mathcal{U} &= \left( X^i + \tilde{X}^i \right) \partial x_i = -b \; \partial x_1 + \left( 1 + a \right) \partial x_2, \\[6pt] \left. \left( f \odot_\Gamma \mathcal{X} \right) \right|_\mathcal{U} &= \left( f \, X^i \right) \partial x_i = \left( \cos a \cos b + 1 \right) \partial x_2. \end{align*} The second line is where a module parts ways with a vector space: the scaling factor is a function, so it stretches the field by a different amount at every point — and it would reverse it wherever \(f\) changed sign, which our particular \(f \geq 0\) never does. Finally, a \((0,2)\)-tensor field costs us nothing at this stage: define \(T \coloneqq df \otimes df\), i.e. \begin{align*} T \colon \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \times \Gamma T\mathcal{M} &\longrightarrow C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \\ \left( \mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2 \right) &\longmapsto T \left( \mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2 \right) \coloneqq df \left\lceil \mathcal{X}_1 \right\rfloor \odot_{C^\infty} df \left\lceil \mathcal{X}_2 \right\rfloor, \end{align*} whose component functions in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) are \(\left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)_{ij} \coloneqq T \left( \partial x_i, \partial x_j \right) = \mathtt{X}_i \, \mathtt{X}_j\), i.e. \begin{align*} \left. T \right|_\mathcal{U} = \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)_{ij} \, dx^i \otimes dx^j, \qquad \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix} \sin^2 a \cos^2 b & \sin a \cos a \sin b \cos b \\[4pt] \sin a \cos a \sin b \cos b & \cos^2 a \sin^2 b \end{bmatrix}_{ij}, \end{align*} and which transforms, as every \((0,2)\)-tensor field must, with one Jacobian factor per (covariant) index: \(\left( T_\mathcal{V} \right)_{kl} = \left( \partial \mathscr{X}^i / \partial \mathscr{Y}^k \right) \left( \partial \mathscr{X}^j / \partial \mathscr{Y}^l \right) \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)_{ij} = \mathtt{Y}_k \, \mathtt{Y}_l\), as it should. Evaluating it on our two fields gives \begin{align*} T \left( \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \right)(p) = \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)_{ij}(p) \, X^i(p) \, \tilde{X}^j(p) = \left( -\cos a \sin b \right) \left( b \sin a \cos b - a \cos a \sin b \right), \end{align*} an element of \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\), built out of nothing but the objects defined in this appendix. 2 For the chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) we remove from \(\mathcal{M}\) the points with \(a \leq 0\), \(b = 0\), since the function \[ \operatorname{atan2}(b, a) = \begin{cases} \arctan\left(b/a\right) & \text{if } a > 0, \\ \arctan\left(b/a\right) + \pi & \text{if } a < 0 \text{ and } b \geq 0, \\ \arctan\left(b/a\right) - \pi & \text{if } a < 0 \text{ and } b < 0, \\ +\pi/2 & \text{if } a = 0 \text{ and } b > 0, \\ -\pi/2 & \text{if } a = 0 \text{ and } b < 0, \\ \text{undefined} & \text{if } a = 0 \text{ and } b = 0, \end{cases} \] is discontinuous there. Removing that closed ray leaves \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) = (0, \infty) \times (-\pi, \pi)\), which is open in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), as a chart image must be: note that the value \(\operatorname{atan2}(b,a) = \pi\) is not attained on \(\mathcal{V}\), and that the origin \(a = b = 0\) is excluded as well. 3 Outside that interval the curve leaves \(\mathcal{V}\) and re-enters it, and its chart representative must be written with the wrapping function \(\operatorname{wrap}_{(-\pi, \pi)}(\lambda) \coloneqq \left( \lambda + \pi \mod 2\pi \right) - \pi\), which returns the unique representative of \(\lambda \mod 2\pi\) in \([-\pi, \pi)\). This is a statement about the chart, not about the curve: \(\delta_{r_0}\) is perfectly smooth on all of \(\mathbb{R}\), it is \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) that cannot see the whole of it.

title: C.5 Examples of Connections, Torsion and Curvature (§§6.1–6.4)
text:
This appendix continues the example of Appendix C.4: same manifold, same two charts, same curves, fields and scalar field. On top of it we now place three different connections, chosen so that between them they display every notion of Chapter 6: \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\), flat and torsion free, whose autoparallels are straight lines in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\); \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\), flat but with torsion, whose autoparallels include the circles \(\delta_{r_0}\); \(
abla^{\kappa}\), torsion free but curved, whose autoparallels are sinusoids and whose parallel transport around closed loops does not return vectors to themselves. A connection is additional structure: nothing in \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty})_2\) singles one out, and in particular the egg-carton shape of \(\mathcal{M}\) inside \(\mathbb{R}^3\) plays no role in what follows. Only once a metric is introduced will a preferred connection appear. As in the rest of the notes, the Einstein summation convention is implied, and the connection coefficient functions follow the convention of Chapter 6, \(\Gamma^i_{jk} \coloneqq dx^i\left\lceil 
abla_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j ightfloor\), whose last lower index labels the direction of differentiation.

title: C.5 Examples of Connections, Torsion and Curvature (§§6.1–6.4)
text:
C.5.1 Setting

We write functions on \(\mathcal{M}\) through the chart coordinates of their argument, \(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a, b)\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(p) = (\beta_1, \beta_2)\), related on \(\mathcal{V}\) by \[ a = \beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \qquad b = \beta_1 \sin \beta_2, \qquad \beta_1 = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} : \] expressions in \(a, b\) refer to the chart \(\mathscr{X}\), and expressions in \(\beta_1, \beta_2\) to the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\). From Appendix C.4 we only need the following objects. The Jacobians of the transition maps (Subsection C.4.2), \[ \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \beta_2 & -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \\ \sin \beta_2 & \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}^s_{j}, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \beta_2 & \sin \beta_2 \\ -\dfrac{\sin \beta_2}{\beta_1} & \dfrac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \end{bmatrix}^i_{l}, \] and hence the relations between the chart-induced basis fields on \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \mathcal{V}\): \[ \partial y_1 = \cos \beta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \sin \beta_2 \, \partial x_2 , \qquad \partial y_2 = -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \, \partial x_2 . \] The curves \(\gamma_{x_0}\) and \(\delta_{r_0}\) (Subsection C.4.3), through their chart representatives, from which their velocity and acceleration components follow by differentiation: \[ \begin{array}{c@{\qquad}|@{\qquad}c} (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{x_0})(\lambda) = (x_0, \, \lambda) & (\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_{x_0})(\lambda) = \left( \sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}, \, \operatorname{atan2}(\lambda, x_0) \right) \\[8pt] (\mathscr{X} \circ \delta_{r_0})(\lambda) = (r_0 \cos \lambda, \, r_0 \sin \lambda) & (\mathscr{Y} \circ \delta_{r_0})(\lambda) = (r_0, \, \lambda), \quad \lambda \in (-\pi, \pi) \end{array} \] The vector fields \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) (Subsection C.4.5), the velocity fields of the two families, whose component functions, in the notation of Section 5.3, are \[ \begin{array}{c@{\qquad}|@{\qquad}c} \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i = \partial x_2 & \left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{V} = y^i \, \partial y_i = \sin \beta_2 \, \partial y_1 + \dfrac{\cos \beta_2}{\beta_1} \, \partial y_2 \\[12pt] \left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \tilde{x}^i \, \partial x_i = -b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2 & \left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{V} = \tilde{y}^i \, \partial y_i = \partial y_2 \end{array} \] The scalar field \(f(p) = \cos a \cos b + 1\) and its differential (Subsection C.4.4), with component functions in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) \[ \left. df \right|_\mathcal{U} = \mathtt{x}_i \, dx^i, \qquad \mathtt{x}_1 = -\sin a \cos b, \qquad \mathtt{x}_2 = -\cos a \sin b . \] The second derivatives of the chart transition, needed below. By Chapter 6 they are the functions \(\frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}(p) = \partial_k \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right]\big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big)\), i.e. the second partial derivatives of \((\beta_1, \beta_2) \mapsto (\beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \beta_1 \sin \beta_2)\): \[ \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^1}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\sin \beta_2 \\ -\sin \beta_2 & -\beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}_{kj}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^2}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \cos \beta_2 \\ \cos \beta_2 & -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}_{kj}. \] Finally, recall how a connection is specified in practice. By Chapter 6, on a chart domain the whole action of \(\nabla\) is fixed by the \(\dim(\mathcal{M})^3 = 8\) connection coefficient functions: for any two vector fields, \(\nabla_\mathcal{Z} \mathcal{W} = \big( \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor w^k \right\rceil + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, w^j z^i \big) \partial x_k\). Conversely, any choice of \(8\) smooth functions on a chart domain defines, through this formula and the Leibniz rule, a connection there. Since \(\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{M}\), choosing the \(\Gamma\)’s in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) defines a connection on the whole manifold, and its coefficients in \(\mathscr{Y}\) then follow from the transformation law.

title: C.5 Examples of Connections, Torsion and Curvature (§§6.1–6.4)
text:
C.5.2 A flat, torsion-free connection: \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\)

Define \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\) on \(\mathcal{M}\) by declaring all its connection coefficient functions in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) to vanish, \[ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_x ight)^i_{jk} = 0, \qquad 	ext{i.e.} \qquad 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j = 0 , \] the analogue on \(\mathcal{M}\) of the familiar derivative of vector fields in the Euclidean plane, hence the label. Coefficients in the polar chart. With \(\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_x = 0\), only the inhomogeneous term of the transformation law survives, \[ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^i_{jk} =  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^s} \,  rac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} =  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \,  rac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^1}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} +  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \,  rac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^2}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}, \] which is symmetric in \(j\) and \(k\), leaving six independent entries. Taking the rows of \(\partial \mathscr{Y}^i / \partial \mathscr{X}^l\) and the second derivatives listed above:  egin{align*} \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^1_{11} &= \cos  eta_2 \cdot 0 + \sin  eta_2 \cdot 0 = 0, \ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^1_{12} = \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^1_{21} &= \cos  eta_2 \, (-\sin  eta_2) + \sin  eta_2 \, \cos  eta_2 = 0, \ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^1_{22} &= \cos  eta_2 \, (- eta_1 \cos  eta_2) + \sin  eta_2 \, (- eta_1 \sin  eta_2) = - eta_1, \ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^2_{11} &= - rac{\sin  eta_2}{ eta_1} \cdot 0 +  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} \cdot 0 = 0, \ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^2_{12} = \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^2_{21} &= - rac{\sin  eta_2}{ eta_1} \, (-\sin  eta_2) +  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} \, \cos  eta_2 =  rac{1}{ eta_1}, \ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y ight)^2_{22} &= - rac{\sin  eta_2}{ eta_1} \, (- eta_1 \cos  eta_2) +  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} \, (- eta_1 \sin  eta_2) = 0 . \end{align*} The same connection thus has vanishing coefficients in one chart and non-vanishing ones in the other: the \(\Gamma\)’s are not the components of a tensor field. In terms of the basis fields, \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_2} \partial y_2 = - eta_1 \, \partial y_1\) and \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_1} \partial y_2 = 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_2} \partial y_1 =  rac{1}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2\), while \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_{\partial y_1} \partial y_1 = 0\). Torsion and curvature. In the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) all \(\Gamma\)’s vanish, so \(\mathtt{T}^i_{jk} = \Gamma^i_{kj} - \Gamma^i_{jk} = 0\) and \(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{jkm} = \partial x_k\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{jm} ightceil - \partial x_m\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{jk} ightceil + \Gamma^i_{rk} \Gamma^r_{jm} - \Gamma^i_{rm} \Gamma^r_{jk} = 0\). Both are tensor fields, so they vanish in every chart: \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\) is flat and torsion free. It is instructive to see this happen in the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\), where the \(\Gamma\)’s do not vanish. Torsion freeness is the symmetry \((\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y)^2_{12} = (\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_y)^2_{21}\). As for the curvature, in two dimensions and thanks to the antisymmetry in the last two indices, the independent components are \(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{j12}\), and, with \(\partial y_k\) acting on functions as \(\partial / \partial  eta_k\),  egin{align*} \mathrm{Riem}^1_{212} &= \partial y_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{22} ightceil - \partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{21} ightceil + \Gamma^1_{r1} \Gamma^r_{22} - \Gamma^1_{r2} \Gamma^r_{21} = -1 - 0 + 0 - \Gamma^1_{22} \Gamma^2_{21} = -1 +  eta_1 \cdot  rac{1}{ eta_1} = 0, \ \mathrm{Riem}^2_{112} &= \partial y_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^2_{12} ightceil - \partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^2_{11} ightceil + \Gamma^2_{r1} \Gamma^r_{12} - \Gamma^2_{r2} \Gamma^r_{11} = - rac{1}{ eta_1^2} - 0 + \Gamma^2_{21} \Gamma^2_{12} - 0 = - rac{1}{ eta_1^2} +  rac{1}{ eta_1^2} = 0, \end{align*} while \(\mathrm{Riem}^1_{112}\) and \(\mathrm{Riem}^2_{212}\) vanish term by term. The derivatives of the \(\Gamma\)’s and their quadratic terms cancel exactly, as they must. ✓ Covariant derivatives of the example fields. In the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) the covariant derivative reduces to the action of the vector field on the component functions. Hence \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{Y}\left\lfloor x^k ightceil \partial x_k = 0, \qquad 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor 	ilde{x}^k ightceil \partial x_k = \partial x_2\left\lfloor -b ightceil \partial x_1 + \partial x_2\left\lfloor a ightceil \partial x_2 = -\partial x_1 , \] since the components of \(\mathcal{X}\) are constant. The same results must come out of the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\), where the components are not constant and the \(\Gamma\)’s compensate for it. With \((
abla_\mathcal{Z} \mathcal{W})^k = \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor w^k ightceil + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, w^j z^i\), \(	ilde{y}^i = (0,1)\) and \(y^i = (\sin  eta_2, \cos  eta_2 /  eta_1)\):  egin{align*} \left( 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} ight)^1 &= \partial y_2\left\lfloor \sin  eta_2 ightceil + \Gamma^1_{22} \, y^2 = \cos  eta_2 -  eta_1 \,  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} = 0, \ \left( 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} ight)^2 &= \partial y_2\left\lfloor  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} ightceil + \Gamma^2_{12} \, y^1 = - rac{\sin  eta_2}{ eta_1} +  rac{\sin  eta_2}{ eta_1} = 0, \quad \checkmark \end{align*} and, since the components of \(\mathcal{Y}\) are constant in \(\mathscr{Y}\), \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = \Gamma^k_{2i} \, y^i \, \partial y_k = \Gamma^1_{22} \, y^2 \, \partial y_1 + \Gamma^2_{21} \, y^1 \, \partial y_2 = -\cos  eta_2 \, \partial y_1 +  rac{\sin  eta_2}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2 , \] which, using the relations between the basis fields, is \(-\cos  eta_2 (\cos  eta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \sin  eta_2 \, \partial x_2) + \sin  eta_2 (-\sin  eta_2 \, \partial x_1 + \cos  eta_2 \, \partial x_2) = -\partial x_1\). ✓ Torsion freeness can also be checked on these two fields: their commutator is \([\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}] = [\partial x_2, -b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2] = \partial x_2\left\lfloor -b ightceil \partial x_1 + \partial x_2\left\lfloor a ightceil \partial x_2 = -\partial x_1\), so that \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} - 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} - [\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}] = -\partial x_1 - 0 + \partial x_1 = 0\). ✓ For the covector field \(df\), the formula \((
abla_\mathcal{Z} df)_k = \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_k ightceil - \Gamma^j_{ki} \, \mathtt{x}_j \, z^i\) gives, in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\), \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} df = \partial x_2\left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_k ightceil dx^k = \sin a \sin b \; dx^1 - \cos a \cos b \; dx^2 , \] i.e. the components of \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}} df\) are the ordinary second partial derivatives of \(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\), as expected for a connection whose coefficients vanish in that chart. Autoparallels. The autoparallel equation \(\ddot{\gamma}^k + \Gamma^k_{ji}(\gamma(\lambda)) \, \dot{\gamma}^i \dot{\gamma}^j = 0\) reads, in each chart, \[  egin{array}{c@{\qquad}|@{\qquad}c} 	ext{chart } \mathscr{X}: & 	ext{chart } \mathscr{Y}: \[4pt]  egin{cases} \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{U} = 0 \ \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0 \end{cases} &  egin{cases} \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} - \gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \,  ig( \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V}  ig)^2 = 0 \[4pt] \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} + \dfrac{2}{\gamma^1_\mathcal{V}} \, \dot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} = 0 \end{cases} \end{array} \] where \(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \coloneqq \mathscr{Y}^1 \circ \gamma\) is the radial chart coordinate along the curve, and in the second equation both \(\Gamma^2_{12}\) and \(\Gamma^2_{21}\) contribute. In the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) the solutions are \((\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma)(\lambda) = (a_0, b_0) + \lambda \, (u, v)\): the autoparallels of \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\) are the curves whose chart representatives in \(\mathscr{X}\) are straight lines, traversed at constant speed. In particular: \(\gamma_{x_0}\) is autoparallel, since \((\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{x_0})(\lambda) = (x_0, \lambda)\). In the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\) its representative is curved, yet it solves the corresponding equations: differentiating it, \[ \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{V} = \left(  rac{\lambda}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}}, \,  rac{x_0}{x_0^2 + \lambda^2} ight), \qquad \ddot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{V} = \left(  rac{x_0^2}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^{3/2}}, \, - rac{2 x_0 \lambda}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^2} ight), \] so that  egin{align*} & rac{x_0^2}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^{3/2}} - \sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2} \,  rac{x_0^2}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^2} = 0, \ &- rac{2 x_0 \lambda}{(x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^2} +  rac{2}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}} \,  rac{\lambda}{\sqrt{x_0^2 + \lambda^2}} \,  rac{x_0}{x_0^2 + \lambda^2} = 0. \quad \checkmark \end{align*} At field level, this is the statement \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor x^k ightceil \partial x_k = 0\). \(\delta_{r_0}\) is not autoparallel. Its acceleration, computed in either chart,  egin{align*} 	ext{chart } \mathscr{X}: \quad a_{\delta}(\lambda) &= \ddot{\delta}^k_\mathcal{U} \, \partial x_k = -r_0 \cos \lambda \, \partial x_1 - r_0 \sin \lambda \, \partial x_2, \ 	ext{chart } \mathscr{Y}: \quad a_{\delta}(\lambda) &=  ig( 0 + \Gamma^1_{22} \cdot 1  ig) \partial y_1 +  ig( 0 + 2 \, \Gamma^2_{12} \cdot 0 \cdot 1  ig) \partial y_2 = -r_0 \, \partial y_1 , \end{align*} is the same vector (use \(\partial y_1 = \cos \lambda \, \partial x_1 + \sin \lambda \, \partial x_2\) along the curve), pointing towards the origin. Since it is not proportional to the velocity \(\partial y_2\), not even a reparametrization of \(\delta_{r_0}\) is autoparallel. At field level, \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{Y} = - eta_1 \, \partial y_1 
eq 0\). Parallel transport. Let \(\mathcal{Z}\) be a vector field along a curve \(\gamma\) with components \(z^k(\lambda)\) in a chart. By the same argument used for the autoparallel equation, \((
abla_{v_{\gamma(\lambda)}} \mathcal{Z})^k = \dot{z}^k + \Gamma^k_{ji}(\gamma(\lambda)) \, z^j \, \dot{\gamma}^i\), so parallel transport along \(\gamma\) is the linear system of ODEs \[ \dot{z}^k(\lambda) + \Gamma^k_{ji} ig( \gamma(\lambda)  ig) \, z^j(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^i(\lambda) = 0 . \] For \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\) in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) this is \(\dot{z}^k = 0\): parallel transport keeps the cartesian components constant, along any curve. Hence \(\mathcal{X}\) is parallel along every curve, whereas \(\mathcal{Y}\) is parallel along none of our curves, e.g. \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = -\partial x_1 
eq 0\) along \(\gamma_{x_0}\). Transporting an initial vector with cartesian components \((c_1, c_2)\) along \(\delta_{r_0}\), where \(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{V} = (0,1)\) and \( eta_1 = r_0\), the polar components must instead solve \[ \dot{z}^1 + \Gamma^1_{22} \, z^2 = \dot{z}^1 - r_0 \, z^2 = 0, \qquad \dot{z}^2 + \Gamma^2_{12} \, z^1 = \dot{z}^2 +  rac{1}{r_0} \, z^1 = 0, \] whose solution is \(z^1(\lambda) = c_1 \cos \lambda + c_2 \sin \lambda\), \(z^2(\lambda) = (-c_1 \sin \lambda + c_2 \cos \lambda) / r_0\). Converting back with \(	extrm{unic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\) gives \(\cos \lambda \, z^1 - r_0 \sin \lambda \, z^2 = c_1\) and \(\sin \lambda \, z^1 + r_0 \cos \lambda \, z^2 = c_2\). ✓ The transported vector keeps its cartesian direction while its polar components rotate. After a full turn it returns to itself, as it must for a flat connection.

title: C.5 Examples of Connections, Torsion and Curvature (§§6.1–6.4)
section: C.5.3 A flat connection with torsion: \(\nabla^{\mathrm{W}}\)
text:
C.5.3 A flat connection with torsion: \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\)

The second connection is built by declaring a frame, rather than a chart, to be parallel. On \(\mathcal{M}^* \coloneqq \mathcal{M} \setminus \{ (0, 0, h(0,0)) \}\), i.e. where \(a^2 + b^2 > 0\), consider the unit radial and angular vector fields \[ e_1 \coloneqq  rac{a \, \partial x_1 + b \, \partial x_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}, \qquad e_2 \coloneqq  rac{-b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}, \] which on \(\mathcal{V}\) read \(e_1 = \partial y_1\) and \(e_2 =  rac{1}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2\). They form a frame at every point of \(\mathcal{M}^*\), but, unlike \(\{ \partial x_i \}\) or \(\{ \partial y_i \}\), not a chart-induced one. Define \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\) by \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Z} \, e_a = 0 \qquad  orall \, \mathcal{Z} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}^*, \; a = 1, 2 . \] By the product rule this fixes the connection completely: any vector field is \(\mathcal{W} = w^a e_a\) with \(w^a \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M}^*)\), and then \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Z} \mathcal{W} = \mathcal{Z}\left\lfloor w^a ightceil e_a\). A connection of this kind, which makes a global frame parallel, is called a teleparallel (or Weitzenböck) connection, hence the label. Coefficients in the polar chart. Since \(\partial y_1 = e_1\) and \(\partial y_2 =  eta_1 \, e_2\), the product rule gives \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial y_k} \partial y_1 = 0, \qquad 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial y_k} \partial y_2 = \partial y_k\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 ightceil e_2 = \delta^1_k \, e_2 =  rac{\delta^1_k}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2 , \] so that the only non-vanishing coefficient function is \[ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y ight)^2_{21} =  rac{1}{ eta_1} \qquad  ig( 	ext{while } \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y ight)^2_{12} = 0  ig). \] Coefficients in the cartesian chart. Inverting the definition of the frame, \[ \partial x_1 =  rac{a \, e_1 - b \, e_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}, \qquad \partial x_2 =  rac{b \, e_1 + a \, e_2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}, \] and the product rule, with the frame fields parallel, gives  egin{align*} 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_k} \partial x_1 &= \partial x_k\left\lfloor  rac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil e_1 - \partial x_k\left\lfloor  rac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil e_2, \ 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_k} \partial x_2 &= \partial x_k\left\lfloor  rac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil e_1 + \partial x_k\left\lfloor  rac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil e_2 . \end{align*} The four derivatives needed are  egin{gather*} \partial x_1\left\lfloor  rac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil =  rac{b^2}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}}, \qquad \partial x_2\left\lfloor  rac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil =  rac{a^2}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}}, \ \partial x_2\left\lfloor  rac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil = \partial x_1\left\lfloor  rac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} ightceil = - rac{a b}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}}, \end{gather*} and, re-expressing \(b \, e_1 + a \, e_2 = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \; \partial x_2\) and \(a \, e_1 - b \, e_2 = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \; \partial x_1\),  egin{align*} 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_1 &=  rac{b \,  ig( b \, e_1 + a \, e_2  ig)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} =  rac{b}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_2, & 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_1 &= - rac{a \,  ig( b \, e_1 + a \, e_2  ig)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} = - rac{a}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_2, \ 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_2 &= - rac{b \,  ig( a \, e_1 - b \, e_2  ig)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} = - rac{b}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_1, & 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_2 &=  rac{a \,  ig( a \, e_1 - b \, e_2  ig)}{(a^2 + b^2)^{3/2}} =  rac{a}{a^2 + b^2} \, \partial x_1, \end{align*} i.e. the non-vanishing coefficient functions in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) are \[ \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x ight)^2_{11} =  rac{b}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x ight)^2_{12} = - rac{a}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x ight)^1_{21} = - rac{b}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x ight)^1_{22} =  rac{a}{a^2 + b^2} . \] The two connections differ by a tensor field. Although neither set of \(\Gamma\)’s is tensorial, their difference is: the inhomogeneous terms, which depend only on the charts, cancel in the transformation law. In the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\), the difference \(D \coloneqq \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}} - \Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}\) has components \[ D^1_{22} = 0 - (- eta_1) =  eta_1, \qquad D^2_{12} = 0 -  rac{1}{ eta_1} = - rac{1}{ eta_1}, \qquad D^2_{21} =  rac{1}{ eta_1} -  rac{1}{ eta_1} = 0, \] and, since \(\Gamma^{\mathrm{E}}_x = 0\), its components in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) must be exactly \(\Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x\). Checking one of them with the \((1,2)\)-tensor transformation law,  egin{align*} D^1_{22} ig|_\mathscr{X} &=  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^1}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^l}  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^s}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2}  rac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^p}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \, D^l_{sp} = \cos  eta_2 \left(  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} ight)^2  eta_1 + \left( - eta_1 \sin  eta_2 ight) \sin  eta_2 \,  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} \left( - rac{1}{ eta_1} ight) \ &=  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1}, \end{align*} which is indeed \(\left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x ight)^1_{22} = a / (a^2 + b^2)\) written in the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\), since \(a =  eta_1 \cos  eta_2\) and \(a^2 + b^2 =  eta_1^2\). ✓Note also that \(D^i_{j1} = 0\): the two connections agree when differentiating along \(\partial y_1\), i.e. radially, and differ only in the angular direction. Torsion. In the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\), \(\mathtt{T}^2_{12} = \Gamma^2_{21} - \Gamma^2_{12} =  rac{1}{ eta_1} = -\mathtt{T}^2_{21}\), all other components vanishing, i.e. \(\mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial y_1, \partial y_2) =  rac{1}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2\). In the chart \(\mathscr{X}\), \[ \mathtt{T}^1_{12} = \Gamma^1_{21} - \Gamma^1_{12} = - rac{b}{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \mathtt{T}^2_{12} = \Gamma^2_{21} - \Gamma^2_{12} =  rac{a}{a^2 + b^2}, \] i.e. \(\mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial x_1, \partial x_2) =  ig( -b \, \partial x_1 + a \, \partial x_2  ig) / (a^2 + b^2) = \mathcal{Y} / (a^2 + b^2)\). Both results describe the same tensor field: since \(\partial y_j =  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \partial x_s\), bilinearity and antisymmetry give \[ \mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial y_1, \partial y_2) = \det\!\left(  rac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} ight) \mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial x_1, \partial x_2) =  eta_1 \cdot  rac{1}{ eta_1^2} \, \partial y_2 =  rac{1}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2 , \] using \(\mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2\) and \(a^2 + b^2 =  eta_1^2\). ✓ The origin of the torsion is transparent in the frame: since \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}} e_a = 0\), \[ \mathtt{T}(\cdot, e_1, e_2) = -[e_1, e_2] = -\Big[ \partial y_1,  rac{1}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2 \Big] = -\partial y_1\left\lfloor  rac{1}{\mathscr{Y}^1} ightceil \partial y_2 =  rac{1}{ eta_1^2} \, \partial y_2 =  rac{1}{ eta_1} \, e_2 : \] a connection that declares a non-chart-induced frame parallel has a torsion measuring how much the frame fields fail to commute. As a last check, take our two fields in the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\), where, in terms of the frame, \(\mathcal{X} = \sin  eta_2 \, \partial y_1 +  rac{\cos  eta_2}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2 = \sin  eta_2 \, e_1 + \cos  eta_2 \, e_2\) and \(\mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2 =  eta_1 \, e_2\). Since the frame is parallel, only the frame components get differentiated: \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 ightceil e_2 = \sin  eta_2 \, e_2, \qquad 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} = \partial y_2\left\lfloor \sin  eta_2 ightceil e_1 + \partial y_2\left\lfloor \cos  eta_2 ightceil e_2 = \cos  eta_2 \, e_1 - \sin  eta_2 \, e_2 , \] where \(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 ightceil = y^1 = \sin  eta_2\). Their commutator, \([\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}] = -\partial x_1 = -\cos  eta_2 \, \partial y_1 +  rac{\sin  eta_2}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2 = -\cos  eta_2 \, e_1 + \sin  eta_2 \, e_2\), was computed in Subsection C.5.2, so that \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} - 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{X} - [\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}] = \sin  eta_2 \, e_2 - \cos  eta_2 \, e_1 + \sin  eta_2 \, e_2 + \cos  eta_2 \, e_1 - \sin  eta_2 \, e_2 = \sin  eta_2 \, e_2 , \] in agreement with \(\mathtt{T}(\cdot, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = y^1 \, \mathtt{T}(\cdot, \partial y_1, \partial y_2) = \sin  eta_2 \,  rac{1}{ eta_1} \, \partial y_2 = \sin  eta_2 \, e_2\), the term with \(y^2\) dropping out by antisymmetry. ✓ Curvature. Since the frame is parallel, \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} e_a - 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} e_a - 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_{[\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}]} e_a = 0\) for \(a = 1, 2\), and by \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M}^*)\)-linearity in the slot of \(\mathcal{Z}\), \(\mathrm{Riem} = 0\): \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\) is flat. In the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\) this is immediate: every term of \(\mathrm{Riem}^i_{j12} = \partial y_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{j2} ightceil - \partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{j1} ightceil + \Gamma^i_{r1} \Gamma^r_{j2} - \Gamma^i_{r2} \Gamma^r_{j1}\) contains either a coefficient with last index \(2\), all of which vanish, or the derivative \(\partial y_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^i_{j1} ightceil\), which vanishes since \(\Gamma^2_{21} = 1/ eta_1\) does not depend on \( eta_2\). Curvature and torsion are thus independent notions: \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\) and \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\) are both flat, and only the latter has torsion. A covariant derivative compared. For the same scalar field \(f\) and direction \(\mathcal{X} = \partial x_2\), the two connections give different covariant derivatives of \(df\). In the chart \(\mathscr{X}\), with \(x^i = (0,1)\), \((
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} df)_k = \partial x_2\left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_k ightceil - \left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_x ight)^j_{k2} \mathtt{x}_j\), so that \[ 
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{X} df = \left( \sin a \sin b -  rac{a \cos a \sin b}{a^2 + b^2} ight) dx^1 + \left( -\cos a \cos b +  rac{a \sin a \cos b}{a^2 + b^2} ight) dx^2 , \] which differs from \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}_\mathcal{X} df\) by the terms coming from \(D\). Autoparallels. In the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\), the autoparallel equation of \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\) contains a single \(\Gamma\), with \(j = 2\), \(i = 1\): \[ \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} = 0, \qquad \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} +  rac{1}{\gamma^1_\mathcal{V}} \, \dot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} = 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad  rac{d}{d\lambda} \Big( \gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} \Big) = 0 . \] Hence \(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) = r_0 + u \lambda\) and \(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V} \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{V} = w\) constant, and the autoparallels are: for \(u = 0\), \(\gamma^2_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) = \varphi_0 + (w / r_0) \, \lambda\): circles traversed at constant speed. In particular \(\delta_{r_0}\), with \(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{V} = (0,1)\), is autoparallel for \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\), while it was not for \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\). At field level, \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2\left\lfloor \mathscr{Y}^1 ightceil e_2 = 0\), since the radial coordinate is constant along the circles; for \(w = 0\), radial lines, \(\gamma^2_\mathcal{V} = \varphi_0\), the only curves that are autoparallel for both connections, in agreement with \(D^i_{j1} = 0\); for \(u, w 
eq 0\), \(\gamma^2_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) = \varphi_0 +  rac{w}{u} \ln\!\left( 1 +  rac{u \lambda}{r_0} ight)\), i.e. \(\gamma^1_\mathcal{V} = r_0 \, e^{u (\gamma^2_\mathcal{V} - \varphi_0) / w}\): logarithmic spirals. The vertical curves \(\gamma_{x_0}\), \(x_0 
eq 0\), are no longer autoparallel: \(\ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{V} = x_0^2 / (x_0^2 + \lambda^2)^{3/2} 
eq 0\). Note that the autoparallel equation only involves the symmetric part of the \(\Gamma\)’s: the torsion-free connection with the same symmetric part as \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\) has exactly the same autoparallels. Likewise, the normal coordinates of Chapter 6 can remove the symmetric part \(\left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y ight)^2_{(12)} =  rac{1}{2 eta_1}\) at any given point, but no chart can remove the antisymmetric part \(\left( \Gamma^{\mathrm{W}}_y ight)^2_{[21]} =  rac{1}{2 eta_1}\), which is fixed by the torsion. Parallel transport. By construction, \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) are parallel along every curve, and a vector field is parallel along \(\gamma\) iff its frame components \(w^a\) are constant along it. Along \(\delta_{r_0}\), \(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{V} = (0,1)\) and all \(\Gamma^k_{j2}\) vanish, so the parallel transport equations reduce to \(\dot{z}^k = 0\) in the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\): parallel transport along the circles keeps the polar components constant. In the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) the transported vector, \( ig( z^1 \cos \lambda - r_0 z^2 \sin \lambda, \; z^1 \sin \lambda + r_0 z^2 \cos \lambda  ig)\), co-rotates with the circle, in sharp contrast with \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\). In particular \(\mathcal{Y} = \partial y_2\) is parallel along the circles, whereas \(\mathcal{X}\), with polar components \((\sin \lambda, \cos \lambda / r_0)\) along \(\delta_{r_0}\), is not.

title: C.5 Examples of Connections, Torsion and Curvature (§§6.1–6.4)
text:
C.5.4 A curved, torsion-free connection: \(
abla^{\kappa}\)

Neither of the previous connections is curved. Fix a constant \(\kappa > 0\) and define \(
abla^{\kappa}\) on \(\mathcal{M}\) by a single non-vanishing coefficient function in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\), \[ \left( \Gamma^{\kappa}_x ight)^1_{22} = \kappa \, a, \qquad 	ext{i.e.} \qquad 
abla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_2 = \kappa \, a \, \partial x_1, \quad 
abla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_1 = 
abla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_1} \partial x_2 = 
abla^{\kappa}_{\partial x_2} \partial x_1 = 0 . \] Torsion and curvature. The coefficients are trivially symmetric in their lower indices, so \(
abla^{\kappa}\) is torsion free. In the Riemann curvature, every quadratic term \(\Gamma^i_{rk} \Gamma^r_{jm}\) can only be non-zero for \(r = 1\), and then contains a vanishing factor \(\Gamma^i_{1k}\); the only non-vanishing derivative is \(\partial x_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{22} ightceil = \kappa\). Hence the only non-vanishing components are \[ \mathrm{Riem}^1_{212} = \partial x_1\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{22} ightceil - \partial x_2\left\lfloor \Gamma^1_{21} ightceil = \kappa = -\mathrm{Riem}^1_{221}, \] and the Ricci curvature, \(\mathrm{Ric}_{ab} = \mathrm{Riem}^m_{amb}\), has the single component \(\mathrm{Ric}_{22} = \mathrm{Riem}^1_{212} = \kappa\), i.e. \(\mathrm{Ric} = \kappa \, dx^2 \otimes dx^2\). Being a tensor field that does not vanish in one chart, the curvature cannot be made to vanish in any other: no choice of chart makes all the \(\Gamma\)’s of \(
abla^\kappa\) vanish on an open set. Autoparallels. The autoparallel equation in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) reads \[ \ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{U} + \kappa \, \gamma^1_\mathcal{U} \,  ig( \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U}  ig)^2 = 0, \qquad \ddot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0 . \] The second equation gives \(\gamma^2_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = b_0 + v \lambda\), and the first then becomes the harmonic oscillator \(\ddot{\gamma}^1_\mathcal{U} + \kappa v^2 \gamma^1_\mathcal{U} = 0\), so that \[ \gamma^1_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = A \cos\! ig( \sqrt{\kappa} \, v \lambda + \psi  ig) \quad \longrightarrow \quad a = A \cos\! ig( \sqrt{\kappa} \, (b - b_0) + \psi  ig) : \] the autoparallels of \(
abla^\kappa\) are sinusoids in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\), all with the same wave number \(\sqrt{\kappa}\), independently of the speed \(v\). Among our curves, only \(\gamma_0\) (\(A = 0\)) is autoparallel; for \(x_0 
eq 0\), \(\gamma_{x_0}\) has acceleration \(
abla^\kappa_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{X} = 
abla^\kappa_{\partial x_2} \partial x_2 = \kappa \, x_0 \, \partial x_1\) along it. Parallel transport around a loop. In the chart \(\mathscr{X}\) the parallel transport equations along a curve with velocity components \(\dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}\) are \(\dot{z}^1 + \kappa \, \gamma^1_\mathcal{U} \, z^2 \, \dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0\) and \(\dot{z}^2 = 0\). Transport a vector with components \((z^1, z^2)\) counterclockwise around the rectangle \([x_0, x_1] 	imes [b_0, b_0 + \Delta b]\): along the two horizontal sides \(\dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 0\), so nothing changes; up the right side, \(a = x_1\) and \(\dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = 1\), so \(z^1\) changes by \(-\kappa \, x_1 \, z^2 \, \Delta b\); down the left side, \(a = x_0\) and \(\dot{\gamma}^2_\mathcal{U} = -1\), so \(z^1\) changes by \(+\kappa \, x_0 \, z^2 \, \Delta b\). After the full loop, \[ \Delta z^1 = -\kappa \, z^2 \, (x_1 - x_0) \, \Delta b = -\mathrm{Riem}^1_{212} \, z^2 	imes 	ext{(area enclosed)}, \qquad \Delta z^2 = 0 : \] the vector does not return to itself, and the mismatch is proportional to the curvature component, to the transported vector and to the enclosed area. Repeating the computation for \(
abla^{\mathrm{E}}\) or \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\) gives \(\Delta z = 0\) for every loop, as expected for flat connections (for \(
abla^{\mathrm{W}}\), loops must avoid the origin).

title: C.6 Example of Variations and Euler–Lagrange Equations (§7.2.1)
text: We follow the variational definition of geodesics of Chapter 7 on a manifold where every step can be done by hand: the Lagrangian in two charts, its Euler–Lagrange equations, how these change between charts, and the length of two families of variations of two curves, one geodesic and one not. Dots denote \(d/d\lambda\), and functions of \(p\) written along a curve are evaluated at \(\gamma(\lambda)\).

title: C.6 Example of Variations and Euler–Lagrange Equations (§7.2.1)
text:
C.6.1 Setting

Manifold. Let \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_2\) be the paraboloid \[ \mathcal{M} \coloneqq \Big\{ p = (a, b, c) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \;\Big|\; c = \frac{1}{4} \big( a^2 + b^2 \big) \Big\}, \] with the topology induced from \(\left( \mathbb{R}^3, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^3} \right)\), and the atlas \(\mathcal{A} \coloneqq \{ (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}), (\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \}\) formed by the cartesian and the polar charts: \[ \begin{array}{c@{\;\;} | @{\;\;} c} \textbf{Chart $(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})$} & \textbf{Chart $(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})$} \\[6pt] \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \\[2pt] \mathscr{X} \colon \mathcal{U} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2 \\ (a, b, c) &\longmapsto \big( a \,,\, b \big) \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \mathcal{V} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \setminus \{ (a, 0, c) \in \mathcal{M} \mid a \leq 0 \} \\[2pt] \mathscr{Y} \colon \mathcal{V} &\longrightarrow \{ (\beta_1, \beta_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid \beta_1 > 0, \; -\pi < \beta_2 < \pi \} \\ (a, b, c) &\longmapsto \big( \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \,,\, \operatorname{atan2}(b, a) \big) \end{aligned} \end{array} \] with inverses \(\mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = \big( \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \frac{1}{4}(\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2) \big)\) and \(\mathscr{Y}^{-1}(\beta_1, \beta_2) = \big( \beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \beta_1 \sin \beta_2, \frac{1}{4} \beta_1^2 \big)\). At a point \(p = (a, b, c) \in \mathcal{V}\) we write \(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a, b)\) and \(\mathscr{Y}(p) = (\beta_1, \beta_2)\), so that \(a = \beta_1 \cos \beta_2\), \(b = \beta_1 \sin \beta_2\) and \(c = \frac{1}{4} \beta_1^2\). The transition map \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}(\beta_1, \beta_2) = (\beta_1 \cos \beta_2, \beta_1 \sin \beta_2)\) and its inverse are smooth on \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V})\) and \(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{V})\), and their Jacobians are \[ \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \right)_p = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \beta_2 & -\beta_1 \sin \beta_2 \\ \sin \beta_2 & \beta_1 \cos \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}_{ik}, \qquad \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \beta_2 & \sin \beta_2 \\ -\sin \beta_2 / \beta_1 & \cos \beta_2 / \beta_1 \end{bmatrix}_{ki}. \] Height. The scalar field \(f(p) \coloneqq c\) has chart representatives \(\big( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = \frac{1}{4} (\alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2)\) and \(\big( f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta_1, \beta_2) = \frac{1}{4} \beta_1^2\), whose partial derivatives give the component functions of \(df\) in each chart: \[ \mathtt{X}_1 = \frac{a}{2}, \qquad \mathtt{X}_2 = \frac{b}{2}, \qquad\qquad \mathtt{Y}_1 = \frac{\beta_1}{2}, \qquad \mathtt{Y}_2 = 0 , \] consistently with \(\mathtt{Y}_k = \big( \partial \mathscr{X}^i / \partial \mathscr{Y}^k \big) \mathtt{X}_i\). Metric. Since \(\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{M}\), the covector fields \(dx^1\), \(dx^2\) are defined on all of \(\mathcal{M}\), and we define, for all \(\mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2 \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\), \[ g(\mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2) \coloneqq dx^1\left\lceil \mathcal{X}_1 \right\rfloor dx^1\left\lceil \mathcal{X}_2 \right\rfloor + dx^2\left\lceil \mathcal{X}_1 \right\rfloor dx^2\left\lceil \mathcal{X}_2 \right\rfloor + df\left\lceil \mathcal{X}_1 \right\rfloor df\left\lceil \mathcal{X}_2 \right\rfloor . \] With \(dx^k\left\lceil \partial x_i \right\rfloor = \delta^k_i\) and \(df\left\lceil \partial x_i \right\rfloor = \mathtt{X}_i\), its components in \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) are \[ (g_\mathscr{X})_{ij} = g(\partial x_i, \partial x_j) = \delta^1_i \delta^1_j + \delta^2_i \delta^2_j + \mathtt{X}_i \, \mathtt{X}_j = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + \frac{a^2}{4} & \frac{ab}{4} \\[2pt] \frac{ab}{4} & 1 + \frac{b^2}{4} \end{bmatrix}_{ij}. \] In \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), the transformation law \((g_\mathscr{Y})_{kl} = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^j}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^l} (g_\mathscr{X})_{ij}\) turns the first two terms into \(\sum_i \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^l}\), i.e. \(1\) for \(k = l = 1\), \(\beta_1^2\) for \(k = l = 2\) and \(0\) otherwise, and the last one into \(\mathtt{Y}_k \, \mathtt{Y}_l\): \[ (g_\mathscr{Y})_{kl} = \begin{bmatrix} W & 0 \\ 0 & \beta_1^2 \end{bmatrix}_{kl}, \qquad W \coloneqq 1 + \frac{\beta_1^2}{4} = 1 + \frac{a^2 + b^2}{4} . \] Both \(\det(g_\mathscr{X}) = W\) and \(\det(g_\mathscr{Y}) = \beta_1^2 \, W\) are positive, and \(g\) is positive definite: a Riemannian metric. Curves. For a smooth curve \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\) we name the component functions of its chart representatives and its height, \[ \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \coloneqq (\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma)(\lambda) = \big( a(\lambda), b(\lambda) \big), \qquad \gamma_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) \coloneqq (\mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma)(\lambda) = \big( r(\lambda), \theta(\lambda) \big), \qquad c(\lambda) \coloneqq (f \circ \gamma)(\lambda), \] the second one for those \(\lambda\) with \(\gamma(\lambda) \in \mathcal{V}\). They are the coordinates \((a, b)\), \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\) and \(c\) of the point \(\gamma(\lambda)\), now as functions of \(\lambda\), so that \(a = r \cos \theta\), \(b = r \sin \theta\) and \(c = \frac{1}{4} (a^2 + b^2) = \frac{1}{4} r^2\). The components of the velocity \(v_{\gamma(\lambda)}\) are \(\dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U} = (\dot{a}, \dot{b})\) and \(\dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{V} = (\dot{r}, \dot{\theta})\), and the rate of change of the height is \[ \dot{c} = (df)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) = \mathtt{X}_i \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} = \frac{1}{2} \big( a \, \dot{a} + b \, \dot{b} \big) = \mathtt{Y}_k \, \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{V} = \frac{1}{2} \, r \, \dot{r} . \] Since \(g\) is Riemannian, \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma = +1\) wherever \(v_\gamma \neq 0\), and the speed reads, in each chart, \[ s_\gamma^2 = (g_\mathscr{X})_{ij} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} = \dot{a}^2 + \dot{b}^2 + \frac{1}{4} \big( a \, \dot{a} + b \, \dot{b} \big)^2 = \dot{a}^2 + \dot{b}^2 + \dot{c}^2 , \qquad s_\gamma^2 = (g_\mathscr{Y})_{kl} \, \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{V} \, \dot{\gamma}^l_\mathcal{V} = W \, \dot{r}^2 + r^2 \, \dot{\theta}^2 , \] the two expressions agreeing since \(\dot{a}^2 + \dot{b}^2 = \dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\theta}^2\) and \(\dot{c}^2 = \frac{1}{4} r^2 \dot{r}^2\). The first one is the euclidean speed of \(\lambda \mapsto (a, b, c) \in \mathbb{R}^3\): \(g\) is the metric induced by \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Euler–Lagrange expressions. For a curve \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma([a,b]) \subseteq \mathcal{U}\), define, for \(m = 1, 2\), \[ (E_\mathscr{X})_m(\lambda) \coloneqq \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ (\partial_{2+m} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})(\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}) \Big] - (\partial_m \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X})(\gamma_\mathcal{U} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}), \] and likewise \((E_\mathscr{Y})_m\) with \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y}\) and \((\gamma_\mathcal{V} ; \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{V})\), so that \(\gamma\) is a geodesic if and only if \(E_\mathscr{X} = 0\) (or \(E_\mathscr{Y} = 0\)). Here \(\partial_1, \partial_2\) differentiate the position slots and \(\partial_3, \partial_4\) the velocity slots of the chart representatives \[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( a, b \, ; x^1_p, x^2_p \big) = \sqrt{ (x^1_p)^2 + (x^2_p)^2 + \tfrac{1}{4} \big( a \, x^1_p + b \, x^2_p \big)^2 }, \qquad \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y}\big( \beta_1, \beta_2 \, ; y^1_p, y^2_p \big) = \sqrt{ W \, (y^1_p)^2 + \beta_1^2 \, (y^2_p)^2 } . \] Every partial derivative of \(\mathcal{L} = \sqrt{F}\) carries a factor \(1 / \mathcal{L}\), which equals \(1 / s_\gamma\) on the curve. Since \(s_\gamma > 0\), we clear it by computing \(s_\gamma \, E\), which vanishes if and only if \(E\) does. Cartesian chart. Partial derivatives. With \(u \coloneqq a \, x^1_p + b \, x^2_p\) and \(\partial \sqrt{F} = \partial F / (2 \sqrt{F})\), \[ \partial_1 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{u \, x^1_p}{4 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}}, \qquad \partial_2 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{u \, x^2_p}{4 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}}, \qquad \partial_3 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{x^1_p + \frac{1}{4} u \, a}{\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}}, \qquad \partial_4 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{x^2_p + \frac{1}{4} u \, b}{\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}} . \] On the curve. With \((a, b \, ; x^1_p, x^2_p) = (a, b \, ; \dot{a}, \dot{b})\): \(u = a \dot{a} + b \dot{b} = 2 \dot{c}\), \(\frac{1}{4} u \, a = \dot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_1\), \(\frac{1}{4} u \, b = \dot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_2\) and \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = s_\gamma\), so \[ \partial_1 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{\dot{c} \, \dot{a}}{2 s_\gamma}, \qquad \partial_2 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{\dot{c} \, \dot{b}}{2 s_\gamma}, \qquad \partial_3 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{\dot{a} + \dot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_1}{s_\gamma}, \qquad \partial_4 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} = \frac{\dot{b} + \dot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_2}{s_\gamma} . \] \(\lambda\)-derivative. By the quotient rule and \(\frac{d}{d\lambda} (\mathtt{X}_1 \circ \gamma) = \frac{1}{2} \dot{a}\), \[ \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ \partial_3 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \big] = \frac{\ddot{a} + \ddot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_1 + \frac{1}{2} \dot{c} \, \dot{a}}{s_\gamma} - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma^2} \big( \dot{a} + \dot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_1 \big). \] Subtracting \(\partial_1 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) cancels the term \(\frac{1}{2} \dot{c} \, \dot{a} / s_\gamma\), and likewise for \(m = 2\): \[ \boxed{ s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{X})_1 = \ddot{a} + \mathtt{X}_1 \, \ddot{c} - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} \big( \dot{a} + \dot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_1 \big), \qquad s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{X})_2 = \ddot{b} + \mathtt{X}_2 \, \ddot{c} - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} \big( \dot{b} + \dot{c} \, \mathtt{X}_2 \big) . } \] Polar chart. Partial derivatives on the curve. With \(\partial_1 W = \frac{1}{2} \beta_1\) and \((\beta_1, \beta_2 \, ; y^1_p, y^2_p) = (r, \theta \, ; \dot{r}, \dot{\theta})\), \[ \partial_1 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = \frac{\frac{1}{4} r \dot{r}^2 + r \dot{\theta}^2}{s_\gamma}, \qquad \partial_2 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = 0, \qquad \partial_3 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = \frac{W \dot{r}}{s_\gamma}, \qquad \partial_4 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = \frac{r^2 \dot{\theta}}{s_\gamma} . \] \(\lambda\)-derivative. By the quotient rule and \(\frac{d}{d\lambda} (W \circ \gamma) = \frac{1}{2} r \dot{r}\), \[ \boxed{ s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{Y})_1 = W \ddot{r} + \tfrac{1}{4} r \dot{r}^2 - r \dot{\theta}^2 - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} \, W \dot{r}, \qquad s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{Y})_2 = r^2 \ddot{\theta} + 2 r \dot{r} \dot{\theta} - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} \, r^2 \dot{\theta} . } \] Since \(\partial_2 \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = 0\) (the angle is cyclic), \((E_\mathscr{Y})_2 = \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ r^2 \dot{\theta} / s_\gamma \big]\), so \(r^2 \dot{\theta} / s_\gamma\) is constant along every geodesic. For a constant-speed parametrization, \(s_\gamma' = 0\) and the last term of every boxed expression drops. Contraction with the velocity. For every curve, \((E_\mathscr{X})_m \, \dot{\gamma}^m_\mathcal{U} = 0\). Using \(\mathtt{X}_1 \dot{a} + \mathtt{X}_2 \dot{b} = \dot{c}\) and \(s_\gamma s_\gamma' = \dot{a} \ddot{a} + \dot{b} \ddot{b} + \dot{c} \ddot{c}\), \[ s_\gamma \, (E_\mathscr{X})_m \, \dot{\gamma}^m_\mathcal{U} = \big( \dot{a} \ddot{a} + \dot{b} \ddot{b} + \dot{c} \ddot{c} \big) - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} \big( \dot{a}^2 + \dot{b}^2 + \dot{c}^2 \big) = s_\gamma s_\gamma' - \frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} \, s_\gamma^2 = 0 . \] Only the component of \(E_\mathscr{X}\) transverse to the curve carries information: a variation with \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ} \propto \dot{\gamma}_\mathcal{U}\) moves the curve along itself, which to first order is a reparametrization and leaves the length unchanged.

title: C.6 Example of Variations and Euler–Lagrange Equations (§7.2.1)
text:
C.6.2 Change of chart

Claim. Along any curve in \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\), \[ \boxed{ (E_\mathscr{Y})_k = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \, (E_\mathscr{X})_i , } \] the transformation law of the components of a covector. Hence \(E_\mathscr{X} = 0 \iff E_\mathscr{Y} = 0\): being a geodesic does not depend on the chart. Proof (any \(d\), any two charts). Let \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \coloneqq \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\) and \(J^i_k \coloneqq \partial_k \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}^i\). Since \(x^i = J^i_l \, y^l\) are the components of the same vector, \(\mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y}(\beta \, ; y) = \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\big( \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}(\beta) \, ; J(\beta) \, y \big)\). Chain rule: \(\partial_{d+k} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = J^i_k \, \partial_{d+i} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\) and \(\partial_k \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = J^i_k \, \partial_i \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} + (\partial_k J^i_l) \, y^l \, \partial_{d+i} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}\). Along the curve, \(\frac{d}{d\lambda} J^i_k = (\partial_l J^i_k) \, \dot{\gamma}^l_\mathcal{V} = (\partial_k J^i_l) \, \dot{\gamma}^l_\mathcal{V}\) by Schwarz’s theorem, so \[ \begin{aligned} (E_\mathscr{Y})_k &= J^i_k \, \frac{d}{d\lambda} \big[ \partial_{d+i} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \big] + (\partial_k J^i_l) \, \dot{\gamma}^l_\mathcal{V} \, \partial_{d+i} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} - J^i_k \, \partial_i \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} - (\partial_k J^i_l) \, \dot{\gamma}^l_\mathcal{V} \, \partial_{d+i} \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X} \\ &= J^i_k \, (E_\mathscr{X})_i . \qquad \square \end{aligned} \]

title: C.6 Example of Variations and Euler–Lagrange Equations (§7.2.1)
text:
C.6.3 Two curves

Consider the meridian \(\gamma\) from \(A \coloneqq \mathscr{X}^{-1}(0, 1)\) to \(B \coloneqq \mathscr{X}^{-1}(0, 3)\), and the arc \(\sigma\) of the parallel \(\beta_1 = 2\) from \(P \coloneqq \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2})\) to \(Q \coloneqq \mathscr{X}^{-1}(-\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2})\) (Figure C.9): \[ \begin{aligned} \gamma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) &= (0, \lambda), & \gamma_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) &= \big( \lambda, \tfrac{\pi}{2} \big), & \lambda &\in [1, 3], \\ \sigma_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) &= (2 \cos \lambda, 2 \sin \lambda), & \sigma_\mathcal{V}(\lambda) &= (2, \lambda), & \lambda &\in \big[ \tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{3\pi}{4} \big]. \end{aligned} \] Figure C.9: The meridian \(\gamma\) (black) from \(A\) to \(B\) and the arc of parallel \(\sigma\) (grey, dashed) from \(P\) to \(Q\) of Subsection C.6.3, on \(\mathcal{M}\) (top) and in the charts \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) (bottom, same scale), with the coordinate lines of \(\mathscr{Y}\) in light grey. Both curves are straight in \(\mathscr{Y}\); only \(\gamma\) is a geodesic. The meridian is a geodesic. Its parametrization does not have constant speed, so the terms with \(s_\gamma'\) matter. Ingredients. \(\dot{a} = \ddot{a} = 0\), \(\dot{b} = 1\), \(\ddot{b} = 0\), \(c = \frac{\lambda^2}{4}\), \(\dot{c} = \frac{\lambda}{2}\), \(\ddot{c} = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\mathtt{X}_1 = 0\), \(\mathtt{X}_2 = \frac{\lambda}{2}\), \(W = 1 + \frac{\lambda^2}{4}\), and \(s_\gamma = \sqrt{1 + \dot{c}^2} = \sqrt{W}\), so \(\frac{s_\gamma'}{s_\gamma} = \frac{\dot{W}}{2W} = \frac{\lambda}{4W}\). Cartesian chart. \(s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{X})_1 = 0\), and \[ s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{X})_2 = 0 + \frac{\lambda}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\lambda}{4W} \Big( 1 + \frac{\lambda}{2} \cdot \frac{\lambda}{2} \Big) = \frac{\lambda}{4} - \frac{\lambda}{4W} \, W = 0 . \] Polar chart. \(r = \lambda\), \(\dot{r} = 1\), \(\ddot{r} = 0\), \(\dot{\theta} = \ddot{\theta} = 0\): \(s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{Y})_1 = 0 + \frac{\lambda}{4} - 0 - \frac{\lambda}{4W} \, W = 0\) and \(s_\gamma (E_\mathscr{Y})_2 = 0\). Length. With \(F(\lambda) \coloneqq \frac{\lambda}{2} \sqrt{W} + \operatorname{arsinh} \frac{\lambda}{2}\), which satisfies \(F' = \sqrt{W}\), \[ L_{[1,3]}[\gamma] = \int_1^3 \sqrt{1 + \tfrac{\lambda^2}{4}} \; d\lambda = F(3) - F(1) = \frac{3 \sqrt{13} - \sqrt{5}}{4} + \operatorname{arsinh} \tfrac{3}{2} - \operatorname{arsinh} \tfrac{1}{2} . \] The parallel is not a geodesic. Ingredients. \(c = 1\), so \(\dot{c} = \ddot{c} = 0\); \(\dot{\sigma}_\mathcal{U} = (-2 \sin \lambda, 2 \cos \lambda)\), \(\ddot{\sigma}_\mathcal{U} = -\sigma_\mathcal{U}\); \(s_\sigma = 2\) and \(s_\sigma' = 0\). Cartesian chart. Only the accelerations survive: \[ (E_\mathscr{X})_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} (-2 \cos \lambda) = -\cos \lambda, \qquad (E_\mathscr{X})_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} (-2 \sin \lambda) = -\sin \lambda . \] Polar chart. \(r = 2\), \(\dot{r} = \ddot{r} = 0\), \(\dot{\theta} = 1\), \(\ddot{\theta} = 0\): \[ (E_\mathscr{Y})_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} (-2) = -1, \qquad (E_\mathscr{Y})_2 = 0 . \] Change of chart. With \(\beta_2 = \lambda\): \(\cos \lambda \, (-\cos \lambda) + \sin \lambda \, (-\sin \lambda) = -1\) and \(-2 \sin \lambda \, (-\cos \lambda) + 2 \cos \lambda \, (-\sin \lambda) = 0\), as the Claim of Subsection C.6.2 requires. ✓ \(E\) has no component along \(\dot{\sigma}\), which points in the direction of \(\partial y_2\). Length. \(L_{[\pi/4, 3\pi/4]}[\sigma] = \int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4} 2 \, d\lambda = \pi\).

title: C.6 Example of Variations and Euler–Lagrange Equations (§7.2.1)
text:
C.6.4 Variations of the meridian

With \(\varphi(\lambda) \coloneqq (\lambda - 1)(3 - \lambda)\), which vanishes at \(\lambda = 1, 3\), and \(\varphi' = 4 - 2\lambda\), consider (Figure C.10) \[ \text{(i)} \quad \mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \big( \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \varphi, \, \lambda \big), \quad \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_\mathscr{X} = (\varphi, 0); \qquad \text{(ii)} \quad \mathscr{Y} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \big( \lambda, \, \tfrac{\pi}{2} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \varphi \big), \quad \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_\mathscr{Y} = (0, \varphi). \] Family (i) pushes \(\gamma\) sideways in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\), family (ii) rotates it in the chart \(\mathscr{Y}\) (admissible for \(|\textrm{\runic ᛊ}| < \frac{\pi}{2}\), since \(\varphi \leq 1\)). Neither is a straight shift in the other chart: e.g. for (ii), \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \lambda \big( -\sin(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} \varphi), \cos(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} \varphi) \big)\) is not affine in \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}\). Figure C.10: Families (i) (top) and (ii) (bottom) of Subsection C.6.4, for deformation parameter \(\pm 0.5\), \(\pm 1\) (blue negative, red positive), on \(\mathcal{M}\) and in both charts. The vectors \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}\) (green, deformation parameter \(1\)) are drawn in the chart that defines each family, where the varied curves are straight shifts of \(\gamma\). First variation. By step 5 of Appendix B.14, in the chart defining each family, \[ \text{(i)} \;\; \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L_{[1,3]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}=0} = -\int_1^3 (E_\mathscr{X})_1 \, \varphi \, d\lambda = 0, \qquad \text{(ii)} \;\; \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L_{[1,3]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}=0} = -\int_1^3 (E_\mathscr{Y})_2 \, \varphi \, d\lambda = 0 . \] Family (ii), exactly. The varied curve has \(r = \lambda\), \(\dot{r} = 1\), \(\dot{\theta} = \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \varphi'\), so \[ L_{[1,3]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] = \int_1^3 \sqrt{W + \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \lambda^2 \varphi'^2} \; d\lambda \;\geq\; \int_1^3 \sqrt{W} \, d\lambda = L_{[1,3]}[\gamma] , \] with equality only for \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0\): rotating any part of the meridian makes it longer. Family (i), to second order. The varied curve has \((a, b; \dot{a}, \dot{b}) = (\textrm{\runic ᛊ} \varphi, \lambda; \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \varphi', 1)\), so \(u = \lambda + \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \varphi \varphi'\) and \[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{X}^2 = \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \varphi'^2 + 1 + \tfrac{1}{4} \big( \lambda + \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \varphi \varphi' \big)^2 = W + \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \big( \varphi'^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \lambda \varphi \varphi' \big) + O(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}^4) . \] With \(\sqrt{W + \delta} = \sqrt{W} + \delta / (2 \sqrt{W}) + O(\delta^2)\), \(L_{[1,3]}[\gamma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] = L_{[1,3]}[\gamma] + \frac{1}{2} \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \, I + O(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}^4)\), where, integrating by parts with \(\frac{1}{2} \lambda \varphi \varphi' = \frac{1}{4} \lambda (\varphi^2)'\), \(\varphi(1) = \varphi(3) = 0\) and \((\lambda W^{-1/2})' = W^{-3/2}\), \[ I = \int_1^3 \frac{\varphi'^2 + \frac{1}{2} \lambda \varphi \varphi'}{\sqrt{W}} \, d\lambda = \int_1^3 \Big( \frac{\varphi'^2}{\sqrt{W}} - \frac{\varphi^2}{4 W^{3/2}} \Big) d\lambda . \] Sign of \(I\). On \([1,3]\), \(\frac{5}{4} \leq W \leq \frac{13}{4}\), and Wirtinger’s inequality for functions vanishing at both ends of an interval of length \(2\) gives \(\int_1^3 \varphi'^2 \, d\lambda \geq \frac{\pi^2}{4} \int_1^3 \varphi^2 \, d\lambda\). Therefore \[ I \;\geq\; \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \cdot \frac{\pi^2}{4} \int_1^3 \varphi^2 \, d\lambda - \frac{1}{4} \Big( \frac{4}{5} \Big)^{3/2} \int_1^3 \varphi^2 \, d\lambda = \Big( \frac{\pi^2}{2 \sqrt{13}} - \frac{2}{5 \sqrt{5}} \Big) \int_1^3 \varphi^2 \, d\lambda > 0 , \] since \(\frac{\pi^2}{2 \sqrt{13}} > 1 > \frac{2}{5 \sqrt{5}}\). The argument only uses \(\varphi(1) = \varphi(3) = 0\), so \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = 0\) is a strict local minimum of the length for every sideways push \(\textrm{\runic ᛉ}_\mathscr{X} = (\varphi, 0)\), not only for this \(\varphi\) (Figure C.12, left).

title: C.6 Example of Variations and Euler–Lagrange Equations (§7.2.1)
text:
C.6.5 Variations of the parallel

With \(\psi(\lambda) \coloneqq -\cos 2\lambda\), which vanishes at \(\lambda = \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{3\pi}{4}\) and is positive in between, and \(\psi' = 2 \sin 2\lambda\), consider (Figure C.11) \[ \text{(i)} \quad \mathscr{X} \circ \sigma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \sigma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_\mathscr{X}, \quad \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_\mathscr{X} = (0, \psi); \qquad \text{(ii)} \quad \mathscr{Y} \circ \sigma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} = \big( 2 + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \psi, \, \lambda \big), \quad \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_\mathscr{Y} = (\psi, 0), \] (ii) being admissible for \(|\textrm{\runic ᛊ}| < 2\). Family (i) pushes \(\sigma\) in the direction of \(\partial x_2\), family (ii) radially, up (\(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} > 0\)) or down (\(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} < 0\)) the wall of the bowl. We write \(L \coloneqq L_{[\pi/4, 3\pi/4]}\). Figure C.11: Families (i) (top) and (ii) (bottom) of Subsection C.6.5, as in Figure C.10. Since \(\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}\) is linear in its first slot, family (ii) is also a straight (radial) shift in \(\mathscr{X}\); family (i) is not a straight shift in \(\mathscr{Y}\). First variation, family (i). With \((E_\mathscr{X})_2 = -\sin \lambda\), and substituting \(w = \cos \lambda\), \(\cos 2\lambda = 2w^2 - 1\), \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L[\sigma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}=0} = \int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4} \sin \lambda \, (-\cos 2\lambda) \, d\lambda = \int_{-\sqrt{2}/2}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \big( 1 - 2w^2 \big) \, dw = 2 \Big( \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} \Big) = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} . \] First variation, family (ii). With \((E_\mathscr{Y})_1 = -1\), \[ \frac{d}{d\textrm{\runic ᛊ}} L[\sigma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] \Big|_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}=0} = \int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4} \psi \, d\lambda = \Big[ -\tfrac{1}{2} \sin 2\lambda \Big]_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4} = 1 . \] The same in the chart \(\mathscr{X}\): there family (ii) is \(\sigma_\mathcal{U} + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \tilde{\textrm{\runic ᛉ}}\) with \(\tilde{\textrm{\runic ᛉ}}^i = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \textrm{\runic ᛉ}_\mathscr{Y}^k = \psi \, (\cos \lambda, \sin \lambda)^i\), and \(-\int (E_\mathscr{X})_i \, \tilde{\textrm{\runic ᛉ}}^i \, d\lambda = \int \psi \, (\cos^2 \lambda + \sin^2 \lambda) \, d\lambda = 1\). ✓ Interpretation. Both derivatives are positive: pushing \(\sigma\) up the bowl lengthens it, pushing it down shortens it, so \(\sigma\) is not the shortest curve from \(P\) to \(Q\). Family (ii), to second order. Here \(r = 2 + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \psi\), \(\dot{r} = \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \psi'\), \(\dot{\theta} = 1\), and \(W = 2 + O(\textrm{\runic ᛊ})\), so \[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y}^2 = (2 + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \psi)^2 + W \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \psi'^2 = 4 + \delta, \qquad \delta = 4 \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \psi + \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \big( \psi^2 + 2 \psi'^2 \big) + O(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}^3) . \] From \(\sqrt{4 + \delta} = 2 + \frac{\delta}{4} - \frac{\delta^2}{64} + O(\delta^3)\), with \(\frac{\delta^2}{64} = \frac{1}{4} \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \psi^2 + O(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}^3)\), the \(\psi^2\) terms cancel: \[ \mathcal{L}_\mathscr{Y} = 2 + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} \, \psi + \tfrac{1}{2} \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 \psi'^2 + O(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}^3), \qquad L[\sigma_{\textrm{\runic ᛊ}}] = \pi + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} + \frac{\pi}{2} \, \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2 + O(\textrm{\runic ᛊ}^3), \] using \(\int \psi \, d\lambda = 1\) and \(\int \psi'^2 \, d\lambda = \int 4 \sin^2 2\lambda \, d\lambda = \pi\). Moving down the bowl shortens the arc (first order), at the cost of the extra radial motion \(\psi'\) (second order); the two balance near \(\textrm{\runic ᛊ} = -\frac{1}{\pi}\), where the length is about \(\pi - \frac{1}{2\pi}\) (Figure C.12, right). Figure C.12: Length of the varied curves as a function of the deformation parameter, for families (i) (blue, solid) and (ii) (orange, dashed). Left: the meridian \(\gamma\): vanishing first variations and a minimum at \(0\) (Subsection C.6.4). Right: the parallel \(\sigma\): tangent lines of slopes \(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\) and \(1\) at \(0\), and the second-order expansion \(\pi + \textrm{\runic ᛊ} + \frac{\pi}{2} \textrm{\runic ᛊ}^2\) of family (ii) (dotted) (Subsection C.6.5).

title: C.7 Example of Integration (§§8.1–8.3)
text: The construction of Chapter 8 on the circle, where every step is a one-variable integral: the metric volume form in three charts, the length of an arc in two of them, and the length of the whole circle from a partition of unity (Figure C.13). Manifold and charts. Let \(\mathcal{M} \coloneqq \{ p = (a, b) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid a^2 + b^2 = R^2 \}\), \(R > 0\), with the topology induced from \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and the charts, given through their inverses, \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{U} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \setminus \{ (R, 0) \}, & \mathscr{X}^{-1}(\alpha) &= R \, (\cos \alpha, \sin \alpha), & \alpha &\in (0, 2\pi), \\ \mathcal{V} &\coloneqq \mathcal{M} \setminus \{ (-R, 0) \}, & \mathscr{Y}^{-1}(\beta) &= R \, (\cos \beta, \sin \beta), & \beta &\in (-\pi, \pi), \\ \mathcal{W} &\coloneqq \{ p \in \mathcal{M} \mid b < 0 \}, & \mathscr{Z}^{-1}(\gamma) &= \big( \gamma, - \sqrt{R^2 - \gamma^2} \big), & \gamma &\in (-R, R), \end{aligned} \] the last one projecting the lower half onto the \(a\)-axis. The transition maps to \(\mathscr{X}\) and their Jacobians are \[ \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}(\beta) = \begin{cases} \beta, & \beta > 0 \\ \beta + 2\pi, & \beta < 0 \end{cases}, \quad \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} = 1 ; \qquad \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{W}\mathcal{U}}(\gamma) = 2\pi - \arccos \frac{\gamma}{R}, \quad \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{W}}(\gamma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{R^2 - \gamma^2}} . \] Both are positive, and so is the one between \(\mathscr{Y}\) and \(\mathscr{Z}\), their quotient on \(\mathcal{V} \cap \mathcal{W} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\): \(\mathcal{A}^\uparrow \coloneqq \{ (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}), (\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}), (\mathcal{W}, \mathscr{Z}) \}\) is an oriented atlas. Metric volume form. The metric induced from \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \(g(\mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2) \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^2 d\xi^k\lceil \mathcal{X}_1 \rfloor \, d\xi^k\lceil \mathcal{X}_2 \rfloor\) with \(\xi^1, \xi^2\) the scalar fields \(p \mapsto a, b\), has in a chart \(\mathscr{X}\) the single component \((g_\mathscr{X})_{11} = \sum_k \big( \partial_1 [ \xi^k \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} ] \big)^2\), the squared speed of \(\mathscr{X}^{-1}\). Hence \[ (g_\mathscr{X})_{11} = (g_\mathscr{Y})_{11} = R^2 \big( \sin^2 + \cos^2 \big) = R^2, \qquad (g_\mathscr{Z})_{11} = 1 + \frac{\gamma^2}{R^2 - \gamma^2} = \frac{R^2}{R^2 - \gamma^2}, \] and, by (8.5), \[ \big( \omega^g_\mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \big)(\alpha) = \big( \omega^g_\mathscr{Y} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \big)(\beta) = R, \qquad \big( \omega^g_\mathscr{Z} \circ \mathscr{Z}^{-1} \big)(\gamma) = \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 - \gamma^2}} , \] in agreement with (8.1): \(\omega^g_\mathscr{Z} = \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{W}} \, \omega^g_\mathscr{X}\). The projection \(\mathscr{Z}\) compresses the circle near the ends of \(\mathcal{W}\), where it becomes vertical, and its density grows there. Integral over a region. Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be the arc \(\alpha \in (\alpha_1, \alpha_2)\), with \(\pi < \alpha_1 < \alpha_2 < 2\pi\), so that \(\overline{\mathcal{D}}\) is compact and contained in \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{W}\), and \(f = 1\). By (8.3), its length in the two charts is, with \(\gamma_i \coloneqq R \cos \alpha_i\), \begin{align*} \text{in } \mathscr{X} : \quad \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega^g &= \int_{\alpha_1}^{\alpha_2} d\alpha \; R = R \, (\alpha_2 - \alpha_1), \\ \text{in } \mathscr{Z} : \quad \int_\mathcal{D} \Omega^g &= \int_{\gamma_1}^{\gamma_2} d\gamma \; \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 - \gamma^2}} = R \Big[ \arcsin \frac{\gamma}{R} \Big]_{\gamma_1}^{\gamma_2} \overset{\substack{\arcsin(\cos \alpha) \, = \, \alpha - 3\pi/2 \\ \text{on } (\pi, 2\pi)}}{=} R \, (\alpha_2 - \alpha_1) . \end{align*} Without the volume form, the chart representatives of \(f\) alone give \(\alpha_2 - \alpha_1\) and \(\gamma_2 - \gamma_1 = R \, (\cos \alpha_2 - \cos \alpha_1)\), which differ. With the chart \(\mathscr{Z}'(a, b) \coloneqq - a\) instead of \(\mathscr{Z}\), the Jacobian, and with it the density \(-R / \sqrt{R^2 - \gamma^2}\), would be negative, and the chart integral would give \(- R \, (\alpha_2 - \alpha_1)\): \(\mathscr{Z}'\) does not belong to \(\mathcal{A}^\uparrow\). Integral over the whole manifold. \(f = 1\) does not vanish near \((R, 0) \notin \mathcal{U}\), nor near \((-R, 0) \notin \mathcal{V}\), so a partition of unity is needed. Let \(\chi : \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1]\) be smooth, with \(\chi = 1\) on \((-\infty, -\frac{1}{2}]\) and \(\chi = 0\) on \([\frac{1}{2}, \infty)\), and \[ \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_1(p) \coloneqq \chi(a / R), \qquad \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_2 \coloneqq 1 - \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_1 . \] \(\operatorname{supp} \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_1 \subseteq \{ a \leq R/2 \} \subset \mathcal{U}\) and \(\operatorname{supp} \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_2 \subseteq \{ a \geq -R/2 \} \subset \mathcal{V}\), so \(\{ \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_1, \textrm{\runic ᚹ}_2 \}\) is a partition of unity subordinate to \(\{ \mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V} \}\). By (8.4), computing each term in the chart of its domain, \[ \int_\mathcal{M} \Omega^g = \int_{0}^{2\pi} d\alpha \; R \, \chi(\cos \alpha) + \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} d\beta \; R \, \big( 1 - \chi(\cos \beta) \big) \overset{2\pi\text{-periodic}}{=} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} d\beta \; R \, \big( \chi(\cos \beta) + 1 - \chi(\cos \beta) \big) = 2 \pi R , \] and \(\chi\), i.e. the partition of unity, drops out. In practice one integrates in \(\mathscr{X}\) alone, \(\int_0^{2\pi} d\alpha \, R = 2\pi R\), ignoring the single missing point \((R, 0)\); that it does not contribute agrees with the result above, but is not covered by (8.3). Figure C.13: Integration on the circle of Section C.7. (a) An arc \(\mathcal{D}\) (orange) in the lower half \(\mathcal{W}\) (green), projected by the chart \(\mathscr{Z}\) onto \((\gamma_1, \gamma_2)\), with the density \(\omega^g_\mathscr{Z} = R / \sqrt{R^2 - \gamma^2}\) (blue), which grows where the projection compresses the circle. (b) The same arc in the angle chart \(\mathscr{X}\), where the density is constant. The two shaded areas are equal, both being the length \(R \, (\alpha_2 - \alpha_1)\) of \(\mathcal{D}\); the two intervals alone, \(\gamma_2 - \gamma_1\) and \(\alpha_2 - \alpha_1\), are not. (c) The partition of unity: \(\textrm{\runic ᚹ}_1 = 1\) on the left arc (blue), \(\textrm{\runic ᚹ}_2 = 1\) on the right arc (orange), and both share the arcs in between (purple). The support of \(\textrm{\runic ᚹ}_1\) avoids the point missing from \(\mathcal{U}\), and that of \(\textrm{\runic ᚹ}_2\) the point missing from \(\mathcal{V}\).

title: C.8 Example of Newton–Cartan Theory (§§9.1–9.5)
text: This appendix illustrates the pseudo-forces of Subsection 9.4 and the encoding of gravity in the connection (Subsection 9.5) on simple worldlines. Without gravity, we follow a uniform circular motion and a uniform straight motion through the same event with the same velocity, in a stratified chart at rest and in two rigidly moving ones. Around a point mass, we keep the circular motion, now an orbit, and follow a body falling radially from rest, also in a chart attached to it, which exhibits the tidal acceleration. Finally, we revisit both settings in a chart which is not stratified. In every case we ask whether the worldline satisfies Newton II with \(\mathcal{F}_\gamma = 0\), i.e. Newton I, and, if not, which force it requires. A force is a vector field along the worldline, so the required force is the same in every chart, and only its component functions change; pseudo-forces, in contrast, appear and disappear with the chart. As in Subsection 9.4.1, the coordinates of a point are written \(\alpha = (\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3)\) in the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) and \(\beta = (\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3)\) in the chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) under study, which is redefined in each item; dots denote derivatives w.r.t. absolute time \(t\). The component functions of a force w.r.t. each chart are written \(f^k_\mathcal{U}(t) \coloneqq (dx^k)_{\gamma(t)}\big( \mathcal{F}_\gamma(t) \big)\) and \(f^k_\mathcal{V}(t) \coloneqq (dy^k)_{\gamma(t)}\big( \mathcal{F}_\gamma(t) \big)\). Being the components of one and the same vector, they are related by the transformation law of vector components, \(f^k_\mathcal{V} = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \, f^l_\mathcal{U}\).

title: C.8 Example of Newton–Cartan Theory (§§9.1–9.5)
text:
C.8.1 Setup

The smooth manifold is \(\mathcal{M} \coloneqq \mathbb{R}^4\), with points \(p = (p_0, p_1, p_2, p_3)\), the standard topology, and the maximal atlas containing the identity chart \(\mathscr{X} : \mathcal{U} = \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}^4\), \(p \mapsto (p_0, p_1, p_2, p_3)\). The absolute time is \(t(p) \coloneqq p_0\), so \(\left. dt \right|_\mathcal{U} = dx^0\) and \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) is stratified.
